In his seventeenth year Ferdinando toured Europe, visiting Rome, Bologna, Ferrara, Venice, Austria and Prague. His personal rule began a year later, though Christina remained the power behind the throne until her death in 1636.

A plague swept through Florence in 1630 and killed a tenth of its people. Unlike the Tuscan nobility, Ferdinando and his brothers stayed in the city and went through it on foot to ease the suffering. Tuscany took part in the Wars of Castro, its last military conflict under the Medici, and defeated the forces of Pope Urban VIII in 1643. The treasury was so empty that the state could not pay interest on its bonds, and the rate was lowered by 0.75 per cent. The economy decayed to the point that barter became common in rural markets, the beginning of a long Tuscan decline.

Ferdinando was fascinated by new instruments and installed hygrometers, barometers, thermometers and telescopes in the Palazzo Pitti. In 1654 he is reported to have invented a sealed-glass spirit thermometer, marked with 360 divisions. His brother Leopoldo established the Accademia del Cimento in 1657 to bring scientists from across Tuscany to Florence, and Ferdinando took an active part in it. Like his father, he was a patron and friend of Galileo, who dedicated his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems to him. He tried to keep the Holy See from holding a full hearing and kept Galileo in Florence until December 1632. In June 1633 the Roman Inquisition convicted Galileo, and after his sentence was commuted to house arrest Ferdinando visited him at his villa.

Ferdinando died on 23 May 1670 of apoplexy and dropsy and was buried in the Basilica of San Lorenzo, the Medici crypt. His marriage to Vittoria was unhappy, but produced two children who reached adulthood: Cosimo, born in 1642, who succeeded him as Cosimo III, and Francesco Maria, born in 1660. He was remembered by his contemporaries as a man of culture and science. His 49-year rule saw the start of the economic decline that his successor Cosimo III made worse.
ferenc-szalasi: Ferenc Szálasi was born on 6 January 1897 in Kassa, now Košice in Slovakia, the son of a soldier, and was of mixed Armenian, German, Hungarian, Slovak and Rusyn ancestry. He studied at military academies and served on the front line for 36 months in the Austro-Hungarian Army in the First World War. In 1925 he became a staff officer of the restored Kingdom of Hungary under Regent Miklós Horthy.

He became a fanatical right-wing nationalist and a proponent of Hungarism, which advocated expanding Hungary back to its borders before the Treaty of Trianon. In 1933 he published a pamphlet, a plan for building the Hungarian state, and a military court expelled him from the General Staff. In 1937 he founded the Hungarian National Socialist Party. Imprisoned in 1938, he was proclaimed leader of the Arrow Cross Party by his followers. He was granted amnesty in 1940 but had to run the party clandestinely after Horthy outlawed it.

After the German occupation of March 1944 the Arrow Cross Party was legalised. When Horthy tried to take Hungary out of the war, the Germans kidnapped his son and threatened to kill him unless Horthy abdicated in favour of Szálasi. Horthy signed under duress, and the Government of National Unity was formed on 16 October 1944. On 4 November Szálasi was sworn in as Leader of the Nation.

His regime imposed martial law, took part in Germany's war effort and restarted the Holocaust in Hungary, which Horthy had halted. His militias were responsible for the murder of 10,000 to 15,000 Hungarian Jews and the deportation of a further 650,000 to death camps. His government lasted 163 days and held authority only in Budapest and its surroundings.

Szálasi and his cabinet fled Hungary shortly before the Siege of Budapest began. American troops captured him at Mattsee in Austria on 6 May 1945, and he was returned to Hungary on 3 October. The People's Tribunal in Budapest, in open sessions begun in February 1946, found him guilty of war crimes and high treason. The historian Peter Kenez wrote that he was so out of touch with reality that he could fairly be described as mad. He was executed by hanging on 12 March 1946.
ferentino: Ferentino is a town and comune in the province of Frosinone in Lazio, 65 kilometres south-east of Rome. It lies on a hill 400 metres above sea level, in the Monti Ernici area. In antiquity it was the town of the Hernici of Ferentinum. It stood just above the Via Latina and, being a strong place, served for the detention of hostages.

Ferentinum took no part in the rising of 306 BCE. Its inhabitants became Roman citizens after 195 BCE, and the place later became a municipium. From 1198 to 1557 Ferentino was the seat of the papal rectorate of Campagna and Marittima province. The town was strong in textiles, linen and embroidery, and in handicraft such as clay bricks, and after World War II it saw heavy industrial growth, mainly in pharmaceuticals.

The town keeps remains of ancient fortifications. The lower part of the outer walls is built of roughly hewn blocks of limestone, with rectangular blocks of tuff above in places. Two gates survive, the Porta Maggiore, a double gate built wholly of tuff blocks, and the Porta Sanguinaria. The acropolis, dating from the 2nd to 1st centuries BCE, has massive retaining walls like those of the lower town, and a building of travertine blocks whose cornice carries two inscriptions of the period of Sulla recording its construction by two censors.

The Cathedral of Sts John and Paul stands on part of the ancient acropolis, rebuilt in 1099 to 1118 on the site of an older church. It contains a Cosmatesque ciborium and a 12th-century mosaic pavement. The Gothic church of Santa Maria Maggiore dates from the 13th and 14th centuries. The Romanesque monastery of Sant'Antonio Abate housed the remains of Pope Celestine V until 1327.
fergana-valley: The Fergana Valley is an intermountain depression between the Tien Shan in the north and the Alay in the south. It is about 300 km long and up to 70 km wide, covering about 22,000 square kilometres, and it crosses eastern Uzbekistan, southern Kyrgyzstan and northern Tajikistan. Its fertility comes from the Naryn and the Kara Darya, which join near Namangan to form the Syr Darya. The climate is dry and continental, with hot summers and frost in December and January. The name Fergana is of Persian origin.

As early as 500 BCE the western part of the valley formed part of Sogdiana, which owed allegiance to the Achaemenid Empire under Darius the Great. In 329 BCE Alexander the Great founded Alexandria Eschate, the Furthest, in the south-west of the valley, at the site of the modern city of Khujand. Chinese chroniclers, drawing on the travels of Zhang Qian and published around 126 BCE, present the region as the country of the Dayuan, possibly descendants of Greek colonists, known for its Heavenly Horses. The Chinese waged war against the Dayuan in 104 BCE to obtain them. The Kushan Empire later ruled the area until the 3rd century CE, when the Sassanid Empire invaded.

Fergana then passed between the Sassanid Empire, the Hephthalite Empire and, from the mid-6th century, the Turkic Khaganates. In the 8th century it was a field of rivalry between Tang China and the expanding Muslim power. The Abbasid victory at the Battle of Talas in 751 led to the disengagement of China from Central Asia. In 819 Ahmad ibn Asad was granted authority over the city of Fergana, a step in the rise of the Samanid Empire. Genghis Khan invaded Transoxiana and Fergana in 1219, and the valley later became part of the Chagatai Khanate. The Babur who founded the Mughal dynasty came from the valley.

The Russian Empire conquered the valley at the end of the 19th century, forming the province of Fergana in 1876 out of the former khanate of Kokand. It became part of the Soviet Union in the 1920s, and the three republics that share it became independent in 1991. The valley is ethnically diverse, populated largely by Uzbek, Tajik and Kyrgyz people. Cotton cultivation, begun by the Soviets, is joined by grains, fruits and vegetables, stock breeding and mining of coal, iron and other minerals.
ferhat-abbas: Ferhat Abbas was born on 24 August 1899 in the village of Taher, Algeria, the son of a caid who had been awarded the rosette of a commander of the Legion of Honor. He was educated at Phillipeville and Constantine, served in the French army medical corps, reaching the rank of sergeant, and studied at the pharmacy school of the University of Algiers.

He then worked as a pharmacist in Sétif, where he entered politics and was elected to the municipal council and to the general council of Constantine. In an article of 1936 he wrote, "I am France", but in 1938 he grew disillusioned as his hopes of equality came to nothing.

In 1938 he organised the Algerian Popular Union, which promoted equal rights for French and Algerians while keeping Algerian culture and language as primary values. After General Giraud refused to let Muslims enlist as equals, he turned to nationalism and issued the Manifesto of the Algerian People on 10 February 1943, condemning French colonial rule and demanding self-determination. The governor general rejected it. With Messali Hadj he formed the Amis du Manifeste et de la Liberté, and he was imprisoned for a year. In 1946 he founded the Union Démocratique du Manifeste Algérien, a moderate party, and was elected to the French Constituent Assembly.

After arrests and the failure of moderate nationalism he fled to Cairo in 1956 and joined the Front de Libération Nationale as the war intensified. He became its delegate to the United Nations in 1957 and on 18 September 1958 president of the Provisional Government of the Algerian Republic, a largely diplomatic post. Talks with Charles de Gaulle failed to end the war, and in 1960 he visited China and the Soviet Union. He resigned on 27 August 1961 and was succeeded by Benyoucef Ben Khedda.

Algeria became independent on 5 July 1962. Abbas was president of the constituent assembly from 25 September 1962 to 15 September 1963, but Ahmed Ben Bella sidelined it, and Abbas resigned in protest. He was expelled from the FLN and held under house arrest from 1964 to 1965. He received the Medal of Resistance on 30 October 1984 and died on 24 December 1985, and he is buried at El Alia Cemetery. His books include La nuit coloniale (1962), Autopsie d'une guerre (1980) and L'indépendance confisquée (1984).
fernan-gonzalez-of-castile: Fernán was the son of Gonzalo Fernández, named count of Arlanza and the Duero around the year 900 and by tradition a descendant of the judge Nuño Rasura. His mother, Muniadona, was so well remembered that Iberian Muslim scholars sometimes recorded later counts of Castile as Ibn Māma Duna, descendant of Muniadona. He grew up in the castle of Lara, where his father had begun to reunite the fractured counties of Old Castile, which had been a single county under Rodrigo of Castile until it was split after the death of his son Diego Rodríguez Porcelos in 885.

Fernán was made count of Castile and Burgos before 931. That year Álvaro Herraméliz, count of Álava, Cerezo and Lantarón, died, and Fernán succeeded him as well, reuniting Rodrigo's county. He also married Álvaro's widow, Sancha Sánchez, sister of King García Sánchez I of Pamplona, a marriage that reinforced political alliances across the Christian north.

Fernán gathered a strong force from the counties of Burgos, Asturias, Santillana, Lantarón, Álava, Castile and Lara. His military skill came to prominence at the Battle of Simancas in 939 and then at Sepúlveda, which he took from the Moors and repopulated. As his power grew, so did his independence from León. Dissatisfied that King Ramiro II of León had distributed his troops among the frontier towns, he rose in rebellion, and in 944 the king gave the county of Castile to his own son Sancho. Fernán was defeated and held prisoner for three years, until he was reconciled with the king by giving his daughter Urraca in marriage to the heir, who became Ordoño III.

After Ramiro's death in 951 León fell into a dynastic crisis, which Fernán turned to his advantage. He first backed Sancho against Ordoño III, then, after Ordoño's early death, abandoned Sancho, by then King Sancho I, to support Ordoño IV, the new husband of his daughter Urraca. In 960, through Navarrese intervention for Sancho, he was captured by García Sánchez I of Pamplona and freed after territorial concessions. He sealed the new alliance by marrying García's daughter Urraca. With León weakened, he settled into autonomy as count, owing only nominal fealty.

Fernán died in 970, and the county passed to his son García Fernández. He was buried in the monastery of San Pedro of Arlanza. His life and feats are recorded in an anonymous poem, the Poem of Fernán González, written between 1250 and 1271 and surviving in an incomplete fifteenth-century copy. He is regarded as the first autonomous count of Castile and the founder of the dynasty that ruled a semi-autonomous Castile, laying the foundations for its later independence as a kingdom.
fernand-braudel: Fernand Braudel was born on 24 August 1902 in Luméville-en-Ornois, in the Meuse, and joined his father, a mathematics teacher, in Paris at the age of seven. He studied at the Sorbonne and gained his agrégation in history in 1923, then taught in Algeria until 1932. There he became fascinated by the Mediterranean and began a doctoral thesis on the foreign policy of Philip II of Spain, working in archives at Simancas, Venice and Dubrovnik. In 1935 he went to Brazil to help build the University of São Paulo. On the voyage home in 1937 he travelled with Lucien Febvre, co-founder of the journal Annales, and came under the influence of the Annales School.

Called up in 1939, Braudel was taken prisoner on 29 June 1940 and held at Mainz, where he became rector of the camp university, and from June 1942 near Lübeck. He drafted his work on the Mediterranean in captivity, without his own books and notes, sending copy books to Febvre in Paris. After 1945 he led the second generation of Annales historians, defended his thesis in 1947 and was elected to the Collège de France in 1949. He headed the Sixième section of the École pratique des hautes études from 1956 and edited the Annales from 1957. He directed the Fondation Maison des Sciences de l'Homme from 1970 until his death and was elected to the Académie française in 1984.

The Mediterranean and the Mediterranean World in the Age of Philip II (1949) was his most influential book. For Braudel there is no single Mediterranean but many seas, bound to the plains, mountains and desert around them. He divided time into three levels: the slow time of geography, the social and economic history of two or three centuries, and the history of events, which he called the time of surfaces.

Civilization and Capitalism, 15th–18th Century (1967–1979) follows how ordinary people made economies work, and traces centres of capitalism in turn: Venice, Antwerp and Genoa, Amsterdam and London. He argued that capitalists were typically monopolists, not entrepreneurs in competitive markets. His last book, The Identity of France, was unfinished at his death on 27 November 1985. He stressed constraints on human action and the lives of slaves, serfs, peasants and the urban poor, and is regarded as a precursor of world-systems theory.
fernando-alvarez-de-toledo-3rd-duke-of-a: Fernando Álvarez de Toledo was born at Piedrahíta, in the province of Ávila, on 29 October 1507, into a prominent Castilian military family. His father, García, died on a campaign on the island of Djerba in 1510, and Fernando was orphaned at the age of three. He was educated at the ducal court at Alba de Tormes in Roman Catholicism and humanism and knew Latin, French, English and German. In 1523, aged sixteen, he joined the troops that took Fuenterrabía from France and Navarre. He inherited the ducal title from his grandfather and served the Spanish monarchs Charles I and Philip II.

His first battle command was the conquest of Tunis in 1535, where the city fell, defended by Hayreddin Barbarossa. In 1542 he ended the French siege of Perpignan. At the Battle of Mühlberg in 1547 he led the Spanish tercios, and a flanking attack by them was largely responsible for the imperial victory over the Elector of Saxony. Sent to Italy as commander in chief, he became governor of Milan in 1555 and viceroy of Naples in 1556. When Pope Paul IV declared Philip deposed as king of Naples, Alba marched on Rome with 12,000 men, entered it in September 1557, and the pope sued for peace.

In 1567 Philip II sent him to Brussels with a powerful army, after the Iconoclasm of 1566. On 5 September he set up the Council of Troubles, known in the Netherlands as the Court of Blood. It condemned thousands, among them the counts of Egmont and Horn, who were executed in Brussels on 5 June 1568. New taxes provoked revolt, which William the Silent supported. The Spanish Fury at Mechelen in 1572 and the surrender of Haarlem, whose garrison of about 2,000 was executed, earned Alba the name Iron Duke. After more than 5,000 executions in five years Philip replaced him with Luis de Requesens, and Alba returned to Spain in 1573.

In 1580, aged 73 and ill, Alba led about 20,000 men into Portugal during the succession crisis, defeated a Portuguese army at Alcántara in late August and entered Lisbon. Philip II became Philip I of Portugal and made Alba viceroy and constable of Portugal. He died in Lisbon on 11 December 1582 and was buried at Alba de Tormes.

Alba has often been considered the most effective general of his generation. His repression in the Netherlands made him a symbol of tyranny in European history and part of the anti-Spanish Black Legend, a reputation that rebel writers used for propaganda.
fernando-belaunde-terry: Fernando Belaúnde was born in Lima on 7 October 1912, the second of four children of a wealthy family. His father, Rafael Belaúnde Diez Canseco, was a professor who later served as prime minister under José Bustamante y Rivero. Persecution of the family during the dictatorship of Augusto B. Leguía led them to move to France in 1924, where he began university studies in engineering. From 1930 to 1935 he studied architecture in the United States, at the University of Miami and then the University of Texas at Austin. Back in Peru in 1936 he designed private homes, founded the magazine El Arquitecto Peruano in 1937 and from 1943 taught architecture and urban planning.

In 1944 he co-founded the National Democratic Front, which elected Bustamante president in 1945, and sat in Congress until General Manuel Odría's coup of 1948. In 1956 he led a slate for election. When the electoral board refused his candidacy, he led a protest that police met with water cannon, known as the manguerazo, and crossed alone to the police chief carrying a Peruvian flag; the government gave way. He lost to Manuel Prado and in July 1956 founded the Acción Popular party at Chincheros, Cuzco. In 1959 he was jailed for twelve days at El Frontón. In 1962 he came second, by under 14,000 votes, to Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre; the military deposed Prado, and Belaúnde won the new election of 1963.

Belaúnde's first term promoted a doctrine he called the Conquest of Peru by Peruvians, aimed at developing the Amazon and other outlying regions. It included the Carretera Marginal de la Selva, a highway linking Chiclayo with Amazonas and San Martín, irrigation and hydroelectric projects, the Banco de la Nación and social housing. In 1964 the armed forces dropped napalm on the Matsés after two loggers were killed, killing hundreds. By 1967 the sol had lost much of its value. A settlement with a Standard Oil subsidiary over the La Brea and Pariñas oil fields forced his cabinet to resign on 1 October 1968, and days later General Juan Velasco Alvarado overthrew him. He spent the next decade teaching in the United States.

Elected again in April 1980 with 45 percent of the vote, he returned newspapers to their owners and finished the highway. The internal conflict with Shining Path began the day before the election; states of emergency were declared in Ayacucho and Apurímac, military officers reportedly committed human rights violations, and thousands died. The El Niño of 1982–83 brought floods and droughts. Alan García of APRA won in 1985, and Belaúnde became senator for life. He died on 4 June 2002.
fernando-de-la-rua: Fernando de la Rúa was born in the city of Córdoba, the son of Eleonora Bruno and Antonio de la Rúa. He attended the local Military Lyceum and graduated with a law degree from the National University of Córdoba at the age of 21. He entered public service in 1963 as an adviser to a minister of President Arturo Illia.

He was elected senator in March 1973 and that September ran for vice president as the running mate of Ricardo Balbín, losing to Juan Perón in a landslide. The 1976 coup removed him from Congress, and he worked as a lawyer for the firm Bunge y Born. After 1983 he lost the Radical Civic Union primary to Raúl Alfonsín but was elected senator. Later he opposed the Pact of Olivos between Alfonsín and President Carlos Menem, which allowed the constitutional amendment of 1994.

The 1994 amendment gave Buenos Aires autonomy and an elected mayor, and in 1996 de la Rúa was the first to hold the office by popular vote. He extended Line D of the Buenos Aires Underground, started the extension of Line B, and built the Roberto Goyeneche avenue in place of a planned highway. He also established the first non-recreational bikeway in the city.

In 1999 he ran for president for the Alliance, a coalition of his party and the Frepaso, and answered Menem's description of him as boring by embracing it in television advertisements. He defeated Eduardo Duhalde by 48.4% to 38.3% on 24 October and took office on 10 December 1999. His vice president, Carlos Álvarez, resigned after alleging that legislators had been bribed to pass a labour law. Three economy ministers followed within a year, and the last, Domingo Cavallo, kept the peso pegged to the dollar and introduced the corralito, which limited bank withdrawals, after a banking panic in November 2001.

Riots and looting broke out on 19 December 2001, and de la Rúa declared a state of emergency. The protests that followed, the cacerolazos, caused 27 deaths and thousands of injuries. Cavallo and the cabinet resigned, and on 20 December de la Rúa resigned to Congress and left the Casa Rosada by helicopter, having served half his term. Congress appointed Adolfo Rodríguez Saá, and then Eduardo Duhalde, who completed the term.

De la Rúa retired from politics. He was indicted over the labour-law bribery claims, over police repression during the crisis, and over the Megacanje debt operation, and was cleared of the first in 2013 and of the Megacanje charge on 6 October 2014. He died of heart failure on 9 July 2019, at the age of 81, and received a state funeral in Congress. His nickname Chupete, meaning pacifier, dated from his youth in politics.
ferrara: Ferrara lies on the Po di Volano, a branch channel of the Po, about 44 kilometres north-east of Bologna. The nearness of the Po has been a constant concern, with recurrent disastrous floods, the latest in 1951. The first documented settlements in the province date from the 6th century BCE. The Etruscan town of Spina, near the ancient mouth of the Po, was lost until modern times, when drainage works in 1922 revealed a necropolis of over 4,000 tombs.

Ferrara first appears in a document of the Lombard king Desiderius of 753, who captured it from the Exarchate of Ravenna. The Franks gave it to the papacy in 754 or 756. In 988 the Church ceded it to the House of Canossa, and at the death of Matilda of Tuscany in 1115 it became a free commune. In the 12th century the Este backed the Ghibelline Salinguerra against the Guelph Adelardi and in the end reaped the benefit. In 1264 Obizzo II d'Este was proclaimed lifelong ruler, ending the communal period.

Borso d'Este was made duke of Modena and Reggio in 1452 by Emperor Frederick III and duke of Ferrara in 1471 by Pope Paul II. Lionello and above all Ercole I were among the most important patrons of the arts in Italy in their time. The Addizione Erculea, planned by Biagio Rossetti for Ercole I, is regarded as one of the most important examples of Renaissance urban planning.

A war against Venice, fought and lost in 1482 to 1484, struck the city hard. Alfonso I, who married Lucrezia Borgia, overcame the papal and Spanish armies at the Battle of Ravenna in 1512 with artillery from his own foundry. An earthquake in 1570 caused the economy to collapse.

When Alfonso II died without heirs in 1597, the House of Este lost Ferrara to the Papal States, under which it remained for almost 300 years, a period of steady decline; in 1792 its population was only 27,000. It was briefly part of the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy from 1805 to 1814, and was restored to the pope in 1815.

Ferrara is a city of Emilia-Romagna and capital of its province. Its Este Castle, begun in 1385 with four bastions and a moat, stands in the centre, and the Cathedral of Saint George was consecrated in 1135. About 9 kilometres of brick walls still encircle the town. Its Jewish community is the only one in Emilia-Romagna with a continuous presence from the Middle Ages to the present. UNESCO has designated the city a World Heritage Site.
feudalism: The word feudal comes from the medieval Latin feudalis, from feudum, meaning fee or fief, first attested in a charter of Charles the Fat in 884. Its ultimate origin is unclear. People of the Middle Ages did not conceive of feudalism as a formal political system. The noun feudalism was in use by the end of the 18th century.

Feudalism usually emerged from the decentralisation of an empire. In the Carolingian Empire of the 9th century, which lacked the bureaucratic infrastructure to support cavalry without allocating land to mounted troops, such soldiers began to secure hereditary rule over their lands, and their power extended to the social, political, judicial and economic spheres.

The classic definition, by François Louis Ganshof in 1944, describes reciprocal legal and military obligations of the warrior nobility, built on lords, vassals and fiefs. A lord made someone his vassal at a commendation ceremony of homage and an oath of fealty, in which the vassal promised to fight at the lord's command and the lord to protect him. The vassal's principal obligation was aid or military service.

Marc Bloch's broader definition of 1939 includes the obligations of all three estates, the nobility, the clergy and the peasantry, who were bound by manorialism, and is called feudal society. Outside Europe the term has been applied most often to Japan under the shoguns and sometimes to medieval Ethiopia, and some scholars have used it for China in the Spring and Autumn period, ancient Egypt, the Parthian Empire and India until the Mughal dynasty.

In France the 11th century saw what historians call a feudal revolution, a fragmentation of powers as castellans and lesser lords took over local rights. Because vassals often pledged themselves to two or more lords, the idea of a liege lord, to whom obligations were superior, developed in the 12th century. Most military aspects of feudalism ended by about 1500, as armies became professional and the Black Death weakened the nobility's hold over the lower classes. On the night of 4 August 1789 the French National Assembly announced that it abolished the feudal system entirely. Since Elizabeth A. R. Brown's The Tyranny of a Construct (1974) and Susan Reynolds's Fiefs and Vassals (1994) medieval historians have debated inconclusively whether feudalism is a useful construct.
feurs: Feurs was founded by the Romans, and its name is a contraction of Forum Segusiavorum, after the forum of the Gallo-Roman town. Ptolemy gives it as the capital of the Gallic Segusiavi, and it appears on the Tabula Peutingeriana. Archaeologists have found a theatre, sewers, milestones, inscriptions, statuettes and pottery that reflect the importance of the Roman town, which lay near major Roman roads. The town gave its name to Forez.

A church dedicated to St Baudile is reported in 960 and a second, dedicated to the Virgin Mary, in 1001. A castle is reported in 1246. In the Middle Ages the town had no bridge over the Loire, but a harbour is recorded in 953 and another near Randans in 1060. Feurs, with the County of Forez, was forfeited to the Constable of Bourbon with his other possessions in 1523 and entered the royal domain in 1531. In 1542 it was attached to the generality of Lyon, created by Henry II.

During the French Revolution Feurs was briefly the capital of the Loire department, from 1793 to 1795. The Revolutionary Court headed by Claude Javogues made many victims there, about 80, almost all executed at the site where Mayor Pierre-Marie Assier erected the Chapel of the Martyrs in 1826. The town lay on one of the first French railways, the Andrézieux to Roanne line opened on 1 August 1832, and workshops building locomotives were set up there. Feurs stands in the Forez plain, between the Monts du Lyonnais to the east and the Forez mountains to the west, and the Lignon du Forez flows into the Loire in the commune. Remains of the Roman forum survive, and a museum of archaeology shows finds from the town.
fezzan: Fezzan is the southwestern region of modern Libya. It is largely desert, broken by mountains, uplands and dry river valleys, or wadis, in the north, where oases allow ancient towns and villages to survive in the Sahara. Only the ash-Shati Valley, the Wadi Irawan, parts of the Tibesti Mountains and a few remote oases can support settled populations, while the dune seas of the Idehan Ubari and the Idehan Murzuq cover most of the rest. In Berber languages the name means rough rocks, and it may also derive from the Greek Phazania, which may mean the country of the pheasants.

From the 5th century BCE to the 5th century CE Fezzan was the home of the Garamantes, who operated the trans-Saharan trade routes between Carthage and later the Roman Empire in North Africa and the Sahelian states of west and central Africa. The Roman generals Septimus Flaccus in 19 BCE and Suetonius Paulinus in 50 CE led small expeditions into the northern Sahara. After the Roman Empire ended, a commercial crisis cut its importance, and desertification greatly reduced the population.

In the 13th and 14th centuries Fezzan was part of the Kanem Empire. Wars against Kanem-Bornu in the early sixteenth century led to the Awlad Muhammad dynasty, with Murzuk as its capital. In 1574 Ottoman Tripolitania invaded and occupied it, though the Turks refrained from exercising much influence. Italy occupied it from 1911 and met resistance from the Sanusiyya Sufi order. Free French troops occupied Murzuk on 16 January 1943 and ran Fezzan from Sabha as the Fezzan-Ghadames Military Territory. When French control ceased in 1951, Fezzan became part of the Kingdom of Libya.

After the formation of Libya in 1934, Fezzan was designated one of the country's three primary provinces, with Tripolitania to the north and Cyrenaica to the northeast. Murzuk and Sabha are its chief towns.
fianarantsoa: Fianarantsoa lies at an average altitude of 1,200 metres in south central Madagascar and is the capital of the Haute Matsiatra Region. Two rivers, the Mandranofotsy in the west and the Tsiandanitra in the east, cross the town; both flow into the Matsiatra river. National road 7, one of the main highways of the island, links it to Antananarivo, 411 km away, and to Toliara, 518 km away, and a railway runs from the town to Manakara on the coast. The town has 191,766 inhabitants. Its name means good education in Malagasy.

The Merina built Fianarantsoa in the early 19th century as the administrative capital of the newly conquered Betsileo kingdoms. It grew into a cultural and intellectual centre for the island. It has some of the oldest Protestant and Lutheran cathedrals in Madagascar, the island's oldest theological seminary, also Lutheran, and the seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Fianarantsoa. A university, named after the town, was built there in 1972, and the many wine producers of the town have given it a reputation as the wine capital of Madagascar.

The Upper Town, the historic centre, has brick houses renovated in their original style and several churches along Rue du Rova. The oldest church in the town, Eglise Antranobiriky, dates from 1859. The largest, the Cathedral of the Holy Name of Jesus, was built from 1871 to 1890, and the neogothic Protestant church Fiangonana Trinité Masombahoaka dates from 1885. The railway station in the Lower Town was inaugurated in 1935, and a memorial in front of it honours the victims of the Malagasy Uprising of 1947. Ranomafana National Park lies 65 km to the north-east.
fianna-fail: Fianna Fáil was founded by Éamon de Valera, a former leader of Sinn Féin. The year before, he had proposed a motion that elected members be allowed to take their seats in Dáil Éireann if the Oath of Allegiance were removed. It failed at the Sinn Féin Ard Fheis, and de Valera and a number of others, including most of Sinn Féin's parliamentary talent, split from the party. His new party adopted its name on 2 April 1926.

Although it also opposed the Treaty settlement, it rejected abstention and aimed to republicanise the Irish Free State from within. It entered the Dáil in 1927. Its platform of economic autarky appealed to farmers, working-class people and the poor, and it largely took over the voters of the Labour Party, whose policy was almost identical.

Fianna Fáil won the 1932 general election and formed its first government on 9 March 1932. Between then and 2011 it was in power for 61 of 79 years, and its first period in office, until February 1948, was its longest at 15 years and 11 months. Its most dominant era was 1932 to 1973, when de Valera, Seán Lemass and Jack Lynch served as Taoiseach, apart from two three-year periods of the Fine Gael leader John A. Costello. Under Lemass in the 1960s the party shifted away from autarky towards free trade and foreign direct investment.

In 1970 the Arms Crisis led Lynch to dismiss the ministers Charles Haughey and Neil Blaney, who were accused of seeking to provide arms to the Provisional Irish Republican Army. In 1985 a large part of the membership left to form the Progressive Democrats under Desmond O'Malley. From 1989 Fianna Fáil governed in coalitions. Under Bertie Ahern, Taoiseach from 1997, it claimed credit for helping to broker the Good Friday Agreement in 1998. In 2011 it fell from the largest party in the Dáil to the third largest, losing 58 of its 78 seats. In 2020 it entered a coalition with Fine Gael and the Green Party.

The party used a cumann system, in which the branch, or cumann, was the basic unit, grouped into district branches and a constituency branch in each constituency. Its enduring commitments are to Irish unity, to the Irish language and to Ireland's tradition of military neutrality.
fiat: On 11 July 1899 Giovanni Agnelli was among the founding members of FIAT, Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino. The first plant opened in 1900 with 35 staff making 24 cars. The first car, the 3½ HP, was based on a design bought from Ceirano GB & C and had a 697 cc boxer twin engine; only 24 were built. The company was known from the beginning for the talent of its engineers. By 1903 it made a small profit and produced 135 cars.

By 1910 FIAT was the largest automotive company in Italy, and the American FIAT Automobile Company opened a plant at Poughkeepsie, which closed when the United States entered the First World War in 1917. During that war FIAT devoted all its factories to supplying the Allies with aircraft, engines, machine guns, trucks and ambulances. By the early 1920s it held 80 per cent of the Italian market. In 1921 workers seized its plants and hoisted the red flag, and Agnelli quit the company until the occupation ended. The Lingotto factory, the first FIAT plant to use assembly lines, was then the largest in Europe, and by 1925 FIAT held 87 per cent of the Italian car market.

In the Second World War FIAT made vehicles and aircraft, among them the CR.42 Falco, for the Army and the Regia Aeronautica and later for the Germans. After Benito Mussolini was overthrown, the National Liberation Committee removed the Agnelli family from leadership because of its ties to his government. They returned in 1963, when Giovanni's grandson Gianni became general manager, and he was chairman from 1966 to 1996. In 1970 FIAT employed more than 100,000 people in Italy and production there reached 1.4 million cars.

FIAT Automobiles was formed in January 2007 from the group's reorganised car business. FIAT merged with Chrysler in 2014 as Fiat-Chrysler Automobiles, and in 2021 it became a subsidiary of Stellantis after the merger with Peugeot SA's PSA Group. It is the largest car maker in Italy and for over twenty years was the largest in Europe and third in the world, until the car industry crisis of the late 1980s.

Outside Italy, Brazil is the largest country of production; FIAT built its first Brazilian plant at Betim in 1973. Nine FIAT Automobiles models have won the European Car of the Year award, from the 124 in 1967 to the 500 in 2008.
fibonacci: Leonardo Bonacci, known as Fibonacci, was an Italian mathematician from the Republic of Pisa, and one modern verdict calls him the most talented Western mathematician of the Middle Ages. The name Fibonacci, short for filius Bonacci, meaning son of Bonacci, first appears in a modern source in an 1838 text by Guglielmo Libri, although a notary named Perizolo called him Lionardo Fibonacci as early as 1506.

He was born around 1170 to Guglielmo, an Italian merchant and customs official who directed a trading post in Bugia, now Béjaïa in Algeria. He travelled there with his father as a young boy and was educated in Bugia, where he learned the Hindu-Arabic numeral system.

Fibonacci saw the advantages of the Hindu-Arabic system, which, unlike the Roman numerals then in use, allowed easy calculation through place value. In 1202 he completed the Liber Abaci, the Book of Calculation, which popularised these numerals in Europe. It presented what he called the modus Indorum, the method of the Indians, with ten digits including a zero and positional notation. The book applied the numerals to commercial bookkeeping, the conversion of weights and measures, the calculation of interest and money-changing. It was well received across educated Europe, and replacing Roman numerals and the abacus made business calculation easier and faster, which helped the growth of banking and accounting.

He was a guest of Emperor Frederick II, who enjoyed mathematics and science. John of Palermo, a member of the court, posed questions based on Arab mathematical works for him to solve. In 1240 the Republic of Pisa granted him a salary, in a decree naming him Leonardo Bigollo, in recognition of his services to the city as an adviser on accounting and as an instructor of its citizens.

The original 1202 manuscript is not known to survive; a copy of 1228 does. Among his other works are the Practica Geometriae of 1220, on surveying and practical geometry, the Flos of 1225, which solves problems posed by Johannes of Palermo, and the Liber quadratorum, on Diophantine equations, dedicated to Frederick II.

The Liber Abaci poses a problem about the growth of a population of rabbits under idealised assumptions. Its solution, generation by generation, is the sequence later called the Fibonacci numbers, in which each number is the sum of the previous two. Fibonacci began with 1, 2, 3 and carried the calculation to the thirteenth place, the value 233. It is the earliest known description of the sequence outside India, where mathematicians had described it as early as the sixth century.
fidel-castro: Fidel Alejandro Castro Ruz was born out of wedlock at his father's farm in Birán on 13 August 1926. His father, Ángel Castro y Argiz, was a migrant from Galicia in north-west Spain who took his household servant, Lina Ruz González, as his mistress and later second wife; they had seven children. At six Castro was sent to live with his teacher in Santiago de Cuba, and he later attended the Jesuit-run Dolores School there and, from 1942, El Colegio de Belén in Havana. In 1945 he began studying law at the University of Havana, where he took up anti-imperialist ideas and became involved in student activism. In 1947 he joined the Party of the Cuban People, founded by Eduardo Chibás.

In 1952 Castro formed a group called The Movement, which ran on a clandestine cell system and gained about 1,200 members in a year, most from Havana's poorer districts. He planned an attack on the Moncada Barracks, a garrison outside Santiago de Cuba, to be launched on 25 July 1953; it failed. After a year's imprisonment he went to Mexico and formed the 26th of July Movement with his brother Raúl Castro and Ernesto Che Guevara. Returning to Cuba, he led a guerrilla war against the forces of Fulgencio Batista from the Sierra Maestra. After Batista's overthrow in 1959 Castro assumed military and political power as prime minister.

The United States came to oppose his government and tried to remove it by assassination attempts, an economic embargo and counter-revolution, including the Bay of Pigs Invasion of 1961. Castro aligned Cuba with the Soviet Union and allowed Soviet nuclear weapons to be placed there, which led to the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962. He declared himself a Marxist–Leninist from December 1961, and Cuba became a one-party state under Communist Party rule. A new constitution in 1976, based on the Soviet Constitution of 1936, ended 16 years of rule by decree, and Castro became president.

After the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991 Castro led Cuba through the economic downturn known as the Special Period. On 31 July 2006, after surgery for intestinal bleeding, he delegated his duties to Raúl Castro, who was elected president by the National Assembly on 24 February 2008. Fidel stepped down as first secretary of the Communist Party in 2011 and died on 25 November 2016, aged 90, of natural causes.

He was the longest-serving non-royal head of state of the 20th and 21st centuries. His supporters regard him as a champion of socialism and anti-imperialism whose government advanced economic and social justice and secured Cuba's independence from American domination. His critics regard him as a dictator whose administration oversaw human rights abuses, the exodus of many Cubans and the impoverishment of the economy.
fidesz: Fidesz was founded in the spring of 1988 as Fiatal Demokraták Szövetsége, the Alliance of Young Democrats, an underground liberal student movement opposed to the ruling Hungarian Socialist Workers' Party. Founding such a movement was semi-illegal at the time, so its founders risked their careers. Membership had an upper age limit of 35 years, abolished at the 1993 congress. In 1989 the movement won the Thorolf Rafto Memorial Prize, received by one of its leaders, Péter Molnár. During the transition to multiparty democracy in 1989 and 1990 it became a political party, and in the 1990 election it entered the National Assembly with about 6 percent of the vote, with Viktor Orbán at its head.

In 1992 Fidesz joined the Liberal International. At its 1993 congress it redefined itself from liberal to civic-centrist, which split the membership: Péter Molnár, Gábor Fodor and Klára Ungár left for the liberal Alliance of Free Democrats, and Orbán was elected chairman. After a disappointing result in 1994 the party grew more conservative, and in 1995 it renamed itself the Hungarian Civic Party and sought links with the national-conservative Hungarian Democratic Forum.

Fidesz first took power at the 1998 election, with Orbán as prime minister, in coalition with the Hungarian Democratic Forum and the Independent Smallholders' Party. In 2000 it left the Liberal International and joined the European People's Party. It narrowly lost the 2002 election to the Hungarian Socialist Party, with 41.07 percent against 42.05 percent, and accused its opponents of electoral fraud. In 2003 it took the name Fidesz – Hungarian Civic Union. In 2004 it won 47.4 percent of the vote in the European Parliament elections and 12 seats. Its nominee László Sólyom was elected President of Hungary in 2005. During its years in opposition between 2002 and 2010 it formed an electoral alliance with the Christian Democratic People's Party.

Fidesz's position has shifted over time. It began on the centre-left, strongly committed to anti-clerical and secular policies, moved to the right from 1994, and by 1998 was the most prominent liberal-conservative force in Hungary, adopting nationalism and Christian democracy in the early 2000s. After winning a parliamentary supermajority in the 2010 election it promulgated a new constitution, the Fundamental Law, in 2011, and it won supermajorities again in 2014, 2018 and 2022.
fief: In ancient Rome a benefice, from the Latin beneficium, was a gift of land for life as a reward for services to the state, and medieval Latin documents continued to call a land grant in exchange for service a beneficium. Later the term feudum, or feodum, replaced it, first attested in 984 although more primitive forms appear up to a century earlier. Why it replaced beneficium is not well established. The most widely held theory, from Marc Bloch, links it to a Frankish word meaning movable goods, so that when land replaced currency as the main store of value the Germanic word displaced the Latin one.

A fief gave the vassal the use of the land and its income, while the granting lord kept ultimate ownership and could in principle recover it in case of disloyalty or death. Originally vassalage did not imply a landholding, but by the 8th century the grant of land was becoming standard. In Francia Charles Martel was the first to make large-scale, systematic use of granting the usufruct of lands to vassals for life, sometimes passing to the second or third generation. By the middle of the 10th century fees had largely become hereditary, and the eldest son had first to do homage and fealty and pay a relief. There never existed a standard feudal system or one type of fief, and customs varied by region.

In the 13th century the term feodum described a dependent tenure held in return for a specified amount of knight service and occasional payments. Knight service in war was far less common than castle-guard, suit in court, attendance in the lord's entourage and hospitality. In northern France in the 12th and 13th centuries a knight's service on offensive campaigns was limited to 40 days. A lord in late 12th-century England and France could also claim wardship and marriage, aids, and escheat, the reversion of the fief when there was no heir. By the 12th century English and French kings and barons began to commute military service for cash payments called scutages, with which they could hire mercenaries.

In England Henry II turned fiefs into important sources of royal income and patronage. The discontent of barons at the arbitrary reliefs claimed under his son King John resulted in Magna Carta of 1215.
fier: Fier lies on the bank of the Gjanica River in the Myzeqe Plain, between the Seman to the north, the Vjosë to the south and the foothills of the Mallakastra Mountains to the south-east. It is near the Adriatic and has a Mediterranean climate. Its name is claimed to derive from the Albanian word fier, meaning fern, since naming places after local plants is common among the Myzeqar Albanians; another hypothesis derives it from the Italian fiera, a trade fair.

The history of the place is bound up with the oil, gas and bitumen deposits nearby. Dioscorides in his Materia Medica describes lumps of bitumen in the river Seman, and Strabo, writing in about 17 CE, describes a rock near Apollonia that emitted fire, with hot springs and asphalt below it.

Near the site lies Apollonia, one of the two most important ancient Greek colonial settlements in present-day Albania, founded by settlers from Corfu and Corinth on land of the Illyrian Taulantii. Its prosperity rested on trade, including trade in slaves, and on pastoral farming, and a mint was set up in the middle of the 5th century BCE. It came under Roman control in 229 BCE. Octavian, later the Emperor Augustus, studied there for six months in 45 and 44 BCE, and Cicero called it a great and important city. It declined as the Vjosë silted up and an earthquake in the 3rd century CE changed the coastline.

In the 14th and 15th centuries Venetian traders used the site of Fier as a marketplace for farm produce from the Myzeqe lowlands. The town was founded in the 19th century by the Vrioni family, and officially in 1864 by Omer Pasha Vrioni II. Kahreman Pasha Vrioni, the local governor, asked French architects to plan a city as an artisan and trade centre, and in 1864 and 1865 a market for 122 merchants was built along the Gjanica.

Its first inhabitants were the servants of Kahreman Pasha and members of Aromanian families who had lived in the area since the early 19th century. In 1918, after Albanian independence from the Ottoman Empire, Fier and its countryside formed a majority Orthodox Christian enclave in which Muslims were roughly 35% of the population. Under communism it became a centre of the oil, bitumen and chemical industries and of power generation.

Fier is the seat of Fier County and Fier Municipality, and is served by the A2 motorway. With the nearby town of Patos it remains the centre of Albania's oil, bitumen and chemical industries. It is a base for visiting the classical sites of Apollonia and Byllis. Its population is mixed, of Muslims and Orthodox Christians, and the municipal unit had 52,926 inhabitants at the 2023 census.
fiesole: Fiesole is a town and comune of the Metropolitan City of Florence in Tuscany, on a height above Florence, about 5 km north-east of that city. Its Latin name was Faesulae, from the Etruscan Viesul, Viśl or Vipsul. It was an important member of the Etruscan confederacy, and the remains of its ancient walls and buildings have been preserved, with an archaeological museum in the town.

The earliest recorded mention dates to 283 BCE, when the Romans conquered the Etruscan town. In Roman times it was the seat of a school of augurs, to which twelve young men were sent each year from Rome to study divination. The old town was destroyed either in the Social War or by Sulla in 80 BCE, in reprisal for supporting the populares, and Sulla colonised it with veterans, who later supported Catilina under Gaius Mallius. In 406 the general Stilicho won a victory near Fiesole over the Vandals and Suebi under Radagaisus. In the Gothic War the town was besieged several times, and in 539 the Byzantine general Justin captured it and razed its fortifications.

For several centuries in the early Middle Ages Fiesole was independent and no less powerful than Florence in the valley below, and wars arose between them. The Florentines sacked it in 1010 and 1025 and conquered it in 1125, obliging its leading families to live in Florence. Dante reflects the rivalry in the Divine Comedy by referring to the beasts of Fiesole. From the 14th century wealthy Florentines had villas in the hills, and one is the setting of the frame story of Boccaccio's Decameron. The Medici built a villa there in the fifteenth century.

The Roman theatre, below the cathedral, has 19 tiers of stone seats and is 34 metres in diameter, and there are remains of Roman baths and of Etruscan walls. The cathedral holds the shrine of Saint Romulus, according to legend the first bishop, and an altarpiece by Pietro Perugino. The Badia, the old cathedral, was built in 1028. The European University Institute is based in the town, in historic buildings such as the Badia Faesolina and the Villa Schifanoia, and several American universities maintain campuses there.
fifa-world-cup: The first international football match was a challenge match played in Glasgow in 1872 between Scotland and England, and the first tournament for nations, the British Home Championship, took place in 1884. Football was a demonstration sport at the Olympic Games of 1900 and 1904, and FIFA, founded in 1904, tried to arrange its own tournament in Switzerland in 1906, which its official history describes as unsuccessful.

After the success of the Olympic football tournaments, FIFA, with its president Jules Rimet as the driving force, looked again at staging a competition outside the Olympics. On 28 May 1928 the FIFA Congress in Amsterdam decided to stage a world championship, and Uruguay, celebrating the centenary of its independence in 1930, was named host of the first tournament.

Early hosts were chosen at meetings of FIFA's congress, and the choices were controversial because travel between South America and Europe took three weeks by boat. Holding the first tournament in Uruguay reduced the European entries to four. The next two were both held in Europe, and Argentina and Uruguay boycotted the 1938 tournament in France, as the South American countries had assumed that the location would alternate between the continents.

The 1950 World Cup in Brazil was the first to include the British football associations, which had withdrawn from FIFA in 1920 and rejoined in 1946. Uruguay, who had boycotted the two previous tournaments, won it by defeating the host nation in the match called the Maracanazo. The tournament was expanded to 24 teams in 1982 and to 32 in 1998, which allowed more teams from Africa, Asia and North America to take part; South Korea finished fourth in 2002 and Morocco fourth in 2022. European and South American teams still dominate, and the finalists of every tournament have come from those two continents.

Since the second World Cup in 1934 qualifying tournaments have been held within the continental zones under their confederations, and the finals are played within a host nation or nations over about a month, first in groups and then in knockout rounds. The trophy has been won by eight national teams, and Brazil are the only team to have played in every tournament.

From 1930 to 1970 the winners received the Jules Rimet Trophy, named in 1946 after the FIFA president who set up the first tournament. Brazil's third victory in 1970 entitled them to keep it, but it was stolen in 1983 and has never been recovered, apparently melted down. A new trophy of solid 18 carat gold, designed by the Italian Silvio Gazzaniga, has been awarded since then. The World Cup was first televised in 1954, and the 2018 tournament was watched by an estimated 3.5 billion people.
fife: Fife is a natural peninsula in eastern Scotland, bordered by the Firth of Tay to the north, the North Sea to the east and the Firth of Forth to the south. The Ochil Hills partly block the route to the west. The coast has small harbours, from the docks at Burntisland and Rosyth to the fishing villages of the East Neuk such as Anstruther and Pittenweem, with their stepped gables.

The Pictish king list and the Poppleton manuscript mention a division of the Pictish realm into seven sub-kingdoms, one of them Fife, recorded as Fib in 1150. The hill-fort of Clatchard Craig near Newburgh was an important Pictish stronghold between the sixth and eighth centuries. The epithet Kingdom of Fife is first recorded only in 1678, and may derive from the quasi-regal privileges of the Earl of Fife. Until the 15th century the earl was considered the principal peer of the Scottish realm and had the right to crown the nation's monarchs.

Fife became an important royal centre from the reign of King Malcolm III, who had his principal home at Dunfermline. Dunfermline Abbey replaced Iona as the burial place of Scotland's royal elite, and Robert I is buried there. The House of Stuart built a palace at Falkland, favouring Fife for its hunting grounds. James VI called the county a beggar's mantle fringed wi gowd, the fringe being a coast of small ports trading wool, linen, coal and salt with the Low Countries.

Fife became a centre of heavy industry in the 19th century. Coal had been mined since at least the 12th century, and the number of pits increased ten-fold in the Victorian period. The Forth and Tay rail bridges linked it with Edinburgh and Dundee, and Kirkcaldy became the world centre of linoleum production. After the Second World War Glenrothes became Scotland's second new town. The county was governed by a county council from 1890 until 1975, when Fife region was created, and Fife Council became a unitary authority in 1996.

Fife is a council area with 373,990 residents in 2025, administered from Glenrothes. Its largest settlement is Dunfermline, which was awarded city status in 2022, and its largest town on the north-east coast is St Andrews. The University of St Andrews is the oldest of the ancient universities of Scotland, and the Old Course there is the world's oldest golf course. Fife has 4,961 listed buildings, among them Falkland Palace, Culross Palace, Dunfermline Abbey and St Andrews Cathedral.
fifteenth-amendment: The amendment grew from Congress's debates over the rights of freedmen after the Civil War. Once the Thirteenth Amendment ended the three-fifths rule, Republicans feared that the Democratic-dominated Southern states would gain House seats, and hoped to offset this by attracting and protecting black votes. The Civil Rights Act of 1866 was passed over President Johnson's veto, and the Fourteenth Amendment was adopted on 28 July 1868. Its second section only reduced a state's representation if it disenfranchised male citizens, which left states free to deny ballot access by race. In 1868 only eight Northern states allowed black men to vote. The election of Ulysses S. Grant that year convinced a majority of Republicans that protecting black male voters mattered to the party's future.

Section 1 provides that the right of citizens to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or any State on account of race, color or previous condition of servitude. Section 2 gives Congress power to enforce the amendment by appropriate legislation.

Representative John Bingham pushed for a wider ban, but a proposal covering nativity, property, education and religion was rejected, as was one banning literacy tests. A conference committee drew up the narrow final text, which mentions no poll taxes and does not guarantee the right to hold office. The House approved it on 25 February 1869 by 144 to 44 and the Senate the next day by 39 to 13, almost entirely along party lines. Senator Charles Sumner abstained because it did not prohibit literacy tests and poll taxes.

The amendment divided the women's suffrage movement, since it barred race discrimination but not sex discrimination. The American Equal Rights Association split into the National Woman Suffrage Association of Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton, who opposed it, and the American Woman Suffrage Association of Lucy Stone and Henry Browne Blackwell, who supported it. Nevada ratified first, on 1 March 1869, and Congress required Virginia, Mississippi, Texas and Georgia to ratify as a condition of regaining representation. It was certified as part of the Constitution on 30 March 1870.

The Supreme Court interpreted the amendment narrowly in the late 19th century. From 1890 to 1910 Southern Democrats adopted new state constitutions and Jim Crow laws, and poll taxes, literacy tests, white primaries and violent intimidation by the Ku Klux Klan disenfranchised most black voters and many poor whites, while grandfather clauses exempted white men.

In the 20th century the Court struck down grandfather clauses in Guinn v. United States in 1915 and dismantled the white primary in the Texas primary cases between 1927 and 1953. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 provided federal oversight of elections in discriminatory jurisdictions and banned literacy tests.
fifth-crusade: Pope Innocent III, disappointed by the Fourth Crusade's failure to recover Jerusalem, issued the bull Quia maior in April 1213 calling all of Christendom to a new crusade, and the decree Ad Liberandam followed in 1215. Few Frenchmen took part in the expedition of 1217, unwilling to go in the company of Germans and Hungarians. Most of the men came from Germany and other lands of the Holy Roman Empire. Emperor Frederick II had taken the cross in 1215 but did not take part in person as promised.

The Ayyubid Sultanate in Egypt was ruled by al-Adil, Saladin's brother, who preferred truces and concessions to war and whose chief concern was Egypt itself. The crusaders therefore chose Egypt as their first target, viewing it as the key to Jerusalem.

Andrew II of Hungary, who had mortgaged his estates to pay for the expedition, reached Acre in autumn 1217. A campaign in Syria that year was inconclusive. The crusaders then turned to Egypt, and the first of their fleet reached Damietta on 27 May 1218. The siege began on 23 June. After a first assault failed, Oliver of Paderborn built a siege engine with a revolving ladder, and the day after the renewed assault began on 24 August 1218 the chain tower that guarded the river was taken.

The cardinal Pelagius Galvani arrived as papal legate and considered himself supreme commander. On 5 November 1219 the crusaders entered Damietta and found it abandoned, filled with the dead and with most of the remaining citizens ill. Al-Kamil offered peace terms that included the return of Jerusalem, but Pelagius rebuked the sultan's envoys, and in July 1221 the army marched south towards Cairo. Defeated at the battle of Mansurah, it was forced to surrender.

The terms of surrender required the crusaders to leave Damietta and Egypt altogether and accepted an eight-year truce. The Crusade ended with nothing gained for the West and much loss of life, resources and reputations. Many had opposed the treaty, bitter that operations had begun before the emperor's forces arrived. John of Brienne was censured for leaving Damietta around Easter 1220 to press his claim to Cilicia, and Pelagius was accused of ineffectual leadership and of rejecting the sultan's offer. The sharpest criticism fell on Frederick II, whose ambition lay in Europe rather than the Holy Land.
fiji: Fiji is an archipelago of 332 islands, of which 106 are inhabited, and 522 smaller islets, in the South Pacific about 2,000 km north-northeast of New Zealand. Only around 10% of its area of some 194,000 square kilometres is land. The two largest islands, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu, account for about three-quarters of the land area. The islands are mountainous, with peaks up to 1,324 metres, and covered with thick tropical forest. Most were formed by volcanic activity beginning around 150 million years ago. The 180° meridian runs through Taveuni, but the International Date Line is bent so that the whole group keeps one time.

Pottery shows that Austronesian peoples had settled Fiji by at least 3500 to 1000 BCE, with Melanesians following about a thousand years later. It is believed that either the Lapita people or the ancestors of the Polynesians settled first, though not much is known of what became of them. Archaeological evidence shows settlement on Moturiki Island from at least 600 BCE and possibly 900 BCE, and some migrants moved on to Samoa, Tonga and even Hawai'i. Trade with neighbouring archipelagos began long before European contact. In the 10th century the Tu'i Tonga Empire was established in Tonga and Fiji came within its sphere of influence, bringing Polynesian customs and language; that empire began to decline in the 13th century.

Europeans first visited in the 17th century. The name Fiji comes from the Tongan pronunciation, Fisi, of the Fijian name Viti, and was first promulgated by Captain James Cook; accounts written until the late 19th century spelled it Feejee. After a brief period as an independent kingdom, the British established the Colony of Fiji in 1874. It was a Crown colony until it gained independence in 1970 as the Dominion of Fiji. After a series of coups, the military government declared a republic in 1987.

Fiji is a parliamentary republic with its capital at Suva on Viti Levu, home to nearly three-quarters of the population. About 54.3% of the people are native Fijians, who are Melanesians with Polynesian ancestry in many cases, and 38.1% are Indo-Fijians, descendants of Indian contract labourers brought by the British in the 19th century. Rotuma, with a culture closer to Tonga and Samoa, has a special administrative status. Rugby sevens is the national sport.
filippo-brunelleschi: Brunelleschi was born in Florence in 1377, the son of Brunellesco di Lippo Lapi, a notary and civil servant, and Giuliana Spini. He received a literary and mathematical education, but being artistically inclined he was apprenticed at 15 as a goldsmith and sculptor in cast bronze, and in December 1398 he became a master.

In 1401 he was one of seven competitors for the second pair of bronze doors of the Florence Baptistery, each making a panel of the Sacrifice of Isaac. The jury could not choose between his panel and that of Lorenzo Ghiberti and proposed that the two collaborate. Brunelleschi refused to give up total control and preferred that the work go to Ghiberti. He later gave up sculpture for architecture and optics.

His first architectural commission was the Ospedale degli Innocenti, a foundling hospital begun in 1419 and opened on 25 January 1445, whose loggia drew clearly on classical forms and became a model across Europe. He also designed the Old Sacristy and the nave of the Basilica of San Lorenzo for the Medici family.

In 1418 he won the competition to build the dome of Florence Cathedral, helped by a brick model made by his friend Donatello. His later works included the Pazzi Chapel, the Basilica of Santo Spirito and Santa Maria degli Angeli, an octagonal church whose funds the government seized in 1437 for a war against Lucca.

The dome was built from 1420 to 1436 with two shells, one within the other, and more than four million bricks. Brunelleschi left no plans of it, and he invented a new hoisting machine and chains of wood and sandstone that act as tension rings. His early biographer Antonio Manetti says that between 1415 and 1420 he made perspective paintings of the Baptistery and the Palazzo Vecchio, and he is credited as the first to describe a precise system of linear perspective. In 1421 he received what is thought to be one of the first modern patents, for a boat to carry goods on the Arno. He died on 15 April 1446 and was buried in the crypt of the cathedral.
filippo-juvarra: Filippo Juvarra was born in Messina on 7 March 1678 into a family of goldsmiths and engravers and worked in the family shop. He studied for the priesthood and was ordained in 1703, while teaching himself architecture from books by Vitruvius and Vignola. He designed festive settings in Messina for the coronation of Philip V in 1701. In 1704 he moved to Rome, where he studied with Carlo and Francesco Fontana. His first independent work was for the stage: he designed sets for operas under the patronage of Cardinal Ottoboni and of the widowed Queen of Poland, Marie Casimire d'Arquien, using scenes drawn at an angle.

In 1706 Juvarra won a contest for the new sacristy of St Peter's, held by Pope Clement XI, and entered the Accademia di San Luca. His Antamoro Chapel of 1708, made with the sculptor Pierre Le Gros, is his only completed architectural work in Rome. In 1714 he was recruited to the Duchy of Savoy by Victor Amadeus II and became chief court architect in Turin. There he built the façade of the Palazzo Madama in 1718–21, a theatrical screen before a grand staircase and a medieval castle. The Basilica of Superga, begun to fulfil a vow Victor Amadeus made during the siege of Turin, took over fourteen years to build and stands on a mountaintop with a dome seventy-five metres high.

He also designed the hunting lodge at Stupinigi (1729–1731), with an oval central pavilion topped by a bronze stag, and worked on the palace of Venaria Reale. In 1719 he went to Portugal, where he planned the palace at Mafra and a palace and cathedral for John V in Lisbon.

After fire destroyed the Royal Alcazar of Madrid on Christmas Eve 1734, Philip V asked Juvarra to supervise a new palace. He moved to Madrid in April 1735 and died suddenly in January 1736, less than nine months after arriving. His pupils, among them Giovanni Battista Sacchetti, carried out his designs. Bernardo Vittone and Benedetto Alfieri followed his manner, and his style fell out of favour with the rise of Neoclassicism. A major exhibition of his designs was held in Genoa and Madrid in 1994.
filippo-maria-visconti: Filippo Maria Visconti was born on 3 September 1392, the son of Gian Galeazzo Visconti and Caterina Visconti. His father died of plague in 1402, and his elder brother Gian Maria became Duke of Milan with their mother's support. Gian Maria came to regard her as a threat and had her imprisoned at Monza on 18 August 1404; she died there on 17 October, and her death was rumoured to have been caused by poison. After Gian Maria was assassinated on 16 May 1412, Filippo Maria allied himself with Beatrice, the widow of the condottiero Facino Cane, gaining access to her late husband's wealth and armies.

Filippo Maria succeeded his brother as Duke of Milan and established his rule over Pavia. His succession was contested by his uncle Estorre Visconti and his cousin Giacomo, who briefly held Milan, but on 16 June 1412 he retook the city. In 1418 he had Beatrice executed at the Castle of Binasco after accusing her of adultery. By employing condottieri such as Francesco Bussone da Carmagnola, Niccolò Piccinino and later Francesco Sforza, he recovered much of the Lombard territory of his father's duchy. His attempt to expand into Romagna in 1423 provoked a war with Florence, which Venice joined in 1425. Venice conquered Brescia, and Filippo Maria was defeated at Maclodio on 12 October 1427. Peace was later signed at Ferrara.

In 1428 he married Marie of Savoy, daughter of his ally Amadeus VIII of Savoy, who later reigned as Antipope Felix V with Visconti's support. Filippo Maria also invited the humanist Gasparino Barzizza to Milan, where he founded a school. The oldest surviving tarot decks, then called carte da trionfi, were likely commissioned by him.

Filippo Maria died on 13 August 1447, the last male of the Visconti line. After a brief republican experiment known as the Ambrosian republic, the duchy passed to Francesco Sforza, who had married Bianca Maria Visconti, Filippo Maria's only child, born to his mistress Agnese del Maino.
fin-de-siecle: Fin de siècle is a French term meaning end of century. It covers the sense of the English phrase turn of the century and also the closing of one era and the beginning of another, and without context it usually means the end of the nineteenth century. The period was widely thought to be one of social degeneracy and at the same time of hope for a new beginning. The cultural hallmarks of the 1880s and 1890s included ennui, cynicism, pessimism and a widespread belief that civilisation leads to decadence. The term is commonly applied to French art and artists, since the traits first appeared in France, but the movement affected many European countries.

B. A. Morel's degeneration theory held that societies can regress as well as progress under a flawed environment, with the effects passed from generation to generation. In Degeneration Max Nordau held that the two dominant traits of the degenerate were ego mania and mysticism, and his work brought the concept of genius back into popular thought. Pessimism spread from the work of Arthur Schopenhauer, and R. H. Goodale counted 235 essays by British and American authors on pessimism between 1871 and 1900. Oscar Wilde joked in An Ideal Husband that optimist and pessimist were the only fashionable religions left.

Decadent writers such as Charles Baudelaire and Arthur Rimbaud influenced their English counterparts, the aesthetes, who held that art should evoke an emotional response and show beauty in the unnatural. Holbrook Jackson listed the characteristics of English decadence as perversity, artificiality, egoism and curiosity. Gothic fiction expressed fears of change and decay through the human body, in works such as Robert Louis Stevenson's The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886), Oscar Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray (1891), H. G. Wells's The Time Machine (1895) and Bram Stoker's Dracula (1897). The age also produced a flood of future war narratives, sold in tens of thousands of copies across Europe, which acted as political advocacy.

The ideas of fin de siècle artists gave the impetus for symbolism and modernism. The political culture of the time was marked by revolt against materialism, rationalism, positivism, bourgeois society and liberal democracy, and favoured emotionalism, irrationalism and vitalism. Its themes were controversial and have been cited as a major influence on fascism and on the beginnings of geopolitics, including the theory of Lebensraum. Michael Heffernan has argued that geopolitics arose in fin de siècle Europe from technological change and the sense that imperialist competition had closed the world's frontiers. Writing of the 1890s, he notes a widespread assumption that the passing of the century would mean a clear break with the past.
finistere: Finistère lies in the extreme west of Brittany. Its prefecture is Quimper, and its largest city is Brest. Other large towns include Concarneau, Morlaix, Carhaix, Quimperlé and Douarnenez, and the department includes the island of Ushant, called Eusa in Breton and Ouessant in French. It is the westernmost department of metropolitan France and has a claim to being the most coastal: 117 of its 277 communes lie on the coast, and its coastline of about 1,250 km makes up almost a quarter of that of Brittany.

The abers, rugged fjord-like inlets, are a notable feature of the north coast. The Pointe de Corsen, at the north-western tip of the department, is the westernmost point of continental France. About 40 kilometres to the south lies the rugged and isolated headland of the Pointe du Raz.

The present department consists of the historical region of Léon and parts of Cornouaille and Trégor, all of them parts of Brittany before the Revolution. Its name comes from the Latin Finis Terræ, meaning the end of the earth. The Breton name, Penn ar Bed, means head or end of the world and resembles the Cornish name of Land's End, Pedn an Wlas. It should not be confused with Fisterra in Galicia, Spain, which has the same origin.

Agriculture, fisheries and food processing occupy an important place in the economy. A military presence, including the Île Longue submarine base and the naval air base at Lanvéoc-Poulmic, together with related industries, employs a significant part of the population. The port of Roscoff has ferry links with Ireland and Great Britain.

Finistère is the area where Breton survives most strongly as a spoken language, and its Breton-speaking schools are called Diwan, Divyezh and Dihun. The Festival de Cornouaille in Quimper celebrates Breton music and traditions. The sculptor Roland Doré made many of the calvaries that stand in the department.
finland: Finland lies approximately between latitudes 60° and 70° N, and only Reykjavík lies further north among world capitals than Helsinki. Its land is predominantly covered by boreal forest, and it has about 168,000 lakes and 179,000 islands; the largest lake, Saimaa, is the fourth largest in Europe. Much of the landscape is a result of the Ice Age, and the terrain is rising by about 1 centimetre a year around the Gulf of Bothnia because of post-glacial rebound, so that the surface area of the country expands by about 7 square kilometres annually. Halti, at 1,324 metres, is the highest point.

The area was settled around 8500 BCE towards the end of the last glacial period, by hunter-gatherers using stone tools. The first pottery appeared in 5200 BCE with the Comb Ceramic culture, and the Corded Ware culture arrived in the south of coastal Finland between 3000 and 2500 BCE and may have coincided with the start of agriculture. In the Iron Age, Finland Proper was the most densely populated area, and main exports were furs, slaves, castoreum and falcons to European courts. At the end of the ninth century, local artefacts had more common features than ever before, which has been interpreted as expressing a common Finnish identity.

From the middle of the 13th century Finland became part of Sweden during the Northern Crusades. In 1809, as a result of the Finnish War, it was captured from Sweden and became an autonomous grand duchy within the Russian Empire, and an independence movement gradually developed. Finland declared its independence after the Russian Revolution of 1917, and a civil war the following year ended in victory for the anticommunist Whites. During World War II Finland fought the Soviet Union in the Winter War and the Continuation War and Nazi Germany in the Lapland War, losing parts of its territory but retaining its independence and democracy.

Finland has a population of 5.7 million, and Helsinki is the capital and largest city. The official languages are Finnish and Swedish, the mother tongues of 83.5 percent and 5.0 percent of the population. It became the first country in Europe to grant universal suffrage in 1906. A new constitution enacted in 2000 made the presidency primarily a ceremonial office, and Finland is now considered a parliamentary republic. It joined the European Union in 1995 and the Eurozone in 1999, and NATO in 2023. National minorities include the Sámi, Roma, Jews and Tatars.
finlandisation: Finlandization means the process by which a powerful country makes a smaller neighbour refrain from opposing its foreign policy while the smaller state keeps its nominal independence and its own political system. The word arose in the West German political debate of the late 1960s and 1970s. It was coined in scholarly debate and made known by the political scientists Richard Löwenthal, Walter Hallstein and Kurt Birrenbach, who feared the effects of a withdrawal of American troops from Germany. Franz Josef Strauss and others used it in response to Willy Brandt's attempts to normalise relations with East Germany. It is often considered pejorative.

Finland had fought the Winter War against the Soviet Union in 1939, losing 9 per cent of its territory, and re-entered the Second World War in 1941 beside Germany. After the Paris Peace Treaty of 1947 it kept democracy and parliamentary government under heavy Soviet pressure. Its foreign relations followed the doctrine of Juho Kusti Paasikivi, who stressed a trusting relationship with the Soviet Union. In April 1948 Finland signed an Agreement of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance, which obliged it to resist attacks by Germany or its allies but also recognised its wish to stay outside great-power conflicts. Finland stayed out of the Marshall Plan and the Warsaw Pact.

Between 1944 and 1946 the Soviet part of the Allied Control Commission demanded that libraries withdraw more than 1,700 books as anti-Soviet, and Finnish censors banned films such as The Manchurian Candidate.
