Possession of such books was never banned, and the censorship never took the form of purging; much of it was self-censorship. Finns reacted in varied ways to the term. Many ordinary Finns found it offensive, while the cartoonist Kari Suomalainen defined it as the art of bowing to the East without mooning the West.

After the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, the treaty of 1948 was replaced by a new treaty with the Russian Federation on a more equal footing, ending the Paasikivi-Kekkonen doctrine. Finland joined the European Union in 1995. After the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Finland applied for NATO membership on 18 May and became a member on 4 April 2023. The word has also been applied to other states near a great power, such as Denmark's attitude toward Germany between 1871 and 1940 and Swiss policy toward Nazi Germany.
finnish-civil-war: Finland had been a grand duchy of the Russian Empire since 1809. Its population grew from 860,000 in 1810 to 3,130,000 in 1917, industry and a labour movement developed, and tension rose over the autocratic rule of the tsar and the undemocratic system of estates inherited from Swedish rule. The main cause of the war was the crisis of the First World War. After the February Revolution of 1917 the Russian Provisional Government restored Finland's autonomy, and after the October Revolution both conservatives and socialists came to support independence, though they disagreed about who should lead the nation.

The final escalation began in early January 1918, when each action by one side drew a counteraction from the other. The Red Guards, led by a section of the Social Democratic Party, held the south, including nearly all the major towns and industrial centres. The Whites, led by General Mannerheim and built around the Jägers trained in Germany and volunteer Civil Guards, held the agrarian centre and north. The Reds' general offensive in February failed.

Mannerheim chose to strike first at Tampere, the main industrial town of the south-west, which held nearly 15,000 heavily armed Red Guards. His assault began on 16 March, and the Whites besieged the town. After German troops landed in April, the Reds' leaders withdrew from Helsinki to Viipuri and then to Petrograd. Thousands of Reds tried to flee to Russia, but most were encircled, and those in the Lahti area surrendered on 1 and 2 May. The war ended on 15 May with the capture of Fort Ino. Both sides carried out executions, known as the White Terror and the Red Terror.

The Whites and German troops captured around 80,000 Red prisoners, including 5,000 women and 1,500 children, and held them in camps such as Suomenlinna and Hämeenlinna. Most of the deaths in the war occurred outside the battlefields, in the camps and the terror. Treason courts examined 76,000 cases and convicted 68,000 Reds, and of 555 death sentences 113 were carried out. About 15,000 children were left orphaned, and many moderate Finns came to think of themselves as citizens of two nations.

A plan for a German-led Finnish monarchy collapsed with Germany's surrender in November 1918, and Finland became an independent republic, confirmed by the Constitution Act of 17 July 1919. The war has several names, among them Civil War, Class War, War of Independence and Red Rebellion, each tied to a political viewpoint.
finnish-war: After concluding the Treaty of Tilsit with Napoleon in 1807, Emperor Alexander I of Russia wrote on 24 September 1807 to King Gustav IV Adolf of Sweden that peace between them depended on Sweden accepting the treaty's limits, which in practice meant cutting off trade with Britain. The king, who viewed Napoleon as the Antichrist, secured an alliance with Britain on 8 February 1808. In Saint Petersburg his stubbornness was seen as a convenient pretext for occupying Finland. Swedish plans assumed that war in winter was impossible, while Russian planners chose a winter offensive, when frozen seas would isolate Finland.

On 21 February 1808, 24,000 Russian troops under Friedrich Wilhelm von Buxhoeveden crossed the border and took Loviisa; war was not declared until April. Helsinki fell on 2 March and Turku on 21 March, as the Swedish army under General Wilhelm Mauritz Klingspor withdrew northwards. Sveaborg, with a garrison of 6,000 men and over 700 cannons, surrendered on 6 May 1808 after prolonged negotiations, its commander Admiral Carl Olof Cronstedt believing resistance futile, and the Russians gained most of the Swedish archipelago fleet intact. Swedish counter-attacks at Siikajoki and Revolax halted the offensive for a time, and Finns rose in guerrilla fighting.

Reinforced to 55,000 men against an estimated 36,000, the Russians attacked again in August, and Count Nikolay Kamensky won the most important victory at Oravais on 14 September. By November 1808 Russian forces had overrun all of Finland, and the Convention of Olkijoki of 19 November obliged the Swedish army to leave. In March 1809 Russian columns crossed the frozen Gulf of Bothnia, occupying the Åland Islands and entering Umeå on 24 March. King Gustav IV, blamed for the loss of Finland, was dethroned by a coup in Stockholm on 13 March, and his uncle became Charles XIII of Sweden.

By the Treaty of Fredrikshamn of 17 September 1809 Sweden also gave up its domains east of the Torne river. The Grand Duchy of Finland kept the Gustavian constitution of 1772 with only slight modifications until 1919, and in 1812 Russia attached to it the areas it had gained from Sweden in the 18th century, known as Old Finland. In Sweden the war was followed by a new constitution and, in 1818, by the establishment of the House of Bernadotte. Two studies of 2015 by the political scientists Jan Teorell and Bo Rothstein argue that the defeat moved Swedish elites to reform the bureaucracy.
fire-temple: Fire rituals are first evident in the 9th century BCE, about the same time as Zoroastrianism itself and the introduction of Atar as a divinity. There is no allusion to a temple of fire in the Avesta proper, nor an Old Persian word for one. Herodotus shows that in the mid-5th century BCE Zoroastrians worshipped to the open sky, ascending mounds to light their fires, so the temple is a later development. The oldest remains identified as a fire temple are on Mount Khajeh, near Lake Hamun in Sistan, tentatively dated to the 3rd or 4th century BCE, rebuilt in the Parthian era and enlarged in Sassanid times.

By the Parthian period there were two kinds of place of worship, the bagin, a sanctuary of a particular divinity with an icon, and the atroshan, a place of burning fire, which became more common as the movement against images gained support. Under the Sassanid dynasty the statues were by law abandoned or replaced by fire altars. There seem to have been virtually only two grades of fire, the Atash-i Vahram, kept continuously burning, and the Atash-i Adaran, a parish fire relit each year. The characteristic Sassanid sanctuary was a domed chamber on a square plan with a pillar at each corner, and Sassanid coins always show a fire altar with flames on the reverse.

Three Great Fires, Adur Burzen-Mihr, Adur Farnbag and Adur Gushnasp, were said to derive from Ahura Mazda and were associated with priests, warriors and farmers; other texts call them symbols of imperial sovereignty. The battles of al-Qādisiyyah in 636 and Nihavānd in 642 were instrumental in the collapse of the Sassanid Empire and of state-sponsored Zoroastrianism, and some fire temples were destroyed or converted into mosques, though others continued. According to Parsi legend, refugees from Khorasan brought the ash of a fire to Gujarat. Its fire was moved from Sanjan to the Bahrot Caves, then to Bansdah and Navsari, and in the 18th century to Udvada.

Fire temples are built to serve the fire within them and are classified by its grade: Atash Dadgah, Atash Adaran and Atash Behram. A Dadgah fire can be consecrated in a few hours by two priests, an Adaran fire requires eight priests and two to three weeks, and a Behram fire gathers sixteen kinds of fire and requires thirty-two priests for a ceremony that can take up to a year. The outer façade of a temple is almost always plain. Only priests may enter the innermost sanctum, which has a double domed roof and no light but the fire's. Worshippers offer dry sandalwood through a priest, who does not preach but tends the fire. Priests hold the ranks of dastur, mobad and herbad.
firestone-tire-and-rubber-company: Harvey S. Firestone founded the company on 3 August 1900 in Akron, Ohio, with 12 employees. It first made solid rubber side-wire tyres for fire apparatus, then pneumatic tyres for wagons, carriages and other vehicles. Akron was also the home of its rival Goodyear and of General Tire and B.F. Goodrich, and Firestone and Goodyear together were the largest suppliers of automotive tyres in North America for over 75 years. In 1906 Henry Ford chose Firestone to supply tyres for his cars, and the close relationship between Harvey Firestone and Ford made the company the original equipment supplier for Ford vehicles.

In 1926 the company opened a rubber plantation of more than a million acres in Liberia, at Harbel, and its first service centre. From then until the outbreak of the First Liberian Civil War in 1990 the Harbel plantation was the largest of its kind in the world. It was planned to employ 350,000 people, more than the number of able-bodied men in the whole country, which created intense pressure for labour. The historian Christine Whyte concluded that the collusion of Firestone and government officials to keep wages low and coerce workers was at best overlooked. In September 1990 rebels under Charles Taylor seized the plantation, and operations fully restarted only in 2003.

The company's first radial tyre, the Firestone 500, began to show tread separation in the 1970s. On 20 October 1978 Firestone recalled over 7 million of them, the largest tyre recall to that date, and in May 1980 the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration fined it $500,000. In late 1979 the company, more than a billion dollars in debt, brought in John Nevin, who closed nine of seventeen plants and moved headquarters to Chicago. In 1988 he negotiated its sale to the Japanese firm Bridgestone.

Firestone is now part of Bridgestone Americas and is based in Nashville, Tennessee. In 2000 a high failure rate of Firestone tyres on Ford Explorers brought lawsuits and a mandatory recall, and in 2001 Bridgestone/Firestone ended its ties to Ford. Its tyres also won every Indianapolis 500 from 1920 to 1966.
firozpur: Firozpur lies on the banks of the Sutlej River in the Firozpur District of Punjab. After the Partition of India in 1947 it became a border town on the India–Pakistan border, and it has memorials to soldiers who died fighting for India. A popular name for the locality is Shaheedon-ki-dharti, 'the land of martyrs'. The name is said to come either from Feroz Shah Tughlaq, sultan of Delhi, or from Feroze Khan, a Manj Rajput chief of the mid-16th century.

The city is said to have been founded by Firoz Shah Tughlaq, who reigned over the Delhi Sultanate from 1351 to 1388, and its fortress is said to date from the 14th century. An epidemic in 1543 sent much of the Bhabra Jain trading community to Kot Ise Khan. Sikh influence was affirmed in 1758, when Adina Beg was defeated, and in 1761 sardars of the Bhangi Misl took hold of Ferozepore, which then held 37 villages.

After the death of the chief Dhanna Singh about 1818–19 his widow Lachhman Kaur ruled it, and in 1823 she enlisted British East India Company help to remove a nephew who had occupied the fort. When she died without issue on 28 September 1835 the territory lapsed to the British, and Henry Lawrence took full charge in 1839.

In 1839 Ferozepur was the British outpost towards Sikh power, and it was the scene of operations in the First Anglo-Sikh War, when the Sikhs crossed the Sutlej in December 1845 and were defeated. It stayed in British hands throughout the Indian Mutiny. Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Orphanage there on 26 October 1877, and the Saragarhi Memorial Gurdwara, opened in 1904, commemorates the 21 Sikh soldiers who died at Saragarhi on 12 September 1897.

On 23 March 1931 the remains of Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev were cremated at Hussainiwala on the Sutlej, a place that passed to Pakistan in 1947 and to India on 17 January 1961 in an exchange of exclaves. Their memorial was begun in 1965 and completed in 1968.

Firozpur Cantonment is a major cantonment of India, and the fort within it, a Sikh Empire-era structure, was reopened to the public on 2 June 2025. The 2011 census counted 110,313 people in the city, 70.5 per cent Hindu and 26.3 per cent Sikh. Moti Bazar and Hira Mandi were once prominent markets for the pearl and diamond trade.
firozpur-district: Firozpur district, also written Ferozepur, is one of the twenty-three districts of the state of Punjab and covers 2,190 square kilometres. Its capital, the city of Firozpur, is described as lying inside ten gates, among them the Amritsari, Zira, Delhi, Multani and Kasuri gates. The district now has three tehsils, Firozpur, Zira and Guru Har Sahai, and six blocks. About 93 per cent of the population spoke Punjabi as a first language at the 2011 census.

In the 18th century Sikh warrior groups called misls united in resisting Mughal rule. In 1763 Hari Singh of the Bhangi Misl sacked Kasur, and his commander Gujjar Singh crossed the Sutlej to take Ferozepur, which he gave to his nephew Gurbakhsh Singh. Around 1792 it passed to Gurbakhsh Singh's son Dhanna Singh, who accepted British protection when Ranjit Singh's favourite, Nihal Singh Atariwala, threatened him; this stopped Ranjit Singh from expanding eastward. Dhanna Singh's widow, Lachhman Kaur, died in 1835 without an heir, and the British then took control of the Ferozepur Jagir.

The First Anglo-Sikh War was fought mainly in the district. The first battle was at Mudki, where the Sikh commander Lal Singh abandoned his troops, and at Ferozeshah another leader, Teja Singh, fled when victory was near. After the Treaty of Lahore of 1846 the British took the land east of the Sutlej and divided it among the districts of Ferozepur, Badhni and Ludhiana. Badhni was dissolved in 1847 and added to Ferozepur. In 1856 the Nawab of Mamdot was removed for the wrongdoings of himself and his son, and his lands joined the district, and in 1884 the western part of Sirsa district, including Fazilka, followed.

After the Partition of Punjab, Firozpur became part of India, and by the 1951 census 349,767 Sikh and Hindu refugees from areas that became Pakistan had settled there. Later changes of boundary reduced its area: in 1972 its Moga and Muktsar tehsils went to a new Faridkot district, and in 2011 Fazilka became a district of its own. Firozpur forms part of the Firozpur division.
first-amendment-to-the-united-states-con: The right to petition for redress of grievances was a principle of the 1215 Magna Carta and of the English Bill of Rights of 1689. In 1776 the Virginia colonial legislature passed a Declaration of Rights that called freedom of the press a bulwark of liberty, and eight other states made similar pledges. After the Constitutional Convention proposed a new constitution on 17 September 1787, George Mason proposed adding a bill of rights. James Madison and other delegates argued that state guarantees were sufficient and that listing rights risked implying that unlisted ones were unprotected, and the proposal was defeated by a unanimous vote of the state delegations. The Bill of Rights was proposed later to answer Anti-Federalist opposition to ratification.

The amendment was adopted on 15 December 1791 as one of the ten amendments of the Bill of Rights. In the original draft it stood third, but the first two articles were not ratified by the states. It prevents Congress from making laws respecting an establishment of religion, prohibiting the free exercise of religion, abridging the freedom of speech or of the press, or limiting the right of peaceable assembly and of petition. Courts have cited Thomas Jefferson's phrase about a wall of separation between church and state in applying the religion clauses, and have held that the amendment also protects freedom of association by implication.

At first the amendment bound only Congress, and many of its provisions were read more narrowly than now. The Supreme Court did not rule on the Alien and Sedition Acts, and punishment for blasphemy was upheld throughout the nineteenth century. During the First World War the Court upheld the conviction of Charles Schenck under the Espionage Act of 1917, with Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. describing a test of clear and present danger.

Beginning with Gitlow v. New York in 1925 the Court applied the amendment to the states through the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Near v. Minnesota in 1931 and New York Times Co. v. United States in 1971 limited prior restraint of publication, and New York Times Co. v. Sullivan in 1964 required public officials suing for libel to prove actual malice.
first-anglo-afghan-war: The war was one of the first major conflicts of the Great Game, the nineteenth-century competition between Britain and Russia for influence in Central Asia. In Britain any Russian advance into Central Asia was assumed to be directed at India, although no Russian tsar seriously planned an invasion. Lord Palmerston and John Hobhouse feared the instability of Afghanistan and Sindh and the growing power of the Sikh kingdom. Scholars now also stress the fear that Dost Mohammad Khan and the Qajar ruler of Iran would ally to end Sikh rule in the Punjab. The British decided to replace Dost Mohammad with a more pliant ruler, the former king Shuja Shah Durrani.

The Army of the Indus, some 21,000 British and Indian troops under John Keane, set out from the Punjab with William Hay Macnaghten as Britain's chief representative, followed by 38,000 camp followers and 30,000 camels. The British occupied Kabul in August 1839 and restored Shuja. Most troops then went back to India, leaving 8,000 in Afghanistan, but Shuja's rule could be kept only by a British presence that the Afghans resented, and Macnaghten's decision to let soldiers bring their families seemed to show that the occupation would be permanent.

On 1 January 1842 an agreement allowed the British garrison of Kabul and its dependents to leave Afghanistan, and the withdrawal began five days later. The column numbered about 16,500, of whom about 4,500 were soldiers and over 12,000 camp followers. Almost all of them died in the mountain passes. The garrisons at Kandahar and Jalalabad held out, and Ghazni was stormed. Akbar Khan was defeated near Jalalabad, and relief forces came from India in the spring.

Lord Ellenborough, who replaced Lord Auckland as governor-general, was under instructions to end the war. He ordered the forces at Kandahar and Jalalabad to leave after inflicting reprisals and securing the release of prisoners. Shuja Shah was assassinated and succeeded by his son Fateh Jang, who abdicated for his brother Shahpur Mirza. Their short reign ended with the return of Dost Mohammad Khan from exile in India.

The campaign cost over one million pounds in the year 1840 to 1841. In Britain Lord Aberdeen and Benjamin Disraeli criticised the war as rash, and the army chaplain G. R. Gleig wrote in 1843 that not one benefit was gained from it. In 1878 the British invaded again, beginning the Second Anglo-Afghan War.
first-anglo-dutch-war: In the 16th century England had supported the Dutch Republic against Spain in the Eighty Years' War. The separate peace between England and Spain in 1604 strained the relationship, and the Dutch, having made peace with Spain in 1648, replaced the English as the dominant traders with the Iberian Peninsula, adding to an English resentment of Dutch trade that had grown since 1590. By the middle of the century the Dutch had the largest merchant fleet in Europe, with more ships than all other states combined, and had conquered most of Portugal's territories and trading posts in the East Indies and Brazil.

Tensions rose when the English Parliament passed the Navigation Act 1651, which required cargo to English ports and colonies to be carried in English ships. The Dutch saw acceptance as subordinating their trade to the English system. The more immediate cause was action by the English navy and privateers: 140 Dutch merchantmen were seized in 1651, and another 30 in January 1652 alone. An English embassy under Oliver St John, which reached The Hague on 7 March 1651 proposing a confederation of the two Commonwealths, left on 2 July without an alliance.

Both nations were unready, and war might have been delayed but for an encounter between the fleets of Lieutenant-Admiral Maarten Tromp and General at Sea Robert Blake near Dover on 29 May 1652. Cromwell's ordinance required foreign fleets to dip their flag in salute. The salute was not given promptly, and Blake opened fire in the brief Battle of Dover; Tromp lost two ships but escorted his convoy to safety. The Grand Pensionary Adriaan Pauw went to London in a last attempt to prevent war, but English demands had become extreme. Parliament declared war on 10 July 1652. Despite a series of victories in 1652 and 1653, the Commonwealth could not blockade Dutch trade, although English privateers inflicted serious losses on Dutch merchant shipping.

The economic damage led to the Treaty of Westminster in 1654, in which the Dutch made minor concessions. They accepted the Navigation Act, paid an indemnity of £85,000 for the East India Company's losses and agreed to salute English warships in the Channel. The Dutch realised few of their own aims. Cromwell dropped his aim of a union subordinating the Dutch and asked instead that the House of Orange be excluded from the stadtholdership. In a secret annexe, the States of Holland passed an Act of Seclusion in May 1654. The commercial issues remained unresolved, and in 1665 they led to the Second Anglo-Dutch War.
first-anglo-sikh-war: Maharaja Ranjit Singh expanded and consolidated the Sikh kingdom of Punjab in the early nineteenth century, as British-controlled territories advanced to its borders. He kept a policy of wary friendship with the British while building up his army with American and European mercenaries as trainers. After his death in 1839 the kingdom fell into disorder: his successors Kharak Singh and Nau Nihal Singh died within months in suspicious circumstances, and Sher Singh was murdered in September 1843. The army grew from 29,000 men in 1839 to over 80,000 in 1845, and its regimental committees formed an alternative source of power. Jind Kaur became regent for her infant son Duleep Singh, with Lal Singh as vizier and Tej Singh as army commander.

The British East India Company had meanwhile built up its strength near the Punjab, with a cantonment at Firozpur, and annexed Sindh in 1843. Most British accounts say their concern was the Sikh army's threat to the border; Sikh and Indian historians say that preparations such as bridging trains and siege batteries show an intent to conquer.

After diplomatic relations broke, the Sikh army began crossing the Sutlej on 11 December 1845, claiming to enter Sikh possessions; the British saw it as hostile and declared war. They won an untidy battle at Mudki on 18 December. At Ferozeshah on 21 December the Sikh artillery caused heavy British casualties, and Hardinge expected defeat, but the British rallied the next morning. Sikh accounts say that Lal Singh held back the irregular cavalry and that Tej Singh withdrew when victory was near.

On 28 January 1846 Sir Harry Smith won at Aliwal. At Sobraon on 10 February the British broke through the Sikh entrenchments, and the pontoon bridge over the Sutlej broke, trapping nearly 20,000 Sikh troops on the east bank. Sikh accounts say Tej Singh deliberately weakened it; British accounts say it broke under the weight of retreating men. None of the trapped soldiers tried to surrender, and the Sikhs lost between 8,000 and 10,000 men.

By the Treaty of Lahore on 9 March 1846 the Sikhs ceded the Jullundur Doab and owed an indemnity of 15 million rupees. Unable to pay, the Durbar ceded Kashmir, Hazarah and the hill country between the Beas and Indus, and Gulab Singh of Jammu bought Kashmir from the Company for 7.5 million rupees under the Treaty of Amritsar. The Treaty of Bhyroval of 16 December 1846 replaced the regent with a British resident, giving the Company control of the government. Resentment led to the Second Anglo-Sikh War within three years.
first-balkan-war: Serbia and Montenegro had secured their independence by 1867, confirmed by the Treaty of Berlin in 1878. Between 1878 and 1912 Greece, Bulgaria and Serbia sponsored insurgent groups in Ottoman Macedonia that fought the government and each other in the Macedonian Struggle. The Young Turk Revolution of July 1908 revived the question of whether Ottoman rule could last. By 1912 the Ottoman Empire, known as the sick man of Europe, was still fighting Italy in Libya and the Dodecanese, and peace came only on 15 October 1912, days after the Balkan war began. Bulgaria was the strongest of the four states of the Balkan League, with some 600,000 men mobilised, while Greece, thought the weakest, was the only member with a meaningful navy.

Montenegro declared war on 8 October 1912. In Thrace the Ottoman command had wrongly expected the main Bulgarian army to go to Macedonia, and the Bulgarians defeated the Ottoman East Army on the Edirne-Kırklareli line. In Macedonia the Greek Army of Thessaly seized Thessaloniki, and the Serbs and Bulgarians won great victories at Kirkkilise, Lüleburgaz, Kumanovo and Monastir. The Greek fleet took Lemnos and kept the Ottoman fleet in the Dardanelles.

Adrianople fell on 11 March 1913 after a two-week bombardment and a final assault by the Bulgarian Second Army and two Serbian divisions. Ottoman casualties in the whole Adrianople campaign reached 23,000 dead, and the Ottoman command lost all hope of regaining the initiative. On 23 April 1913 the garrison of Shkodër surrendered, starved, to the Montenegrins. The Ottoman government had declared war with its mobilisation only partly complete, and 580,000 Ottoman soldiers in the Balkans faced 912,000 of the League.

The Treaty of London ended the war on 30 May 1913. All Ottoman territory west of the Enez-Kıyıköy line passed to the Balkan League, and Albania was declared independent. The Ottomans lost 83 per cent of their European territories and 69 per cent of their European population. Many civilians were killed or driven from their homes, and both sides committed war crimes. Serbia and Greece, which occupied most of the territory meant for Albania, withdrew only reluctantly. Greece and Serbia signed a military alliance against Bulgaria on 1 May 1913, and Bulgaria, disputing the division of Macedonia, attacked its former allies on 16 June 1913, beginning the Second Balkan War.
first-battle-of-panipat: In 1504 Babur took control of the kingdom of his late uncle Ulugh Beg II, based on Kabul and Ghazni. Opposed by Muhammad Shaybani to the north-west, he sought to expand south-east into Punjab, and by 1519 he had reached the Chenab River. Most of North India belonged to the Delhi Sultanate under Ibrahim Lodi of the Lodi dynasty, who was locked in a power struggle with relatives and ministers.

Daulat Khan Lodi, Governor of Punjab, offered to defect to Babur. When Babur set out for Lahore in 1524 he found Daulat driven out by Ibrahim's forces, but the Lodi army that marched out against him was routed. Babur took Jhelum, Sialkot, Kalanaur and Dipalpur, put Dipalpur under Alam Khan, a rebel uncle of Ibrahim, and returned to Kabul. He crossed the Indus again in December 1525 and, after securing Punjab, advanced towards Delhi.

At Panipat Babur met a much larger army. Ibrahim's force is reported to have had an effective strength of between 50,000 and 70,000 men with 1,000 war elephants, but it lacked gunpowder weapons. Babur had 12,000 men, at least part of them with matchlock muskets, a cavalry that fought as horse archers, and between 15 and 20 cannons. He defended his position with 700 wagons tied together in a line, with a breastwork for musketeers between every second wagon and sally points 150 riders wide for the cavalry. His right flank rested on the city of Panipat, and on the left he dug a trench filled with branches against cavalry.

When Ibrahim attacked on 21 April 1526, the frontage Babur presented was too narrow for him to use his numbers. Musket and cannon fire pinned Ibrahim's centre while horse archers harried the flanks and rear, and the noise of the cannon panicked the elephants and added to the casualties. Ibrahim and 20,000 of his men were killed, and thousands more died in the retreat.

The battle was one of the earliest in which gunpowder weapons were used on the Indian subcontinent. It was a decisive military victory for Babur and gave him new lands, beginning a new phase in the establishment of the Mughal Empire in the heart of the subcontinent, an empire that lasted over 300 years. To secure his position, however, Babur still had to fight the Mewar ruler Rana Sanga at Khanwa in 1527 and the eastern Afghans at the Ghaghra River in 1529.
first-battle-of-the-marne: Germany declared war on France on 3 August 1914. Under the Schlieffen Plan, as revised by Helmuth von Moltke, the German armies were to sweep through Belgium and into France, capture Paris and destroy the French army within about six weeks, so that Germany could then turn on Russia. August brought bloody battles that the Germans mostly won, and the French and British retreated southward for more than 250 km in what is called the Great Retreat. The French commander, Joseph Joffre, kept his army in order and reinforced it with troops from his eastern flank and with reserve units.

By early September the German armies were exhausted and had outrun their supplies. Kluck's 1st Army turned south-east and crossed the Marne on 3 September, unaware that a new French army, the 6th, was guarding Paris to his west. Joseph Gallieni, the military governor of Paris, saw that the German right flank was vulnerable, and on 4 September Joffre ordered a counter-offensive. The battle was fought from 5 to 12 September along a front of 230 km between Paris and Verdun.

On 5 September part of the French 6th Army met a German reserve corps near the Ourcq river, which held it for 24 hours and warned Kluck. He turned his army west to face the threat, which opened a gap of 50 km between his army and Bülow's 2nd Army. French aerial reconnaissance found the gap, and the French 5th Army and the British force advanced into it. By 9 September the German 1st and 2nd Armies were at risk of encirclement and were ordered to retreat to the Aisne, where the Germans dug in on the heights.

The retreat ended the Schlieffen Plan. Moltke is said to have told Kaiser Wilhelm II that Germany had lost the war, though whether he did is not known; on 14 September he was replaced by Erich von Falkenhayn, officially because of ill health.

Both sides then tried to outflank each other's northern wings in the Race to the Sea, which ended at the First Battle of Ypres and led to a stalemate of trench warfare on the Western Front that lasted four years. No exact casualty counts exist, since the battle is hard to separate from others in August and September. The historian Holger Herwig called it the most important land battle of the 20th century, and in French tradition it is the Miracle on the Marne.
first-boer-war: Boer farmers had moved north from the Cape after Britain acquired it in 1814, and the Great Trek followed the abolition of slavery in the British Empire in 1834. Britain recognised the independence of the Transvaal in the Sand River Convention of 1852.

The discovery of diamonds in 1867 ended the isolation of the Boer republics and drew British imperial interest, and in 1875 Lord Carnarvon tried to organise a federation of British and Boer territories, which the Boer leaders refused. The Transvaal under President T. F. Burgers was bankrupt, with tax problems and a war against the Pedi under Sekhukhune. Sir Theophilus Shepstone was sent as special commissioner, and on 12 April 1877 the annexation was proclaimed in Pretoria.

The war began on 16 December 1880 with shots at Potchefstroom. On 20 December the Boers ambushed a column of the 94th Foot under Lieutenant-Colonel Philip Robert Anstruther at Bronkhorstspruit, and the six small British forts in the Transvaal were besieged from late December.

The Boers had no regular army: farmers organised in commandos, skilled hunters and marksmen who fought from cover on horseback, while the British relied on volleys and formations. Major-General Sir George Pomeroy Colley set out to relieve the forts with about 1,200 men. He was repulsed at Laing's Nek on 28 January 1881 and lost half his escort at the Ingogo River on 8 February.

On 14 February hostilities were suspended for negotiations offered by Kruger, but on the night of 26 February Colley took some 400 men to the top of Majuba Hill. At dawn the Boers stormed it, and within thirty minutes the British were swept off the summit. They lost 92 killed, 134 wounded and 59 prisoners, and Colley was shot dead trying to rally his men.

Gladstone's government, wary of a costly distant war, ordered a truce. Sir Evelyn Wood signed an armistice on 6 March, and a treaty was signed with Kruger on 23 March 1881. Under the Pretoria Convention, signed on 3 August and ratified on 25 October, the Boers accepted the Queen's nominal rule and British control of external relations and African affairs, in return for self-government.

It was the first conflict since the American War of Independence in which Britain was decisively defeated and forced to sign a peace on unfavourable terms. Historians lay much of the blame on Colley's command, with poor intelligence and communications. The discovery of gold on the Witwatersrand in 1886 revived British interest, and in the Second Boer War, which broke out in 1899, one British slogan was Remember Majuba.
first-bulgarian-empire: The Bulgars were Turkic semi-nomadic warrior tribes of the Pontic–Caspian steppe and the Volga region. The Bulgars of Asparuh crossed the Danube into Scythia Minor, a nominal Byzantine province, in the 670s. In 680 the Byzantine Emperor Constantine IV led a large army and fleet against them but suffered a disastrous defeat at Onglos, in or near the Danube Delta. The Bulgars crossed the Balkan Mountains into Thrace, and in 681 the Byzantines signed a treaty acknowledging Bulgaria as an independent state, ceding the lands north of the Balkan Mountains and agreeing to pay an annual tribute. It was the first state the Byzantine Empire recognised in the Balkans.

After Khan Sevar died in 753 the Dulo clan died out, and in fifteen years seven khans reigned and all were murdered. Under Krum (r. 803–814) Bulgaria doubled in size and destroyed the Avar Khaganate. Boris I decided by 863 to accept Christianity, and in 866 he executed 52 leading nobles after an anti-Christian rebellion. The Council of Preslav in 893 made Old Bulgarian the language of state and church.

Under Simeon I (r. 893–927) the empire reached its largest extent. He defeated the Byzantines at Boulgarophygon in 896 and annihilated their army at Anchialus in 917, and the Bulgarians besieged Constantinople in 923 and 924 without success. From 968 the Kievan prince Sviatoslav I invaded, and the Byzantine emperor John I Tzimiskes forced him out in 971. In 1014 Basil II crushed the Bulgarians at the Battle of Kleidion and ordered 15,000 prisoners blinded, sparing every hundredth man one eye to guide the rest home. By 1018 the last strongholds had surrendered.

The Glagolitic alphabet, created by Cyril and Methodius, reached Bulgaria with their disciples in 886, and the Early Cyrillic alphabet was invented in the capital Preslav. Old Church Slavonic literature flourished under Simeon I and spread north, becoming the lingua franca of much of Eastern Europe. The fully independent Bulgarian Patriarchate was recognised in 927. The Madara Rider, a relief carved in a cliff, was listed by UNESCO in 1979. The Second Bulgarian Empire followed in 1185.
first-carlist-war: Before the war Spain was in deep social, economic and political crisis. Its population was about 12.3 million, and between 1824 and 1833 the state's average annual income was barely more than half its level before the wars. In 1823 Ferdinand VII repealed the Spanish Constitution of 1812, which had abolished the fueros, and in the Ominous Decade that followed he suppressed his enemies and the press with the help of a militia, the Voluntarios Realistas, which reached 284,000 men in 1832.

The Basque provinces had kept a relative autonomy since supporting Philip V in the War of the Spanish Succession. The western Basque provinces and Navarre sided with Carlos because he was willing to uphold their institutions and laws, though historians disagree on whether the cause there was essentially one for the fueros. The Liberals held the institutions, almost the whole army and the cities, and had the support of the United Kingdom, France and Portugal.

Tomás de Zumalacárregui, the Carlist commander in Navarre, swore an oath to uphold the fueros and made his base in the Amescoas, near Estella, where 3,000 volunteers joined him. In April 1834 France, Great Britain, Spain and Portugal signed the treaty of the Quadruple Alliance. Both sides shot prisoners; the most notorious case was at Heredia, where 118 Liberal prisoners were executed on Zumalacárregui's order. After his death in 1835 the Liberals slowly regained the initiative. In 1837 the Royal Expedition reached the walls of Madrid but retreated after the Battle of Aranzueque, while in the east Ramón Cabrera held the initiative.

The war was the deadliest civil war of nineteenth-century Europe, responsible for the deaths of 5% of the 1833 population, with military casualties about half that number. Bilbao fell from 15,000 to 10,234 inhabitants. In October 1839 the Basques kept a reduced form of home rule, covering taxation and the military draft, in exchange for their incorporation into a centralised Spain. In 1840 General Baldomero Espartero became premier and regent with the support of the Progressives. The war is often compared with the Spanish Civil War a century later; Mark Lawrence writes that it offered a comparable struggle between legitimist Carlists and modernising Liberals.
first-continental-congress: The First Continental Congress met from 5 September to 26 October 1774 at Carpenters' Hall in Philadelphia, at the beginning of the American Revolution. It was organised just after the British Navy blockaded Boston Harbor and Parliament passed the punitive Intolerable Acts in response to the Boston Tea Party. Delegates came from twelve of the Thirteen Colonies; Georgia did not attend, because Loyalist sentiment there outweighed Patriot views, and it joined only the following year. Delegates were chosen by the people, by the colonial legislature or by a colony's Committee of Correspondence.

Peyton Randolph of Virginia was elected president on the opening day. He served until 22 October, when ill health forced him to retire, and Henry Middleton of South Carolina took his place. Charles Thomson, leader of the Philadelphia Committee of Correspondence, became secretary. On 6 September Thomas Cushing proposed that sessions begin with a prayer, and Samuel Adams proposed the Reverend Jacob Duché to lead it.

The delegates were not of one mind. Conservatives such as Joseph Galloway, John Dickinson, John Jay and Edward Rutledge wanted to pressure Parliament to rescind its acts and bring about reconciliation. Others, among them Patrick Henry, Roger Sherman, Samuel Adams and John Adams, wanted a decisive statement of colonial rights and liberties. Roger Sherman denied the legislative authority of Parliament, and Patrick Henry held that a completely new system of government was needed. Joseph Galloway proposed a Plan of Union, which the delegates tabled and later struck from the record. The Congress's first act was to adopt the Suffolk Resolves, drawn up by several Massachusetts counties, which declared grievances, called for a boycott of British goods and urged each colony to train its own militia.

In the end the voices of compromise prevailed, and the Congress did not call for independence. On 20 October it signed the Continental Association in its Declaration and Resolves, a compact to boycott British goods from 1 December 1774 unless Parliament repealed the Intolerable Acts, with committees of observation and inspection in each colony to enforce it. Exports to Britain were to cease after 10 September 1775 if the acts stood. The delegates also planned an end to the import of slaves from 1 December, and drew up a Petition to the King. Imports from Britain fell by 97 percent in 1775.

Every colonial assembly except New York's approved the proceedings. The petition failed, and the outbreak of fighting in April 1775 cut short the boycott's chance of changing British policy. The Second Continental Congress met in Philadelphia the following May, after the Battles of Lexington and Concord, to organise the colonies' defence in the American Revolutionary War.
first-council-of-nicaea: The council grew out of a dispute among the clergy of Alexandria about the nature of Jesus and his relation to God the Father, which scholars date between 318 and 322. Archbishop Alexander taught that the Son was eternally generated from the Father, while the presbyter Arius held that the Father alone was eternal and that the Son was created and subordinate. A local council of bishops from Egypt and Libya sided with Alexander, and Arius was excommunicated and exiled, then sought support elsewhere in the east. Arius' teaching is known partly from his few surviving writings but chiefly from his opponents.

In 324 Constantine defeated Licinius and became sole ruler of the empire. He learned of the quarrel, probably from Eusebius of Nicomedia, and urged both men to reconcile. When that failed he summoned the bishops to Nicaea and paid the expenses, including their travel, from the imperial treasury.

The council met from May until the end of July 325. Reports of attendance range from 250 to 300, the traditional figure of 318 being given by Athanasius, while lists of signatories hold 200 to 220 names. Almost all came from the eastern half of the empire. Hosius of Corduba may have presided, and two presbyters represented Pope Sylvester I. Constantine opened it with a speech in Latin, though most present spoke Greek. No acts of the council survive, so its work is known from later accounts, such as those of Eusebius of Caesarea and Athanasius.

The council settled the question of the divine nature of the Son and drew up the first part of the Nicene Creed. It ordered uniform observance of the date of Easter, ending reliance on the Jewish community to identify the lunar month of Nisan. It dealt with the Melitian schism in Egypt and issued twenty canons on church discipline.

Nicaea was the first attempt to gather a general council representing the church in every part of the empire, and it set a precedent for later councils to adopt creeds and canons. It did not end the conflict. Arians and Melitians soon regained nearly all the rights they had lost, and Arianism remained a subject of debate for the rest of the fourth century. Constantine's son Constantius II and Valens, who ruled the east after him, both favoured Arianism.

Popular accounts credit the council with things it did not do. There is no record of any discussion of the biblical canon, and the story that books were chosen by whether they fell from an altar was popularised by Voltaire from an account of 887. Constantine did not force the homoousian view on the bishops, and was baptised some eleven or twelve years later.
first-crusade: The expedition began with a request for help. In March 1095 the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos sent envoys to the Council of Piacenza to ask Pope Urban II for military support against the advancing Seljuk Turks. Urban responded favourably, perhaps hoping to heal the East-West Schism of forty years earlier. Later that year, at the Council of Clermont, he urged Christians to undertake an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Adhemar of Le Puy was the first to take the cross. The response was far greater than the pope or Alexios expected, and most of those who answered were poor people with little fighting skill rather than knights.

Thousands of mostly poor Christians, led by the French priest Peter the Hermit, set out first. This People's Crusade passed through Germany, where it took part in anti-Jewish violence, including the Rhineland massacres, and was destroyed by a Turkish ambush led by Kilij Arslan I at the Battle of Civetot in October 1096. The main armies left in August 1096 under princes including Raymond IV of Toulouse, Godfrey of Bouillon and his brother Baldwin of Boulogne, Bohemond of Taranto and Robert Curthose of Normandy, and gathered at Constantinople by April 1097. Estimates of their numbers run to as many as 100,000 with non-combatants.

In Anatolia the crusaders took Nicaea in June 1097 and defeated Kilij Arslan at the Battle of Dorylaeum on 1 July. The siege of Antioch began on 20 October 1097 and the city was captured in June 1098. The crusaders reached Jerusalem, then held by the Fatimids, in June 1099, with perhaps only 12,000 men left, and took it by assault on 15 July. Crusader eyewitnesses leave little doubt that there was great slaughter in the city, though some historians think later sources exaggerated its scale.

A council in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre made Godfrey of Bouillon leader of Jerusalem after Raymond of Toulouse refused the crown. In August 1099 the crusaders defeated a Fatimid force at the Battle of Ascalon, which ended the expedition, and most of them then went home. Four states were established: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch and the County of Tripoli. When Godfrey died a year later, Baldwin became the first Latin king of Jerusalem.

Latin Christendom regarded the success as the work of divine providence. This form of religious warfare remained popular for centuries, and the First Crusade became one of the most written-about events of the medieval period.
first-fitna: Under Umar, who was caliph from 634, the conquests of Byzantine and Sasanian lands brought revenue to the Muslims, and provincial governors ruled with considerable autonomy. Uthman succeeded Umar after the latter's assassination in 644. He relied on his Umayyad relatives and appointed his kinsmen to nearly all the important governorships, which led to accusations of nepotism and to resentment among other members of the Quraysh. As the flow of spoils slowed and he demanded that provincial surplus be forwarded to him, opposition grew, above all in Iraq and Egypt. Dissidents from both provinces marched on Medina and killed Uthman in June 656. Ali was then recognised as caliph.

Aisha, Talha and Zubayr opposed Ali, demanding vengeance for Uthman and a new election. Ali defeated them at the Battle of the Camel, outside Basra, on 8 December 656. Talha and Zubayr were killed, and Ali sent Aisha back to Medina and announced a pardon. Mu'awiya, the governor of Syria and Uthman's cousin, whom Ali had tried to dismiss, then declared war, demanding vengeance for Uthman. The armies met at Siffin in July 657. When the balance turned towards Ali, the Syrians raised copies of the Quran on their lances and asked for arbitration, and Ali accepted under pressure from his own army.

The arbitration, agreed on 2 August 657, went badly for Ali, and a group that rejected it, the Kharijites, gathered at Nahrawan and declared both Ali and Mu'awiya infidels. They killed civilians who did not share their views, and Ali's forces destroyed them at the Battle of Nahrawan. In 658 Mu'awiya sent about 6,000 Syrian troops under Amr ibn al-As into Egypt and took the province, depriving Ali of one of his wealthiest regions. A raid under Busr ibn Abi Artat then went through the Hejaz and Yemen, executing supporters of Ali.

In late 660 Ali and Mu'awiya agreed to stop fighting. In January 661 Ali was assassinated at the Great Mosque of Kufa by the Kharijite Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam. His son Hasan was proclaimed caliph in Kufa, but his forces suffered defections as Mu'awiya marched on the city with a large army. Hasan made a treaty ceding the caliphate, with a general amnesty and a provision that a council would choose the caliph after Mu'awiya's death. Mu'awiya was recognised as caliph, and the Umayyad Caliphate followed.
first-french-empire: The empire grew out of the Consulate. On 9 November 1799 troops led by Napoleon Bonaparte seized control in a coup planned with Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès, and Bonaparte outmaneuvered Sieyès to become First Consul. He was made First Consul for life in 1802, after a plebiscite that gave 3,653,600 votes in favour and 8,272 against. On 18 May 1804 the Senate gave him the title Emperor of the French, and on 2 December 1804 he was crowned in Notre-Dame de Paris by Pope Pius VII. The state nevertheless continued to be formally called the French Republic until October 1808.

In the War of the Third Coalition the French army won a string of victories over Austrian and Russian forces, most notably at Austerlitz in 1805. Napoleon created the Confederation of the Rhine, and on 6 August 1806 the Habsburgs abdicated the title of Holy Roman Emperor. He destroyed the Prussian armies at Jena and Auerstedt, and the Treaties of Tilsit removed about half of Prussia's territory. To build satellite states he installed relatives as rulers, among them his brother Joseph Bonaparte at Naples, later King of Spain.

The Continental System, a blockade against Britain, strained the alliance with Russia, and the seizure of the Spanish throne provoked a guerrilla war across the Iberian Peninsula. Austria was defeated at Wagram in 1809 and ceded the Illyrian Provinces. In 1812 Napoleon invaded Russia and lost nearly his whole army. After defeat at Leipzig in 1813, Paris capitulated on 30 March 1814, and Napoleon abdicated at Fontainebleau on 11 April. He returned from Elba and revived the empire in the Hundred Days of 1815, but was defeated at Waterloo and exiled to Saint Helena, where he died in 1821.

At its height in 1812 the empire had 130 departments and a population of over 44 million, and ruled some 90 million subjects across Europe. The Napoleonic Code increased legal equality, established jury systems and legalised divorce, while seigneurial dues and justice were abolished, as were aristocratic privileges everywhere except Poland. Napoleon preserved many social gains of the Revolution while suppressing political liberty: he rejected electoral democracy and freedom of the press, though his rule included public education and the emancipation of the Jews.
first-indochina-war: Vietnam was absorbed into French Indochina in stages between 1858 and 1887, and Vietnamese nationalism grew until World War II broke French control. After the Japanese surrender in August 1945, Emperor Bảo Đại abdicated on 25 August and handed power to the Viet Minh, and on 2 September Ho Chi Minh proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. Allied commanders had placed the south under British Admiral Mountbatten, and on 23 September 1945 French forces overthrew the Viet Minh administration in Saigon. A preliminary accord of March 1946 recognised the Democratic Republic as a free state within a French Union, but talks in Paris broke down over independence and the reunification of Cochinchina.

Full war broke out between French and Viet Minh forces in December 1946. In 1947 Ho Chi Minh and General Võ Nguyên Giáp withdrew into the mountainous Việt Bắc, while the French took the main towns by March. In 1949 France united Cochinchina, Annam and Tonkin as the State of Vietnam within the French Union under Bảo Đại. About 325,000 of the 500,000 French troops were Indochinese, and soldiers came from across the French colonial empire, since governments forbade sending metropolitan recruits.

The Chinese Communist victory of 1949 changed the war. In 1950 China and the Soviet Union recognised the Democratic Republic, while the United States recognised the State of Vietnam and began to aid France. Giáp reorganised his forces into five infantry divisions, and the conflict came to resemble a conventional war. The Battle of Dien Bien Phu in 1954, the last major battle, ended in a decisive French defeat.

The Geneva Conference opened in May 1954, and the accords were signed on 21 July. They set a ceasefire, which took effect on 11 August, and divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel, with a free election planned for 1956 to reunify the country. France undertook to respect the independence of Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia.

Estimates put military deaths at 400,000 to 842,707 and civilian deaths at 125,000 to 400,000. Both sides committed war crimes. French troops killed over 200 women and children in the Mỹ Trạch massacre of 29 November 1947, and one historian estimates that the Viet Minh assassinated 100,000 to 150,000 civilians. In France leftists called it the dirty war. The Algerian War began on 1 November 1954, and an Algerian leader praised the victory at Dien Bien Phu as an incentive to insurrection.
first-intermediate-period: The First Intermediate Period spanned about 125 years, from c. 2181 to c. 2055 BCE, after the end of the Old Kingdom. It comprises the Seventh Dynasty, mostly considered spurious by Egyptologists, the Eighth, Ninth and Tenth, and part of the Eleventh. Several causes for the Old Kingdom's fall are given, some only hypothetical. One is the very long reign of Pepi II, the last major pharaoh of the Sixth Dynasty, who outlived many heirs and so created problems of succession. Another was the rise of provincial nomarchs, whose posts had become hereditary and who built tombs in their own domains, raised armies and fought their neighbours. A third is low Nile floods in a drier climate, bringing famine, but there is no consensus.

Little is known of the Seventh and Eighth Dynasties at Memphis. Manetho describes 70 kings who ruled for 70 days, almost certainly an exaggeration for disorganised kingship. The Ninth and Tenth Dynasties arose at Heracleopolis, each with nineteen listed rulers, while in the south warlords dominated. Ankhtifi, whose tomb was found in 1928 at Mo'alla, 30 kilometres south of Luxor, ruled the nomes of Hierakonpolis and Edfu but failed to take the Theban nome. His tomb autobiography claims he rescued Egypt from famine: "I gave bread to the hungry and did not allow anyone to die".

The Theban kings descended from Intef, nomarch of Thebes. Intef II began the assault on the north, particularly at Abydos, and Intef III completed its conquest and moved into Middle Egypt. Mentuhotep II then defeated the Heracleopolitan kings and reunified the country, beginning the Middle Kingdom.

The Egyptologists Georg Steindorff and Henri Frankfort coined the term in 1926, and the period is often called a dark age. Ludwig David Morenz has argued it was not one and proposed the name Period of Regions. Very little monumental evidence survives. The Theban kings developed a distinctive Pre-Unification Theban Style of relief and built saff tombs at El-Tarif. The Ipuwer Papyrus, which modern scholarship does not date to the period but which may refer to it, records impoverishment in Egypt.
first-intifada: Israel captured the West Bank, Jerusalem, the Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip from Jordan and Egypt in the Six-Day War of 1967, and the occupation was approaching its twentieth year when the uprising began. Israel opened its labour market to Palestinians from the occupied territories, who did mostly unskilled or semi-skilled work, and by 1987 over 40 percent of the Palestinian workforce worked in Israel daily. Land expropriation, high birthrates and limited land for building and farming raised population density and unemployment, and only one in eight college-educated Palestinians could find work in their field.

The expansion of the Palestinian university system, which drew students from refugee camps, villages and small towns, produced a new elite from lower social strata that was more activist and more confrontational. Israeli administrators, pursuing an iron fist policy of deportations, house demolitions and curfews, believed Palestinian resistance was exhausted.

In December 1987 an Israeli truck collided with cars of Palestinian workers at the Erez checkpoint, killing four, three of them from the Jabalia refugee camp in Gaza. Rumours spread that it was a deliberate reprisal for the stabbing of an Israeli businessman in Gaza two days earlier, an intention Israel denied. Mass funerals led to demonstrations, and on the following day teenagers threw stones at military vehicles and soldiers opened fire.

The uprising spread through strikes, boycotts of Israeli institutions, refusal to pay taxes, graffiti, barricades and the throwing of stones and Molotov cocktails. No single person or organisation began it. Local committees, and the Unified National Leadership of the Uprising, issued communiques and set up underground schools, medical care and food aid. The PLO and its chairman Yassir Arafat chose an unarmed strategy. Israel deployed about 80,000 soldiers, and on 16 April 1988 the PLO leader Khalil al-Wazir was assassinated in Tunis by an Israeli commando squad.

In the first thirteen months 332 Palestinians and 12 Israelis were killed. Over the whole six years the Israeli army killed at least 1,087 Palestinians, and 100 Israeli civilians and 60 soldiers died. An estimated 822 Palestinians were killed by other Palestinians as alleged collaborators between 1988 and April 1994. Human Rights Watch criticised the use of lethal force, and images of soldiers beating adolescents led to the adoption of plastic bullets.

In November 1988 the Palestine National Council in Algiers voted to recognise Israel, accept the relevant United Nations resolutions and adopt the principle of two states on the borders of 1967. Jordan cut its administrative and financial ties to the West Bank. The uprising lasted until the Madrid Conference of 1991, although some date its end to 1993, the year the Oslo Accords were signed. Hamas, which opposed negotiation, grew as a rival to the PLO during these years.
first-italian-war-of-independence: In 1848 revolutions broke out across Europe. Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies granted a constitution on 23 January, Leopold II of Tuscany and Charles Albert of Sardinia followed on 17 February, and Pope Pius IX did so for the Papal States on 14 March. Sicily, except Messina, rose against the Bourbons. Riots in Milan, the Five Days, and in Venice drove the Austrians from both cities, and from 23 March they fell back into the fortresses of the Quadrilateral: Peschiera, Verona, Mantua and Legnago. The Austrian army in Lombardy–Venetia was commanded by the 81-year-old Josef Radetzky, whose soldiers were well trained and knew the ground.

On 23 March 1848 the Kingdom of Sardinia declared war on Austria, and its army of about 65,000 men crossed the Ticino. After fighting at Goito Bridge and Pastrengo, the Papal States and the Two Sicilies withdrew from the war, though some of their troops stayed on as volunteers. Radetzky took Vicenza in June, and in the battle of Custoza from 22 to 27 July he defeated the Piedmontese. Charles Albert then sought a truce, Milan surrendered, and the Salasco armistice followed in August.

Meanwhile a separate popular war was fought by revolutionaries. Pius IX fled Rome on 24 November 1848, after the assassination of his interior minister, and Giuseppe Garibaldi commanded volunteers. Charles Albert reopened the war on 20 March 1849 under a Polish general, Wojciech Chrzanowski, but Radetzky invaded Sardinia and beat his army at Novara on 23 March. That night Charles Albert, finding his commanders against going on, declared that he would abdicate.

The defeat at Novara echoed across Italy. Leopold II returned to Tuscany, and Austrian troops imposed the restoration at Livorno on 10 and 11 May 1849. Genoa revolted on 1 April 1849, fearing that the Albertine Statute would be abolished. Neapolitan forces under Carlo Filangieri took Catania on 7 April and entered Palermo on 15 May, ending the Kingdom of Sicily. Louis Napoleon sent an expedition to restore Pius IX in Rome, where the Roman Republic fell by 2 July. Venice, besieged by Julius Jacob von Haynau from 28 April, held out until 22 August 1849, when the war ended. Victor Emmanuel succeeded his father in Sardinia.
first-italo-ethiopian-war: Italian troops landed at Massawa on 5 February 1885 to replace the departing Egyptians. After an Ethiopian force under Ras Alula destroyed an Italian column at the Battle of Dogali in 1887, the Italians held back for a time. On 2 May 1889 Menelik II, newly proclaimed emperor, signed the Treaty of Wuchale with Italy. The Italian and Amharic texts differed: the Italian version made Ethiopia conduct its foreign affairs through Italy, effectively a protectorate, while the Amharic version did not.

Menelik learned of the Italian reading in 1890, when Queen Victoria's reply told him that Britain could not deal with Ethiopia directly. In 1893 he repudiated the treaty. Italy, led by Prime Minister Francesco Crispi, who sought a second Roman empire, turned to force. Menelik meanwhile imported large numbers of rifles and artillery from Russia, France and others.

In December 1894 the Italians crossed the Mareb River into Tigray. General Oreste Baratieri defeated Ras Mengesha Yohannes at Coatit in January 1895 and again at Senafe, then occupied Adigrat and Adwa. On 17 September 1895 Menelik called his men to arms, and leaders of every region answered, assembling an army of over 100,000. On 7 December 1895 Ras Makonnen overran the Italian position at Amba Alagi, killing Major Pietro Toselli.

Menelik and Empress Taytu Betul joined the siege of the fort at Mekele, which surrendered on 21 January 1896 after its water was cut off; the garrison was allowed to leave. On 1 March 1896 at Adwa three Italian brigades, separated on mountain tracks, met an Ethiopian army of between 73,000 and 120,000. By noon they were in retreat. Estimates put Italian dead at between 5,900 and 6,133, with thousands captured; the Italians left behind their artillery.

News of the defeat brought riots in Italian cities, and within two weeks Crispi was forced to resign. Talks failed when Italy would accept the end of its protectorate claim only if Ethiopia took no protection from another power. The Treaty of Addis Ababa of October 1896 set the borders of Eritrea and obliged Italy to recognise Ethiopia's independence. Captured Eritrean askaris, regarded as traitors, had their right hands and left feet amputated; Italian prisoners were generally treated better.

Britain and France sent missions to Addis Ababa, and France signed a treaty in March 1897. As one of the first decisive victories of an African army over a European colonial power, the war became a symbol of pan-Africanism. Ethiopian sovereignty lasted until the Second Italo-Ethiopian War of 1935–36.
first-jewish-roman-war: Judaea fell to the Roman Republic in 63 BCE, when Pompey intervened in a succession war between the brothers Hyrcanus and Aristobolus. He entered the Temple's Holy of Holies, which only the High Priest was permitted to do, abolished the Jewish monarchy and made Hyrcanus High Priest alone. Judaea later became a province ruled directly by governors, marked by oppression, social divisions and rising religious and ethnic tension. Most scholars see the revolt as an expression of Jewish nationalism, partly inspired by the successful Maccabean revolt against the Seleucids. In May 66 violence broke out in Caesarea after a Greek sacrificed birds at the entrance of a synagogue, and Governor Gessius Florus then looted the Temple treasury and massacred residents of Jerusalem.

Rebels killed the Roman garrison in Jerusalem. Cestius Gallus, the governor of Syria, invaded but was defeated at Bethoron, and a provisional government led by the former High Priest Ananus ben Ananus appointed Josephus commander of Galilee. In 67 Vespasian invaded Galilee and captured Yodfat, Tarichaea and Gamla. Refugees and rebels crowded into Jerusalem, where a three-way factional war developed between Eleazar ben Simon, John of Gischala and Simon bar Giora. Nero died in 68, and when the legions proclaimed Vespasian emperor he left for Rome.

His son Titus returned in the winter of 69 and 70 with more than 48,000 troops and began the siege of Jerusalem in the spring of 70, when the city was swollen with Passover pilgrims. Jerusalem fell in the summer of 70, and the Romans destroyed the Temple and razed the city. Titus and Vespasian held a triumph in Rome in 71. Roman forces under Sextus Lucilius Bassus took Herodium and Machaerus, and the last stronghold, Masada, fell in 73 or 74.

Many Jews died in battles, sieges and famine, were displaced or were sold into slavery. Josephus claimed that 1.1 million died in Jerusalem, a figure widely considered exaggerated. The aristocracy, including the High Priesthood, collapsed, as did the Sanhedrin. Legio X Fretensis garrisoned Jerusalem for nearly two centuries, and the Flavian dynasty commemorated the victory in monuments and coinage and imposed a punitive tax on all Jews.

The destruction of the Second Temple ended sacrifices and the High Priesthood, and the Sadducees and Essenes disappeared from the record. The Pharisees, who had largely opposed the revolt, survived, and the rabbinic sages emerged as leaders and established a centre at Yavneh. The revolt is seen as one stage in the gradual separation of Christianity from Judaism. Two further Jewish revolts against Rome followed in the second century, among them the Bar Kokhba Revolt of 132 to 136. The main source for the war is Josephus, who led the defence of Galilee and was later held captive and then received Roman citizenship.
first-macedonian-war: While Rome was occupied by its war with Carthage, Philip V of Macedon saw a chance to extend his power westward. According to the historian Polybius, he was urged on by Demetrius of Pharos, whom the Romans had made ruler of most of coastal Illyria before he turned against them and fled to Philip's court in 219 BCE. After Hannibal's victory at Lake Trasimene in June 217 BCE, Demetrius advised Philip to make peace with the Aetolians and turn to Illyria and Italy. A peace was concluded at Naupactus.

Philip spent the winter of 217 to 216 BCE building a fleet of 100 small fast galleys, lembi, of the Illyrian kind. When he heard of a Roman squadron near Apollonia he retreated in panic, which Polybius says cost him his best chance in Illyria. After Hannibal's victory at Cannae in 216 BCE Philip sent ambassadors to Hannibal, and they agreed a treaty in the summer of 215 BCE. Roman forces captured the emissaries on their way home and found the terms.

In the late summer of 214 BCE Philip took Oricum with 120 lembi and besieged Apollonia. The Roman propraetor Marcus Valerius Laevinus retook Oricum, and in Livy's account a force of 2,000 men under Quintus Naevius Crista entered Apollonia by night and routed Philip's camp. Philip burned his fleet and withdrew over the mountains. In 213 and 212 BCE he advanced in Illyria by land and captured Lissus, which gave him access to the Adriatic.

In 211 BCE Laevinus made a treaty with the Aetolian League: the Aetolians would fight on land and the Romans at sea, Rome would keep slaves and booty, and Aetolia would receive any territory taken. Attalus I of Pergamon, Elis, Sparta and Messenia were allowed to join. In 210 BCE Laevinus and the Aetolians took Phocian Anticyra, and Rome enslaved its inhabitants. Philip fought on in Greece, winning two battles at Lamia in 209 BCE. Attempts at peace by neutral trading states, among them Egypt, Rhodes, Athens and Chios, failed. In 208 BCE Philip took Opus when Attalus was caught off guard and barely escaped to his ships.

The escape of Attalus proved the turning point. Attalus returned to Pergamon when Prusias I of Bithynia moved against it, and Philip resumed the offensive against the Aetolians. In 206 BCE they sued for a separate peace on terms set by Philip, without Rome's consent. In 205 BCE the Romans sent Publius Sempronius Tuditanus with 35 ships and 11,000 men to Dyrrachium. Finding no allies left in Greece, and having kept Philip from aiding Hannibal, Rome agreed to the Peace of Phoenice in 205 BCE. There had been no decisive engagements, and the war ended in a stalemate.
first-mexican-empire: The Spanish Empire broke apart after Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808, and in 1810 the priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla began the Mexican War of Independence, a decade of fighting between insurgents and royalists. Hidalgo was executed in 1811 and his successor José María Morelos in 1815. When Liberals in Spain restored the Spanish Constitution of 1812 in 1820, curtailing the privileges of established elites, Mexican elites saw their interests threatened. Agustín de Iturbide, an officer of the Spanish army, then drew up the Plan of Iguala and allied with the insurgent leader Vicente Guerrero.

The plan rested on three guarantees: an independent constitutional monarchy governed by a Spanish prince, equal rights for all Americanos and Spaniards born in Spain, and the exclusive position of the Roman Catholic Church. Viceroy Juan O'Donojú signed the Treaty of Córdoba on 24 August 1821. Ferdinand VII of Spain rejected it and no Spanish prince would accept the throne.

On the night of 18 May 1822 a sergeant, Pío Marcha, and the first infantry regiment began a demonstration for Iturbide to be made emperor, and crowds joined them. The next day Congress voted 67 to 15 in his favour, short of a legal quorum, and he was crowned on 21 July 1822. The treasury was bankrupt, the court was planned to outdo the viceroy's, and the government resorted to forced loans. Congress and the emperor clashed over a supreme court, a veto and military tribunals, and fifteen deputies were arrested in August on suspicion of a republican plot.

Iturbide dissolved Congress on 31 October 1822 and replaced it with a National Institutional Junta of his supporters. In December Antonio López de Santa Anna began a rebellion for a republic at Veracruz, and on 1 February 1823 officers proclaimed the Plan of Casa Mata, pledging to restore Congress. Most of Mexico proclaimed for it by March. Iturbide reconvened Congress on 4 March, presented his abdication on 19 March, and left the capital after an agreement of 26 March.

The empire's territory matched the Viceroyalty of New Spain, without Cuba, Santo Domingo and the Philippines, and the Central American lands of the Captaincy General of Guatemala were annexed shortly after it began. It reached its maximum extent, from northern California to Central America, excluding Panama.

After the abdication the Central American provinces formed the Federal Republic of Central America on 1 July 1823, and only Chiapas stayed with Mexico. Power passed to a republican provisional government in 1823 and 1824, which abolished the monarchy and established the First Mexican Republic. Later cessions, mostly to the United States, reduced Mexico to less than half of its maximum extent.
first-nagorno-karabakh-war: Armenians and Azerbaijanis fought over Karabakh as the Russian Empire dissolved in 1917 and 1918, and in April 1920 the Soviet Eleventh Army invaded the Caucasus. On 4 July 1921 the Caucasus Bureau voted 4 to 3 to assign Nagorno-Karabakh to the Armenian Soviet republic, but a day later it reversed the decision and left the region within the Azerbaijan SSR. Armenian discontent was voiced after Stalin's death: about 2,500 Karabakh Armenians signed a petition in 1963 asking for transfer to Armenia or Russia, and there were large demonstrations in Yerevan in 1965 and 1977.

On 20 February 1988 the parliament of the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Oblast voted to unite the region with Armenia. Inter-ethnic clashes followed and grew more violent as the Soviet Union disintegrated, including the pogroms at Sumgait in 1988 and Baku in 1990 against Armenians and the Gugark pogrom in 1988 against Azerbaijanis.

In late 1991 both sides sought weapons from the Soviet military stores. Azerbaijan had the early advantage, with five divisions and five air bases against Armenia's three divisions and no airfields. Azerbaijani forces blockaded Stepanakert, the capital of Nagorno-Karabakh, through the winter of 1991 and 1992 and shelled it, and Armenian volunteers formed detachments of about forty men. Full-scale fighting began in early 1992, and the Khojaly Massacre of that year, confirmed by Human Rights Watch and Memorial, was among the atrocities attributed to the war.

In June 1992 Azerbaijani forces took back dozens of villages in the Shahumian region. In early 1993 Armenian forces overran northern Karabakh and captured seven Azerbaijani-majority districts outside the enclave. Russia shipped large quantities of arms to Armenia in 1993, and Turkey sided with Azerbaijan. The United Nations Security Council passed resolutions 874 and 884 in October and November 1993, recognising Nagorno-Karabakh as a region of Azerbaijan.

By the end Armenians held the enclave and surrounding territory, including the Lachin corridor linking it to Armenia. About 724,000 Azerbaijanis were expelled from Armenia, Nagorno-Karabakh and the surrounding territories, and 300,000 to 500,000 Armenians were displaced. Russia mediated a ceasefire agreed on 5 May 1994, which took effect on 12 May and was signed by the defence ministers of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the Republic of Artsakh.
Mediation by the OSCE Minsk Group from 1995 produced no peace treaty. Armenian forces held about 9 per cent of Azerbaijan's territory outside the enclave until a second war began in September 2020.
first-nations-in-canada: First Nations is a term for Indigenous peoples in Canada who are neither Inuit nor Métis. Traditionally they lived south of the tree line and mainly south of the Arctic Circle. The government adopted the term officially in the 1980s to replace Indian band, after people began to use it in the activism of the 1970s to avoid the word Indian, which some considered offensive. It has no legal definition.

Their cultures span thousands of years, and many oral traditions describe historical events such as the Cascadia earthquake of 1700. Peoples had settled and established trade routes across what is now Canada by between 500 BCE and 1000 CE, among them the Haida and Salish on the Pacific coast, the Blackfoot on the prairies, the Cree in the northern woodlands, the Anishinaabe and Iroquois around the Great Lakes, and the Mi'kmaq on the Atlantic coast.

Prolonged contact with Europeans came only after permanent settlements in the 17th and 18th centuries. Trade strengthened more organised political entities such as the Iroquois Confederation. The population is estimated at between 200,000 and two million in the late 15th century, and colonisation brought a decrease of 40 to 80 percent, through epidemics of influenza, measles and smallpox, conflicts over the fur trade, and loss of land. In the late 1630s smallpox killed more than half of the Huron.

Between 1875 and 1885 settlers and hunters brought the bison almost to extinction, and the Canadian Pacific Railway brought settlers onto Indigenous land. Many nations had negotiated treaties for food and help to begin farming, but Lieutenant-Governor Edgar Dewdney cut rations, and between 1880 and 1885 about 3,000 Indigenous people starved to death in the North-West Territories. Amendments to the Indian Act in 1905 and 1911 made it easier to expropriate reserve land. More than 6,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis served with British forces in the two world wars.

The federal ban on potlatch and Sun Dance ceremonies ended in 1951, and in 1960 First Nations people gained the right to vote in federal elections without losing their Indian status. The White Paper of 1969 proposed abolishing the Indian Act and treating First Nations as an ethnic minority. The residential school system, a network of boarding schools run by Christian churches, was created to isolate Indigenous children from their own culture, and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission concluded in 2015 that it was a cultural genocide. Over thirty Indigenous languages are spoken, most only in Canada, and many are in decline.
first-opium-war: Trade between China and Europe long favoured China, which sustained a trade surplus paid for in silver. The British realised they could reduce their deficit by selling opium produced in India, and sales of Indian opium to China began in 1781 and grew as the East India Company consolidated its control of India. By 1838 the British were selling roughly 1,400 long tons a year. Within the Chinese administration, some officials such as Xu Naiji argued for legalising and taxing opium, while others, later led by Lin Zexu, regarded the trade as a moral evil. The Daoguang Emperor rejected legalisation and in 1839 sent Lin Zexu to Guangzhou to halt the trade completely.

In March 1839 Lin forced British dealers to hand over 1,420 tonnes of opium, which he had destroyed in public on Humen Beach on 3 June. Tension rose after British sailors beat to death a villager, Lin Weixi, in July, and Charles Elliot refused to hand the accused over to Chinese authorities. Fighting began after the Qing blockade of foreign ships. The British government, urged by merchants who demanded compensation, sent an expedition that arrived in late June 1840. After the Second Battle of Chuenpi on 7 January 1841 the British occupied Hong Kong.

Henry Pottinger replaced Elliot as superintendent in August 1841 and moved operations north. British steamships such as the Nemesis could move against winds and tides, and naval guns out-ranged most Qing artillery. In 1842 the fleet advanced up the Yangtze and captured the emperor's tax barges, sharply reducing his revenue. It took Wusong and Baoshan and occupied the outskirts of Shanghai in June. The Treaty of Nanking was signed aboard HMS Cornwallis on 29 August 1842.

The treaty granted an indemnity and extraterritoriality to British subjects, opened five treaty ports and ceded Hong Kong Island in perpetuity. It was the first of the unequal treaties, and the Treaty of the Bogue recognised Britain as an equal of China. The United States and France concluded similar treaties in 1844. The unrest that followed formed the background of the Taiping Rebellion, and a Second Opium War was fought in 1856 to 1860.

The war was contested in Britain. William Ewart Gladstone called it a war unjust in its origin, and he feared the judgments of God on England for its iniquity towards China. Historians still debate whether it was avoidable. Some stress Britain's expanding trade, while others argue that Lord Palmerston's government went to war to uphold national honour. Twentieth-century nationalists in China consider 1839 the start of a century of humiliation.
