first-partition-of-poland: By the late 18th century the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth had fallen from the rank of a European power to a country under heavy Russian influence, with the Russian tsar effectively choosing its monarchs. Russian victories over the Ottomans in the Russo-Turkish War of 1768 to 1774 endangered Habsburg interests, and Austria began to consider war. Frederick II of Prussia, whose army and treasury the Seven Years' War had weakened, sought a peaceful solution. His brother Prince Henry was told at Saint Petersburg that Prussia might claim some Polish land, and Frederick then proposed a partition by Austria, Prussia and Russia, with the largest share going to Austria.

The Commonwealth was also weakened by civil war against the Bar Confederation, which opposed Russian control. The three powers justified their action as compensation for a troublesome neighbour and a remedy for Polish anarchy.

Prussia and Russia agreed at Saint Petersburg on 6 February 1772, and the partition agreement was signed in Vienna on 19 February. In early August troops of all three powers entered the Commonwealth and occupied the agreed provinces, and the treaty on their gains was signed on 5 August and ratified on 22 September. The Bar Confederation held out: Wawel Castle fell at the end of April, and Częstochowa, commanded by Casimir Pulaski, in late August. Its members fled abroad or were deported to Siberia.

Prussia took most of Royal Prussia, joining East Prussia to Brandenburg, but not Danzig or Thorn: 36,000 square kilometres and about 600,000 people. Frederick became King of Prussia rather than King in Prussia. Austria received 83,000 square kilometres and 2,650,000 people, including Galicia and the salt mines of Bochnia and Wieliczka. Russia gained 92,000 square kilometres and 1,300,000 people. The Commonwealth lost about 211,000 square kilometres, 30 percent of its territory, and about a third of its population.

The European powers reacted with indifference, and only a few voices, such as Edmund Burke's, were raised in objection. Armies occupied Warsaw to compel the calling of the Sejm, and fewer than half the usual deputies attended this Partition Sejm. On 18 September 1773 a committee of thirty signed the treaty of cession, renouncing all Commonwealth claims to the lost lands.
first-punic-war: The Roman Republic had been expanding in southern Italy for a century and by 272 BCE had conquered the peninsula south of the River Arno. Carthage, with its capital in what is now Tunisia, dominated southern Spain, much of the North African coast, the Balearic Islands, Corsica, Sardinia and the western half of Sicily. Most of what is known of the war comes from Polybius, a Greek sent to Rome as a hostage in 167 BCE, whose Histories were written about a century after the war.

The war began in 264 BCE when the Romans gained a foothold at Messana in Sicily. Syracuse allied with them, and a large Carthaginian army sent to lift the siege of Akragas was heavily defeated in 262 BCE. Land fighting was mostly sieges and raids, so the Romans turned to the sea. In 260 BCE they built a fleet using a shipwrecked Carthaginian quinquereme as a model, and they introduced the corvus, a bridge with a spike that let legionaries board enemy ships instead of ramming them.

In 256 BCE the Romans sailed with 330 warships and won the Battle of Cape Ecnomus, possibly the largest naval battle in history by the number of combatants. Their invasion of North Africa at first went well, but a storm later destroyed most of the fleet sent home, with over 100,000 men lost. They rebuilt repeatedly and took Panormus. By 248 BCE Carthage held only Lilybaeum and Drepana, and Hamilcar Barca held out from Eryx with guerrilla tactics. In 243 BCE the Romans built a new fleet and blockaded the garrisons, and in 241 BCE they destroyed the Carthaginian relief fleet at the Battle of the Aegates Islands.

Carthage paid large reparations and Sicily became a Roman province. Both states were exhausted. Rome became the leading military power in the western Mediterranean, and building about 1,000 galleys laid the base for its maritime dominance for 600 years. Carthage's unpaid foreign troops rebelled, and the revolt was put down with great difficulty and savagery. In 237 BCE the Romans took Carthage's planned expedition to Sardinia as an act of war and made it cede Sardinia and Corsica and pay a further 1,200 talents. This resentment is considered a cause of the Second Punic War of 218 BCE.
first-schleswig-war: At the beginning of 1848 Denmark included the Duchy of Schleswig, and the king of Denmark ruled the duchies of Holstein and Saxe-Lauenburg within the German Confederation. Germans made up a third of the country's population, and the three duchies accounted for half of Denmark's economy. Schleswig was divided between a Danish-speaking north and a Low German-speaking south, while Holstein and Lauenburg were entirely German. Danish nationalists held that Schleswig, but not Holstein, should be part of Denmark, while German nationalists wanted Schleswig and Holstein kept together. A legally questionable change to the rules of succession added to the dispute.

In March 1848 the Low German-speaking population of Schleswig, Holstein and Lauenburg rebelled and set up a provisional government and army. Prince Frederick of Noer took the fortress of Rendsburg, whose gates were open, and won over its garrison. The German Confederation supported the rebels, and most of the German troops were Prussian. The Danes won at Bov on 9 April, and Prussian forces crossed into Schleswig on 19 April and won at Schleswig on 23 April. Russia opposed any advance towards Jutland, and Nicholas I ordered a mobilisation and sent a squadron of the Baltic fleet to Danish waters. Prussia signed the armistice of Malmö on 26 August 1848.

The war resumed on 3 April 1849 and ended in another truce on 10 July. In 1850 Prussia and Denmark signed a peace at Berlin on 2 July, and Danish troops moved against the rebels in Holstein. The Danes won the Battle of Idstedt on 24 and 25 July 1850. The Schleswig-Holstein army was disbanded on 1 April 1851.

The London Protocol of 8 May 1852 confirmed the Danish king as duke of the duchies, which were to remain independent entities, with Schleswig having no greater constitutional tie to Denmark than Holstein. The settlement did not resolve the issue, because the German Diet refused to recognise it. The Second Schleswig War of 1864 ended with the king of Denmark transferring the duchies to Austria and Prussia.
first-serbian-uprising: Serbia had been under Ottoman rule since the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, and by the 18th century Serbs faced heavy taxation, discrimination and the devshirme, which required Christian families to provide sons for the Ottoman military. The Sanjak of Smederevo, also called the Pashalik of Belgrade, held about 368,000 people before 1804. Austria occupied much of it from 1788 to 1791, and many Serbs had fought in the Serbian Freikorps of the Austrian army.

In 1793 and 1796 Sultan Selim III issued firmans that gave the Serbs more rights, but in 1801 four Janissaries, the Dahije, killed the Belgrade Vizier Hadži Mustafa Pasha, divided the sanjak among themselves in defiance of the Sultan, suspended Serbian autonomy, raised taxes and imposed forced labour. At the end of January 1804 they executed between 70 and 150 village leaders, merchants and priests in what became known as the Slaughter of the Knezes.

On 14 February 1804 Serbian leaders gathered at Orašac and chose Đorđe Petrović, known as Karađorđe, a cattle trader with military experience, as their leader. They quickly took Šumadija, and the Ottoman government at first told neighbouring pashas not to help the Dahije; Milenko Stojković captured and beheaded the Dahije on 5–6 August 1804. When talks broke down in 1805, Selim ordered the rebels crushed, and the Serbs defeated his army at Ivankovac that year, then an Ottoman army at Mišar in 1806.

Rebels led by Petar Dobrnjac took Belgrade in December 1806, and Karađorđe proclaimed it the capital on 8 January 1807. The rebels set up a government with an assembly and a ruling council, abolished forced labour and feudal obligations and reduced taxes. Russian forces, fighting the parallel Russo-Turkish War, helped at Malajnica in July 1807. In 1809 Serbian forces were defeated at Čegar, where the commander Stevan Sinđelić fired into his gunpowder magazine rather than see his men captured, and the Ottomans built the Skull Tower from Serbian skulls.

The Treaty of Bucharest of May 1812 between Russia and the Ottomans promised the Serbs a general amnesty and control of their own affairs, but required Ottoman garrisons in fortresses. Karađorđe sought absolute power while his dukes tried to limit it, and the Ottomans reconquered Serbia in 1813. Karađorđe and other leaders fled. Villages were burned and thousands were sold into slavery, 1,800 women and children on 17 October 1813 alone, and Serbian institutions were abolished.

The Serbs were the first Christian population in Ottoman history to rise up against the Sultan and set up a short-lived independent state, and the rising became a symbol of nation-building in the Balkans. A Second Serbian Uprising began in April 1815 under Miloš Obrenović and eventually turned Serbia into a semi-autonomous state.
first-sino-japanese-war: Korea was a Qing tributary state in the late 19th century, while Japan, transformed by the reforms that followed the Meiji Restoration of 1868, regarded it as a target of expansion. Japan opened Korea to trade by the treaty of 1876, and from 1879 Li Hongzhang directed China's Korea policy. After the Imo Incident of 1882 the Qing stationed troops in Seoul and sent advisers, and Yuan Shikai trained a new Korean military formation.

A reformist faction in Korea, the Enlightenment Party, looked to Japan, and in December 1884 it staged the Kapsin Coup with the help of the Japanese minister. In late April 1894 the Donghak Rebellion, the largest peasant rebellion in Korean history, broke out against oppressive taxation, and the Korean government asked for Qing help.

China sent between 2,465 and 2,800 troops in June, and Japan, which held that it had not been notified as the 1885 Convention of Tientsin required, landed a larger force at Incheon. Japanese troops seized the Korean king in Seoul on 23 July 1894 and set up a pro-Japanese government. On 25 July the Japanese Navy won the Battle of Pungdo and sank the transport Kowshing, which was carrying 1,200 Qing reinforcements. War was declared on 1 August.

After the Battle of Pyongyang on 15 September the Qing troops withdrew to Manchuria. The Beiyang Fleet was decisively defeated at the Battle of the Yalu River two days later. The Japanese Army invaded Manchuria and took Port Arthur on 21 November 1894, after which Japanese forces killed civilians in the Port Arthur Massacre, with unconfirmed estimates in the thousands. Weihaiwei fell on 12 February 1895 after a siege lasting 23 days. The Qing court began negotiations in early March, and Japanese forces occupied the Pescadores Islands later that month.

The Treaty of Shimonoseki was signed on 17 April 1895. China recognised Korea's total independence and ceded the Liaodong Peninsula, Taiwan and the Penghu Islands. It also paid a large indemnity. On 23 April Russia, Germany and France applied diplomatic pressure in the Triple Intervention, and Japan gave up the Liaodong Peninsula in exchange for a larger indemnity. Taiwan's inhabitants resisted the cession with a guerrilla campaign lasting nearly two years.

The war exposed the limits of the Qing effort to modernise its military and shifted regional dominance in East Asia from China to Japan. Historians link the defeat to the political upheavals led by Sun Yat-sen and Kang Youwei that ended in the 1911 Revolution. In Korea, the Japanese-sponsored Kabo Reforms of 1894 to 1896 abolished legal slavery and the privileges of the yangban class. Tension between Russia and Japan over Manchuria grew in the years that followed.
first-turkic-khaganate: The khaganate was founded by the Ashina clan under Bumin Qaghan and his brother Istami. In 546 Bumin made a preemptive strike against the Uyghur and Tiele groups planning to revolt against their overlords, the Rouran, and expected a Rouran princess in marriage as his reward. The Rouran khagan Yujiulu Anagui rebuked him, calling him a blacksmith slave.

Chinese chronicles record the phrase, and some take it to show that the Turks specialised in metallurgy, though it may describe a form of vassalage rather than literal slavery. Bumin allied with the Western Wei by marrying Princess Changle and in 552 defeated Anagui north of Huaihuang, effectively ending the Rouran, who had dominated the eastern steppe for a century and a half.

Bumin declared himself Illig Khagan at Otuken but died within months, and the empire was divided between his son Muqan Qaghan, who ruled the east and defeated the Hephthalites, and Istami, who bore the title Yabghu of the West. In 557 Istami allied with Khosrow I of the Sasanian Empire to destroy the Hephthalites.

In 576 the Göktürks crossed the Kerch Strait into the Crimea, and five years later laid siege to Chersonesus. They sent embassies to Constantinople, one of which arrived in 568 and discussed an alliance with Justin II, but a Byzantine embassy of 575-576 was received with hostility, and the alliance broke down. In 589 the Sasanians attacked and defeated the Turks.

When the fourth ruler, Taspar Qaghan, died in 581, the realm split over the succession, and four rivals claimed the title, played off against each other by the Sui and Tang. Istami's son Tardu made a bid for independence, and Ishbara in the east acknowledged the suzerainty of Emperor Yang of Sui.

Sui diplomacy incited a revolt of the Tiele vassals that ended Tardu's reign in 603, leaving an eastern and a western khaganate. Illig Qaghan reached the Wei River near Chang'an in 626 and agreed to withdraw, but in 630 a Tang army under Li Jing defeated the Eastern Turks at the Battle of Yinshan. The Western khaganate, known as the Onoq, fell to the Tang general Su Dingfang in 657.

Tang rule left a member of the Ashina clan as a puppet khagan, and in 657 the Tang installed two khagans over the ten arrows, the tribes of the Western Turks, with Chinese titles. Ilterish Qaghan founded the Second Turkic Khaganate after rebelling against the Tang, and it lasted until the Uyghur Khaganate overthrew it in 744. The Old Turkic script was invented in the first half of the sixth century, and the Göktürks spoke a Siberian Turkic language that was the direct predecessor of the Orkhon Turkic of the Second Khaganate.
first-vienna-award: From 1933 Hungary coordinated its foreign policy closely with that of Nazi Germany, hoping to revise the borders set by the Treaty of Trianon of 1920. In June 1933 the Hungarian prime minister Gyula Gömbös met Adolf Hitler, and they concluded that Czechoslovakia was a principal obstacle to a rearrangement of Central Europe. The Munich Agreement of September 1938 partitioned Czechoslovakia and set a three-month period to settle Hungarian demands, but Hungary pressed for talks at once, with border conflicts and sabotage. On 5 October 1938 Hungarian troops attacked Czechoslovak positions near Jesenské, and paramilitaries of the Rongyos Gárda entered Carpathian Ruthenia on 6 October.

Slovakia declared autonomy on 6 October. Czechoslovak and Hungarian delegations met at Komárno from 9 to 13 October 1938, the Czechoslovak side led by Jozef Tiso and the Hungarian by Kálmán Kánya and Pál Teleki. The talks deadlocked on 13 October, and Hungary partly mobilised. Czechoslovakia proposed the Ribbentrop line on 22 October, offering territory with 494,646 Hungarians and 168,632 Slovaks. Hungary rejected it and demanded arbitration, and France and Britain had lost interest in Czechoslovakia.

The award was made in Vienna's Belvedere Palace on 2 November 1938 by the German foreign minister Joachim von Ribbentrop and the Italian foreign minister Galeazzo Ciano. Czechoslovakia gave up southern Slovakia and southern Carpathian Ruthenia, including Košice, Uzhhorod and Mukachevo. Slovakia lost 10,390 square kilometres with 854,277 inhabitants by the census of 1930, 503,980 of them Hungarians. Czechoslovakia also lost its direct railway link to Carpathian Ruthenia and to Romania.

Tiso announced the result on the radio that evening and blamed the central government. The award led to anti-Hungarian feeling in Slovakia, which Slovaks marked on each anniversary. In mid-March 1939 Hitler allowed Hungary to occupy the rest of Carpathian Rus', which gave Hungary a common border with Poland. Only about 60,000 Hungarians remained in Slovakia, and the new border did not follow ethnic lines: only 8 of 79 villages around Košice had a Hungarian majority. The Treaty of Paris, signed on 10 February 1947, declared the award null and void and restored the frontier of 1 January 1938, except for three villages south of Bratislava.
first-world-war: For much of the 19th century the major European powers kept a tenuous balance known as the Concert of Europe. Victory in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871 allowed Otto von Bismarck to consolidate a German Empire, and French policy then aimed to avenge the defeat. Germany and Austria-Hungary formed the Dual Alliance in 1879, which became the Triple Alliance when Italy joined in 1882.

On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir presumptive to Emperor Franz Joseph I, visited Sarajevo. Six assassins of the Young Bosnia movement lined his route. A grenade injured two aides, but an hour later Gavrilo Princip shot and fatally wounded the Archduke and his wife Sophie.

Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July, and Russia mobilised in Serbia's defence. In early August Germany declared war on Russia and France, and the United Kingdom entered after Germany invaded Belgium. The German advance was halted in September, and the Western Front settled into a near-continuous line of trenches. Battles at Verdun, the Somme and Passchendaele failed to break the stalemate.

The Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers in November 1914. The United States joined the Allies in April 1917 after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare, and Soviet Russia made a separate peace in March 1918. The Allied Hundred Days Offensive from August 1918 collapsed the German front line, and the war ended with the Armistice of 11 November 1918.

Four dynasties fell: the Romanovs, the Hohenzollerns, the Habsburgs and the Ottomans. Poland, Finland, the Baltic states, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia were among the new states. Under the Treaty of Versailles, signed on 28 June 1919, Germany lost territory, was disarmed and had to pay large reparations.

Estimates put the deaths at 15 to 22 million and about 23 million wounded military personnel. Of 60 million European military personnel mobilised, an estimated 8 million were killed. The war also drew women into industry in unprecedented numbers, which aided the struggle for women's voting rights.
firth-of-forth: The Firth of Forth is a bay and inlet of the North Sea that separates Fife to the north from Lothian to the south. Further inland it becomes the estuary of the River Forth and several other rivers. It was formed as a fjord by the Forth Glacier in the last glacial period, which scoured out the existing Forth Valley, and over time natural processes turned most of it into a wide bay with gently sloping banks. Its name combines the Scots word firth, a cognate of fjord, with Forth, from a Proto-Celtic word meaning slow running. It was Bodotria in Roman times, Myrkvifiörd in the Norse sagas and, in an early Welsh name, the sea of Iudeu.

The Romans reportedly made a bridge of around 900 boats, probably at South Queensferry. In the 10th century the river was regarded as the boundary of Scotia and was sometimes called the Scots Water. Culross, on the Fife shore, was established in the 6th century and was the birthplace of Saint Kentigern. The inner firth, between the Kincardine and Forth bridges, has lost about half of its former intertidal area to land reclamation, partly for farming but mainly for industry.

The firth was the site of heavy industry and docks, among them Grangemouth, Leith, Methil, Inverkeithing and the naval dockyard at Rosyth. It is crossed by bridges at two places. The Forth Bridge, a railway bridge on the Edinburgh to Aberdeen line, was begun in 1882 and opened on 4 March 1890. The Kincardine Bridge opened in October 1936 and the Forth Road Bridge on 4 September 1964. From 1964 to 1982 a tunnel dug by coal miners ran under the firth, linking the Kinneil colliery on the south side with the Valleyfield colliery on the north. The Clackmannanshire Bridge was completed in November 2008, and the Queensferry Crossing, begun in 2011, was formally opened on 4 September 2017.

The firth is a Site of Special Scientific Interest. The Firth of Forth Islands Special Protection Area holds more than 90,000 breeding seabirds every year, and there is a bird observatory on the Isle of May. Its islands include Bass Rock, Inchcolm, Inchkeith and the Isle of May. The European oyster, fished to extinction here by the 1900s, has been reintroduced in the 21st century. Edinburgh, Leith and Kirkcaldy are among the many towns on its shores.
firuz-shah-tughluq: Nasir al-Din Firuz Shah was born in 1309, the son of Sipahsalar Malik Rajab, brother of Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq, the founder of the dynasty, and of a princess from Abohar in the Punjab. His father died when he was seven, and Ghiyath al-Din raised him and trained him with his cousin Muhammad bin Tughluq in the duties of state. Under Muhammad he held the rank of deputy of the lord chamberlain with command of twelve thousand horses. The addition of Tughluq to his name is reported to be a later convenience, as Persian and contemporary sources call him only Firuz Shah.

Firuz succeeded Muhammad bin Tughluq on 23 March 1351 on the banks of the Indus, where Muhammad had died. According to the Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, he defeated a Mongol raiding party at the outset. A minister at Delhi, the Khwaja-i-Jahan, had meanwhile set up a supposed son of Muhammad as sultan on a false report of Firuz's death, but he submitted. In 1353 Firuz marched on Bengal against Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah, who withdrew to Ekdala; Firuz is said to have refused to annex the marshy country.

His second Bengal campaign began in 1358, after Ilyas Shah killed the king of Sonargaon and the king's son-in-law Zafar Khan took refuge at Hisar, and it ended in a treaty with Ilyas Shah's son Sikandar Shah. In 1360 he invaded Odisha and in the same period besieged the Rai of Kangra at Nagarkot for six months. His campaign against Thatta in 1362 lost three quarters of his horses to disease, and he withdrew to Gujarat, returning in 1363 to receive the submission of the Sindh rulers and an annual tribute of 400,000 tankas.

Firuz was a Sufi Muslim who adopted Sharia policies and banned practices theologians thought un-Islamic, and he persecuted sects they considered heretical. He ended harsh punishments such as the cutting off of hands, lowered the land taxes Muhammad had raised, and allowed sons to inherit their fathers' posts and jagirs. His reign has been described as an age of corruption.

Firuz founded or built Hisar, Firozpur, Fatehabad, Hansi, Jaunpur and Firozabad, dug five major canals and built more than 300 villages, sarais, gardens and madrasas. He replaced the top storeys of the Qutb Minar after lightning struck it in 1368 and brought two Ashokan pillars to Delhi, re-erecting one at Firuz Shah Kotla.

Hindu works were translated from Sanskrit into Persian and Arabic, and he founded hospitals for the poor. In 1387 he made his son Muhammad Shah III his successor, but the nobles turned against him, and Firuz named his great-grandson Tughluq Khan. He died in 1388 after reigning for 37 years and was buried at Hauz Khas, Delhi, beside a madrasa he built in 1352 to 1353.
five-dynasties-and-ten-kingdoms-period: After the An Lushan Rebellion of 755 to 763, large regional administrations called circuit commissions were laid over the old prefectures, and they became the boundaries of the later southern regimes. By the early 10th century the Tang government had given the jiedushi, the regional military governors, such powers that they were de facto independent, with hereditary succession and armies that rivalled the palace armies. Many states were independent long before 907, and the key event was their recognition as sovereign by foreign powers.

Five dynastic states followed one another in the Central Plain: Later Liang, Later Tang, Later Jin, Later Han and Later Zhou. The term Five Dynasties was coined by Song historians and reflects the view that the successive regimes at Kaifeng held the Mandate of Heaven. Zhu Wen founded the first after forcing the last Tang emperor to abdicate in his favour, and the rest and the Song itself emerged from a military organisation led by Shatuo Turks. The Later Zhou under Chai Rong conquered much of Southern Tang between 956 and 958. In 960 Zhao Kuangyin staged a coup and founded the Northern Song, the official end of the Five Dynasties.

In the south more than a dozen states existed at once, of which ten are traditionally called the Ten Kingdoms. They included Wuyue, Min, Southern Han, Former Shu, Later Shu, Jingnan, Southern Tang and Northern Han. Their founders were mostly men of low social status who rose through military ability. The south was more stable than the north, and its kingdoms promoted trade, land reclamation and infrastructure. Commerce grew so fast that bank drafts called flying money partly met a shortage of metal currency.

The Song dynasty subdued the remaining southern states. It swept away Jingnan in 963, Later Shu in 965, Southern Han in 971 and Southern Tang in 975, and Wuyue gave up its land in 978. The last regime, Northern Han, held out until the Song conquered it in 979. The Liao dynasty remained in the north.

Chronicles written from the northern viewpoint, the Old History and the New History, organised the period around the Five Dynasties and presented the Ten Kingdoms as illegitimate. The period turned away from the international mood of the Tang and was a transition towards the national culture of the Song, and the Song adopted a distinctively southern Chinese cultural outlook. The tradition that it was a time of judicial abuse reflects both real problems and the bias of Confucian historians.
flag-of-denmark: The white-on-red cross emblem dates from the age of the Crusades. The earliest known undisputed colour rendering of the Dannebrog is in the Gelre Armorial, of about 1340 to 1370, which shows such a banner beside the arms of the king of Denmark. Valdemar IV displayed a cross in his arms on a seal of 1356. Why the kings began to display it is unknown. Caspar Paludan-Müller suggested a banner sent by the pope during the Livonian Crusade, and Adolf Ditlev Jørgensen the banner of the Knights Hospitaller.

The origin legend was written down in the 1520s by Christiern Pedersen and the friar Petrus Olai. In Olai's most influential version the Danes under Valdemar II were close to defeat at the Battle of Lindanise, near Tallinn in Estonia, on 15 June 1219. Bishop Anders Sunesen prayed on a hill with his arms raised, and the Danes advanced while they stayed up, a story almost identical to Exodus 17. As defeat threatened, the flag fell from the sky, the king showed it to the troops, and they won. Other versions place the event at Fellin in 1208.

The Dannebrog, meaning red cloth, is a red flag with a white Nordic cross extending to the edges, its vertical arm shifted towards the hoist. A regulation of 1748, still in force, sets the cross at one seventh of the flag's height. No official definition of the red exists. The swallow-tailed Splitflag is used on land, and a deeper red Orlogsflag at sea by the navy.

According to tradition the original flag was lost at the Battle of Hemmingstedt on 17 February 1500 and recaptured by Frederik II in 1559, though contemporary records of the battle do not mention its loss. It was used as a maritime flag from the sixteenth century, and became the flag of the whole army from 1842. In the early nineteenth century, with Romantic nationalism, it came to be seen as representing the nation. A circular of 7 January 1834 outlawed its private use, and a regulation of 7 July 1854 permitted it, after the national enthusiasm of the First Schleswig War. It is often said to be the oldest national flag in continuous use.
flanders: Flanders is mainly flat and incorporates the whole Belgian coast on the North Sea. The word has had several meanings. It first named the County of Flanders, which existed from the 8th century, in Latin Flandria, until the French First Republic absorbed it, and which until the 1600s also extended over parts of what are now France and the Netherlands. French Flanders, in the department of Nord, and Zeelandic Flanders, in the Dutch province of Zeeland, are historically Flemish regions. In the 19th and 20th centuries the term Flemish, which also came to mean the Dutch language, led people to call the Dutch-speaking part of Belgium Flanders.

Julius Caesar described the area as the less developed and more warlike part of Gallia Belgica. The County of Flanders was a feudal fief of West Francia. Its first certain count, Baldwin I of Flanders, is reported in a document of 862, when he eloped with a daughter of his king, Charles the Bald. Cities such as Ghent and Bruges, and later Antwerp in the Duchy of Brabant, made the region one of the richest and most urbanised parts of Europe, weaving the wool of neighbouring lands into cloth, and a sophisticated culture developed there that rivalled that of northern Italy.

The county was weakened when districts fell under direct French royal rule in the late 12th century, and the remaining parts came under Baldwin V of Hainaut in 1191. Charles V was born in Ghent in 1500 and inherited the Seventeen Provinces in 1506. His Pragmatic Sanction of 1549 made the Low Countries an entity separate from the Holy Roman Empire and from France, and on his abdication in 1556 they passed to his son Philip II of Spain. Antwerp became the second-largest city in Europe north of the Alps by 1560.

In 1830 the Belgian Revolution split Belgium from the Netherlands, and the Treaty of London of 1839 confirmed Belgian independence. Dutch became an official language in public secondary schools in 1873, and in 1898 Dutch and French were declared equal in laws and royal orders. The first Flemish university opened in 1930.

Flanders is the Dutch-speaking northern part of Belgium. The Flemish Region and the Flemish Community form one body with a parliament and government, as constitutional institutions of the Kingdom of Belgium. The official capital is Brussels, which lies in its own region. Flanders covers 45 per cent of the territory of Belgium but holds more than half its population.
flavius-aetius: Aetius was born at Durostorum in Moesia Secunda, the son of Gaudentius, a Roman general, and an aristocratic mother from Italy. As a boy he served at the imperial court. Between 405 and 408 he was a hostage at the court of the Visigothic king Alaric I and then at that of the Hun king Uldin. In 423 Honorius died and Joannes took the western throne. Aetius served him and brought Hun troops after Joannes was killed at Ravenna in 425. He then made terms with Galla Placidia, the mother of Valentinian III, sent the Huns home and was made commander of the army in Gaul.

In Gaul he defeated the Visigoths under Theodoric I, who were besieging Arelate, and fought the Salian Franks, the Juthungi and the Bagaudae. In 430 he and the army accused the senior commander Felix of plotting against him, and some sources believe Aetius had Felix killed. After a rivalry with Bonifacius ended at the Battle of Rimini, where Bonifacius was fatally wounded, Aetius took refuge with the Huns and returned to power with their help. From 433 to 450 he was the dominant figure in the Western Empire. He defeated the Burgundians in 436 and sent Hun troops against them the next year.

In 451 Attila invaded Gaul. Aetius persuaded the Visigoths of Theodoric I, the Armoricans, Salian Franks, some Saxons and the Burgundians to join him. On 20 June 451 the joint army fought Attila at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains, where Theodoric died. Attila invaded Italy in 452 and razed Aquileia, but Aetius could only harass him with a small force. Attila turned back after meeting an embassy that included Pope Leo I.

In 453 Aetius betrothed his son Gaudentius to Valentinian's daughter, but the emperor feared he wanted the throne for his son. According to Priscus, on 21 September 454 Valentinian leapt up as Aetius delivered a financial account and, with the chamberlain Heraclius, struck him dead with a sword. In March 455 two Huns who had been friends of Aetius killed Valentinian.

Aetius has often been called the last of the Romans. Edward Gibbon wrote that Attila's retreat confessed the last victory won in the name of the Western Roman Empire. J. B. Bury thought the battle less decisive than the Germanic victory at Nedao three years later. His death was followed by a rapid fragmentation of the West.
flax: Flax, also called common flax or line, is the flowering plant Linum usitatissimum, of the family Linaceae. It is an annual that grows to about 1.2 metres, and its fruit is a dry capsule holding glossy brown seeds. The species is known only as a cultivated plant and appears to have been domesticated just once, from a wild species, Linum bienne, called pale flax. Its species name, usitatissimum, means most useful. The word flax may refer to the plant or to its unspun fibres, and cloth woven from the fibres is linen.

Flax is native to the region from the eastern Mediterranean to India and was first domesticated in the Fertile Crescent. The earliest evidence of its use comes from Dzudzuana Cave in the present-day Republic of Georgia, where spun, dyed and knotted wild flax fibres date to about 30,000 years ago. Domesticated oilseed flax with larger seeds is attested at Tell Ramad in Syria, and flax fabric fragments from Çatalhöyük in Turkey date to about 9,000 years ago. The crop reached Switzerland and Germany by 5,000 years ago, and in China and India it was cultivated at least that long ago.

Flax was cultivated extensively in ancient Egypt, where temple walls bore paintings of flowering flax and mummies were wrapped in linen. Egyptian priests wore only linen, because flax symbolised purity. The Romans used it for their sails. Production declined with the Roman Empire, and Charlemagne revived the crop in the eighth century CE with laws that publicised the hygiene of linen and the health of linseed oil. Flanders became the major centre of the European linen industry in the Middle Ages.

The fibres taken from the stem are two to three times as strong as cotton fibres. To prepare them, the plants are pulled up with their roots, to keep the fibres long, then dried and retted, a process that breaks down the pectins binding the fibres to the straw, before the fibres are separated. The seeds are pressed for linseed oil, one of the oldest commercial oils, used as a drying oil in paints and varnishes and in products such as linoleum. Europe and North America depended on flax for cloth until the 19th century, and by the early 20th century cheap cotton had concentrated production in northern Russia, which supplied about 90 per cent of the world's output.
flec: The Treaty of Simulambuco, signed on 1 February 1885, made Cabinda a Portuguese protectorate, which was at once linked to the much larger colony of Angola. Cabindan separatists such as the FLEC maintain that the treaty recognised the territory's special status. In 1956 the Estado Novo of António Salazar made Cabinda an integral part of Angola, shortly after a reminder from the United Nations that Portugal had an obligation to report on its self-governing territories.

In 1963 three of the groups seeking independence, the Movement for the Liberation of the Enclave of Cabinda, the Action Committee of the Cabinda National Union and the Mayombe National Alliance, merged to form the FLEC at a conference in Pointe-Noire in Congo-Brazzaville. It was the main liberation movement but not the only one, competing for support with the Movement for the Liberation of Cabinda and the Union of Cabindan People.

With the independence of Angola in 1975, Cabinda became an exclave province of the new state, and the FLEC fought what it calls the Cabinda War in the region of the former kingdoms of Kakongo, Loango and N'Goyo. The movement broke into factions, among them FLEC-Ranque Franque, FLEC-N'Zita under Henrique N'zita Tiago and FLEC-Lubota under Francisco Xavier Lubota, with further groups formed in 1977, 1979 and 1996. In December 2002 the Angolan Armed Forces announced the capture of FLEC-Renovada, and in October 2006 FLEC-FAC asked the African Union's Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights to intervene.

During the Cold War the FLEC received support from Mobutu Sese Seko of neighbouring Zaire, and limited support from Gabon and France; these supporters sought Cabinda's independence to secure oil rights. In the 1980s it also had help from UNITA and from South Africa. In May 2000 FLEC-FAC kidnapped three foreign employees and one local employee of a Portuguese contractor, who were released within two months. On 8 January 2010 gunmen attacked the bus of the Togo national football team in Cabinda, killing the assistant coach, the team spokesman and the driver. An offshoot of the FLEC claimed responsibility; its spokesman said the attack had been aimed at the Angolan escort.
flensburg: Flensburg lies in the north of Schleswig-Holstein, very close to the German–Danish border, at the innermost tip of the Flensburg Firth, an inlet of the Baltic Sea. After Glücksburg and Westerland it is Germany's northernmost town, and its eastern shore is part of the Angeln peninsula. After Kiel and Lübeck it is the third-largest urban area in Schleswig-Holstein.

Danish settlers founded Flensburg at the latest by 1200, and German merchants soon joined them. Its town rights were confirmed in 1284, and it became one of the most important towns of the Duchy of Schleswig. Because Schleswig, unlike Holstein, did not belong to the Holy Roman Empire, Flensburg was not a member of the Hanseatic League, though it kept contacts with it. After the League's fall in the 16th century its merchants traded as far as the Mediterranean, Greenland and the Caribbean, in herring, sugar and whale oil. The Thirty Years' War ended this boom, and the town became Protestant and ever more German, while the countryside remained Danish.

Flensburg passed to Prussia after the Second Schleswig War in 1864. At the election to the North German Reichstag in 1867 it still had a Danish majority, which lasted until about 1880, when immigration of workers and the replacement of the bureaucracy by southern Germans shifted it. After the Second World War a strong pro-Danish movement sought to unite Schleswig north of the Eider with Denmark, and for some years the town council was dominated by Danish parties. From 2 May 1945 until early June it was the seat of the Flensburg Government, the final administrative form of Nazi Germany.

Flensburg is the cultural and organisational centre of the Danish minority of Southern Schleswig, which runs its own schools, libraries and Lutheran churches. The bilingual Flensborg Avis is published there. The Old Town was largely spared in the Second World War and remains compact and well preserved. The University of Flensburg was founded in 1946 as a pedagogical college and became a university in 1994.
fletcher-christian: Fletcher Christian was born on 25 September 1764 at Moorland Close, near Cockermouth in Cumberland. His father Charles, an attorney descended from Manx gentry, died in 1768, when Fletcher was not yet four. By 1779 his mother Ann had run up debts of nearly £6,500, and the family lost Moorland Close and fled to the Isle of Man, where English creditors had no power. Fletcher spent seven years at the Cockermouth Free School, where William Wordsworth was a younger contemporary, six years his junior.

Christian joined the Royal Navy as a cabin boy at seventeen, later than usual, and served over a year on a ship of the line with his future commander William Bligh. He was then a midshipman and master's mate on HMS Eurydice on a voyage to India, and afterwards joined Bligh's merchant ship Britannia, later as second mate. In 1787 Bligh recruited him for the Bounty, whose task was to carry breadfruit plants from Tahiti to the West Indies; he was master's mate and was made acting lieutenant halfway through the voyage.

The Bounty reached Tahiti on 26 October 1788, and Christian spent five months there. On 28 April 1789, some 1,300 miles west of Tahiti, near Tonga, he led a mutiny. Eighteen mutineers set Bligh adrift in a small boat with eighteen of the twenty-two loyal crew. Accounts differ on motive: some point to the attractions of Tahiti, while Christian's brother Edward argued that Bligh had treated the men harshly.

After the mutiny Christian went back to Tahiti, where he married Maimiti, a chief's daughter, and tried unsuccessfully to settle on Tubuai. He then sailed with eight other mutineers, six Tahitian men and eleven Tahitian women to Pitcairn Island, where the Bounty was stripped and burned. The effective enslavement of the Tahitian men by the mutineers led to an uprising in which most of the men died. When the American ship Topaz called in 1808 only John Adams was alive among the mutineers; he said Christian had been murdered, but gave conflicting accounts to later visitors. Christian's death is dated 20 September 1793. Rumours that he returned to England have persisted.
flinders-island: Flinders Island covers about 1,367 square kilometres in the Bass Strait, northeast of the island of Tasmania, of which it is now part, and lies 54 kilometres from Cape Portland on 40° south, in the zone known as the Roaring Forties. It is about 62 kilometres from north to south and 37 kilometres from east to west. Granite ridges run the length of the island, and about a third of it is mountainous and rugged. Mount Strzelecki in the south west, at 782 metres, is its highest peak. Sandy dunes and coastal lagoons mark the eastern shore.

People first reached the island at least 35,000 years ago, when they crossed the land bridge that later became Bass Strait. A population remained until about 4,500 years ago and then died out, succumbing to thirst and hunger after an acute El Niño climate shift. Tobias Furneaux recorded some of the south-eastern islands of the group in 1773, and Matthew Flinders charted the islands in 1798 before completing, with George Bass, the first circumnavigation of Tasmania, which proved it to be an island. Flinders called the largest island Great Island. Phillip Parker King later named it after Flinders.

In the late 18th century sealers and Aboriginal women, most of them kidnapped from mainland groups, often lived on the island. Seal stocks collapsed, and the last sealing permit was issued in 1828. Many sealers' families stayed, living by cattle grazing and muttonbirding. From 1831 the remnants of the Tasmanian Aboriginal population were exiled first to a place called The Lagoons, and in 1833 to the Wybalenna Aboriginal Establishment at Settlement Point. About 180 survivors were held there, and around 130 died at Wybalenna alone.

After a campaign against the commandant, Henry Jeanneret, that included a petition to Queen Victoria, the remaining 47 people were moved in 1847 to Oyster Cove Station, 56 kilometres south of Hobart. Freehold land was given out from the late 19th century, the Municipality of Flinders Island was set up in 1903, and a proper settlement scheme began only in the 1950s.

The island is part of the Municipality of Flinders Island and is the only island of the Furneaux Group with more than one permanent settlement. Whitemark, which has the main airstrip, and Lady Barron are the largest settlements. Strzelecki National Park covers the area around Mount Strzelecki, and two stretches of the island are recognised as Important Bird Areas. The island is the only remaining habitat of a subspecies of the common wombat.
flintshire: Flintshire is a maritime county, bounded on the north by the Dee estuary and the Irish Sea, on the east by Cheshire, on the west by Denbighshire and on the south by Wrexham County Borough. The Clwydian Range occupies much of the west, and its highest point, Moel Famau, rises to 554 metres. The main rivers are the Dee and the River Alyn. The county is considered part of the Welsh Marches and belonged to the historic Earldom of Chester and Flint.

At the time of the Roman invasion the area was inhabited by the Deceangli, a Celtic tribe who seem to have submitted with little resistance. Lead and silver were worked there, and several Roman ingots of lead bear the name DECEANGI. The region later formed the Hundred of Englefield, became part of the Kingdom of Mercia by the 8th century, and at the Norman conquest in 1066 was held by Edwin of Tegeingl, from whose lordship the county's coat of arms is derived.

In the 13th century the hundreds of Atiscross and Exestan passed from the Earldom of Chester to the expanding Kingdom of Gwynedd after numerous military campaigns. These lands, with the detached territory of Maelor Saesneg, formed the main areas of the county established by the Statute of Rhuddlan in 1284 under Edward I. The Laws in Wales Acts of 1535 to 1542 consolidated it under Henry VIII.

Flintshire was an administrative county from 1889 until 1974, when it was merged with Denbighshire and Edeyrnion Rural District to form Clwyd. The present county was formed in 1996, and its boundaries differ from the historic county: English Maelor went to Wrexham County Borough, and St Asaph, Prestatyn and Rhyl to Denbighshire.

The county covers 169 square miles and had a population of 155,000 in 2021. Connah's Quay is the largest town, followed by Buckley, Flint and Mold. The east is industrial and includes the Deeside conurbation, while the coast further west is developed for tourism, notably at Talacre.

The county held much of the North Wales Coalfield, whose last colliery, at Point of Ayr, closed in 1996. Steelmaking at Shotton ended in 1980, with the loss of 6,500 jobs in one day, though coated steel is still produced there. Airbus makes aircraft wings at Broughton.
flora-tristan: Flora Tristan was born on 7 April 1803. Her father, Mariano Eusebio Antonio Tristán y Moscoso, was a colonel in the Spanish Navy from Arequipa in Peru, and her mother, Anne-Pierre Laisnay, was French. After her father's death in 1807 the family's circumstances changed drastically. In 1821, aged seventeen, she married the engraver and lithographer André Chazal, for whose brother she worked as a colourist. They had three children, and she left the marital home in March 1825. Divorce had been abolished in France in 1816, so she obtained only a separation of property in 1828 and for several years lived under assumed names to escape her husband.

In 1833 Tristan travelled to Arequipa to claim her paternal inheritance, which her uncle held, and stayed in Peru until 16 July 1834. She never secured the inheritance, but her travel diary of post-independence Peru was published in 1838 as Peregrinations of a Pariah. She described Lima's women as freer and more influential than any others she knew. On 20 December 1837 she signed a petition to the Chamber of Deputies for the restoration of divorce, and in 1838 she addressed another against capital punishment. On 10 September 1838 Chazal shot her in the chest; he was sentenced to twenty years' hard labour, later commuted to imprisonment.

Her later works included Promenades in London (1840). In 1843 she left Paris to tour France promoting The Workers' Union, meeting groups of worker activists and urging them to break down occupational, regional and political barriers and to seek national and global working-class solidarity. She held that socialism was possible only with the emancipation of the sexes, drawing on Saint-Simon and Fourier while rejecting the idea that the benevolence of the ruling class would bring socialism.

Tristan died suddenly in 1844; her symptoms in the preceding months match what is now understood as typhoid fever, though the exact cause is not known. After her death her followers tried to carry out her plan for a Workers' Union with little success. According to the historian Maurice Agulhon, her visit to Toulon radicalised its workers and contributed to the 1845 strike at the arsenal. In October 1848 French workers placed a monument on her tomb, and close to eight thousand marched to her grave singing a song from The Workers' Union. She is described as a thinker who joined feminism with socialism, and was the grandmother of the painter Paul Gauguin.
florence: Florence lies about 275 kilometres north-west of Rome, in a basin formed by the hills of Careggi, Fiesole, Settignano, Arcetri, Poggio Imperiale and Bellosguardo. The Arno river flows through it. The name derives from the Latin Florentia, meaning the Flourishing Town, from florēre, to flourish or blossom, and the modern Italian name Firenze descends from it through the older Fiorenza.

Florence was founded as a Roman garrison in 59 BCE in an area previously inhabited by an Etruscan settlement whose name is unknown. After a long period as a flourishing trading and banking medieval commune, it became the birthplace of the Italian Renaissance and was one of the most important cities in Europe from the 14th to the 16th centuries. In 1200 the city had 50,000 people, and by 1300 its population was 120,000, with another 300,000 in the surrounding Contado.

It was the Republic of Florence from 1115 to 1532, then a duchy and, from 1569 to 1801, part of the Grand Duchy of Tuscany. Its turbulent political history includes periods of rule by the powerful Medici family and numerous religious and republican revolutions. From 1865 to 1871 it was the capital of the Kingdom of Italy.

The language spoken in the city in the 14th century came to be accepted as the model for Italian. The works of the Tuscans Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio led to the Florentine dialect being adopted as the basis of a national literary language. The University of Florence was first founded in 1321 and recognised by Pope Clement VI in 1349.

Florence is the capital and most populous city of the Italian region of Tuscany. UNESCO declared its historic centre a World Heritage Site in 1982. The centre lies within medieval walls built in the 14th century. The domed cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore, known as the Duomo, has a dome built by Filippo Brunelleschi that is still the largest in brick and mortar in the world. The Campanile, partly designed by Giotto, the Baptistery, the Palazzo Vecchio and the Uffizi Gallery are among its landmarks. The city was home to Giotto, Donatello, Masaccio, Botticelli, Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo, and it is known as the Cradle of the Renaissance.
florence-cathedral: Santa Maria del Fiore was built on the site of Florence's second cathedral, dedicated to Saint Reparata. According to Giovanni Villani's Nuova Cronica, the old building was crumbling and too small for the growing city, and other Tuscan cities, Pisa and Siena among them, were rebuilding their cathedrals. The city council approved Arnolfo di Cambio's design in 1294, and Cardinal Valeriana, the first papal legate ever sent to Florence, laid the first stone on 9 September 1296. The project was to last 140 years.

After Arnolfo died in 1302 work slowed for almost 50 years. The discovery of the relics of Saint Zenobius in 1330 gave it new impetus, and in 1331 the wool merchants' guild, the Arte della Lana, took over its patronage. In 1334 it appointed Giotto, who began the campanile. He died on 8 January 1337, and Andrea Pisano continued until the Black Death halted work in 1348.

The cathedral is a basilica in the shape of a Latin cross, with a wide central nave of four square bays and an aisle on either side. Its trilobate apses were meant to evoke a flower, in homage to Fiorenza, the city of flowers. It is 153 m long and 38 m wide, and its dome rises 114.5 m. The exterior is faced with polychrome marble panels in green, pink and white.

The dome was planned from the start without external buttresses. In 1367 the model of Neri di Fioravanti was chosen over a rival's, a decision described as one of the first events of the Italian Renaissance, since Gothic flying buttresses were thought ugly and were forbidden in Florence. The original façade was dismantled in 1587 and 1588 on the orders of Grand Duke Francesco I de' Medici. The present Gothic Revival façade by Emilio De Fabris was built from 1876 to 1887.

The interior is Late Gothic and bare, which suits the austerity of the mendicant orders. Because public funds paid for the cathedral, its notable works honour Florentine heroes: Dante appears in a fresco of 1465 by Domenico di Michelino, and Paolo Uccello and Andrea del Castagno painted the condottieri Sir John Hawkwood and Niccolò da Tolentino as riders in 1436 and 1456. In 1475 the astronomer Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli pierced a hole in the dome to make a meridian line.

Cracks in the dome were seen even before it was finished. In 1694 two major cracks were measured at up to 29 mm, and a commission proposed iron belts, but after long debate the dome was left as it was. Excavations from 1965 to 1974 uncovered Roman houses and the ruins of Santa Reparata, and Filippo Brunelleschi's simple tomb lies in the crypt.
floriano-peixoto: Floriano Vieira Peixoto was born on 30 April 1839 in the province of Alagoas and moved to Rio de Janeiro at the age of sixteen to finish his secondary education. In 1858 he entered the Military School of Rio de Janeiro, graduating as a second lieutenant in 1861. During the Paraguayan War he served in the 1st Battalion of Homeland Volunteers, later as its commander, and took part in the battles of Tuyutí, Ytororó, Lomas Valentinas and Angostura.

He returned to the capital in 1870 and took a bachelor's degree in physical and mathematical sciences. Promoted marshal in 1874, he served for just over a year from 1884 as president of the province of Mato Grosso. At the Proclamation of the Republic he refused to lead imperial resistance to the coup, became Minister of War in 1890 and was elected vice president in February 1891.

Peixoto rose to the presidency in November 1891, after Deodoro da Fonseca resigned amid a severe political crisis and an economic crisis worsened by the collapse of the Encilhamento bubble. His policies ended the successive economic crises of the years since 1889, and the economy stabilised and grew again. In 1892 a group of senior officers published the Manifesto of the 13 Generals, arguing that the constitution required him to call new elections rather than finish Deodoro's term.

In 1893 the Second Naval Revolt and the Federalist Revolution broke out, the latter in Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina and Paraná. Peixoto put both down by force, which earned him the nickname Iron Marshal and increased the centralisation of power. His supporters formed the cult known as Florianism, the first significant political movement in Brazil centred on a republican figure. He left the presidency on 15 November 1894.

Peixoto died at Barra Mansa, in the state of Rio de Janeiro, on 29 June 1895, from chronic liver disease, most often identified by historians as cirrhosis. He had been seriously ill for months. He is also called the Consolidator of the Republic. Views of his rule were sharply divided at the time; later generations of Brazilians came to regard it as necessary, and preferable to a continuing cycle of civil war. Nossa Senhora do Desterro, the capital of Santa Catarina, was renamed Florianópolis after the defeat of the federalist rebels there.
florida: About two-thirds of Florida occupies a peninsula between the Gulf of Mexico, the Atlantic Ocean and the Straits of Florida, and it extends northwest into a panhandle. It is the only state that borders both the Gulf and the Atlantic, and it has the longest coastline in the contiguous United States, about 2,170 kilometres. Its climate varies from subtropical in the north to tropical in the south. Everglades National Park is the largest tropical wilderness in the United States, and the Florida Reef is the only living coral barrier reef in the continental United States.

The first inhabitants, the Paleo-Indians, entered Florida at least 14,000 years ago. By the 16th century the major groups included the Apalachee, the Timucua, the Ais, the Mayaimi, the Tequesta and the Calusa. Juan Ponce de León sighted the peninsula on 2 April 1513, and it was the first region of what is now the contiguous United States to be visited and settled by Europeans. The story that he sought the Fountain of Youth is apocryphal and appeared only long after his death. An estimated 700,000 Native Americans lived in Florida in the 1520s, but by 1700 only around 2,000 remained.

Spain founded St. Augustine in 1565, the oldest continuously inhabited European-established settlement in the United States. Britain held Florida briefly from 1763, and Spain recovered it in 1783. Spain later ceded it to the United States. It was the main location of the Seminole Wars (1816–1858), became the 27th state on 3 March 1845, and seceded on 10 January 1861 as one of the seven original Confederate States, returning to the Union on 25 June 1868.

Florida is a state of the United States, with Tallahassee as its capital and 67 counties. Its most populous city is Jacksonville, and the Miami metropolitan area is the largest in the state. Miami Beach's Art Deco District belongs to the state's large collection of Art Deco and Streamline Moderne buildings, and St. Augustine preserves Spanish revival and other early styles.
florida-keys: The Florida Keys are a coral cay archipelago forming the southernmost part of the continental United States. They begin about 24 kilometres south of Miami and extend in an arc south-southwest and then westward to Key West, the westernmost of the inhabited islands, and on to the uninhabited Dry Tortugas. The islands divide the Atlantic Ocean from the Gulf of Mexico and define one edge of Florida Bay. The southern part of Key West is 150 kilometres from Cuba. The total land area is 356 square kilometres.

The northern and central keys are the exposed portions of an ancient coral reef, the Key Largo Limestone, which formed when sea levels stood about 7.6 metres above the present level, beginning some 130,000 years ago. The islands from Big Pine Key to the Marquesas Keys are exposed Miami Limestone. Just offshore lies the Florida Reef, which extends 270 kilometres. The climate is closer to that of the Caribbean than to the rest of Florida.

The Keys were originally inhabited by the Calusa and Tequesta peoples and were charted by Juan Ponce de León in 1513. He named the islands Los Martires, the Martyrs, because from a distance they looked like suffering men. The word key comes from the Spanish cayo, meaning small island. For many years Key West was the largest town in Florida and grew prosperous on revenue from wrecking. It was well placed for trade with Cuba and the Bahamas and lay on the main trade route from New Orleans. Improved navigation led to fewer shipwrecks, and Key West declined in the late 19th century.

The Keys were long reachable only by water. Henry Flagler's Overseas Railway was completed in the early 1910s after hurricanes disrupted the work in 1906, 1909 and 1910. On Labor Day, 2 September 1935, the strongest hurricane to strike the United States made landfall near Islamorada, with a storm surge more than 5.3 metres high. More than 400 people were killed, including more than 200 First World War veterans working on the roadway, whose evacuation train failed to reach them. The storm ended the railway, and U.S. Highway 1 replaced it.

The Overseas Highway, a 204-kilometre section of U.S. 1, runs over most of the inhabited islands, in places on converted railway bridges. The Seven Mile Bridge, built of concrete on pilings, connects Knight's Key to Little Duck Key. Key West is the county seat of Monroe County, and the major industries are fishing and tourism. Many Cubans settled in the Keys after the Cuban Revolution. The waters around the Keys form the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, and Dry Tortugas National Park lies about 110 kilometres west of Key West.
flying-buttress: A flying buttress has two parts: a massive pier, a vertical block of masonry standing away from the building wall, and an arch, the flyer, that bridges the gap between pier and wall. It is called flying because it does not touch the wall at ground level, as an ordinary buttress does. It carries to the ground the lateral forces that arise from stone vaults and from wind on roofs. In Gothic churches two flyers were often set one above the other: the lower, below the springing of the vault, resisted the thrust of the vault, while the upper resisted the wind on the roof. The pier was usually capped with a pinnacle, often ornamented with crockets, whose weight added vertical load.

The system developed in late antiquity and flourished in the Gothic period, from the 12th to the 16th century. Early examples survive on the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna and the Rotunda of Galerius in Thessaloniki. Byzantine and Romanesque buildings supplied precursors. At Durham Cathedral arches carry the thrust of the aisle vault but are hidden under the gallery roof. By the 1160s architects in the Île-de-France used longer, finer arches running over the roofs of the side aisles from the clerestory wall to a heavy pier, so that they were visible from outside. Saint-Germain-des-Prés, completed in 1163, has them round its apse, and those of Notre Dame de Paris, built in 1180, were among the earliest on a Gothic cathedral.
To build one, carpenters made temporary wooden frames, called centring, on the ground, hoisted them into place and fixed them to the piers; these held the stones until the mortar cured.

The advantage was that outer walls no longer had to be thick and heavy, so that wall surface could be reduced and larger windows, often of stained glass, opened. Early flyers were heavier than needed, as at Chartres Cathedral around 1210, and later builders narrowed them, as at Amiens, Le Mans and Beauvais. Late Gothic flyers carried crockets and sculpted figures in niches. Renaissance architecture preferred thick walls and gave up the form, but in the early 20th century the Canadian engineer William P. Anderson revived it to build lighthouses. It has also been used to prop leaning walls, as at Chaddesley Corbett in Worcestershire.
foligno: Foligno stands in the province of Perugia in east central Umbria, on the Topino river where it leaves the Apennines and enters the wide plain of the Clitunno river system. It lies 40 kilometres south-east of Perugia and 6 kilometres south of Spello, at an elevation of 235 metres. The town stands along the Via Flaminia, where four major roads converge, matching its four gates. Its name derives from an Umbrian form, Fulginia, which became the Roman Fulginium and is linked to the cult of the goddess Fulginia. Of its Roman past no significant trace remains except the regular street plan of the centre and three Roman bridges on the Topino.

The origins of the town are uncertain. Cicero refers to the municipium and prefecture of Fulginia, and Pliny lists it among the cities of Umbria. Totila seized the city in 546, and Belisarius recovered it for the Empire four years later. When the Lombard king Alboin occupied Umbria in 571 and founded the Duchy of Spoleto, Foligno was included in it. Saracen raids in 840 and Hungarian invasions in 915 and 924 caused further damage. Under Pope Innocent III the town passed with much of Umbria under the authority of the Church.

The Trinci family rose to power in the late Middle Ages. On 30 November 1367 Pope Urban V appointed Trincia II as vicar of Foligno for an annual tribute of a sparrowhawk, and Gregory XI later confirmed him. Trincia II was thrown from the windows of the Palazzo Trinci in 1377. Ugolino Trinci acquired the Palazzo Governativo in 1398, and in 1439 it passed from the Trinci to the municipality. Foligno experienced French rule in 1798 to 1799 and again in 1809 to 1814. After 1816 it was a seat of district government under the papacy until Italian unification.

The first printed edition of Dante's Divina Commedia was produced in the Orfini Palace at Foligno on 5 and 6 April 1472 by Johannes Numeister and Evangelista Angelini, with sheets for 300 copies. Foligno also produced the almanac Barbanera in the 18th century, together with Spello. The Palazzo Trinci, decorated by Gentile da Fabriano, and the cathedral of San Feliciano are among its landmarks, and Raphael's Madonna of Foligno once stood on the high altar of the church of Sant'Anna. Foligno is a rail junction on the line from Rome to Ancona. Allied bombing in the Second World War destroyed about 80 per cent of the city, and an earthquake in 1997 caused serious damage.
folketing: From 1849 to 1953 the Folketing was one of the two houses of the bicameral Rigsdag, the other being the Landsting. The houses differed in their sizes, franchises and electoral systems. The Folketing was elected by common vote among men and consisted mainly of independent farmers, traders and merchants as well as the educated classes. From 1866 to 1915 the right to vote for the Landsting was restricted to the wealthiest, and some of its members were appointed by the king, so that it predominantly represented the landed gentry and other conservatives. From 1915 both men and women could vote for both houses.

In the following decades law-making took place mainly in the Folketing, and the Landsting came to be regarded as a superfluous rubber stamp. In 1953 a revised constitution was adopted by a referendum, which eliminated the Landsting and made the Folketing the sole chamber. Christiansborg Palace, nicknamed Borgen, the castle, has been the seat of parliament since 1849. The office of Speaker was created in 1850, and its first holder was Carl Christoffer Georg Andræ.

No single party has had a majority of 90 seats since the 1903 elections, because a party needs only 2 per cent of the national vote to gain representation. All Danish governments since then have been coalitions or one-party minority governments. A government may take office without a vote of confidence and stay as long as it does not lose a vote of no confidence, so that it must assemble a majority for each piece of legislation.

The Folketing passes all laws, approves the cabinet and supervises the government, and it adopts the state's budgets and approves its accounts. The monarch's role is in practice limited to signing the laws, which must be done within 30 days of their adoption. Of its 179 members, 175 are elected in Denmark proper and two each in Greenland and the Faroe Islands. Of the 175, 135 seats are elected by proportional representation in 10 constituencies by the D'Hondt method and 40 levelling seats make up the difference between constituency and nationwide votes.

Members have immunity from criminal charges unless caught red-handed or unless the Folketing lifts it, which it has almost always done. Debates can be held behind closed doors, though this has not happened since 9 April 1940, the day of the German invasion. The members are allocated into thirty standing committees.
fon-people: The Fon are the largest ethnic group in Benin. They speak Fongbe, one of the Gbe languages of the Bight of Benin, and also live in south-west Togo. Their history was kept orally until the late medieval era. According to oral histories, they originated at Tado, an Aja kingdom near the Togo–Benin border. One group moved to Allada with king Lande Ajahouto, and when his sons quarrelled over the succession a group followed his middle son Do-Aklin to the Abomey plateau and founded the kingdom of Dahomey about 1620.

The claim of an origin in Allada is not recorded in contemporary sources before the late 18th century and is probably an attempt by the dynasty at Agbome to legitimise its conquest of Allada in the 1720s.

Dahomey expanded in the early 18th century, particularly under King Agaja until the 1740s, and reached the Atlantic coast from its inland capital Abomey. It became one of the main economic and military powers of the coast, second only to the Oyo Empire. Slavery long predated Dahomey, but its rulers and merchants, established on the coast between 1700 and 1740, entered the Atlantic trade, and Dahomey controlled the port of Ouidah. The Fon were both victims and victimisers. Under Oyo overlordship Dahomey had to supply slaves as annual tribute, many of them Fon men, which led to its reliance on an all-female military unit, the Agoji or Mino, known as the Dahomey Amazons.

After the slave trade was outlawed the king turned to palm oil and leased the ports to the French, who read the agreement as a cession. A French attack in 1890 led to the annexation of Dahomey as a colony in 1892. It gained independence in 1960.

The Fon are traditionally settled farmers, growing cassava, maize and yams, with palm oil as a cash crop. Their culture is patrilineal, and villages are usually headed by a hereditary chief. The traditional religion, Vodun, has public gods, personal gods, ancestral spirits and charms. Fon belief holds a female Supreme Being, Nana Buluku, who gave birth to Mawu-Lisa, the moon and sun, who created the universe with the trickster Legba and the cosmic serpent Aido Hwedo. Many Fon are Christian, but most continue to practise Vodun, which through the slave trade influenced Haitian Vodou and Candomblé.
fontainebleau: Fontainebleau is a commune 55.5 kilometres south-south-east of Paris, in the Seine-et-Marne department, of which it is a sub-prefecture. Its land area is the largest of any commune in the Île-de-France, larger than Paris itself. The Forest of Fontainebleau, a former royal hunting park, surrounds the town and is protected by France's Office National des Forêts. It is popular with hikers, horse riders and climbers.

The name was taken in the sixteenth century from the Fontaine Belle-Eau, a spring in the château garden. Louis VII endowed the hamlet with a royal hunting lodge and chapel in the mid-twelfth century, and Louis IX, who called it his wilderness, built a country house and a hospital. Philip the Fair was born there in 1268 and died there in 1314. Francis I turned the country house into a palace in the largest of his building projects, and from 1528 the court there entertained the new ideas known as the Renaissance. Every monarch from Francis I to Louis XV renovated it.

On 18 October 1685 Louis XIV signed the Edict of Fontainebleau there, revoking the Edict of Nantes and the right of Huguenots to worship publicly. Many Protestants were forced to convert, killed or driven into exile. The Treaty of Fontainebleau of 29 October 1807 allowed French troops to cross Spain to invade Portugal. Pope Pius VII arrived at the château as Napoleon's prisoner on 20 June 1812 and stayed in his apartments until 23 January 1814. On 20 April 1814 Napoleon bade farewell to the Old Guard in the courtyard, now called the Courtyard of Goodbyes, and the Treaty of Fontainebleau of 1814 stripped him of his powers and sent him to Elba.

Until the nineteenth century Fontainebleau was a village and suburb of Avon. In 1946 it hosted the Franco-Vietnamese Conference, which ended in failure, and until 1967 it held Allied land forces headquarters for Central Europe.

About 300,000 people visit the palace each year and more than 13 million the forest. The town is home to the European campus of the INSEAD business school, and the mystic George Gurdjieff and the writer Katherine Mansfield are buried in the cemetery at Avon.
foot-binding: Several stories tell of foot binding before its establishment under the Song dynasty. One concerns Pan Yunu, a consort of the Southern Qi emperor Xiao Baojuan, whose dancing was said to make lotus flowers spring from her steps, though there is no evidence that she bound her feet. Another links the custom to the 10th-century emperor Li Yu of the Southern Tang, who asked his concubine Yao Niang to bind her feet in white silk and dance on a golden lotus; others, it was said, then imitated her.

Admiration for small feet existed earlier: a Tang tale of about 850, that of Ye Xian, contains elements of the Cinderella story. Odoric of Pordenone mentioned foot binding in the 14th century, but Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta did not, which may show that it was not yet widespread. By the Ming period it was a status symbol, and its rise coincided with a decline of women's dance.

Binding began before the arch had fully developed, usually between the ages of four and nine, often in winter, when numb feet made the pain less sharp. The foot was soaked in a mixture of herbs and animal blood, the toenails cut back, and the toes curled under and pressed into the sole until they broke. Long cotton bandages were wound in a figure of eight and tightened with each pass, forcing the arch to break and the heel and ball of the foot together.

Practice varied by region and class. Infection was the commonest problem, and poor circulation left injuries unhealed. It is thought that as many as 10 per cent of girls may have died of gangrene and other infections. Frontier peoples such as the Uyghurs, Manchus, Mongols and Tibetans generally did not practise it.

Interpretations differ. Some see fashion and beauty, since a woman with small lotus feet could marry more prestigiously; others point to the seclusion of women, or to a wish to keep daughters at handwork. Laurel Bossen and Hill Gates reject the idea that it was thought more beautiful or won better marriages.

Some Chinese writers opposed the custom in the 18th century, and the Taiping leaders outlawed it where they ruled. Christian missionaries and Chinese reformers, among them the early feminist Qiu Jin, campaigned against it in the late 19th century. It began to die out in the early 20th century, upper-class and urban women giving it up sooner than poorer rural women.
football-war: The nickname suggests that a football match caused the war, but its causes lay deeper, in land reform in Honduras and in immigration and demographic problems in El Salvador. El Salvador was overpopulated, with too few jobs, and 5 per cent of its farms occupied 70 per cent of the land. Many Salvadorans migrated to Honduras to work on banana plantations, and by 1969 more than 300,000 lived there. A Honduran land reform law, fully enforced by 1967, took land occupied by Salvadoran immigrants and redistributed it to native-born Hondurans, and thousands of Salvadoran labourers were expelled.

In June 1969 the two countries met in a two-leg qualifier for the 1970 FIFA World Cup. Honduras won the first game, at Tegucigalpa on 8 June, and El Salvador the second, at San Salvador on 15 June, each accompanied by harassment and riots. On 26 June El Salvador broke off diplomatic ties, saying that around 12,000 Salvadorans had been forced to flee Honduras.

The war began on 14 July 1969 at about 6 in the evening, when the Salvadoran air force attacked Honduran airfields, mainly Toncontín International Airport, where the Honduran air force kept half of its aircraft. The Salvadoran army then invaded on two fronts, one towards the Sula Valley and the other along the Pan-American Highway towards Tegucigalpa. On 15 July the Honduran air force bombed targets in El Salvador, among them the Ilopango International Airport and oil facilities.

On 16 July, in the only major battle of the war, Salvadoran troops surrounded Nueva Ocotepeque, and Honduran forces retreated with civilians. Both fronts then stalled for want of ammunition and because of growing Honduran resistance. The war was the last conflict in which piston-engined fighters fought each other.

A ceasefire arranged by the Organization of American States took effect at midnight on 18 July and required Salvadoran troops to withdraw within 96 hours. El Salvador delayed until it had guarantees for the Salvadorans still in Honduras, and gave way after the OAS threatened sanctions. Its troops left on 2 August 1969. Most historians agree that civilians accounted for the majority of the losses. Estimates of Salvadorans displaced run from 60,000 to 130,000, and their return to an overpopulated country was one cause of the Salvadoran Civil War about a decade later. Trade between the two countries stopped, and a peace treaty was signed in Lima on 30 October 1980.
forbes-burnham: Burnham was born in Kitty, a suburb of Georgetown, to a schoolmaster, James Ethelbert Burnham, and Rachel Abigail Sampson, in an Afro-Guyanese Methodist household. After returning from his studies in the United Kingdom in 1949 he set up a law practice and became leader of the British Guiana Labour Party. In the election of 27 April 1953, the first with universal suffrage, the People's Progressive Party (PPP) won 18 of 24 seats and Burnham became Minister of Education. On 12 and 13 February 1955 the party split into Burnhamite and Jaganite factions; Jagan favoured a socialist domestic policy, Burnham's faction was more moderate. After the 1957 election Burnham formed the People's National Congress (PNC).

Opposition to the PPP government's budget of 31 January 1962 led to mass demonstrations and the rioting of 16 February 1962, "Black Friday", in which 56 businesses were destroyed; the PNC was accused of leading the mobs. Declassified documents show that the United States government under John F. Kennedy came to regard Jagan as a communist and approved intervention against his government, and that from 1962 to 1968 Burnham received support from the Central Intelligence Agency. A December 1964 election under proportional representation gave the PPP 46% and the PNC 41%; Burnham formed a coalition with Peter D'Aguiar's United Force and became premier on 14 December.

After independence in 1966 he passed a National Security Act allowing detention without trial for up to 90 days. An independent review could verify only 15% of the overseas votes that gave the PNC a majority in 1968. On 23 February 1970 he declared a co-operative republic and nationalised the main foreign-owned industries. A constitution of 1980 created an executive presidency, which Burnham won with 76% of the official vote, though observers protested that Indo-Guyanese voters were prevented from voting in places. In 1978 909 members of Jim Jones's Peoples Temple, which Burnham had allowed to settle in Guyana, died at Jonestown.

Burnham died of heart failure during throat surgery in Georgetown on 6 August 1985, aged 62. His legacy remains disputed. His successor Desmond Hoyte called him a great leader, while the historian Moe Taylor called his premiership a deeply divisive chapter in Guyana's recent history, and John Prados described him as a dictatorial figure.
