His administration has been accused of discrimination against Indo-Guyanese and of electoral fraud and state violence, including complicity in the car-bomb death of the historian Walter Rodney on 13 June 1980.
forbidden-city: Construction began in 1406, after the Yongle Emperor, the son of the Hongwu Emperor, moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing. The materials included whole logs of precious Phoebe zhennan wood from the jungles of southwestern China, large blocks of marble from quarries near Beijing, and golden bricks, specially baked paving bricks from Suzhou, laid on the floors of the major halls.

The Chinese name Zijincheng means Purple Forbidden City. Zi, purple, refers to the North Star, which in traditional astrology was the heavenly abode of the Jade Emperor; the Forbidden City was its earthly counterpart. The name first formally appeared in 1576.

The complex is a rectangle measuring 961 m from north to south and 753 m from east to west, enclosed by a wall 7.9 m high and a moat 52 m wide. It has 980 surviving buildings with 8,886 bays of rooms; the common claim of 9,999 rooms is a myth not supported by survey evidence. At the heart of the Outer Court a three-tiered white marble terrace carries three halls, the Hall of Supreme Harmony, the Hall of Central Harmony and the Hall of Preserving Harmony. The first is the largest surviving wooden structure in China. Almost all roofs bear yellow glazed tiles, yellow being the emperor's colour.

From 1420 to 1644 the palace was the seat of the Ming dynasty. In April 1644 rebel forces under Li Zicheng captured it, and he soon fled before the armies of the former Ming general Wu Sangui and the Manchus, setting fire to parts of it. By October a ceremony there proclaimed the young Shunzhi Emperor ruler of all China under the Qing. The Qing renamed some principal buildings to stress harmony rather than supremacy and made the nameplates bilingual in Chinese and Manchu. Anglo-French forces occupied it in 1860 during the Second Opium War, and Empress Dowager Cixi fled in 1900 during the Boxer Rebellion.

Under the Qing the emperor lived and worked almost entirely in the Inner Court, using the Outer Court for ceremony. From 1933 the threat of Japanese invasion forced the evacuation of the museum's most important collections.
forcalquier: Forcalquier lies between the Lure Mountain and Luberon ranges, about 30 km south of Sisteron and 10 km west of the Durance river. Its Latin name, Furnus Calcarius, comes from the lime kilns used in Roman times, and a Roman bridge still stands in the valley to the south of the town. The town is built round the slopes of a steep conical hill.

At the end of the 11th century a family of the counts of Provence created the county of Forcalquier. In the Middle Ages the town was the capital of Haute-Provence along the Durance, a territory that included Manosque, Sisteron, Gap and Embrun. It minted its own currency, and its church was raised to the status of a concathedral.

The counts of Forcalquier grew powerful enough to defy the counts of Provence. The rivalry ended in 1195, when Gersende de Sabran, countess of Forcalquier, married Alfonso II, count of Provence, and their son Ramon Bérenger IV inherited both counties.

The hill is crowned by the octagonal chapel of Notre Dame de Provence, built in 1875 where the medieval citadel stood until its destruction in 1601. The oldest part of the town surrounds the Place Saint-Michel, with a Renaissance fountain of 1511 and doorways from the 12th to 16th centuries. The 12th-century concathedral of Notre Dame de l'Assomption stands across from the Place du Bourguet. Franciscans, called cordeliers for their rope belts, built a convent in the 13th century, occupied by monks until the Revolution. The Port de Cordeliers is all that remains of the town walls. The municipal museum holds prehistoric and Gallo-Roman objects, glass and local pottery.
fort-de-france: Fort-de-France lies on the west coast of Martinique, at the northern entrance to the large Fort-de-France Bay and at the mouth of the Madame River. The city occupies a narrow plain between the hills and the sea but can be reached by road from all parts of the island. Its climate is tropical rainforest, warm and humid all year, with hurricanes a frequent threat from July to November.

Before French settlement the area was known as Iguanacaera, which in the Kariʼnja language means Iguana Island. In 1638 Jacques Dyel du Parquet, first governor of Martinique, had Fort Saint Louis built to protect against attack. The fort was soon destroyed and was rebuilt in 1669, when Louis XIV appointed the Marquis of Baas governor general, and it was built to a design of Vauban. In the 1680s the area was settled and became the French colonial capital in the Caribbean, governed by the Code Noir, the decree Louis XIV issued in 1685 to regulate slavery in the French colonies.

Called Fort-Royal, the administrative capital was overshadowed by Saint-Pierre, the oldest city on the island, known as the Paris of the Caribbean. A British expedition captured the city in 1762, and the Treaty of Paris returned the island to France. A fire in 1890 razed part of the city, and the town hall was completed in 1901. The eruption of Mount Pelée in 1902 destroyed Saint-Pierre and made Fort-de-France economically important. Until 1918 it had an inadequate water supply and was notorious for yellow fever.

Fort-de-France is the capital of Martinique, an overseas department and region of France. Fort Saint Louis is a French naval base. Its sights include Fort Desaix, the park called La Savane, a botanical garden and the cathedral. Its inhabitants are called Foyalais, after Foyal, the Creole form of the old name Fort-Royal. The psychiatrist and political philosopher Frantz Fanon, born in 1925, is among its notable natives.
fort-jesus: Fort Jesus stands on Mombasa Island and was built by order of King Felipe II of Spain, who also reigned as Filipe I of Portugal, to guard the Old Port of Mombasa. It was the only fort the Portuguese maintained on the Swahili coast. Its designer, Giovanni Battista Cairati of Milan, was chief architect for the Portuguese possessions in the East, and the master builder was Gaspar Rodrigues; the fort was Cairati's last overseas work.

The design is Renaissance, but the masonry techniques, materials and labour are believed to have come from the local Swahili people. The fort is roughly square with four bulwarks at its corners, and seen from above its plan has the outline of a person lying on the back with the head towards the sea. It was the first European-style fort outside Europe designed to resist cannon fire.

The Portuguese lost the fort in 1631 to Sultan Yusuf ibn al-Hasan of Mombasa and recaptured it in 1632, after which they refurbished it and added fortifications. It was won and lost at least nine times in the following centuries. Omani Arabs under Saif bin Sultan took it in 1698 after a long siege, which ended the Portuguese presence on the coast, although the Portuguese briefly reoccupied it in 1728 and 1729 with the help of the Swahili city-states. The Omanis took it again in 1837 and used it as barracks. The British occupied it in 1895, after the East Africa Protectorate was established, and made it a prison.

The Portuguese walls were 15 metres high, and the Omanis added three more. The Omanis also left inscriptions from the Koran on door posts and ceiling beams and a hall with five stone pillars, while the Portuguese built a cistern for rainwater and the Arabs sank a well too salty for anything but washing.

In 1958 the fort was declared a historic monument and a national museum, and James Kirkman excavated it from 1958 to 1971. UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site in 2011. It is Mombasa's most visited attraction and houses a museum, a conservation laboratory and an education department.
fort-portal: Fort Portal, formerly called Kabarole, a name that means let them see, lies in Kabarole District in the Western Region of Uganda. It is about 296 kilometres by road west of Kampala, the capital and largest city of Uganda, on an all-tarmac two-lane highway. It stands at an average elevation of 1,523 metres above sea level, at 0°39' north and 30°16' east. The town takes its name from the British diplomat Sir Gerald Portal, whose base was there. It is the seat of Kabarole District and has been the seat of the Tooro Kingdom.

On 1 July 2020 Fort Portal was raised from municipality to a tourism city. In 2019, in preparation for the grant of city status, it annexed several surrounding neighbourhoods and sub-counties, among them Karago, Ibaale Parish, Burungu Parish, Karambi sub-county, Bukuku sub-county and parts of Busoro sub-county. The national census of 2002 counted about 41,000 people, and the census of August 2014 put the population at 54,275. The Uganda Bureau of Statistics estimated 60,800 for mid-2020 and calculated an average annual growth of 2.12 per cent between 2014 and 2020.

The city has three hospitals. Fort Portal Regional Referral Hospital, with 300 beds, is public and administered by the Ministry of Health. Holy Family Virika Hospital, with 155 beds, belongs to the Roman Catholic Diocese of Fort Portal, and Kabarole Missionary Hospital, with 100 beds, is run by the Church of Uganda and was originally founded by John Edward Church of the Church Mission Society.

It has three institutions of higher learning: the main campus of Mountains of the Moon University, once private and now public, in the city centre; the main campus of Uganda Pentecostal University, a private university affiliated with the Pentecostal movement; and the Fins Medical University, founded in 2018. St Mary's Minor Seminary, a Catholic secondary school for prospective priests, is also in the city. Natives of the city include the singer Juliana Kanyomozi, the journalist Andrew Mwenda and the physician Margaret Blick Kigozi, born there in 1950.
fort-ross: Fort Ross stands on the northern California coast in what is now Sonoma County. The earliest people known at the site lived there in the Upper Archaic period, and the main occupation began about 1500 CE. The area was a large part of Kashaya Pomo territory, which they called Metini, and archaeological data suggest the Kashaya moved there sometime between 1000 and 500 BCE. The Spanish sometimes called the fort the Presidio Ruso.

Russian hunting parties had reached California aboard American ships in the early nineteenth century. In 1806 Nikolay Rezanov, a director of the Russian-American Company, visited San Francisco to arrange food supplies for the Alaskan colony, and his captain, Lt. Khvostov, charted the coast to the north and found it unoccupied by other European powers. Rezanov recommended a settlement. On 15 March 1812 Ivan Kuskov arrived at Bodega Bay with 25 Russians and 80 Native Alaskans, and on 11 September 1812 the fortress was dedicated on the name-day of Emperor Alexander I. Four ships were later built there.

By 1817 sea otters had been practically eliminated from the area. Between 1824 and 1836 Mexican explorers found Russian farms inland from the fort, and Governor José Figueroa gave land to Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo to counter the encroachment. By 1839 the settlement's agricultural importance had decreased, and after a trade agreement of 1838 with the Hudson's Bay Company it was no longer needed to feed Alaska. It was sold in 1841 to John Sutter for 30,000 dollars. Some Russian historians assert that the sum was never paid, while a Sutter biography reports that his agent paid 19,788 dollars in 1849.

The California Historical Landmarks Commission bought the stockade in 1903, and the state received it in 1906. Fort Ross is part of Fort Ross State Historic Park, a California Historical Landmark and a National Historic Landmark. Excavations in 1990 to 1992 identified 135 graves in its cemetery, with the consent of the Russian Orthodox Church, Kashaya Pomo and Alaskan Native associations. The Rotchev House became a house museum in 2010.
fougeres: Fougères is a commune and sub-prefecture of the department of Ille-et-Vilaine, in Brittany, on the edge of Brittany, Maine and Normandy. It lies 40 kilometres from Rennes, 58 kilometres from Mont-Saint-Michel and 330 kilometres from Paris. Megalithic monuments in the forest of Fougères suggest that the area was inhabited in the Neolithic era. The town stood at the crossing of two Roman roads, one from Chartres to Carhaix and the other from Avranches to Nantes. It is built on rock, and the castle stands not on a height but on a deposit of hard metamorphic rock, which protected it from attack by mining and from underground.

The creation of Fougères dates to the Middle Ages. Its castle was first mentioned around the end of the 10th century as a simple wooden fortification on a rocky ridge dominating the Nançon valley and its marshes. From the 12th century the population moved away from the banks of the Nançon, and the town grew in two parishes, Saint-Sulpice for the lower town and Saint-Léonard for the upper. Tanners, weavers and drapers developed their crafts in the lower town. A belfry, the first built in Brittany, was erected in 1397 with money from local merchants, who modelled it on Flemish examples seen in their travels. The castle formed part of the Duchy of Brittany's ultimately unsuccessful defence against French aggression, together with Vitré.

In the 16th century the town lost its defensive role. During the French Revolution the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and the levée en masse triggered the rebellion known as the Chouannerie. In 1793 the Vendéens and Chouans seized the town, and Republicans took it a few weeks later. For eight years the town and its region passed from hand to hand, with massacres and looting, and the Chouan leader in the Fougères area was the young general Aimé du Boisguy. In the 19th century shoemaking replaced older crafts, and the population rose from 9,344 in 1856 to 20,952 in 1901. Workers struck in the shoe factories in the winter of 1906–07, and Jean Jaurès came to support them.

Fougères has been classified as a town of art and history since 1985. Its castle, a medieval stronghold on a granite ledge, is its most visited site. A large section of the town wall survives, and the Notre-Dame Gate of the 15th century, with a double drawbridge, is the only fortified town gate left. The churches of Saint-Sulpice and Saint-Léonard both date from the 15th century, and the town hall was completed in 1535. Shoemaking, once the town's chief industry, has almost disappeared. The Tour de France has started and finished stages in the town.
four-asian-tigers: Hong Kong was the first of the four to industrialise, developing a textile industry in the 1950s, and by the 1960s its factories in the British colony also made clothing, electronics and plastics for export. After Singapore's independence from Malaysia, its Economic Development Board set up industrial estates and attracted foreign investment with tax incentives. Taiwan and South Korea began to industrialise in the mid-1960s with heavy government involvement. All four were inspired by the Japanese economic miracle and invested in infrastructure and education, and all benefited from economic support from the United States.

By the end of the 1960s the four economies had far more physical and human capital than other countries at similar levels of development. By 1965 all four had achieved universal primary education, and South Korea's secondary enrolment reached 88 percent by 1987. They kept budget deficits within limits, and Hong Kong, Singapore and Taiwan did not borrow from abroad.

Their export policies differed. Hong Kong and Singapore adopted free-trade regimes, since their domestic markets were small, while South Korea and Taiwan used export incentives, and the governments of Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan promoted particular exporting industries. Together they grew by an average of 7.5 percent a year for three decades. The 1997 Asian financial crisis was a setback: South Korea was hit hardest, its currency falling by between 35 and 50 percent, while Singapore and Taiwan were relatively unscathed.

The causes of the growth are disputed. A World Bank report of 1993, The East Asian Miracle, credited neoliberal policies, including export orientation, low taxes and minimal welfare states. Other analyses argue that state intervention and industrial policy mattered much more, and the economist Dani Rodrik holds that the miracle cannot be understood without the role of government policy.

A cultural explanation points to Confucianism, which is said to have valued stability, hard work, discipline and respect for authority, and Lee Kuan Yew of Singapore advocated Asian values. Critics note that mainland China, the birthplace of Confucianism, did not share the success in the same years, and in 1996 Joseph Stiglitz observed that the Confucian heritage had not long before been cited to explain why these countries had not grown. The four have been proposed as models for other developing countries, especially the Tiger Cub economies of Southeast Asia.
four-books-and-five-classics: The Four Books and Five Classics are traditionally believed to have been written, edited or commented on by Confucius or one of his disciples. Several of the Five Classics were already prominent in the Warring States period. Under the Western Han dynasty, which adopted Confucianism as its official ideology, the texts became part of the state-sponsored curriculum, and it was then that they were first considered together as the Five Classics. The Four Books were selected much later, by the Song dynasty scholar Zhu Xi, as a general introduction to Confucian thought.

The Five Classics are the Classic of Poetry, a collection of 305 poems; the Book of Documents, speeches alleged to come from rulers and officials of the early Zhou period and before; the Book of Rites, on ancient rites and court ceremonies; the I Ching, a divination system; and the Spring and Autumn Annals, a record of the State of Lu for 722–481 BCE. A sixth, the Classic of Music, was lost.

The Four Books are the Great Learning, originally a chapter of the Book of Rites; the Doctrine of the Mean, another chapter of it, attributed to Confucius's grandson Zisi; the Analects, speeches of Confucius and his disciples; and the Mencius, long dialogues between Mencius and the kings of his time.

Traditionally it was thought that Confucius compiled or edited the Five Classics, and that he cut the Classic of Poetry from 3,000 pieces to 305. Many twentieth-century scholars hold that he had nothing to do with editing the classics, while others take the view that he and his followers contributed to their formation. For over 2,000 years he was believed to have written or edited them.

The Han adoption of Confucianism as state orthodoxy led to their preservation, and the Song revival made them the basis of orthodoxy in the examinations. Zhu Xi (1130–1200) fixed the texts of the Four Books and wrote commentaries whose interpretations came to be accepted as those of Confucius himself. In the Ming and Qing dynasties the Four Books formed the core of the civil service examinations.
fourteen-points: The United States entered the First World War on 6 April 1917, in part because of Germany's resumption of submarine warfare and the Zimmermann telegram. President Woodrow Wilson wanted to separate American participation from the nationalist disputes of the European powers. The need for moral aims grew when the Bolsheviks disclosed secret treaties made between the Allies, and Wilson was also responding to Vladimir Lenin's Decree on Peace of November 1917. Three days before his speech, the British prime minister David Lloyd George had set out British war aims at Caxton Hall, and Wilson briefly considered abandoning his own, but his adviser Edward M. House persuaded him to go ahead.

Wilson delivered the Fourteen Points in a speech on war aims and peace terms to the United States Congress on 8 January 1918. They rested on the research of the Inquiry, a team of about 150 advisers led by House.

The first four points called for open covenants of peace openly arrived at, absolute freedom of navigation on the seas, the removal of economic barriers, and guarantees that national armaments would be reduced to the lowest point consistent with domestic safety. Points ten to thirteen dealt with colonial disputes and the autonomous development of peoples, and point thirteen called for a reborn Polish state with free and secure access to the sea.

The speech was spread as Allied propaganda, translated into many languages, and dropped behind German lines. In October 1918 the German chancellor Prince Max of Baden asked Wilson for an armistice and peace negotiations on the basis of the Fourteen Points. In Germany they became a symbol of the promised basis of peace, and through the interwar period critics argued that the Treaty of Versailles contradicted them. The Allied leaders Georges Clemenceau, Lloyd George and Vittorio Emanuele Orlando were sceptical of Wilsonian idealism, and Theodore Roosevelt called the document high-sounding and meaningless.

At the Paris peace conference the points guided disputes over Alsace-Lorraine, the Rhineland and Danzig, which the treaty made a Free City with special Polish rights. They also drew the attention of anti-colonial leaders, who saw an opportunity to seek independence. The Korean March First Movement of 1919 and the Egyptian Revolution of 1919 followed, and the Allies did not support either.
fourth-council-of-the-lateran: Pope Innocent III first thought of an ecumenical council in November 1199. On 19 April 1213 he summoned one in the letter Vineam Domini, which spoke of the urgent need to recover the Holy Land and to reform the Church. The long interval before it met allowed many bishops to attend. In preparing for it Innocent had old St Peter's Basilica extensively refurbished as the centrepiece of the council. The measures it took against Jews came after hostility that had grown during his reign, partly through the Crusades, and after a campaign against the Talmud as part of the effort against heresy.

The council opened at the Lateran Palace on 11 November 1215, St Martin's Day, after a preliminary legal session on 4 November. Innocent preached on the recovery of the Holy Land and on heretics. On 14 November there were violent scenes between supporters of Simon de Montfort and those of the Count of Toulouse. Raymond VI of Toulouse, his son, later Raymond VII, and Raymond-Roger of Foix attended to dispute the confiscation of their territories. All of Raymond VI's lands were confiscated except Provence, which was kept in trust for Raymond VII, and Toulouse was awarded to Simon de Montfort.

At the second plenary session on 20 November, bishops who opposed the designation of Frederick II as Holy Roman Emperor disrupted proceedings. The council ended on 30 November, when Innocent preached on the Nicene Creed and raised a relic of the True Cross. Its seventy-one canons were not debated but were formally adopted on the last day. Anne J. Duggan reports a scholarly consensus that Innocent drafted them himself.

The council had three objectives: crusading, Church reform and combating heresy. Its canons covered Church elections, taxation, marriage, tithes, simony and Judaism, and it condemned the teaching of the Joachimites. It ordered that Jews and Muslims be marked out by their dress, which some historians, among them R. I. Moore, see as a step towards a persecuting society. Between 404 and 412 bishops, over 800 abbots and priors and representatives of several monarchs attended, making it the largest ecumenical council between Chalcedon and the Second Vatican Council. Duggan calls it the most influential council under papal leadership before the end of the fourteenth century. Dissemination of the canons was patchy, and local application varied.
fourth-crusade: Pope Innocent III, who succeeded to the papacy in January 1198, made the preaching of a new crusade the main goal of his pontificate. The Ayyubid Sultanate under Saladin had taken Jerusalem in 1187, and the Third Crusade had ended in 1192 without recovering it. The intended target of the new expedition was Egypt, the centre of Ayyubid power. In 1201 the Republic of Venice contracted with the crusader leaders to build a fleet to carry the army. The leaders greatly overestimated how many men would sail from Venice, since many chose other ports, and about 12,000 arrived instead of the expected 33,500. They could not pay the agreed price of 85,000 silver marks.

In lieu of payment, the Doge Enrico Dandolo proposed that the crusaders help Venice attack the rebellious city of Zara. The sack of Zara in November 1202 was the first attack by a Catholic crusader army on a Catholic city, and the Pope briefly excommunicated the army.

In January 1203 the leaders agreed with the Byzantine prince Alexios Angelos to divert to Constantinople and restore his father Isaac II Angelos as emperor, with the promise of payment and support for the crusade. The army reached Constantinople on 23 June 1203, and Alexios IV was crowned co-emperor in August. He could not raise the promised sums, and a popular uprising deposed him in January 1204. The crusaders decided on outright conquest after his murder on 8 February.

The crusaders sacked Constantinople for three days in April 1204. Many civilians were killed, churches and monasteries were looted, and ancient and medieval works of art were stolen or ruined. Eyewitnesses including Niketas Choniates and Geoffrey of Villehardouin accuse the crusaders of rapacity. Several leaders, including Simon de Montfort, refused to take part in the attacks on Zara and Constantinople, and many crusaders had sailed directly to the Holy Land.

A treaty apportioned the Byzantine Empire between Venice and the crusader leaders. Baldwin of Flanders became emperor of the Latin Empire based in Constantinople, and Boniface of Montferrat founded the Kingdom of Thessalonica. Byzantine refugees founded successor states at Nicaea, Trebizond and Epirus, and the Nicaean Empire retook Constantinople in July 1261. Greeks call the period of Western rule in their lands the Frankokratia.

Historians regard the crusade as having solidified the East-West Schism and dealt a lasting blow to Byzantine power, leaving the restored empire territorially diminished and exposed to the expanding Ottomans. Sir Steven Runciman wrote in 1954 that there was never a greater crime against humanity than the Fourth Crusade. Whether the capture of Constantinople was the aim from the start is debated, and the traditional view was challenged by Donald E. Queller and Thomas F. Madden in their book of 1997.
france: Celtic tribes known as Gauls settled the area in the Iron Age. Ionian Greeks from Phocaea founded Massalia around 600 BCE, and the Romans conquered the south of Gaul around 125 BCE. Julius Caesar conquered the rest and overcame a revolt by the Gallic chieftain Vercingetorix in 52 BCE, after which Gaul was divided into provinces and a Gallo-Roman culture developed. In the 5th century the Visigoths, the Burgundians and the Franks settled in the region. The Franks formed the kingdom of Francia, the heartland of the Carolingian Empire, and the Treaty of Verdun of 843 partitioned that empire, with West Francia evolving into the Kingdom of France.

In the High Middle Ages France was a powerful but decentralised feudal kingdom. After Philip II defeated the Angevin Empire and won the Battle of Bouvines, it became more centralised. From the mid-14th to the mid-15th centuries a dynastic conflict with England, the Hundred Years' War, followed. The 16th century brought the French Renaissance, the French Wars of Religion between Catholics and Huguenots, and the emergence of a French colonial empire. Under Louis XIV the nation built Europe's strongest army.

The French Revolution of 1789 overthrew the ancien régime and produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man. Napoleon Bonaparte established the First French Empire and subjugated much of continental Europe. Later came the Bourbon Restoration, the Second Republic and the Second French Empire under Napoleon III, which collapsed during the Franco-Prussian War in 1870 and gave way to the Third Republic. France emerged victorious from World War I at great human and economic cost, and surrendered and was occupied by Germany in 1940. After liberation in 1944 the Fourth Republic was established and later dissolved over the course of the Algerian War. Charles de Gaulle formed the Fifth Republic in 1958, and Algeria and most French colonies became independent in the 1960s.

Metropolitan France covers 551,500 square kilometres and is bordered by the Pyrenees, the Alps, the Jura Mountains and the Rhine along much of its edge. The estimated population is 69,081,996, and Paris is the capital. France is a unitary semi-presidential republic under the Constitution of 1958, with a president elected for five years and a bicameral Parliament. It is one of the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council and has 54 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
france-albert-rene: France-Albert René was born on 16 November 1935 in Victoria, on Mahé, to Price René, a plantation manager, and Luisa Morgan René, a seamstress. At 17 he won a scholarship to study theology at a seminary in Switzerland, then turned to law in England, graduating from King's College London in 1957 and working as a barrister. In Britain he took part in Labour Party politics and adopted a moderate socialism. He returned to Seychelles in 1964, practised law, launched a newspaper, The People, and helped found the Seychelles People's United Party, which campaigned for socialism and independence from Britain.

Seychelles became independent on 29 June 1976, with James Mancham as first president and René as prime minister. On 4 June 1977, while Mancham was in London, between 60 and 200 Tanzanian-trained supporters of René seized strategic sites on Mahé; three men were killed in the crossfire at a police station. René was sworn in as president on 5 June and called himself an Indian Ocean socialist, oriented towards Tanzania's Julius Nyerere. He denied prior knowledge of the coup, though a participant told a truth commission in 2019 and 2020 that he had helped plan it.

René's party, renamed the Seychelles People's Progressive Front in 1978, was the only legal party from 1979 to 1991, and presidential elections were yes-or-no votes. His government introduced universal healthcare and education and built an offshore financial sector alongside tourism. It survived several coup attempts, among them one in November 1981 sponsored by South Africa and led by the mercenary Mike Hoare, an army mutiny in August 1982 and a 1986 attempt by Defence Minister Ogilvy Berlouis, when India sent a warship. The constitution was amended on 27 December 1991 to allow parties, and René won the multiparty elections of July 1993, and again in 1998 and 2001.

René announced on 24 February 2004 that he would step down, and he left the presidency on 14 July, remaining leader of his party as its patron and founder. He died of respiratory failure on 27 February 2019, aged 83. The historian Kevin Shillington wrote a biography of his early political life, which René endorsed in 2014. His government's social programmes are often credited with improving conditions for the majority Creole population.
france-preseren: France Prešeren was born on 3 December 1800 in the Upper Carniolan village of Vrba, then in the Habsburg monarchy, the third of eight children of a well-off farmer and a better-educated mother. At eight he attended schools run by the Catholic clergy, and in 1812 he entered the State Gymnasium in Ljubljana, where he learned Latin, Greek and German, then the language of education and administration among Slovenes. The poet Valentin Vodnik encouraged him to write in Slovene, and he befriended the future philologist Matija Čop. In 1821 he began studying law at the University of Vienna, where he read Homer, Goethe, Dante and Petrarch.

After taking his law degree in 1828 Prešeren worked in Ljubljana as an assistant to lawyers, and he filed as many as six applications before he was allowed to open his own firm in Kranj in 1846. In 1833 he met Julija Primic, the daughter of a rich merchant, who became the unfulfilled love of his life; she married another man in 1835. Around 1836 he began a lasting relationship with Ana Jelovšek, with whom he had three children.

His first important poem, A Farewell to Youth, was written in 1828 and published in 1830 in the almanac Krajnska čbelica, which also printed The Water Man, the first Slovene ballad. Čop persuaded him to adopt Romanic poetic forms, and he became a master of the sonnet. A Wreath of Sonnets, fifteen sonnets published on 22 February 1834, joins his unhappy love to the theme of an unhappy, subjugated homeland. After Čop drowned in 1835 he wrote the epic-lyric poem The Baptism on the Savica, set in the forced Christianisation of the Carantanians, predecessors of the Slovenes. In 1844 he wrote the patriotic poem Zdravljica, A Toast, and in 1847 a volume of his collected poems appeared.

Prešeren lived in conflict with the civil and religious establishment and developed severe alcoholism and liver disease. He died in Kranj on 8 February 1849. Recognition came slowly, and a new edition of his poems in 1866, with an essay by Josip Stritar setting him in a European context, secured his standing as the leading Slovene poet. His monument in Ljubljana's central square, now Prešeren Square, dates from 1905, and Prešeren Day, the anniversary of his death, became a Slovene cultural holiday in 1945. Zdravljica was declared the national anthem of Slovenia in 1989.
francesc-macia: Francesc Macià i Llussà was born on 21 September 1859 in Vilanova i la Geltrú, Catalonia. Soon after his father's death, when he was 16, he entered the Military Academy of Guadalajara to join the Corps of Engineers, specialising in bridges, railways and telegraphs. He asked to be sent to Cuba but was posted to Barcelona, Madrid and Seville, rising from telegrapher to captain and eventually lieutenant-colonel, and he favoured modernising the army.

In 1887 he was transferred to Lleida, where he met his wife Eugènia Lamarca. In November 1905 army officers wrecked the offices of the satirical journal ¡Cu-Cut! and of La Veu de Catalunya. Macià publicly condemned this, and his superiors transferred him to Santoña in Cantabria.

Elected for Solidaritat Catalana in April 1907, he was re-elected deputy in 1914, 1916, 1918, 1919, 1920 and 1923, and moved from Catalan regionalism towards left-wing independence. In 1919 he founded the Nationalist Democratic Federation, which proposed a federal or confederal Spain, and in 1922 the independence party Estat Català. After Miguel Primo de Rivera's coup in September 1923 he took refuge in Perpignan.

In 1926 he planned the Prats de Molló plot, an insurrection in Roussillon with 50 to 100 Italian mercenaries, which the French gendarmerie stopped. He was convicted and fined, but the failure made him popular in Catalonia. From Brussels he founded the Casal Català there, returned to Spain in April 1930 after a pardon and, after another brief exile, in February 1931.

In March 1931 Estat Català joined Lluís Companys's Catalan Republican Party and the L'Opinió group to form the Republican Left of Catalonia, with Macià as leader. After local elections in April 1931 brought down Alfonso XIII, he proclaimed the Catalan Republic from the balcony of the Palau de la Generalitat on 14 April, a few hours before the Second Spanish Republic was proclaimed in Madrid, hoping for an Iberian Confederation. Three ministers from Madrid reached agreement with him three days later, and the republic became the Generalitat of Catalonia.

The provisional Generalitat drafted a statute of autonomy, which the Spanish Congress approved on 9 September 1932 after many changes. The Republican Left won a landslide in the first Catalan parliamentary election on 20 November 1932, and Macià was officially appointed President of the Generalitat, holding the post until his death. He died of appendicitis in Barcelona on 25 December 1933. His funeral drew a massive demonstration of grief, and he is buried in Montjuïc Cemetery. His papers are preserved in the National Archive of Catalonia and the library of the University of Barcelona. He achieved the first successful establishment of self-government for Catalonia in modern times.
francesca-da-rimini: Francesca was the daughter of Guido I da Polenta of Ravenna. She married Giovanni Malatesta, also called Gianciotto or Giovanni the Lame, son of Malatesta da Verucchio, lord of Rimini, in or around 1275. The marriage was political: Guido had been at war with the Malatesta family, and the match secured a peace negotiated between the two houses. In Rimini she fell in love with Giovanni's younger brother Paolo, who was also married, and the affair continued for some ten years. Giovanni surprised them in her bedroom at some time between 1283 and 1286 and killed them both.

Dante Alighieri, her contemporary, placed her in the fifth canto of the Inferno, in the second circle of hell, reserved for the lustful, where she and Paolo are buffeted by violent winds. Dante probably knew of her through her nephew Guido Novello da Polenta, who hosted him in Ravenna at the end of his life. She is the first soul in hell proper to be given a substantial speaking role, and her account is the first historical record of her.

She introduces herself by her city of birth, says that love seized her and led the pair to one death, and recalls that their love began as they read the tale of Lancelot, a book she calls Galeotto, and that they read no further that day. Commentators have noted that she presents herself as passive and refuses responsibility, and that Dante treats her with compassion: at the end of her speech he faints like a dead body falling.

Soon after Dante, legends grew up around her. Giovanni Boccaccio's commentary on the Divine Comedy says that Guido, fearing that Francesca would refuse the lame Giovanni, sent the handsome Paolo to stand in for him at the wedding, so that she discovered the deception only the next morning. This is very likely a fabrication, since she can hardly have failed to know both brothers, and Boccaccio was born in 1313, some 27 years after her death, though many later commentators repeated it and none earlier had mentioned anything like it.

In the nineteenth century the story inspired many plays, operas and symphonic works, among them Silvio Pellico's tragedy of 1818, Ary Scheffer's paintings, Tchaikovsky's symphonic poem of 1876 and Rachmaninoff's one-act opera of 1906. Gabriele D'Annunzio's tragedy of 1901 and Riccardo Zandonai's opera of 1914 followed, and Rodin's marble The Kiss of 1888 is also associated with the lovers.
francesco-crispi: Francesco Crispi was born in Sicily on 4 October 1818 into a family of Italo-Albanian origin. His paternal family came from Palazzo Adriano, a community founded in the later fifteenth century by Orthodox or Greek Catholic Albanians, the Arbëreshë, and his grandfather was an Arbëreshë Orthodox priest. In December 1847 he was sent to Palermo to prepare the revolution against King Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies, which began on 12 January 1848, the king's birthday.

After it failed he went into exile, first in Marseille, then in Turin, where he worked as a journalist and befriended Giuseppe Mazzini, and later in Malta and London. He returned to Italy in June 1859, and in 1860 he took part in the Expedition of the Thousand and became First Secretary of State in Garibaldi's provisional government in Sicily.

Elected in 1861 for the Historical Left, Crispi kept his seat in every legislature until his death. He was known as the most aggressive member of his group, and in 1864 he abandoned Mazzini for the monarchy, writing that the monarchy united them and the republic would divide them. He became President of the Chamber of Deputies in 1876 and, in December 1877, Minister of the Interior, but was forced to resign in March 1878 after being accused of bigamy. In 1883 he opposed the coalition politics known as Trasformismo and founded the Dissident Left, called the Pentarchy.

Crispi became prime minister on 29 July 1887, the first from Southern Italy, and in his first term also served as foreign minister and interior minister. With Giuseppe Zanardelli he abolished the death penalty, repealed anti-strike laws and reformed the penal code and public health, and he strengthened the role of the prime minister. He saw France as the permanent enemy, visited Bismarck to consult on the Triple Alliance, and turned to imperialism in Africa against Ethiopia. He resigned on 6 February 1891 after a budget deficit cost him his majority.

He returned in December 1893, amid disturbances in Sicily and the Banca Romana scandal. The Fasci Siciliani, a democratic and socialist movement of poor workers, were suppressed under martial law, and after an anarchist tried to shoot him on 16 June 1894 he passed anti-anarchist laws that were also used against socialists. Italian forces beat the Mahdists at Agordat in December 1893 and occupied Kassala in 1894. His second term ended on 14 June 1896 after the defeat at Adwa, and he died on 11 August 1901.
francesco-foscari: Francesco Foscari was born on 19 June 1373, the eldest son of Nicolò Foscari and Cateruzia Michiel. The Foscari were a family of only moderate importance who had secured a hereditary place in the Great Council of Venice after the Serrata, the closing of the council, and rose in prominence during the fourteenth century.

His father became a member of the Council of Ten. Francesco served the republic as ambassador, president of the Council of Forty, member of the Council of Ten, inquisitor, Procurator of St Mark's and avogador de comùn before his election as doge in 1423, in which he defeated the other candidate, Pietro Loredan. He married twice: first Maria Priuli, then in 1415 Marina Nani.

His dogeship lasted 34 years, 6 months and 8 days, the longest in Venetian history, and coincided with the early Italian Renaissance, when Venice grew in prominence in art, humanism and diplomacy. His task was to lead the republic through long wars in Lombardy against Milan, governed by the Visconti, who sought to dominate northern Italy.

The wars marked a critical phase in the republic's expansion onto the mainland, the Domini di Terraferma. They were very costly to a city whose wealth and power lay at sea. Venice abandoned its ally Florence during his leadership and was eventually overcome by Milan's forces under Francesco Sforza, who soon made peace with Florence and left Venice alone. The humanist senator Bernardo Giustiniani justified the mainland wars in Foscari's funeral oration.

In 1445 the Council of Ten tried his only surviving son Jacopo for bribery and corruption and exiled him. Two further trials followed, in 1450 and 1456; in the second Jacopo confessed that he had appealed for help to Sultan Mehmed II and to the Duke of Milan, both enemies of Venice. He was imprisoned on Crete and died there soon after. The news led Foscari to withdraw from his duties, and in October 1457 the Council of Ten forced him to abdicate. He died within days, and public outcry over this brought him a state funeral.

He was painted in profile by Lazzaro Bastiani and commissioned a bronze plaquette from Donatello. A figure of him kneeling before St Mark stood above the portal of the Doge's Palace until the revolutionary government dismantled it in 1797, and his monument by Antonio Bregno and his brother Paolo stands in Santa Maria dei Frari. Lord Byron's play The Two Foscari of 1821 was the basis of Giuseppe Verdi's opera I due Foscari, first performed in Rome on 3 November 1844.
francesco-guicciardini: Francesco Guicciardini was born in Florence on 6 March 1483, the third of eleven children of Piero di Iacopo Guicciardini. The family belonged to the Florentine oligarchy and supported the Medici. His godfather was the philosopher Marsilio Ficino, and he received a humanist education before studying law at the Universities of Ferrara and Padua until 1505. At twenty-three he was appointed by the Signoria to teach legal studies at the Florentine Studio. In 1508 he married Maria Salviati, daughter of Alamanno Salviati, and in the same year wrote a family memoir and began his Ricordi, a collection of personal maxims.

In 1512 the Signoria sent him as ambassador to Ferdinand the Catholic of Aragon. He came to regard Ferdinand as a model of political deceit. Pope Leo X made him governor of Reggio in 1516 and of Modena in 1517, and in 1523 Clement VII appointed him viceregent of the Romagna.

He urged Clement to join the League of Cognac in 1526 against Charles V, and was made lieutenant-general of the papal army, though he could not move its commander to act. The Sack of Rome followed in 1527. Florence's new republic declared him a rebel in March 1530. After the city fell to imperial troops, he was charged with punishing those who had resisted the Medici, and Benedetto Varchi called him more cruel than the others.

He governed Bologna from 1531 and later advised Alessandro de' Medici, defending him before Charles V at Naples in 1535. Cosimo de' Medici dismissed him soon after taking power, and he retired to his villa at Arcetri, where he died in 1540 without male heirs.

None of his works was published in his lifetime. The first sixteen of the twenty books of his History of Italy appeared in 1561, and the first English translation in 1579. The Ricordi, about 220 maxims, and his other writings came to light only after his descendants opened the family archives in 1857. He wrote the History in his last years, drawing on government records and his own experience, and he traced events to the self-interest of the emperors, princes and popes in command.

He corresponded with Niccolò Machiavelli until the latter's death in 1527, but objected that Machiavelli put things too absolutely, and he did not agree that Rome could serve as a perfect norm. Like many Florentine aristocrats he favoured a mixed republican government on the Venetian model, though he worked closely with the Medici.
francesco-ii-sforza: Francesco was born on 4 February 1495, the second son of Ludovico Sforza and Beatrice d'Este. After his father was removed from Milan in the course of the Italian Wars, he was brought to the court of Emperor Maximilian I, who had married Francesco's cousin Bianca Maria Sforza. He lived briefly at court in Innsbruck and was then assigned a tutor and lived at the castle of Steyr with twenty-one followers. Maximilian backed his ambition of an ecclesiastical career as a canon in Cologne, but the Cologne chapter rejected him despite the imperial support.

In August 1512 Francesco put his judicial studies on hold after his brother Massimiliano was elected duke of Milan at the Diet of Mantua. In 1521 Emperor Charles V reconquered Milan from the French after the Battle of Vaprio d'Adda, and Francesco was appointed its duke. His sovereignty remained limited by the occupation of Milan by Spanish troops. He returned to a state depleted by twenty years of combat and promoted a cultural and economic recovery.

Francesco fought on the emperor's side at the Battle of Bicocca in 1522. In 1526 he changed sides and joined the League of Cognac with Francis I of France, Pope Clement VII and the Republic of Florence, and he was besieged in the Castello Sforzesco. On 4 May 1534 he married Christina of Denmark, the 12-year-old niece of Charles V and daughter of Christian II of Denmark and Isabella of Austria. By then, a survivor of a poisoning attempt, he used a cane to walk and had paralysed hands.

Francesco died on 1 November 1535, and the marriage remained childless. His death sparked the Italian War of 1535. His half-brother Giovanni Paolo reclaimed the Duchy of Milan briefly but died in the same year under mysterious circumstances. Francesco was the last member of the Sforza family to hold the title of duke.
francesco-morosini: Francesco Morosini was born in Venice on 26 February 1619 to Pietro and Maria Morosini, of a prominent family that had given the Republic several doges and generals. He received a classical education but was far more interested in battles and strategy, and enlisted in the Venetian army young. In 1638 he took part in an expedition against the Bey of Tunis, and on 10 June 1640, aged 21, he was appointed galley captain in the navy. He fought the Barbary corsairs and in 1643 took part in the War of Castro. By September 1647 he had been promoted to Captain of the Gulf.

The Cretan War gave Morosini his opportunity. He succeeded Alvise Mocenigo as Captain-General of the Venetian forces in Crete in 1654, when the island was almost lost and the capital, Candia, was under siege. In 1647 he had forced his way into the port of Chios, where he bombarded 80 Ottoman galleys, and in 1659 he set fire to a fleet of light vessels at Çeşme. Candia was reduced almost to rubble, and the dead are put at 150,000 to 200,000 Ottoman soldiers and 30,000 Venetian and allied defenders.

On 6 September 1669 he signed a peace and surrendered the city. The Venetians kept their artillery and three fortresses on Crete, and the Ottomans returned Klis in Dalmatia. His enemies, led by Antonio Barbaro, accused him of acting without the Senate's authorisation, and an inquiry cleared him entirely.

When the Great Turkish War began in 1683 he was appointed Captain General of the Sea, leading 10,000 to 15,000 men and about 50 ships. He took Lefkada in 1684, landed on the Peloponnese in 1685 with the help of the local Greek population and, with his lieutenant Otto Wilhelm Königsmarck, took Pylos, Modon, Argos and Nafplio in 1686. By 1687 only Monemvasia remained, and the Venetians established the Kingdom of the Morea. On 26 September 1687 a mortar shell partly destroyed the Parthenon, where the Ottomans stored gunpowder, during the siege of Athens. The Venetians held the city for nearly six months before plague and an approaching Ottoman army forced them out on 10 April 1688.

Morosini was unanimously elected Doge on 3 April 1688 while still campaigning in the Levant, and the Senate asked him to stay at his post. The siege of Negroponte from July to October 1688 failed after plague killed thousands of the besiegers, Königsmarck among them. He reached Venice on 11 January 1690 to a triumphal welcome. In 1693 the seventy-four-year-old Doge sailed again as Captain General, took Salamis, Spetses and Hydra, fell ill and died at Nafplio in January 1694. He was buried in the Church of Santo Stefano in Venice.
francesco-sforza: Francesco Sforza was born at Cigoli, near San Miniato in Tuscany, one of the seven illegitimate sons of the condottiero Muzio Sforza and Lucia de Martini. He spent his childhood at Tricarico in present-day Basilicata, whose marquisate King Ladislaus of Naples granted him in 1412. In 1418 he married Polissena Ruffo, a Calabrese noblewoman, and from 1419 he fought beside his father, gaining a name for bending metal bars with his bare hands. He later proved an expert tactician and a skilled field commander.

After his father's death during the War of L'Aquila, Sforza took part in the final defeat of Braccio da Montone, then served the Neapolitan army, Pope Martin V and Filippo Maria Visconti, Duke of Milan. Pay governed a mercenary's loyalty: in 1433-1435 he led the Milanese attack on the Papal States but, after conquering Ancona, changed sides and obtained the title of vicar of the city from Pope Eugene IV. He served both Florence and Venice in the later 1430s, and for a time was held prisoner at the castle of Mortara after falling into disgrace.

On 25 October 1441 he married Bianca Maria at Cremona, under the agreements that ended the war between Milan and Venice. He then allied with René of Anjou, pretender to the Neapolitan throne, and marched south, before defeating Niccolò Piccinino with the help of Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta and the Venetians. At the Battle of Montolmo in 1444 he defeated Francesco Piccinino, and was rewarded with the title of capitano generale of the duchy's armies.

Famine and riots in Milan led its senate to entrust him with the duchy, and he entered the city as duke on 26 February 1450, the first time a lay institution had handed over such a title. He never obtained investiture from the Holy Roman Emperor; that came only in 1494, when Emperor Maximilian I invested his son Ludovico Sforza. As duke he built an efficient system of taxation, founded the Ospedale Maggiore in Milan, restored the Palazzo ducale and had the Naviglio d'Adda dug. His friendship with Cosimo de' Medici of Florence led to the Peace of Lodi and then to the Italian League, a defensive alliance that stabilised most of Italy.

Edward IV of England made him a knight of the Garter in 1463. Sforza suffered from hydropsy and gout, and when a rumour of his death in 1462 set off a riot in Milan, he survived four more years, dying in March 1466. His son Galeazzo Maria Sforza succeeded him. Ludovico later commissioned Leonardo da Vinci to design an equestrian monument to him; Leonardo finished a clay horse in 1492, but the statue was never built.
francis-drake: Francis Drake was born at Crowndale Farm in Tavistock, Devon. His birth date is not recorded, and the estimates drawn from contemporary texts and portraits differ by a few years. As a child he was placed in the household of a relative, the Plymouth sea captain William Hawkins, and began his training as an apprentice on Hawkins's boats. He is thought to have served as a seaman on the last two of the four slaving voyages that Hawkins's ships made between 1562 and 1569.

In 1572 Drake led his first independent enterprise, leaving Plymouth on 24 May with 73 men in two small vessels to attack Nombre de Dios on the Isthmus of Panama, where the treasure of Peru was brought ashore. In 1575 he was present at the Rathlin Island massacre in Ireland, where troops under Sir John Norris killed all 200 defenders of the castle, despite its surrender, and several hundred men, women and children of Clan MacDonnell. His circumnavigation began on 13 December 1577. In its course he had his co-commander Thomas Doughty tried and executed, entered the Pacific, raided Spanish ports and ships and captured the treasure ship Cacafuego.

He reached Plymouth on 26 September 1580 with 59 of his crew, and Elizabeth I awarded him a knighthood aboard the Golden Hind in 1581. After war broke out between England and Spain in 1585 he led an expedition that took Vigo, Santo Domingo and Cartagena. In April 1587 he entered the harbour of Cádiz and damaged ships gathered for the Armada, delaying the Spanish invasion by a year. In 1588, as vice admiral on the Revenge, he fought the Armada under Lord Howard of Effingham and captured the galleon Nuestra Señora del Rosario. The English armada he led in 1589 failed.

In 1595 Drake failed to take Las Palmas and was defeated at San Juan de Puerto Rico. An attempt to cross the isthmus to Panama was repulsed, and on 28 January 1596 he died of dysentery, aged about 56, at anchor off Portobelo. The Drake Passage is named after him. Scholars hold two views of him: an older tradition, in Julian Corbett's 1898 biography, treats him as the most important figure in the founding of the British navy, while another places him within privateering. The Spanish branded him a pirate and called him El Draque.
francis-duke-of-guise: François de Lorraine was born at Bar-le-Duc on 17 February 1519, the son of Claude de Lorraine, created Duke of Guise in 1527, and Antoinette de Bourbon. His sister Mary of Guise married King James V of Scotland and was the mother of Mary, Queen of Scots, and his younger brother was Charles, Cardinal of Lorraine.

He was raised with his cousin, the future Henry II of France, though his detractors stressed his foreign origin as a prince étranger from the Duchy of Lorraine. At the Second Siege of Boulogne in 1545 a lance pierced both his cheeks, and the scar earned him the nickname Le Balafré. In 1548 he married Anna d'Este, daughter of Ercole II d'Este, Duke of Ferrara.

Made Grand Chamberlain of France in 1551, Guise won renown in 1552 by defending Metz against Charles V and defeated imperial troops again at Renty in 1554. In 1557 he led an army into Italy to aid Pope Paul IV, but his advance into Naples failed against the Duke of Alba and he retreated. Recalled to France after Montmorency's defeat at St Quentin and made Lieutenant-General, he captured Calais from the English on 7 January 1558, a large propaganda victory, then Thionville and Arlon.

The accession of Francis II on 10 July 1559, husband of Guise's niece Mary, made the Guises supreme in the royal council. After the Huguenot conspiracy of Amboise was put down in March 1560, with 1,200 executed, their power was at its height, but the king's death on 5 December 1560 ended it. Guise then joined Montmorency and Saint-André in a triumvirate opposed to Catherine de' Medici's concessions to Protestants.

On 1 March 1562, as Guise passed through Wassy, a massacre of Protestants took place. How far he was responsible is not known, but the Massacre of Vassy kindled open conflict in the French Wars of Religion. Guise retook Rouen after a month's siege and turned the Battle of Dreux on 19 December to the Catholic advantage, with the Huguenot leader Condé captured.

While about to take Orléans, he was wounded on 18 February 1563 by the Huguenot Jean de Poltrot de Méré and died six days later at Château Corney. Poltrot implicated Coligny and Théodore de Bèze, though he later retracted and Coligny denied responsibility. A bitter feud arose between Guise's son Henry and Coligny, which culminated in the St Bartholomew's Day massacre.
francis-duke-of-teck: Francis was born on 28 August 1837 in Esseg, Slavonia (now Osijek, Croatia), and was known as Count Francis von Hohenstein until 1863. His father, Duke Alexander of Württemberg, was the son of Duke Louis of Württemberg. His mother was the Hungarian Countess Claudine Rhédey de Kis-Rhéde, created Countess von Hohenstein in her own right by Emperor Ferdinand I of Austria. The marriage was morganatic, so Francis had no succession rights to the Kingdom of Württemberg. He studied at the Imperial and Royal Technical Military Academy from 1849 to 1853 and joined the Imperial Austrian Army as a lieutenant in 1854.

As an orderly officer under Count von Wimpffen in Italy during the Austro-Sardinian War, he won a gold medal for distinguished service at the Battle of Solferino in 1859. He served in the Austro-Prussian War and left the Austrian Army when he married and moved to England in 1866. In Britain he held honorary colonelcies of volunteer units, and in 1882 he was attached to the staff of Sir Garnet Wolseley in the Egyptian campaign, receiving a medal for the Battle of Tel-el-Kebir. He became a major-general in the British Army in 1893 and a Generalleutnant in the German Army in 1895.

Because he was the product of a morganatic marriage and had little income, Francis was not an acceptable husband for princesses of most European royal houses. He married Princess Mary Adelaide of Cambridge, a daughter of Prince Adolphus, Duke of Cambridge, on 12 June 1866 at St Anne's Church, Kew. They had one daughter and three sons, and the King of Württemberg created him Duke of Teck in 1871.

The couple lived on Mary Adelaide's Parliamentary allowance of £5,000 a year, with some help from her mother, and Queen Victoria refused requests for more. They were given a grace-and-favour apartment in Kensington Palace and White Lodge in Richmond Park, but ran up large debts and in 1883 left Britain for the continent, returning in 1885. Queen Victoria granted him the style of Highness on 1 July 1887. Their fortunes improved when their daughter Princess Victoria Mary, known as May, became engaged in 1891 to Prince Albert Victor, Duke of Clarence; he died six weeks later, and May then accepted a proposal from his brother Prince George, Duke of York.

After his wife's death in 1897 the duke, always irascible, suffered mental decline, and he died of a stroke on 21 January 1900 at White Lodge. He was buried next to his wife in the Royal Vault at St George's Chapel, Windsor Castle. His daughter became Queen Mary, consort of George V, and he was the maternal grandfather of Edward VIII and George VI.
francis-i-holy-roman-emperor: Francis was born on 8 December 1708 in Lunéville, in Lorraine, the fourth and oldest surviving son of Leopold, Duke of Lorraine, and Élisabeth Charlotte d'Orléans. Through his grandmother Eleonore, a daughter of Emperor Ferdinand III, he was connected with the Habsburgs. Emperor Charles VI favoured the family and had meant his daughter Maria Theresa to marry Francis's older brother Léopold Clément. When Léopold Clément died, Charles adopted the younger brother as his future son-in-law, and Francis was brought up in Vienna alongside Maria Theresa, with whom a real affection arose.

At 15 he was established in the Silesian Duchy of Teschen, and he succeeded his father as Duke of Lorraine in 1729. In 1731 he was initiated into freemasonry at a specially convened lodge in The Hague, and in 1732 he became lord lieutenant of Hungary, at Maria Theresa's wish to have him closer.

The War of the Polish Succession began in 1733, and France seized Lorraine, since its chief minister, Cardinal Fleury, feared Austrian power so close to France. Under the peace terms Stanisław Leszczyński, the losing claimant to the Polish throne, received Lorraine, and Francis became heir to the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, which he received in 1737. He married Maria Theresa in February 1736, though he had hesitated three times before agreeing, and his mother and his brother Prince Charles Alexander opposed the loss of Lorraine.

After Charles VI died in 1740, Francis and Maria Theresa ruled the Habsburg domains, and she gave him responsibility for finance, which he handled well. In the Treaty of Füssen she secured his election as emperor on 13 September 1745, and he was crowned at Frankfurt am Main on 4 October. He succeeded Charles VII and was the last non-Habsburg monarch of the Empire; she made him co-regent of her hereditary lands.

Francis died suddenly in his carriage on 18 August 1765, while returning from the opera at Innsbruck, and is buried in the Imperial Crypt in Vienna. He and Maria Theresa had sixteen children, among them Marie Antoinette, the last pre-revolutionary queen consort of France. His eldest son Joseph II succeeded him as emperor, and his younger son Peter Leopold, later Emperor Leopold II, as Grand Duke of Tuscany.
francis-ii-rakoczi: Francis II Rákóczi was born on 27 March 1676 in Borša Castle, the son of Francis I Rákóczi and Ilona Zrínyi, and belonged to a family that had already given Transylvania princes. His father died when he was four months old. The emperor Leopold I kept legal guardianship, while his mother raised him at Munkács. She defended that castle against Antonio Carafa's siege for three years before capitulating in 1688, after which the children were taken to Vienna.

In 1694 he married Princess Charlotte Amalie of Hesse-Wanfried and took over his estates, which made him the richest landlord in Hungary. When remnants of Imre Thököly's army rose in his lands after the Treaty of Karlowitz of 1699, they asked him to lead them, but he declined and returned to Vienna. There he became a friend of Count Miklós Bercsényi.

Rákóczi's contacts with France, which sought allies against Habsburg power, were seized by an Austrian spy. He was arrested and held at Wiener Neustadt, with death the likely sentence, but escaped to Poland with the help of his wife and the prison commander. In 1703, with the War of the Spanish Succession drawing Austrian troops away, the Kuruc forces rose and asked him to lead them. Most nobles held back, but Hajduk soldiers joined, and by late September 1703 he controlled most of Hungary east and north of the Danube.

The Diet at Szécsény in September 1705 elected him ruling prince of the Confederated Estates, and he refused the crown offered to him so that the war would not seem driven by ambition. The victory of Austrian and British forces at Blenheim in 1704 had cut him off from French and Bavarian support, and from 1706 his army was forced back. The Diet of Ónod declared the Habsburgs deposed on 13 June 1707. After a fall from his horse at Trencsén on 3 August 1708 his men fled, and he left for Poland on 21 February 1711.

The Peace of Szatmár, negotiated by Sándor Károlyi, saw 12,000 rebels lay down their arms on 1 May 1711. Rákóczi refused its terms and lost his estates. He then lived in Poland, England and France, and in 1717 accepted an Ottoman invitation, settling at Tekirdağ, where a Hungarian colony grew up around him. He died there on 8 April 1735.

His remains were moved in 1906 to St. Elisabeth Cathedral in Košice. He is regarded in Hungary as a national hero, and an equestrian statue stands before the Hungarian Parliament Building. His memoirs, written in French, and his meditations survive.
francis-xavier: Francis Xavier was born on 7 April 1506 in the Castle of Xavier in the Kingdom of Navarre, the youngest son of an influential noble family. His father, Don Juan de Jasso y Atondo, was president of the Royal Council of Navarre and later finance minister to King John III of Navarre.

On 15 August 1534 he and six other students met in a crypt on Montmartre, Paris: Ignatius of Loyola, Alfonso Salmeron, Diego Laínez, Nicolás Bobadilla, Peter Faber and Simão Rodrigues. They took private vows of poverty, chastity and obedience to the Pope and vowed to go to the Holy Land. Xavier was ordained on 24 June 1537, and Pope Paul III approved the Society of Jesus in 1540.

King John III of Portugal asked for Jesuit missionaries for his possessions in India, where he believed Christian values were eroding among the Portuguese. Xavier left Lisbon on 7 April 1541 with a papal brief naming him apostolic nuncio to the East, and reached Goa on 6 May 1542. His first task was to restore Christianity among the Portuguese settlers, many of whom, according to recent critical accounts, had been sent out from the jails and lower ranks of Portuguese society.

In 1545 he went to Malacca, and from about January 1546 he preached in the Maluku Islands, including Ambon, Ternate and Morotai. In Malacca in December 1547 he met Anjirō, the first Japanese Christian, who later served as interpreter. Xavier left Goa on 15 April 1549 for Japan with Anjirō, Cosme de Torres and Juan Fernández, carrying gifts for the King of Japan. He set out for China again in April 1552, but was refused recognition of his title in Malacca, and he died on Shangchuan Island on 3 December 1552.

He was first buried on a beach at Shangchuan Island, and in 1553 his body was taken to Malacca and then to Goa, where his relics are kept in the Bom Jesus Basilica. He was beatified by Pope Paul V on 25 October 1619 and canonised by Pope Gregory XV on 12 March 1622, and Pope Pius XI named him co-patron of all foreign missions in 1927. He is also co-patron of Navarre.

Called the Apostle of the Indies, he is said to have converted more people than anyone since Paul the Apostle. His efforts most affected religious practice in India and the East Indies, with less success in Japan and Borneo. In Japan and China Christians later went underground.
francis-younghusband: Francis Edward Younghusband was born on 31 May 1863 at Murree, in the Punjab of British India, into a military family. His uncle Robert Shaw was a noted explorer of Central Asia. He was brought to England as an infant and educated by two aunts at Freshford, near Bath, before entering Clifton College in 1876 and the Royal Military College, Sandhurst, in 1881. He was commissioned in the 1st King's Dragoon Guards in May 1882.

In 1886 and 1887, on leave, Younghusband travelled across Asia from Peking, exploring Manchuria and then crossing the Taklamakan Desert to Chinese Turkestan. He pioneered a route from Kashgar to India through the Mustagh Pass. For this he was elected the youngest member of the Royal Geographical Society and received its Patron's Medal in 1890. In 1889 he was sent with Gurkha soldiers to investigate an uncharted region north of Ladakh, where he dined with his Russian counterpart Captain Bronislav Grombchevsky, and later dealt with Safdar Ali, the ruler of Hunza. He joined the Indian Political Service and spent the winter of 1890 at Kashgar with George Macartney, taking part in the rivalry with Russia known as the Great Game.

In 1903 Lord Curzon appointed him to head the Tibet Frontier Commission, with the stated aim of settling disputes over the Sikkim and Tibet border. The expedition exceeded its instructions and became in effect an invasion. Near Guru, troops with rifles and machine guns routed 600 to 700 Tibetan troops armed with hoes, swords and flintlocks. The expedition lost 202 men in action and 411 to other causes. The Convention of Lhasa that Younghusband signed with Tibetan officials was repudiated by the British government, which feared for its trade and relations with the Qing dynasty. He was made Knight Commander of the Order of the Star of India in December 1904.

Younghusband served as British Resident in Kashmir from 1906 and returned to Britain in 1909. He was president of the Royal Geographical Society from 1919 and chaired the Mount Everest Committee from 1921, which coordinated the early British expeditions. After a mystical experience during his retreat from Tibet he turned to religious writing, advanced ideas of a living universe, and founded the World Congress of Faiths in 1936. He suffered a stroke in July 1942 after addressing one of its meetings and died on 31 July 1942 at Lytchett Minster, Dorset.
franciscans: Francis of Assisi was the son of a rich cloth merchant who gave up his wealth. In 1209 a sermon on Matthew 10:9 made such an impression on him that he decided to devote himself wholly to apostolic poverty, and he began to preach repentance, barefoot and in a rough garment. Bernard of Quintavalle joined him, and within a year he had 11 companions, who lived in the deserted leper colony of Rivo Torto near Assisi and travelled through the mountains of Umbria. The name Ordo Fratrum Minorum, the Order of Lesser Brothers, expresses his rejection of wealth, and he gave his followers the simple tunic of peasants as their habit.

The original Rule approved by Pope Innocent III did not allow the ownership of property, and the friars begged for food while preaching. Clare of Assisi, under Francis's guidance, founded the Poor Clares, and a Third Order was created for men and women who stayed in secular life.

The friars reached the Holy Land in 1217, and in 1219 Francis went to Egypt with the Fifth Crusade and met the Sultan Malik al-Kamil. The extreme poverty required of members was relaxed in the final revision of the Rule in 1223, and how strictly to observe it became a major source of conflict within the order, with numerous secessions. After 1232 Brother Elias gathered money for a great basilica at Assisi, which alienated the zealots, and in the 14th century the quarrels produced a number of separate congregations. In about 1236 Pope Gregory IX appointed the Franciscans, with the Dominicans, as inquisitors, and in 1252 Pope Innocent IV approved their use of torture to extract confessions.

In New Spain the first three Flemish friars arrived in 1523, and in May 1524 the Twelve Apostles of Mexico came, led by Martín de Valencia. They built the Convento Grande de San Francisco, which was the Franciscan headquarters of New Spain for the next three hundred years. Pedro de Gante began the evangelisation and studied Nahuatl through the children of the Indian elite of Tetzcoco.

The First Order comprises three groups, each with its own minister general: the Friars Minor, called the Observants, the Conventuals, formed in 1209, and the Capuchins, founded in 1520. In 1897 Pope Leo XIII combined several smaller orders into the present Order of Friars Minor. Franciscans view creation as good, and Francis expressed affection for animals and natural objects in his Canticle of the Creatures. Among the early members were the scholastics Alexander of Hales, Bonaventure and John Duns Scotus, and the scholar Roger Bacon.
francisco-de-almeida: Francisco de Almeida was born at Lisbon, a son of Lopo de Almeida, first Count of Abrantes, and Brites da Silva. As was usual in his social circle he joined the military young. He took part in the Battle of Toro in 1476, fought in several conflicts in Morocco, and in 1492 joined the Castilians in the conquest of Granada. He also served as a counsellor to King John II of Portugal. His brothers included two bishops, an ambassador to the Holy See and the head of the Order of Malta in Portugal.

In 1505 King Manuel I made Almeida, then in his mid-fifties, the first viceroy of Portuguese India. He sailed from Lisbon on 25 March 1505 with 22 ships and about 1,500 soldiers. His orders were to bring the spice trade under Portuguese control, build forts along the East African and Indian coasts, make alliances with local rulers and set up trading posts. In July 1505 his ships attacked Kilwa, where a fort was built, and Mombasa was taken, plundered and burned with the help of its rival, the Sultan of Melinde.

In India he was to build four forts, on Anjediva Island, at Cannanore, Cochin and Quilon, and he began Fort Anjediva and Fort St Angelo at Cannanore in 1505. In March 1506 his son Lourenço de Almeida defeated the fleet of the Zamorin of Calicut at Cannanore, but in March 1508 an Egyptian fleet defeated Lourenço at Chaul, and he was killed. Almeida set out to avenge him. On 3 February 1509 he won the naval Battle of Diu against a joint fleet of the Mamluk Sultanate, the Zamorin and the Sultan of Gujarat, which had support from the Republic of Venice. Afonso de Albuquerque, who bore a commission to replace him, was held under arrest for three months.

The victory at Diu led the Ottomans and Egyptians to leave the Indian Ocean and gave Portugal a trade monopoly there for more than a century, until the Dutch and English ended it. Almeida sailed for Portugal in December 1509. At Table Bay near the Cape of Good Hope, on 1 March 1510, a raid on the cattle of the nearby Khoe-speaking people, the ǃUriǁ'aikua, ended in an attack in which Almeida and 64 of his men died, among them 11 captains. His body was recovered the same afternoon and buried on the shore.
francisco-de-miranda: Francisco de Miranda was born in Caracas and baptised on 5 April 1750. His father, Sebastián de Miranda Ravelo, was an immigrant from the Canary Islands who had become a wealthy merchant, and his mother came from a wealthy Venezuelan family. His father faced discrimination from rivals because of his Canarian roots, and the white aristocracy, the Mantuanos, resented his appointment as captain of a local militia. Miranda studied at the Royal and Pontifical University of Caracas from 1762 and left La Guaira for Cádiz on 25 January 1771. In Madrid he studied languages and political science, began a personal library and trained as an officer. He saw his first combat in the Siege of Melilla in 1774 and 1775.

In 1781 he was sent secretly to Jamaica to arrange the release of 900 prisoners of war and to carry out espionage. Warned of his coming arrest, he fled to the United States, arriving at New Bern, North Carolina, on 10 July 1783. From 1785 he lived in Europe, travelling through Britain, Prussia, Sweden and Russia, where Catherine the Great protected him from an Inquisition order for his arrest.

From 1791 he served the French Revolution as a maréchal de camp and befriended the Girondins Brissot and Pétion. He served under Dumouriez in the Army of the North and took part in the 1792 campaign, including the Battle of Valmy. In 1806 he raised about 200 volunteers in New York and sailed for Venezuela on 2 February in the Leander. Jefferson and Madison met him but did not involve the United States. He waited in Trinidad for reinforcements that never came.

Venezuela achieved de facto independence on 19 April 1810, when the Supreme Junta of Caracas deposed the colonial administrators. A delegation that included Simón Bolívar and Andrés Bello persuaded Miranda to return, and he was received at La Guaira in 1811. The following year republican forces failed to subdue the royalist provinces, the loss of the Spanish market hit the cocoa trade, and a powerful earthquake struck mostly republican areas. Miranda was forced to sign an armistice with the royalists.

Bolívar and others considered the capitulation treason, arrested him and handed him to the Spanish at La Guaira. He died in the prison at La Carraca, outside Cádiz, on 14 July 1816, aged 66, and was buried in a mass grave, so an empty tomb stands for him in the National Pantheon of Venezuela. He had envisaged an independent empire of all former Spanish and Portuguese territories under a hereditary emperor called the Inca, and the name Colombia was his.
francisco-de-orellana: Orellana was born in Trujillo in western Spain, and biographers still quote various birth dates. He was a close friend of Francisco Pizarro, the conquistador of Peru, also born in Trujillo, and possibly a cousin. He travelled to the New World, probably in 1527, served in Nicaragua, and joined Pizarro's army in Peru in 1533. He supported Pizarro in his conflict with Diego de Almagro in 1538, was appointed governor of La Culata, and re-established the town of Guayaquil.

In 1540 Gonzalo Pizarro arrived in Quito and was charged by his half-brother Francisco with an expedition to find the Land of Cinnamon, thought to lie to the east. Orellana was one of his lieutenants and joined the expedition in March 1541. At the confluence of the Coca and the Napo his men threatened mutiny if they did not go on, and on 26 December 1541 he agreed to be elected chief of a new expedition. He set off with the Dominican Gaspar de Carvajal, who chronicled the voyage, and 50 men, and they built a second brigantine, the Victoria.

They reached the Negro River on 3 June 1542 and entered the Amazon. The name Amazon is said to come from a battle with a tribe whose women fought alongside the men, which Orellana likened to the mythical Amazons of Herodotus. They reached the Atlantic on 26 August 1542 and sailed along the coast to Cubagua Island near Venezuela. Orellana then went to Spain, where Prince Philip appointed him governor of New Andalusia on 13 February 1544, with a charter to explore and settle the Amazonian lands with 300 men and 100 horses.

Orellana sailed from Sanlucar on 11 May 1545 with four ships. An epidemic in the Cape Verde Islands killed 98 of his men, and one ship was lost in the crossing. He reached the coast of Brazil in December 1545, and 57 men died while a riverboat was built. One ship was wrecked on a riverbank. Orellana died on the river in November 1546, according to his wife from illness and grief, and the survivors reached the Spanish base on Margarita Island.
