Carvajal's chronicle was long thought a fantasy, but geoglyphs and terra preta have been taken to support its observation of a flourishing civilization along the Amazon. Orellana Province in Ecuador is named after him, and the Amazon was once called the Orellana River.
francisco-de-paula-santander: Francisco José de Paula Santander y Omaña was born on 2 April 1792 in Villa del Rosario, near Cúcuta, in the Viceroyalty of New Granada. His father, Juan Agustín Santander Colmenares, was governor of the rural town of San Faustino de los Ríos and grew cocoa and coffee. Both parents descended from aristocratic Spanish families, and the family owned haciendas and had wide influence in the region. In 1805 he went to Santa Fe de Bogotá to study, and he was a law student at the University of Santo Tomás when the revolt of 20 July 1810 began the process of independence.

At eighteen Santander left his studies and on 26 October 1810 enlisted as a flag-bearer in the National Guard. He served in the civil war between Centralists and Federalists and was wounded and captured in 1813. Released, he served under Manuel del Castillo y Rada and Simón Bolívar in the defence of the Cúcuta Valley. After the Spanish reconquest of New Granada under General Pablo Morillo, he fled to Casanare and joined Venezuelan Patriot forces.

In 1818 Bolívar named him commander of the vanguard of the Liberator Army of New Granada and sent him to raise an army in Casanare. In the campaign of 1819 he led troops at Paya, Gameza, the Vargas Swamp and Boyacá.

Congress at Cúcuta elected him Vice-President of Gran Colombia in 1821, with Bolívar as President, defeating Antonio Nariño by 38 votes to 19. With Bolívar away, Santander governed. The two had been close allies, but they diverged over the rule of law. Santander wished to punish José Antonio Páez and the Venezuelan rebels of 1826, whereas Bolívar granted an amnesty. He also opposed Bolívar's attempt to extend the constitution drafted for Bolivia, with its lifelong presidency, which he thought close to monarchism. In 1828 Bolívar accused him of plotting his assassination. No evidence of guilt was found, yet he was sentenced to death, and the sentence was commuted to four years of exile in Europe and the United States.

Santander returned in 1832 and Congress of the Republic of New Granada elected him President. He sought ties with industrialised nations while avoiding high tariffs, and he ordered Spanish officers still in captivity executed, among them General José Sardá, on 23 July 1833. Later he sat as a representative for Bogotá. He took to his bed in April 1840 and died on 6 May 1840.

He is known in Colombia as the Man of the Laws, with Bolívar as the Liberator. His reputation has been contested because of such acts as the execution of prisoners after Boyacá, and conservatives such as Laureano Gómez vilified him for opposing the Church's influence over public education.
francisco-de-quevedo: Francisco Gómez de Quevedo y Santibáñez Villegas was born in Madrid on 14 September 1580 into a family of hidalgos from Cantabria. His father was secretary to Maria of Spain, and his mother was lady-in-waiting to the queen. Orphaned by six, he attended the Jesuit Imperial School and the university at Alcalá de Henares from 1596 to 1600. He had a club foot and poor sight, and because he wore pince-nez the word quevedos came to mean pince-nez in Spanish. By 1606 he was a well-known man of letters, befriended by Miguel de Cervantes and Lope de Vega.

In 1613 Quevedo went to Italy as secretary to Pedro Téllez-Girón, 3rd Duke of Osuna, and worked at court to win him the viceroyalty of Naples in 1616. He was made a knight of Santiago in 1618. When Osuna fell in 1620 Quevedo was exiled to Torre de Juan Abad, a fiefdom his mother had bought him, whose inhabitants refused to acknowledge him. He wrote some of his best poetry there and studied Seneca, becoming a leading figure of Spanish Neostoicism.

Philip IV's accession in 1621 ended his exile, and under the Count-Duke of Olivares he returned to court, becoming secretary to the king in 1632. A forced marriage in 1634 lasted about three months. He quarrelled with many writers, above all Luis de Góngora, mocking his obscure vocabulary in the sonnet Aguja de navegar cultos and his prominent nose in A una nariz. In 1639 Quevedo was arrested and his books confiscated, and he was taken to the convent of San Marcos in León. He left in 1643, frail and ill, and withdrew to Torre de Juan Abad.

Quevedo wrote in the style called conceptismo, marked by rapid rhythm, simple vocabulary, witty metaphor and wordplay. His vast poetry ranges from satire to love poems and philosophical pieces and was not published in book form in his lifetime. His one novel, the picaresque Vida del Buscón, appeared in 1626, and Los Sueños, five satirical dream-visions, in 1627. He wrote about fifteen theological and ascetic books and political works such as La política de Dios. His writings also include antisemitic attacks on Jews and on Portuguese new Christians. He died at Villanueva de los Infantes on 8 September 1645.
francisco-de-vitoria: Francisco de Vitoria was born around 1483 in Burgos to noble families of Alava and Burgos, and scholars have proposed years from 1480 to 1492 before settling on 1483. He became a Dominican at the convent of San Pablo in Burgos in 1505. Around 1508 he went to the College Saint-Jacques in Paris, where he studied arts and theology, was influenced by Desiderius Erasmus, and met the Thomist revival led by Peter Crockaert, who taught from Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologica instead of Peter Lombard's Sentences. In 1523 he returned to Spain to teach theology at the College of San Gregorio in Valladolid, where young Dominicans were trained for missionary work in the New World.

In September 1524 he was elected to the prima chair of theology at the University of Salamanca, the senior chair of theology in Spain, and held it until his death. He made the Summa Theologica the basis of the university's theological teaching, and his students included Domingo de Soto and Melchor Cano. Charles V sought his counsel on the Indies and named him imperial theologian for the Council of Trent in 1545, but illness kept him from travelling.

Vitoria published nothing in his lifetime. His lectures and his annual relectiones, about fifteen between 1528 and 1540 of which thirteen survive, are known from students' notes and were published after his death as the Relectiones Theologicae. In De Indis of 1539 he asked whether the inhabitants of the Indies were true masters of their property and public affairs before the Spaniards came. He rejected four arguments against their rights, mortal sin, lack of belief, madness and irrationality, and denied that they could be understood as slaves by nature in Aristotelian terms. He concluded that neither the pope nor Charles V had a rightful claim over Indian lives or property, and that they should not be forcibly converted.

In De iure belli he held that the conditions for a just war were wholly lacking in the Indies, and he denied the legitimacy of the Requerimiento, the document Spaniards read to Indians before hostilities. He saw justification for intervention only to protect victims seized for human sacrifice. He also asserted the right of the Spaniards to travel and trade freely, and held that unlawful resistance to those rights could justify a just war ending in Spanish rule.

Vitoria died in Salamanca on 12 August 1546 and was buried at the Convento de San Esteban. His influence, for example on Hugo Grotius, was significant, and he has been described as a father of international law along with Alberico Gentili and Grotius. His writings have been read as supporting opposite policies, and Antony Anghie and others argue that his humanitarianism legitimised conquest.
francisco-de-zurbaran: Francisco de Zurbarán was born in 1598 in Fuente de Cantos, Extremadura, and was baptised on 7 November. His father Luis was a haberdasher. In 1614 he was sent to Seville to apprentice for three years with Pedro Díaz de Villanueva, of whom little is known. He married María Paet in 1617 and, after her death in 1624, the wealthy widow Beatriz de Morales in 1625. A contract of 17 January 1626 with the Dominican monastery of San Pablo el Real in Seville for 21 paintings, fourteen of them on the life of Saint Dominic, established him as a painter.

In 1628 the Mercedarians of Seville commissioned 22 paintings for their cloister, and in 1629 the elders of Seville invited him to settle there. In 1631 he painted the altarpiece of The Apotheosis of Saint Thomas Aquinas, his largest composition. Around 1630 he became painter to Philip IV, and in the 1630s he painted the Labours of Hercules for the Hall of Realms in Madrid, his only group of mythological subjects.

After 1640 his austere style was compared unfavourably with Murillo's sentimental religiosity, and his reputation declined. From the late 1630s his workshop exported many paintings to South America. He married a third time in 1644, and in 1658 moved to Madrid in search of work and renewed contact with Velázquez. He died on 27 August 1664. Popular myth has him dying in poverty, but his estate was valued at about 20,000 reales.

Zurbarán was nicknamed the Spanish Caravaggio for his forceful use of chiaroscuro, though it is unknown whether he saw Caravaggio's paintings. Juan Sánchez Cotán and the polychrome sculpture of Seville are thought to have shaped his severe compositions. He painted from nature and used a lay-figure to study drapery, with a special gift for white robes, hence the many Carthusians in his work. His subjects were mostly ascetic religious vigils, often a single figure against a dark, featureless background, and his settings resemble shallow theatre stages. His late works, such as Saint Francis, show Murillo's and Titian's influence in looser brushwork.
francisco-del-rosario-sanchez: Sánchez was born in Santo Domingo on 9 March 1817. His mother, Olaya del Rosario Belén, was a free woman of colour; his father, Narciso Sánchez Ramona, a descendant of slaves, worked in the cattle and meat trade. The parents married only in 1819, which is why he bore his mother's surname before his father's. He was taught first by his mother and then by the Peruvian priest Gaspar Hernández. Juan Pablo Duarte, a classmate, recruited him to La Trinitaria, founded in 1838.

When Duarte and others left the country on 2 August 1843 to escape Haitian persecution, Sánchez, who was ill, stayed behind in hiding and took over the leadership of the movement. On the night of 27 February 1844 his men took the Ozama Fortress, and at the Puerta del Conde, after Matías Ramón Mella fired his blunderbuss, he raised the flag. He presided over the Central Government Board, and assured freed people who had mutinied under Santiago Basora that slavery would not return.

Pedro Santana marched on Santo Domingo and on 12 July 1844 drove the Trinitarios from the board. On 22 August Duarte, Sánchez and Mella were declared traitors and deported for life. He lived as a teacher in Curaçao until an amnesty granted by President Manuel Jimenes in 1848. Back home, he sided with Buenaventura Báez against Santana, was exiled again to Curaçao, returned in August 1856 and became governor of the province of Santo Domingo, and in 1859 was banished a third time, to Saint Thomas.

In 1861 Sánchez formed the Dominican Revolutionary Board and obtained from the Haitian president Fabre Geffrard passage through Haitian territory and weapons for a force of 500 men. He entered through Hondo Valle on 1 June 1861. When Haiti withdrew its support under threat from a Spanish squadron at Port-au-Prince, the expedition turned back. On 20 June Sánchez was ambushed near Hondo Valle by Santiago de Óleo, a former ally, wounded in the leg and groin, and captured.

A war council at San Juan under General Domingo Lazala tried the prisoners; Sánchez, conducting his own defence, asked that he alone be condemned. He was shot at San Juan de la Maguana on 4 July 1861 with some twenty companions, some of whom were finished off with machetes and clubs. Spain withdrew from the country in 1865. Dominicans honour him with Duarte and Mella as a founder of the republic, and the Order of Merit of Duarte, Sánchez and Mella bears his name.
francisco-franco: Francisco Franco Bahamonde was born on 4 December 1892 in Ferrol, Galicia, into a family that had given the Spanish Navy officers for six generations. He would have followed his father into the navy, but after the Spanish-American War the Naval Academy admitted no new entrants from 1906 to 1913. He entered the Infantry Academy at Toledo in 1907 and graduated in July 1910 as a second lieutenant. Serving in Morocco, where officers could win promotion on the battlefield, he became a brigadier general in 1926 at the age of 33.

A conservative and monarchist, Franco regretted the end of the monarchy in 1931 but did not challenge the Second Republic. He led the suppression of the 1934 uprising in Asturias, and after the Popular Front won the 1936 election he was sent to the Canary Islands. He joined the military coup of July 1936 and took command of the 30,000 soldiers of the Army of Africa, securing the Moroccan protectorate in part by the summary execution of some 200 senior officers loyal to the Republic. With aircraft from Italy and Germany he began an air bridge to Seville.

Franco was proclaimed Generalísimo and head of state of the Nationalists in October 1936. On 19 April 1937 he merged the Falange and the Carlist parties into a single party. Barcelona fell in January 1939 and Madrid on 28 March, and he proclaimed victory on 1 April 1939. Repression followed. Paul Preston estimates that Franco's forces killed about 420,000 people in the war and afterwards, while Antony Beevor cites at least 35,000 official executions after 1939, and figures vary widely. Spain stayed non-belligerent in the Second World War though it supported the Axis, and the economy grew rapidly from the late 1950s.

In 1969 Franco named Prince Juan Carlos de Borbón as his heir. He died on 20 November 1975, aged 82, and was entombed in the Valley of the Fallen; in 2018 the government approved legal changes that led to plans to exhume his remains. His legacy remains disputed. Scholars debate whether his regime should be called fascist, a military dictatorship or something between, and Paul Preston and Stanley Payne hold differing views.
francisco-i-madero: Francisco Ignacio Madero González was born on 30 October 1873 at the hacienda of El Rosario in Parras de la Fuente, Coahuila, into one of Mexico's wealthiest families. His grandfather Evaristo Madero Elizondo built a large fortune, in part by shipping cotton to Mexican ports during the American Civil War. Between 1886 and 1892 Francisco was educated in France and the United States, at the Lycée Hoche in Versailles, the École des Hautes Études Commerciales in Paris and the University of California, Berkeley. In Paris he took up Spiritism and came to believe he was a medium. Returning in 1893, he managed a family hacienda at San Pedro, where he installed irrigation and built schools, hospitals and a soap factory.

After Bernardo Reyes violently crushed a demonstration on 2 April 1903, Madero, who believed his dead brother's spirit was advising him, decided to enter politics. He founded the Benito Juárez Democratic Club, lost a municipal election in 1904 and started opposition newspapers. His 1908 book The Presidential Succession in 1910 urged voters to stop Díaz's reelection, and he funded the Anti-Reelectionist Party. Díaz had said in 1908 that the 1910 election would be free. The regime arrested Madero on 6 June 1910, and about 5,000 other members of the movement were jailed. A fraudulent election on 21 June gave Díaz a huge majority.

Madero fled to San Antonio, Texas, and issued the Plan of San Luis Potosí, which declared the election void and called for revolt on 20 November 1910. It also promised the return of land to villages and Indian communities. After a defeat at Casas Grandes he gave up military command, and Pancho Villa and Pascual Orozco took Ciudad Juárez against his orders. Díaz resigned on 25 May 1911 under the Treaty of Ciudad Juárez. Madero kept the Federal Army and demobilised the revolutionaries. Elected in a landslide, he was sworn in as president on 6 November 1911.

His slowness on land reform led Emiliano Zapata to proclaim the Plan of Ayala on 25 November 1911, and Orozco rebelled in 1912. Conservatives opposed him, and the press he had freed criticised him. In February 1913 Félix Díaz, Bernardo Reyes and Victoriano Huerta led a coup, supported by the United States, during the Ten Tragic Days of 9 to 19 February. Huerta switched sides, and Madero was arrested and forced to resign. He and Vice President José María Pino Suárez were murdered, and his brother Gustavo A. Madero was kidnapped, tortured and killed.

His death united revolutionaries against Huerta. Venustiano Carranza, governor of Coahuila, led the Constitutionalist Army. He was known as the Apostle of Democracy, and the Monument to the Revolution, completed in 1938, holds his remains.
francisco-jimenez-de-cisneros: He was born Gonzalo Jiménez de Cisneros at Torrelaguna in Castile in 1436, the son of hidalgos. He studied at Alcalá de Henares and Salamanca, took a law degree in 1456 and worked in Rome as a consistorial advocate from 1459. Back in Castile he rose in the secular clergy as vicar general of Cardinal Pedro González de Mendoza's diocese of Sigüenza. In 1484, at forty-eight, he became a Franciscan friar, taking the name Francisco and living an ascetic life that he kept even at the height of his power. In 1492 Mendoza recommended him to Isabella I as her confessor, a post that carried political weight.

After Mendoza died in 1495, Isabella obtained a papal bull naming Cisneros to the Archdiocese of Toledo, the richest in Spain, together with the office of chancellor of Castile. He resisted for six months and accepted only after a second bull. He reformed the Franciscans, requiring celibacy and residence in their parishes, and extended the reforms to other mendicant orders by 1498. Despite opposition from the order's Minister General, he imposed them with the queen's backing.

In 1499 he went with the Inquisition's court to Granada, where he set aside Hernando de Talavera's slow, peaceful conversion of the Muslims, calling it giving pearls to pigs, and ordered forced mass conversion and the burning of Arabic manuscripts, at least 5,000 by the lowest contemporary figure, except those on medicine. The unconverted rose in the First Rebellion of the Alpujarras. It was suppressed, and the Muslims were offered baptism or exile, contrary to the terms of Granada's surrender.

After Isabella's death in 1504 he helped mediate the Treaty of Villafafila, and when Philip I died in 1506 he set up a regent government. Ferdinand II made him Grand Inquisitor for Castile and León in 1507 and obtained a cardinal's hat for him. In 1509 he accompanied the force that took Oran in a single day.

When Ferdinand died on 23 January 1516 Cisneros became regent of Castile for the sixteen-year-old Charles, later Charles V. He fixed the courts at Madrid, established a standing army by drilling townsmen, and ordered most of the fortresses of Navarre demolished. He fell ill in September 1517 on the way to meet Charles at Valladolid and died at Roa on 8 November 1517.

The University of Alcalá, founded in 1500 and opened in 1508 at his expense, held at one time 7,000 students. The Complutensian Polyglot Bible, begun in 1502 and finished in April 1517, set Greek, Latin and Hebrew columns side by side; he died before it was published. He also revived the Mozarabic liturgy. A cause for his beatification was opened in 1669, and he was given the title of Venerable.
francisco-largo-caballero: Francisco Largo Caballero was born in Madrid on 15 October 1869. He left school at the age of seven, was largely self-educated and made his living as a stuccoer of walls. He took part in a construction workers' strike in 1890 and joined the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) in 1894. In his early career he concentrated on municipal politics and burial societies and disapproved of the methods of the anarchist union, the Confederación Nacional del Trabajo (CNT). When the party's founder Pablo Iglesias died in 1925, Largo Caballero became head of the party and of the Workers' General Union (UGT).

He began as a moderate. He advocated a degree of cooperation between the UGT and the military government of General Miguel Primo de Rivera, which let the union go on working, and this began his long conflict with Indalecio Prieto, who opposed any collaboration. From 1931 to 1933 he was Minister of Labour in the first governments of the Second Republic. He tried to improve the lot of landless labourers in the rural south, setting up mixed juries to arbitrate in agrarian disputes and introducing an eight-hour day in the countryside.

After the right-wing CEDA won the elections of 19 November 1933, he turned sharply left. In January 1934 he wrote in El Socialista, Harmony? No! Class war! The historian Angel Smith judges his radicalism almost purely rhetorical. In October 1934 he was one of the leaders of the failed workers' rising, mainly in Asturias, which was put down by the government. It damaged him politically, and Prieto and Manuel Azaña gained the initiative.

After the Popular Front won the elections of February 1936 and the military coup of 17 July began the civil war, President Azaña asked Largo Caballero to form a government on 4 September 1936. He was prime minister and also minister of war, and on 4 November he persuaded the CNT to join the government, with four members in junior ministries. During his term he grew disenchanted with the communists and clashed with the Soviet ambassador Marcel Rosenberg.

The Barcelona May Days of 3 to 8 May 1937 caused a crisis. His attempt to defend the POUM, one of the parties involved, set moderate Socialist ministers such as Prieto and the Communists against him, and he resigned on 17 May 1937; Juan Negrín succeeded him. After the Republic's defeat in 1939 he fled to France, was arrested during the German occupation and held in the Sachsenhausen camp from 1943 to 1945. He died in Paris in 1946, and his remains were returned to Madrid in 1978.
francisco-morazan: José Francisco Morazán Quezada was born on 3 October 1792 in Tegucigalpa, then part of the Captaincy General of Guatemala. His father, Eusebio Morazán, was a criollo from the Antilles whose ancestors were Corsican, and his mother, Guadalupe Quezada, came from a distinguished family of Tegucigalpa. Despite his mixed ancestry he was recorded as Spanish on his baptismal certificate, to avoid discrimination under the colonial casta system. Central America declared independence from Spain on 15 September 1821. Morazán then joined a militia in Tegucigalpa that opposed annexation to the First Mexican Empire, and he rose to prominence at the Battle of La Trinidad on 11 November 1827.

In early 1829 Morazán led an army from Ahuachapán into Guatemala, and after overthrowing President Manuel José Arce he ran the government dictatorially until June 1829. He won the 1830 presidential election against the conservative José Cecilio del Valle and was inaugurated on 16 September. His liberal reforms included freedom of the press, speech and religion, secular marriage, and the abolition of government-aided tithing, which made him powerful enemies. His period of rule was marked by bitter infighting between liberals and conservatives. Del Valle won the next election but died before taking office, and Morazán won the new election and was sworn in on 14 February 1835.

The federation broke apart from 1837, when a cholera epidemic and resistance to the introduction of trial by jury helped ignite revolt. Conservatives rallied around Rafael Carrera and divided Central America into five nations. Elected head of state of El Salvador on 13 July 1839, Morazán faced a war declared by Carrera. On 18 March 1840 he marched on Guatemala City in a last attempt to restore the union, but Carrera's force of about 5,000 men assaulted him from all sides, and he escaped with a small escort.

Morazán went into exile on 8 April 1840, living in Panama and then Peru. He returned to El Salvador in January 1842 and then moved against Costa Rican head of state Braulio Carrillo. On 11 September 1842 a popular movement opposed to him rose in San José, and after 88 hours of fighting he tried to break the siege. He was executed on 15 September 1842.

At his death many across Central America saw him as a tyrant, but by the 1880s he was widely revered as a hero. Statues were raised in San Salvador in 1882 and Tegucigalpa in 1883, and the centenary of his birth was marked across the region in 1892. Honduras named him Father of the Nation in 1942.
francisco-pizarro: Francisco Pizarro was born in Trujillo, in the Crown of Castile, probably in the 1470s, the illegitimate son of the infantry colonel Gonzalo Pizarro and Francisca González, a woman of poor means. Little attention was paid to his education, and he grew up and remained illiterate. In 1513 he accompanied Vasco Núñez de Balboa across the Isthmus of Panama to the Pacific. Under the governor Pedro Arias Dávila he was assigned a repartimiento, arrested Balboa on the governor's orders, and served as mayor of Panama City from 1519 to 1523.

In 1524 Pizarro formed a partnership with the priest Hernando de Luque and the soldier Diego de Almagro to explore and conquer the south. His first expedition left Panama in November 1524 and failed, and the second, from March 1526, produced Bartolomé Ruiz's capture of a balsa raft carrying textiles, gold, silver and emeralds. When the new governor refused a third expedition, Pizarro went to Spain, and Queen Isabel signed the Capitulación de Toledo on 6 July 1529, naming him governor of New Castile, a grant that later angered Almagro, who held lesser positions.

The third expedition left with three ships, 180 men and 27 horses. In May 1532 Pizarro founded San Miguel de Piura, the first Spanish settlement in Peru, and on 24 September he advanced inland with 200 men. At Cajamarca in November 1532 he captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa. Atahualpa filled a room with gold as a ransom, but Pizarro charged him with crimes and had him garrotted in July 1533. He entered Cuzco that year and founded Lima in January 1535, and in 1537 he was made 1st Marquess of the Conquest.

On 26 June 1541 about twenty supporters of Diego de Almagro II stormed Pizarro's palace in Lima and killed him, and he reportedly drew a cross in his blood before dying. His remains were buried under the cathedral.

He destroyed the Inca state and ruled the area for almost a decade. The Inca religion was replaced by Christianity, and much of the local population was reduced to effective serfdom under the encomienda system. He is reviled for ordering Atahualpa's death despite the ransom, which he kept after paying the king his due, and some Peruvians, particularly those of indigenous descent, regard him negatively.
francisco-solano-lopez: Francisco Solano López was born in Manorá, a district of Asunción. His father, Carlos Antonio López, became president in 1841 and commissioned him a brigadier general in 1844, at the age of 17. He studied fortifications and artillery in Rio de Janeiro and Asunción and commanded Paraguayan forces on the Argentine frontier during the Platine Wars.

In 1853 he was sent to Europe as minister plenipotentiary to Britain, France and the Kingdom of Sardinia, and spent more than a year and a half there, mostly in Paris. He bought arms and steamers, brought back European military methods, and set up the first electric telegraph in South America. In Paris he met the Irish-born Eliza Lynch, who returned with him and lived with him until his death. Back in Paraguay he became Minister of War and in 1862 Vice President.

When his father died in 1862, Congress proclaimed López president for ten years. He kept the economic protectionism of his predecessors but abandoned strict isolation, hoping to make Paraguay a third force between Argentina and the Empire of Brazil in the Rio de la Plata basin. He allied with Uruguay's government, introduced compulsory military service and built one of the best-trained, though poorly equipped, armies in the region.

When Brazil invaded Uruguay in October 1864, López seized a Brazilian steamer and declared war that December, invading Mato Grosso. After Argentina refused passage across Corrientes, he declared war on Argentina on 13 April 1865. On 1 May 1865 Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay signed the Treaty of the Triple Alliance, aiming to overthrow his government. The destruction of the Paraguayan fleet at Riachuelo on 11 June 1865 gave the Allies control of the rivers. Talks with Bartolomé Mitre in 1866 failed. In 1868, believing in a conspiracy, he had several hundred people executed, among them relatives, ministers, officers, clergy and foreigners.

Allied troops took Asunción on 1 January 1869. López retreated north and made a last stand at Cerro Corá, where Brazilian forces reached his camp on 1 March 1870. Wounded, he refused General José Antônio Correia da Câmara's call to surrender and died in the struggle. His last words are disputed: "I die for my nation" or "I die with my nation".

Paraguay lost between a quarter and a third of its territory, and at least half its people died. Paraguayans still debate whether he was a leader who held on to the end or one who led the country into a war it could not win. Others in Latin America see him as a defender of small nations. 1 March is a national holiday, and he lies in the National Pantheon of the Heroes in Asunción.
franco-dutch-war: France had backed the Dutch Republic during the Eighty Years War against Spain, and the Peace of Münster of 1648 confirmed Dutch independence and closed the Scheldt estuary, which benefited Amsterdam by removing its rival Antwerp. After the death of William II of Orange in 1650, political control passed to the urban patricians, the Regenten, and Johan de Witt was Grand Pensionary from 1653 to 1672. The States of Holland refused to support a division of the Spanish Netherlands, which convinced Louis XIV that his aims could only be reached by force.

The French offensive began on 4 May 1672, with Turenne's main army of 50,000 and a second force under Condé. By 5 June the French had taken Rheinberg, Orsoy and Burick with little resistance, and they crossed the Rhine, fighting the Battle of Tolhuis on 12 June. William of Orange withdrew behind the Holland Water Line, the flooding of which had been ordered only on 8 June. The Dutch remember 1672 as the Rampjaar, the Disaster Year. Rioting in the cities of Holland replaced Regenten with Orangist partisans, and French peace terms of 1 July caused outrage.

The position stabilised by late July. Emperor Leopold I, Spain and Brandenburg-Prussia came to the Dutch side, and England left the war in February 1674. In 1673 the French took Maastricht, which surrendered on 30 June. In 1674 they overran Franche-Comté in under six weeks, and Turenne won a winter campaign in Alsace that ended in January 1675. William was halted by Condé at the Battle of Seneffe. Sweden, France's ally, invaded Brandenburg and was beaten at Fehrbellin.

Neither side won a decisive victory. By 1677 France held Franche-Comté and had made gains in the Spanish Netherlands and Alsace, helped by victory at the Battle of Cassel and by Vauban's line of fortresses. The Peace of Nijmegen of September 1678 returned Charleroi and Ghent to Spain, while France received all of Franche-Comté and towns including Ypres, Valenciennes and Saint-Omer. All but Ypres remain French. The terms were worse than those on offer in July 1672.

Louis came to be called the Sun King in the years after the war. William of Orange became dominant in Dutch domestic politics, and this helped him build the anti-French Grand Alliance of the Nine Years' War (1688-1697) and the War of the Spanish Succession (1701-1714).
franco-prussian-war: The war grew out of the unification of the German states under Otto von Bismarck. France had been the dominant power of continental Europe after the Franco-Austrian War of 1859, and the decisive Prussian victory over Austria in 1866 appeared to call that position into question. In 1870 Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen was offered the vacant Spanish throne and withdrew his acceptance, but the French ambassador then asked King Wilhelm I at Ems to renounce any future claim. Wilhelm refused, and Bismarck made the report of the exchange public in altered wording. Crowds in Paris demanded war.

France mobilised on 15 July 1870, and its parliament voted for war the next day. The German coalition mobilised more effectively, and its forces were superior in numbers, training and leadership and made better use of railways and artillery.

France invaded German territory on 2 August, and German armies entered north-eastern France on 4 August. French defeats followed at Wissembourg, Spicheren and Wörth, and the largest battle of the war, at Gravelotte on 18 August, drove Marshal Bazaine's Army of the Rhine back into Metz. At the Battle of Sedan on 1 September the Prussians surrounded the Army of Châlons, and on 2 September Napoleon III surrendered with 104,000 of his soldiers.

On 4 September a popular uprising overthrew the Second Empire, and Jules Favre, Léon Gambetta and General Louis-Jules Trochu proclaimed a Government of National Defence and the Third Republic. The Germans began the siege of Paris on 19 September. Bazaine's army at Metz surrendered on 26 October. Paris, starving, fell on 28 January 1871, and an armistice was agreed.

In the last days of the war the German states proclaimed the German Empire under Wilhelm I. By the Treaty of Frankfurt of 10 May 1871, France paid an indemnity of five billion francs and ceded most of Alsace and parts of Lorraine, which became the Imperial Territory of Alsace-Lorraine.

In France the war ended imperial rule and began the first lasting republican government. Resentment at its handling led to the Paris Commune, held from 18 March until the army retook Paris in the Semaine Sanglante of 21 to 28 May. The defeat also produced revanchism in France, a demand for revenge and the return of Alsace and Lorraine. Germany supplanted France as the dominant land power, and other armies adopted the Prussian general staff, universal conscription and detailed mobilisation systems.
franco-spanish-war-1635-1659: In the first stages of the Thirty Years' War France avoided direct involvement, financing Habsburg opponents such as the Dutch Republic and backing the Swedish intervention. After the Imperial-Spanish victory at Nördlingen in September 1634 forced the Swedes out of southern Germany, and most of their German allies made peace at Prague in April 1635, Louis XIII and Richelieu decided on direct intervention. France signed an anti-Spanish alliance with the Dutch and the Treaty of Compiègne with Sweden, and declared war on Spain in May 1635.

A French army of 27,000 defeated the Spanish at Les Avins in May 1635 but lost heavily to disease at Leuven and withdrew. In 1636 a Spanish incursion reached Corbie and caused panic in Paris, but the Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand of Austria retreated for lack of supplies. With the French in Alsace, Spain had to supply Flanders by sea, and in 1639 the Dutch destroyed a large Spanish supply fleet at the Battle of the Downs. Taxes and the cost of the war led to open revolts in Portugal and Catalonia in 1640, which France supported.

On 19 May 1643, five days after the death of Louis XIII, Louis II de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, defeated the Spanish Army of Flanders at Rocroi. The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 recognised Dutch independence and, under the Treaty of Münster, gave France strategic places in Alsace and Lorraine and Pinerolo, but left France and Spain at war. Spain backed French rebels in the Fronde, and in 1657 Cardinal Mazarin allied France with the Commonwealth of England.

Under the Treaty of the Pyrenees, signed on 5 November 1659, France gained Artois, Hainaut and Roussillon, which fixed the border along the Pyrenees but divided the historic Principality of Catalonia. Spain recognised the French gains of Westphalia, France withdrew support from Portugal, and Condé regained his titles and possessions. The treaty included the marriage contract of Louis XIV and Maria Theresa of Spain, which he later used to justify the War of Devolution.

Traditional historiography saw the war as the start of France replacing Spain as the predominant European power. Most historians now view it as militarily indecisive, a stalemate from 1637 to 1659, though Spain's economic and military power declined abruptly after 1659 and it became less able to defend territory outside Peninsular Spain without foreign help.
franco-thai-war: The Franco-Siamese Crisis of 1893 and the Franco-Siamese Treaty of 1907 left Siam without the territories of Laos and Cambodia, a loss later seen in Thailand as a national humiliation. Plaek Phibunsongkhram, known as Phibun, became prime minister on 16 December 1938 and had a propaganda campaign run to reclaim lost territories. Siam was renamed Thailand in June 1939. France signed a non-aggression treaty with Thailand on 12 June 1940, days before the fall of France. That defeat left the colonial administration in Indochina cut off from help, and Japan forced the French to allow it military bases. The apparent submissiveness of the French led Phibun to believe France would not resist seriously.

The Vichy French army in Indochina numbered about 50,000 men, 12,000 of them French, with only 20 tanks; the Royal Thai Army had 60,000 men and nearly one hundred armoured vehicles. Border skirmishes along the Mekong began in October 1940, and Thai aircraft bombed Vientiane, Phnom Penh, Sisophon and Battambang. On 5 January 1941, after a reported French attack on Aranyaprathet, two Thai armies attacked Laos and Cambodia. They overran Laos swiftly, while French forces in Cambodia rallied. A French counterattack on 16 January failed in the fiercest fight of the war.

On 17 January a French squadron surprised a Thai detachment at anchor off Ko Chang, sinking two torpedo boats and disabling a coastal defence ship without French casualties. Japan then mediated. A ceasefire took effect on 28 January, and armistice documents were signed aboard the cruiser Natori on 31 January.

A peace treaty signed in Tokyo on 9 May 1941 had France, coerced by Japan, give up the disputed border territories: Battambang and Pailin, Siem Reap, Banteay Meanchey and Oddar Meanchey, Preah Vihear, and Xaignabouli with part of Luang Prabang. Because Japan wished to keep its relationship with Vichy, the Thais accepted only a quarter of the territory they had gained and paid six million piastres to the French. In Thailand the settlement was seen as a personal triumph for Phibun, who erected the Victory Monument in Bangkok. The real beneficiary was Japan, which extended its influence in both countries; it invaded Thailand on 8 December 1941, and Thailand was allied with Japan until 1945.
francois-duvalier: François Duvalier was born in Port-au-Prince on 14 April 1907, the son of Duval Duvalier, a justice of the peace, teacher and journalist whose family came from Martinique, and Ulyssia Abraham, a baker. He completed a degree in medicine at the University of Haiti in 1934 and spent a year at the University of Michigan studying public health. From 1943 he took part in a campaign to control typhus, yaws, malaria and other tropical diseases, and his patients called him Papa Doc. The racism and violence of the United States occupation of Haiti, which began in 1915, inspired a black nationalism in him, and in 1938 he co-founded the journal Les Griots.

Duvalier became Director General of the National Public Health Service in 1946 and Minister of Health and Labor in 1949 under President Dumarsais Estimé. He left the government after Paul Magloire's coup of 1950 and went into hiding in the countryside in 1954. In the 1957 campaign he stood against the mulatto landowner Louis Déjoie, appealing to the black majority's resentment of the small mulatto elite. He was elected president on 22 September 1957 with 679,884 votes to Déjoie's 266,992, although there are accounts of fraud and intimidation.

After an attempted coup in July 1958 he dismissed the general staff and turned the Presidential Guard into an elite corps. In 1959 he created the militia known as the Tonton Macoute, which by 1961 was twice as big as the army. A sole-candidate election in 1961 extended his term, and a referendum on 14 June 1964 made him president for life, with ballots reportedly premarked yes. His government is estimated to have killed between 30,000 and 60,000 people, and many educated professionals fled to New York, Miami, Montreal, Paris and African states.

He cultivated a personality cult that drew on Vodou, modelling his image on the lwa Baron Samedi, and he expelled foreign bishops, which brought his excommunication. A concordat of 15 August 1966 lifted it and let him nominate Haitian bishops.

Duvalier died of heart disease and diabetes on 21 April 1971, aged 64, and his 19-year-old son Jean-Claude, called Baby Doc, succeeded him. He had suffered a heart attack in 1959, and he had been a diabetic since early adulthood. The regime fell on 8 February 1986, when a crowd attacked his mausoleum. Many books treat the Duvalier era, the best known being Graham Greene's novel The Comedians.
francois-fenelon: François de Salignac de la Mothe-Fénelon was born on 6 August 1651 at the Château de Fénelon in Sainte-Mondane, Périgord, into an old noble family reduced to modest means, in which fifteen generations had held the bishopric of nearby Sarlat. Private tutors taught him the Greek and Latin classics, and his uncle arranged his studies in Paris, where he preached a public sermon at 15. He was ordained about 1675.

In 1679 the Archbishop of Paris made him director of the Nouvelles-Catholiques, a community for young Huguenot girls about to join the Catholic Church, and in 1687 he published his Treatise on the Education of Girls. After Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, he preached to Protestants in Saintonge at Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet's suggestion.

In 1689 he became tutor to the seven-year-old Duke of Burgundy, second in line to the throne. For his pupil he wrote Fables, Dialogues of the Dead and, in 1693 and 1694, The Adventures of Telemachus, a novel about the son of Ulysses that also attacks the divine-right absolute monarchy of Louis XIV's France. It contains the line that good kings are rare and most monarchs bad.

Published in 1699, it was a best seller across Europe and supplied the plot of Mozart's opera Idomeneo. It is read as the programme of the circle of the Duc de Beauvilliers and the Duc de Chevreuse, who hoped for a less centralised monarchy after the king's death. Fénelon also argued that all wars are civil wars, since each person owes more to humanity than to a single country.

Fénelon defended the Quietism of his cousin Madame Guyon. He refused to sign Bossuet's Instructions on the states of prayer and set out his own view in the Maxims of the Saints. Louis XIV removed him as tutor and confined him to the archdiocese of Cambrai, and on 12 March 1699 the Inquisition condemned the book, Pope Innocent XII listing 23 propositions. Fénelon at once submitted. Telemachus angered the king the same year, so the confinement stayed. He sheltered refugees from the War of the Spanish Succession in his palace, wrote against the Jansenist party and died on 7 January 1715.
francois-grimaldi: Francesco Grimaldi, called François in French, was the son of Guglielmo Grimaldi and his wife Giacobina or Giacoba, a Genoese noblewoman. His family descended from Grimaldo Canella, a twelfth-century Genoese statesman who served several times as Consul of Genoa. In the 13th and 14th centuries the cities of northern Italy were torn by the conflict between Guelphs, who were allied to the Pope, and Ghibellines, who supported the Holy Roman Emperor. The Grimaldi were among the most influential families of Genoa and held to the Guelph side.

In 1295 Guelph forces from Liguria under Francesco Grimaldi were routed by a Ghibelline advance and had to take refuge on the Rock of Monaco. In the same year he married Aurelia del Carretto, the widow of his cousin Lanfranco Grimaldi. On 8 January 1297 he dressed as a Franciscan friar and led a small band of followers to the gates of Monaco's castle, where they were let in, and seized it together with his cousin Rainier I, Lord of Cagnes. The coat of arms of Monaco recalls the event with two friars holding swords. The citadel was held for four years, until the Ghibelline stronghold was worn down by prolonged Genoese attack.

Francesco failed to establish Grimaldi rule over Monaco, though this was the family's first attempt. The Grimaldi later resolved to regain the territory because of its value as a base for the maritime trade that was the source of the family's wealth. His marriage was childless, so the modern Grimaldi are not his descendants. After his death in 1309 he was succeeded by his cousin and stepson Rainier I of Monaco, Lord of Cagnes, from whom the later rulers descend. In 1419, more than a century after the coup, three Grimaldi brothers, Ambroise, Antoine and Jean, bought Monaco from Queen Yolande of Aragon in the name of the family, which became the undisputed ruler of the Rock.
francois-guizot: François Guizot was born on 4 October 1787 at Nîmes into a bourgeois Protestant family. His father was executed on the scaffold there on 8 April 1794, during the Reign of Terror, when François was six. His mother took him to Geneva, where he was educated, and in 1805 he arrived in Paris as a tutor. He began writing for the journal Publiciste and in 1812 married Pauline de Meulan, a fellow contributor. Under the Restoration he was one of the leaders of the Doctrinaires, a small party attached to the charter and the crown that favoured the juste milieu, a middle path between absolutism and popular government. In 1822 his lectures were banned.

After the July Revolution of 1830 he supported the constitutional monarchy of Louis Philippe I. In 1832 he became minister of public instruction and carried the law of 28 June 1833, which established primary education in France. He also revived the Académie des Sciences Morales et Politiques and founded the Société de l'histoire de France, which published medieval chronicles at the state's expense. He went to London as ambassador in the spring of 1840. From 29 October 1840 he led the government for nearly eight years, as foreign minister and, after Marshal Soult retired, as prime minister from September 1847.

With Lord Aberdeen he built an understanding between France and Britain, and Napoleon's ashes were brought from St Helena. Opponents called his foreign policy subservient to England, and he answered that they would never reach the height of his disdain. He was unpopular with the more advanced liberals for restricting the vote to propertied men. When he banned the reform banquets in January 1848, the opposition grew, and on 23 February 1848 the king told him he doubted he could keep him as prime minister. Guizot resigned and escaped to London, where he arrived on 3 March.

He never returned to public life and spent most of each year at Val Richer in Normandy, supporting himself by writing. His works include histories of England under Cromwell, the Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire de mon temps, and a history of France told to his grandchildren. He was elected to the Académie Française in 1836. He died in 1874, after reciting verses of Pierre Corneille and texts from the Bible, according to report.

In the 1820s his Histoire générale de la civilisation en Europe was admired by John Stuart Mill, Goethe and Alexis de Tocqueville. His critics call him a conservative or reactionary for resisting universal suffrage, but he defended representative government against both absolutism and the excesses of democracy, and he called for the abolition of capital punishment.
francois-michel-le-tellier-marquis-de-lo: Louvois was born in Paris on 18 January 1641, the son of Michel Le Tellier and Élisabeth Turpin. His father instructed him in the management of state affairs, and the young man won the king's confidence; in 1666 he succeeded his father as war minister. In the War of Devolution (1667 to 1668) Turenne noticed his talents and taught him the art of supplying armies. After the peace of Aix-la-Chapelle he devoted himself to organising the French army. The years from 1668 to 1672 were, in the words of Camille Rousset, years of preparation, when Lionne laboured to find allies, Colbert money and Louvois soldiers for Louis XIV.

With his father, Louvois oversaw an increase in the French Army to 340,000 soldiers, which fought four wars between 1667 and 1713. According to Cathal Nolan he created the Régiment du Roi in 1663 and founded the Royal-Artillerie regiment in 1673. He reorganised the army and exercised strict control over officers, which slowed tactical and operational responses. His logistics were more successful: he improved the magazine system left by his father and built up enough grain and wagons to supply his armies with 200,000 rations a day for up to six months in the Franco-Dutch War (1672 to 1678). He also founded the Hôtel des Invalides and reorganised the military orders of merit.

Louvois had a prominent part in the capture of Strasbourg in 1681 and in the revocation of the Edict of Nantes. He annulled a clause of the revocation allowing some liberty of conscience, with the phrase that the king wished the worst harshness on those who would not share his religion, and he claimed credit for inventing the dragonnades. After Colbert died in 1683 he took over the ministry of public buildings, and in 1688 he began the collection of plans-reliefs of French strongholds, now the Musée des Plans-Reliefs.

Louvois died suddenly of apoplexy on 16 July 1691 after leaving the king's cabinet, although Voltaire claimed he died while taking the waters at Balaruc, and the suddenness of his death caused suspicion of poison. Historians credit him with creating the civilian role of minister of war. French writers have compared him with Carnot, since both reorganised armies with existing resources and new systems, though his methods were unscrupulous in his private life and his work, including harsh measures against Huguenots.
francois-mitterrand: François Mitterrand was born on 26 October 1916 in Jarnac, Charente, into a devoutly Catholic and conservative family; his father was a stationmaster. He studied at the École Libre des Sciences Politiques in Paris. Called up in 1938, he was wounded by shrapnel on 14 June 1940 and captured by the Germans on 21 June. He escaped from a prisoner-of-war camp on 28 November 1941 with forged papers, and then worked as a mid-level official of the Vichy government looking after prisoners of war. In 1943 he built up a resistance network of former prisoners. His wartime conduct caused much controversy in France in the 1980s and 1990s.

Under the Fourth Republic Mitterrand held ministerial office several times, among them Minister of the Interior in the cabinet of Pierre Mendès-France in 1954–1955, when he had to direct the response to the Algerian War of Independence. In 1958 he was one of the few who opposed Charles de Gaulle's plan for a Fifth Republic, and his book Le Coup d'État permanent (1964) criticised de Gaulle's personal power. In 1971 he became first secretary of the Socialist Party, arguing that an alliance with the Communists was necessary to win power. He was the left's standard bearer in 1965 and 1974.

On 10 May 1981 Mitterrand became the first socialist President of the Fifth Republic. His first term began with nationalisation of key firms and a 39-hour work week, alongside the abolition of the death penalty, but facing economic tensions he soon turned to austerity and market liberalisation. In July 1985 French intelligence agents sank the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland, killing a photographer.

He was re-elected in 1988, and twice governed in cohabitation with conservative cabinets led by Jacques Chirac and Édouard Balladur. With the German chancellor Helmut Kohl he advanced European integration through the Maastricht Treaty. He left office in 1995 and died in Paris on 8 January 1996 of prostate cancer, which had been concealed for most of his presidency.
francois-ravaillac: Ravaillac was born in 1578 at Angoulême into an educated family. His grandfather François Ravaillac was the prosecutor in Angoulême, and two of his maternal uncles were canons of Angoulême Cathedral. His father, Jean Ravaillac, was a violent man whose misdeeds caused a public scandal and legal difficulties, while his mother, Françoise Dubreuil, was known for her Catholic piety. He worked first as a servant and later as a school teacher. Obsessed with religion, he sought admission to the ascetic Feuillants order but was dismissed after a short probation for being prey to visions. An application to the Society of Jesus in 1606 was also unsuccessful.

In 1609 Ravaillac claimed a vision instructing him to convince King Henry IV of France to convert the Huguenots to Catholicism. Between Pentecost 1609 and May 1610 he made three trips to Paris to tell the king, lodging with Charlotte du Tillet, mistress of the duc d'Épernon. Unable to meet him, he interpreted Henry's decision to invade the Spanish Netherlands as the start of a war against the Pope, and resolved to kill the king.

On 14 May 1610 he waited in the Rue de la Ferronnerie. The king's coach was halted by a blockage in the street, and Ravaillac climbed onto the wheel and stabbed Henry to death. The Duke of Montbazon, riding with the king, was wounded. Ravaillac was seized and taken to the Hôtel de Retz to avoid a lynching, then to the Conciergerie.

He was frequently tortured to make him name accomplices, but denied he had any and said he had acted alone. The king had been on his way to visit Maximilien de Béthune at the Arsenal to make final preparations for intervention in the War of the Jülich Succession. According to the account, Ravaillac had seen that the king wanted to make war on the Pope, in order to transfer the Holy See to Paris.

On 27 May 1610 Ravaillac was taken to the Place de Grève in Paris, tortured a last time and pulled apart by four horses, a method reserved for regicides. His parents were forced into exile, and the rest of his family was ordered never to use the name Ravaillac again. In January 1611 Jacqueline d'Escoman denounced the duc d'Épernon as responsible for the king's death and was jailed for life. Philippe Erlanger concluded that Ravaillac, the king's mistress Henriette d'Entragues and Charlotte du Tillet planned the assassination, while Roland Mousnier held that he had no accomplices but his confessors. Later ages saw Ravaillac as an evil figure, though a few Catholics viewed him as a hero.
francois-tombalbaye: François Tombalbaye was born on 15 June 1918 in the village of Bessada in southern Chad, near Koumra. His father was a prominent trader and he belonged to the Sara, the main ethnic group of the five southern prefectures. He attended a primary school run by Protestant missionaries in Sarh and studied to become a teacher in Brazzaville, since Chad had no such schools. During the Second World War he fought for Free France. In 1946 or 1947 he formed a chapter of the Chadian Progressive Party in Sarh, and in 1949 the French authorities revoked his teaching post as punishment for his political activism.

Tombalbaye won a seat in the colonial territorial assembly in 1952, succeeded Gabriel Lisette as leader of the party in March 1959 and led the independent state from 11 August 1960. He banned the other parties, dissolved the National Assembly in 1963 after rioting and began replacing French administrators with local staff. A programme of Africanization largely ignored the Muslim north and centre. On 1 November 1965 riots over taxes and corruption in Guéra Prefecture caused 500 deaths and spread, and the rebel FROLINAT, based in Sudan, took up arms. Tombalbaye called on France, which agreed to help on condition of reforms; he accepted in 1969, and prisoners were released.

In 1971 an attempted coup with links to Muammar al-Gaddafi was uncovered, and he cut relations with Libya. Drought gripped the country, and by the end of 1972 over 1,000 political prisoners had been arrested. In August 1973 he replaced his party with the National Movement for the Cultural and Social Revolution, renamed Fort-Lamy as N'Djamena and took the name N'Garta. Under authenticité, missionaries were expelled and non-Muslim men in the south had to undergo yondo initiation rites, including floggings and scarification, to gain promotion. These rites were native only to a subgroup of the Sara.

His support in the south dwindled, and he made arbitrary promotions and demotions in the army. On 13 April 1975, after some leading officers had been arrested over an alleged coup, he was reportedly shot in his palace and died of his wounds. His body was buried in secret at Faya. The military installed Félix Malloum, by then a general, as head of state.
franconia: Franconia is not a political entity with a fixed area, and it is debated whether some districts belong to it. It is defined by its history, its culture and especially the East Franconian dialect, and in part by the territory of the former Duchy of Franconia and the Franconian Circle. Most of it lies north and south of the River Main and its tributary the Regnitz, in the three Bavarian districts of Lower, Middle and Upper Franconia. Upland ranges such as the Franconian Jura, the Fichtel Mountains, the Rhön and the Spessart surround it. Its highest mountain is the Schneeberg in the Fichtel Mountains, at 1,051 metres.

Fossil finds show people were living in the region about 600,000 years ago. In the Iron Age, from about 800 BCE, the Celts were the first people discernible there, and they built hill forts and settlements such as the one Ptolemy called oppidum Menosgada on the Staffelberg. As Rome expanded in the first century BCE and Germanic tribes advanced from the north, Celtic culture declined. The southern parts came under Roman control, but most of the region stayed in free Germania.

The Franks gained the region through victories over the Alamanni and Thuringians in the 6th century. Its name does not mean it was the homeland of the Franks, since it was only partly settled by Franks from the Rhineland. After the Frankish Empire was divided, East Francia was formed from the territories of the dioceses of Mainz, Worms, Würzburg and Speyer, and Bamberg was added later. Slavs began to settle the north-east from the 7th century. Irish and Anglo-Saxon monks first spread Christianity strongly there, and Saint Kilian was martyred at Würzburg in the late 7th century. Saint Boniface probably carried the mission to the ordinary people.

On 2 July 1500, under Emperor Maximilian I, the Empire was divided into Imperial Circles, and the Franconian Circle was formed in 1512. The region was severely affected by Kleinstaaterei, a patchwork of tiny states, and the bishops of Würzburg used the nominal title of Duke of Franconia. In 1559 the circle was given jurisdiction over coinage. After the Holy Roman Empire ended, Napoleon's restructuring of the south German states gave most of Franconia to Bavaria.

Franconia is divided among Bavaria, Thuringia, Baden-Württemberg and Hesse, and its largest part belongs to Bavaria. Its largest city is Nuremberg, followed by Fürth, Würzburg and Erlangen, and the region has roughly five million inhabitants. Franconians count as one of the four tribes of Bavaria. Large areas of Middle and Upper Franconia are Protestant, while Lower Franconia and western Upper Franconia are mostly Catholic, reflecting the territories of the Franconian Circle.
francysk-skaryna: Francysk Skaryna was born into a wealthy family of Polotsk, then a major trade and manufacturing centre of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. His father, Luka Skaryna, and his older brother Ivan were merchants. The date of his birth is unknown. In 1504 he is recorded as a student at Jagiellonian University, where he graduated Bachelor of Arts in 1506, and in 1512 he received a doctorate in medicine at the University of Padua, having asked to take the examination there without, it seems, studying in the city. Whether he was Catholic or Orthodox is not known for certain.

By 1517 Skaryna was in Prague, where he rented a printing house from a merchant named Severin and began publishing a new translation of the Bible with his own prefaces. His Psalter appeared on 6 August 1517, and on 10 August 1518 he issued four books at once. The Bible of twenty-three books printed from 1517 to 1519 under the name Biblia Ruska was the second printed Bible of the Slavic world, after a Czech edition. All were in quarto, in a Church Slavonic with many Ruthenian words and some Polish and Czech influence.

Skaryna added his own comments, forewords, afterwords and prints with his image, which no other Bible of Eastern Europe has. In his prefaces he said that he wanted ordinary people to become acquainted with wisdom and science. In 1522 he opened the first printing house in Vilnius and published The Little Travel Book, followed by the Apostol in 1525. He tried to sell his books in Moscow in the late 1520s or early 1530s without success.

After his brother's death in 1529 Skaryna went to Poznań for a share of Ivan's property. In 1532 he served as doctor and secretary to John, Bishop of Vilnius, and when Ivan's creditors had him imprisoned in Poznań for several months, royal certificates of 21 and 25 November 1532 exempted him from every jurisdiction but the King's.

The last record of him dates from 1534, when he moved to Prague. He is presumed to have died between 1551 and 29 January 1552. Some Belarusian scholars see him as a Renaissance figure comparable to Copernicus and Erasmus, though the Oktoikh of Schweipolt Fiol, printed in 1491, was an earlier Cyrillic book.
frankenstein: Mary Shelley's mother, Mary Wollstonecraft, died of infection eleven days after her birth, and she grew up among the writers and political figures who gathered at the home of her father, William Godwin. She met Percy Bysshe Shelley at sixteen, and in the summer of 1816 she, Percy and Claire Clairmont visited Lord Byron at the Villa Diodati by Lake Geneva. It was the rainy summer known as the Year Without a Summer, after the eruption of Mount Tambora in 1815, and the party stayed indoors reading German ghost stories. Byron proposed that each of them write a ghost story.

Shelley could think of nothing for days. After a night of talk about the principle of life and galvanism, she imagined a pale student of unhallowed arts kneeling beside the thing he had put together. She finished writing in April or May 1817.

Victor Frankenstein, born in Naples to an upper-class Genevese family, is obsessed with alchemy in youth and then turns to chemistry and electricity. At the University of Ingolstadt he finds a way to create life and assembles a large humanoid creature from body parts. Repelled when it awakens, he flees. In Shelley's text Victor discovers an unknown principle of life and does not say how it works; the electric jolt and the stitched-together image come from James Whale's 1931 film.

The creature teaches himself to speak and read, learns his origin from papers in his clothes, and is driven away by a family he has watched. Embittered, he travels to Geneva, kills Victor's younger brother William and frames the servant Justine, who is executed. He then asks Victor to make him a female companion. He compares himself to Adam and to the fallen angel of Milton, and the subtitle The Modern Prometheus alludes to the Titan who gave fire to humans.

Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus appeared anonymously on 1 January 1818 in three volumes, in an edition of 500 copies, with a preface by Percy Shelley and a dedication to Godwin. The second English edition, of 11 August 1823, named Mary Shelley as author after the success of Richard Brinsley Peake's stage play Presumption, which she attended on 29 August 1823.

The revised one-volume edition of 31 October 1831 added a new introduction and a more moral tone, and it is the one most widely read. The novel has influenced literature and popular culture and produced a genre of horror stories, films and plays, and the name Frankenstein is often wrongly given to the creature.
frankenthal: Frankenthal was first mentioned in 772. An Augustinian monastery was built there in 1119, and its ruins, known after the founder as the Erkenbertruine, still stand in the town centre. In the second half of the 16th century people from Flanders, persecuted for their religious beliefs, settled in the town. They were industrious and artistic, brought economic prosperity and included important carpet weavers, jewellers and artists, whose Frankenthaler Malerschule, or Frankenthal school of painting, acquired some fame. In 1577 Count Palatine Johann Casimir raised the settlement to the status of a city.

In 1600 Frankenthal was converted into a fortress. In 1621 English soldiers under Sir Horace Vere garrisoned it and the Spanish besieged it during the Thirty Years' War, after which troops of the opposing sides occupied it in turn. Trade and industry were ruined, and the town was not rebuilt until 1682. French troops burnt it to the ground in 1689 in the War of the Grand Alliance, and it did not fully recover for more than fifty years.

In 1750 Elector Charles Theodore made Frankenthal a centre of industry. A port was built between 1772 and 1781, factories were opened and mulberry trees were planted for silk production. The porcelain factory opened in 1755 and remained in production until 1800. The town came under French occupation in 1797 and passed to Bavaria in 1816, and modern industrialisation began around 1859. The synagogue built in 1884 was burnt to the ground on Kristallnacht in 1938, and a bombing raid in 1943 almost destroyed the town centre. Since 1946 Frankenthal has been part of the state of Rhineland-Palatinate, and it had 49,051 inhabitants in 2022 and some medium-sized industries.
frankfurt: Frankfurt lies on both sides of the river Main, south-east of the Taunus mountain range, in the western part of Germany. Its downtown is north of the Main in the Altstadt, the historical centre. The southern part of the city holds the Frankfurt City Forest, Germany's largest forest within a city. A ring-shaped Green Belt, formally created in 1991, covers a third of the administrative area.

The name derives from Franconofurd, from the Germanic tribe of the Franks and furt, a ford where the river was shallow enough to cross on foot. The first written records of 794 give Frankonovurd in Old High German and Vadum Francorum in Latin.

The first traces of Roman settlement along the river Nidda date to the reign of Emperor Vespasian, from 69 to 79 CE, and Nida was a Roman civitas capital. Alemanni and Franks later lived in the area, and in 794 Charlemagne presided over an imperial assembly and church synod at which Franconofurd was first mentioned. It was one of the two capitals of his grandson Louis the German, together with Regensburg, and Louis founded the collegiate church, rededicated in 1239 to Bartholomew the Apostle and now Frankfurt Cathedral.

Frankfurt has been an imperial city since 1372. As the Free City of Frankfurt it was a city state for nearly five centuries and one of the most important cities of the Holy Roman Empire, as a site of imperial coronations. It lost its sovereignty when the empire collapsed in 1806, regained it in 1815 and lost it again in 1866, when the Kingdom of Prussia annexed it after the Austro-Prussian War. It has been part of the state of Hesse since 1945.

Frankfurt am Main is the most populous city in the German state of Hesse, with 778,589 inhabitants. It is a financial centre, home to the European Central Bank, the Deutsche Bundesbank and the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, and Frankfurt Airport is the busiest in Germany.

The Römer, a complex of nine houses that the city council acquired in 1405 from a wealthy merchant family, is the city hall. Its Kaisersaal, the Emperor's Hall, is where newly crowned emperors held their banquets. The Römer was partly destroyed in the Second World War and rebuilt, and the Goethe House, where Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was born in 1749, was destroyed and rebuilt in 1947.
frankfurt-parliament: The assembly was part of the outcome of the March Revolution in the states of the German Confederation. Opposition politicians demanded basic and civic rights, liberal governments in the states and above all a German nation-state with a pan-German constitution and a popular assembly. On 5 March 1848 they met at the Heidelberg Assembly and resolved to form a pre-parliament, which sat in St Paul's Church in Frankfurt from 31 March to 3 April. It decided to cooperate with the Confederate Diet in forming a national constitutional assembly, with one deputy for every 50,000 inhabitants.

The assembly was elected on 1 May 1848 and opened on 18 May in the Paulskirche, with 379 deputies present. Heinrich von Gagern was elected president. Because it had not been created by the German Confederation, it had no head of state, no government and no legal legitimation, and powers such as France and Russia declined to recognise it. On 28 June it voted for a Provisional Central Power and the next day chose Archduke John of Austria as Regent of the Empire. In November 1848 the Austrian army executed the deputy Robert Blum in Vienna, despite his parliamentary immunity, which showed how dependent the assembly was on the goodwill of the states.

The deputies began drafting the constitution on 19 October 1848. It passed on 27 March 1849 by 267 votes to 263, with a hereditary emperor, a directly elected lower house and a House of the States. On 28 March the assembly chose the Prussian king as emperor.

Frederick William IV refused the crown, on the grounds that the constitution and the offer abridged the rights of the princes, and Prussia rejected the constitution on 21 April 1849. The Austrian deputies had left Frankfurt on 5 April, and Gagern resigned on 10 May. Revolts followed in Dresden, the Palatinate and Baden. On 31 May the remaining deputies decided to move to Stuttgart, and from 6 June a rump parliament of 154 deputies met there. On 18 June the Württemberg army occupied the chamber and expelled the deputies from other states. In the 20th century major elements of the Frankfurt constitution became models for the Weimar Constitution of 1919 and the Basic Law of 1949.
frankfurt-rhine-main: The Rhine-Main Metropolitan Region lies in the central-western part of Germany and stretches over parts of three states: Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate and Bavaria. It is named after its core city, Frankfurt, and the two rivers Rhine and Main. Its largest cities are Frankfurt am Main, Wiesbaden, Mainz, Darmstadt, Offenbach, Worms, Hanau and Aschaffenburg. The German Federal Ministry of Transport, Building and Urban Affairs designates it a European Metropolitan Region, and it covers roughly 13,000 square kilometres with a population above 5.9 million. It is the third-largest metropolitan region in Germany after Rhine-Ruhr and Berlin-Brandenburg.

The region is polycentric, but Frankfurt's economic size and political weight give it a monocentric relation with its commuter belt. Since the early 1970s the Frankfurt am Main metropolitan area has been defined as the cities of Frankfurt and Offenbach and their neighbouring districts. The Regierungsbezirk Darmstadt of Hesse lies entirely inside the region and adds Darmstadt and Wiesbaden, and a wider ring takes in Mainz in Rhineland-Palatinate and Aschaffenburg in Bavaria.

Its central position in south-western Germany made it an important industrial and transport centre once industrialisation began in the middle of the nineteenth century, and the area's growth is traced chiefly to favourable communications that promoted early industrialisation.

Banking, trade and logistics have largely replaced heavy industry. The European Central Bank is headquartered in Frankfurt am Main. The chemical industry has a long presence, notably in the Industriepark Höchst on the south-western edge of Frankfurt, which hosts over 90 chemical, pharmaceutical and healthcare firms. Insurers have offices in Darmstadt and Wiesbaden. Frankfurt Airport is the busiest in Germany by passenger numbers, and the Frankfurt am Main Hauptbahnhof and the Frankfurter Kreuz are among Europe's busiest rail and road interchanges. An S-Bahn network runs from Wiesbaden and Mainz in the west to Hanau in the east.

The region has five universities and over 20 colleges, with more than 200,000 students. Three public research universities, Goethe University Frankfurt, Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz and TU Darmstadt, form the Rhine Main Universities alliance.
franklin-d-roosevelt: Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born on 30 January 1882 in Hyde Park, New York, to James Roosevelt I and his second wife, Sara Ann Delano, who were sixth cousins from wealthy families. Apart from a stint in public school in Germany at nine, he was educated by tutors until 14, when he entered Groton School, whose headmaster Endicott Peabody urged students into public service. He graduated from Harvard University and married Eleanor Roosevelt, a niece of Theodore Roosevelt, on 17 March 1905.

In the Democratic landslide of 1910 Roosevelt won a surprising victory for a strongly Republican seat in the New York State Senate. In August 1921, at Campobello Island, he fell ill with what was diagnosed as polio, which left him permanently paralyzed from the waist down. He taught himself to walk short distances with iron braces and in 1926 established a rehabilitation centre at Warm Springs, Georgia.

He was elected governor of New York in 1928 by less than one percent. After winning the Democratic nomination on the fourth ballot in 1932, he pledged a new deal for the American people and defeated President Herbert Hoover.

Roosevelt had declined in health since at least 1940. On 12 April 1945, at the Little White House in Warm Springs, he said he had a terrific headache, slumped forward while sitting for a portrait, and was pronounced dead of a massive intracerebral hemorrhage, aged 63. The expansion of government programmes under Roosevelt redefined the role of government in the United States and permanently increased the power of the president at the expense of Congress. Surviving programmes include the Securities and Exchange Commission, the National Labor Relations Act and Social Security.
frankokratia: Frankokratia, also called Latinokratia, and for the Venetian domains the Venetian Occupation, names the collection of primarily French and Italian states, fiefs and colonies established on the territory of the partitioned Byzantine Empire after the Sack of Constantinople in 1204 during the Fourth Crusade. The terms come from Franks, the name the Orthodox Greeks gave to Western French and Italians whose homelands had once belonged to the Frankish Empire. The period's span differs by region, because the situation was volatile: Frankish states fragmented and changed hands, and Greek successor states reconquered many areas.

The Latin Empire (1204 to 1261), centred on Constantinople and covering Thrace and Bithynia, claimed nominal suzerainty over the other crusader states. It shrank to little more than its capital, which Michael VIII Palaiologos of the Empire of Nicaea captured in 1261. Among the other Latin states, the Kingdom of Thessalonica (1205 to 1224) fell to the Despotate of Epirus, and the Principality of Achaea (1205 to 1432) in the Peloponnese became the strongest, until the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea conquered it. The Duchy of Athens (1205 to 1458) passed to the Catalan Company in 1311 and to the Acciaiuoli family in 1388. The Duchy of the Archipelago, founded by the Sanudo family in 1207, lasted until 1579.

Genoese families such as the Gattilusi held Lesbos and other north-eastern Aegean islands, and the Maona company held Chios until 1566. The Republic of Venice built the most durable holdings: the Kingdom of Candia on Crete (1211 to 1715), Corfu for most of the period from 1386 to 1797, the coastal fortresses of Modon and Coron, held until 1500, and the whole island of Negroponte from 1390 to 1470. The Knights Hospitaller held Rhodes from 1310 until the Ottomans ousted them in 1522. Many areas were captured by the Ottomans between the 14th and 17th centuries, and the Ionian Islands and some islands and forts stayed Venetian until the turn of the 19th century, though the Byzantine Empire itself was restored in 1261.

The Franks left a mark on the Greek language. The fragmentation of the Byzantine world caused communication problems and divided the common language into dialects, and since the Franks used the speech of ordinary people for administration, the prestige of the literary language declined. Latin loanwords, mostly Italian and including Venetian, then French, entered Greek. The vocabulary of feudal law and property was mainly French, while that of trade and shipping was Italian. Frankish place names are the most significant influence, and a number of Greek given names are of Frankish origin.
frans-hals: Hals was born in 1582 or 1583 in Antwerp, the son of the cloth merchant Franchois Fransz Hals van Mechelen. His parents fled to Haarlem in the new Dutch Republic during the Fall of Antwerp in 1584 and 1585, and he lived there for the rest of his life. He studied under the Flemish émigré Karel van Mander, whose Mannerist influence is barely noticeable in his work. In 1610 he joined the Haarlem Guild of Saint Luke and began to earn money restoring pictures for the town council, which had confiscated Catholic religious art. With the market for religious themes gone, he turned to portraiture.

His earliest known work is the portrait of Jacobus Zaffius of 1611, and his breakthrough came in 1616 with the life-sized group portrait The Banquet of the Officers of the St George Militia Company. His best-known sitter was René Descartes, painted in 1649. He married Anneke Harmensdochter around 1610, and after her death in 1615 he married Lysbeth Reyniers in 1617, and they had eight children.

Hals painted wealthy citizens, civic guards and the regents of local hospitals, and also itinerant players, fishwives and tavern figures. In his group portraits each sitter is shown differently, with unidealised faces and a variety of poses. Between 1620 and 1640 he painted many married couples as pairs of panels, and only once on a single canvas. He worked with visible brushstrokes, which earlier painters had treated as a flaw, though most of his works were built up in layers rather than thrown onto the canvas in one go.

His palette darkened over his life, probably because of the sober dress of his Protestant sitters.
