Unlike Rembrandt, he refused to travel to his clients, and when he began a militia portrait in Amsterdam it was finished by Pieter Codde because he insisted that the sitters come to Haarlem. Five of his sons became painters, as did his brother Dirck Hals.

Hals lived so long that he went out of fashion and fell into financial difficulty. In 1652 he sold his belongings to settle a debt with a baker, and in 1664 the city gave him an annuity of 200 florins. He died in Haarlem on 26 August 1666 and was buried in the Grote Kerk. His reputation waned, and for two centuries some of his paintings sold for a few pounds or shillings. From the 1860s the critic Théophile Thoré-Bürger restored his standing. His technique influenced Édouard Manet, Claude Monet, Gustave Courbet and others, and Vincent van Gogh wrote to his brother of the joy of seeing a Frans Hals. Several of his main works hang in the Frans Hals Museum in Haarlem.
frantisek-palacky: František Palacký was born on 14 June 1798 at Hodslavice, a village in north-eastern Moravia. His ancestors had belonged to the Bohemian Brethren and had kept their Protestant faith in secret through the years of persecution. His father was a schoolmaster. In 1812 he was sent to the Evangelic Lutheran Lyceum at Bratislava, where he met the philologist Pavel J. Šafařík and became a zealous student of Slavic languages; he mastered 11 languages.

He settled in Prague in 1823 and found a friend in Josef Dobrovský, who introduced him to Count Sternberg and his brother Francis, founder of the Society of the Bohemian Museum. The society collected documents on Bohemian history in order to reawaken national sentiment. In 1825 Palacký became the first editor of its journal, Časopis Českého musea.

His principal work was Dějiny národu českého v Čechách a v Moravě, the History of the Czech Nation in Bohemia and Moravia, which runs to 1526 and the end of Czech independence. He said that in writing of the later period he would have to lie. It rested on research in the archives of Bohemia and the libraries of the chief cities of Europe, and the first volume appeared in German in 1836. Police censorship hindered it, especially over his account of the Hussite movement: he had to cut passages and accept others interpolated by the censors. After censorship ended in 1848 he published a new edition, completed in 1876, which restored the original form.

The Revolution of 1848 drew him into politics. In his Letter to Frankfurt he declined to join the preliminary parliament, since as a Czech he had no interest in German affairs. In June he presided over the Slavic Congress at Prague, and he sat in the Reichstag at Kroměříž from October 1848 to March 1849. He favoured a strong Austrian empire, a federation of southern German and Slavonic states retaining their rights, a view called Austroslavism, and was offered a post in the Pillersdorf cabinet. The collapse of the federal idea in 1852 led him to retire from politics.

After the concessions of 1860 and 1861 he became a life member of the Austrian senate, and in the Bohemian Diet he led the nationalist-federal party. He sought a Czech kingdom of Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia, and attended the Panslavist congress in Moscow in 1867. He died in Prague on 26 May 1876. He is counted as one of the three Fathers of the nation, with Charles IV and Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk.
frantz-fanon: Frantz Fanon was born on 20 July 1925 in Fort-de-France, Martinique, then part of the French colonial empire, into a middle-class family. His father was a customs officer and his mother a shopkeeper. After the fall of France in June 1940, Martinique came under the control of naval elements loyal to the Vichy regime, whose rule Fanon later described as that of authentic racists. In January 1943 he left for the British colony of Dominica to join Allied sympathisers, and after a local uprising overthrew the regime in June 1943 he returned and enlisted in the 5th Antillean Marching Battalion of the Free French Forces. He later studied at the University of Lyon, including literature, drama and philosophy, and qualified as a psychiatrist in 1951.

Fanon did his residency at Saint-Alban-sur-Limagnole under François Tosquelles, who emphasised the role of culture in psychopathology. While finishing his residency in Lyon he published Black Skin, White Masks in 1952, an analysis of the psychological effects of colonial subjugation on black people. The book began as a doctoral dissertation that Lyon rejected. From 1953 he worked in Algeria as head of a service at the Blida-Joinville Psychiatric Hospital. He developed sociotherapy and trained nurses and interns.

After the Algerian revolution began in November 1954, Fanon joined the Front de Libération Nationale (FLN). He treated both French soldiers who had carried out torture and Algerian victims of it. In November 1956 he submitted a letter of resignation to the Resident Minister, and he was expelled from Algeria in January 1957. He then moved to Tunis, wrote for the FLN newspaper Al Moudjahid and served as ambassador to Ghana for the Provisional Algerian Government.

A Dying Colonialism, published in 1959, recounts how Algerians changed old cultural patterns during the revolution. In The Wretched of the Earth, published shortly before his death, Fanon defends the right of a colonised people to use violence to gain independence. He also describes the forces leading either to national independence or to neocolonialism, and the French government censored the book. He was influenced by Jean-Paul Sartre, Jacques Lacan, Marxism and the Négritude of Aimé Césaire. Fanon died on 6 December 1961, having gone to the United States for leukaemia treatment in October. His work influenced Steve Biko in South Africa, Amílcar Cabral in Guinea-Bissau and the Black Power movement in the United States.
franz-conrad-von-hotzendorf: Franz Xaver Josef Conrad von Hötzendorf was born on 11 November 1852 in Penzing, a suburb of Vienna, into an Austrian officers' family. His father, a retired colonel of hussars, had fought at Leipzig. He was educated at the Theresian Military Academy in Wiener Neustadt, took an interest in natural science and in Darwin's theory of evolution, and was commissioned in 1871. After the Kriegsschule he joined the General Staff in 1876, served in Bosnia and Herzegovina after the Treaty of Berlin and became a popular professor of tactics in Vienna in 1888. His books on infantry tactics sold well.

At the suggestion of Archduke Franz Ferdinand he became Chief of the General Staff in November 1906. He saw conflict as always inevitable and held that the fate of nations was decided on the battlefield rather than at diplomatic conferences. He proposed preventive war against Serbia in 1906, in 1908 to 1909, in 1912 to 1913 and in May 1914, and Hew Strachan counts twenty-five such proposals between 1 January 1913 and 1 January 1914. His differences with Foreign Minister Aehrenthal, who rejected his plan for preventive war against Italy, led to his dismissal in 1911, and he returned in December 1912.

His war plans assumed more soldiers than were available, with better training than they had, and relied on railway timetables of the 1870s. In August 1914 an army of 460,000 men sent into Serbia was defeated, and the offensive against Russia through Galicia brought the loss of Lemberg, though Conrad's forces won at Limanowa in December 1914. Austria-Hungary suffered nearly a million casualties, many in efforts to relieve Przemyśl, which surrendered in April 1915.

From 1915 his troops depended increasingly on German support and command. Emperor Charles I made him a field marshal in November 1916 but dismissed him as Chief of Staff in March 1917, after the failure of his Trentino Offensive. He then commanded an army group on the Italian front until he retired in the summer of 1918. He married Virginia von Reininghaus in 1915 after a long affair, and after his death in 1925 a journal was found that held more than 3,000 letters to her which he had never sent. The historian John Leslie describes him as a loner who was politically inept.
franz-grillparzer: Franz Grillparzer was born in Vienna on 15 January 1791. His father, a lawyer ruined by Napoleon's invasion, wanted him to follow the same profession, and Franz entered the University of Vienna in 1807 as a student of jurisprudence, and his father died two years later. After his degree in 1811 he tutored privately, and in 1813 he became a clerk at the Imperial Hofkammer. In 1832 he became director of its archives and held the post until he retired in 1856. He regarded his official career merely as a means of independence, and he never married. From early youth he had a strong literary impulse, and he studied Spanish drama, especially Pedro Calderón de la Barca.

The Ancestress, published in 1816, was a gruesome fate-tragedy, and its first performances in 1817 brought him wide recognition. Sappho followed in 1818, and in 1821 he completed the trilogy The Golden Fleece. Some critics consider its last part, Medea, his highest achievement. He wrote King Ottokar's Fortune and Rise in 1823, but difficulties with the censor delayed its performance until 19 February 1825.

His only comedy, Woe to Him Who Lies, failed at its premiere on 6 March 1838, and he turned his back on the theatre. After that he published only the fragment Esther, but three finished tragedies were found among his papers, among them The Jewess of Toledo and Libussa. He also wrote the novella The Poor Musician in 1848.

After 1840 he almost passed from the memory of his contemporaries. Heinrich Laube became artistic director of Vienna's court theatre in 1849 and staged his forgotten works, and Grillparzer became the most popular author of the day, ranked with Goethe and Schiller. He was made a member of the Academy of Sciences and in 1861 was elected to the Austrian Herrenhaus. His eightieth birthday was marked by all classes from the court downwards.

He died in Vienna on 21 January 1872. He was buried first in the Währinger Cemetery, now Schubertpark, and now lies at Hietzing Cemetery. He is regarded as the national poet of Austria, and the Grillparzer Prize and Grillparzer Ring are named after him. He wrote the oration for Ludwig van Beethoven's funeral and the epitaph for Franz Schubert.
franz-joseph-i: Franz Joseph was born on 18 August 1830 at Schönbrunn Palace in Vienna, the eldest son of Archduke Franz Karl and Sophie, Princess of Bavaria. His uncle Ferdinand, emperor from 1835, was disabled by seizures and his father was unambitious, so his politically ambitious mother raised him as a future emperor, stressing devotion, responsibility and diligence. During the Revolutions of 1848 he joined Field Marshal Radetzky's campaign in Italy and received his baptism of fire at Santa Lucia on 5 May. In December 1848 Ferdinand abdicated at Olomouc as part of Felix zu Schwarzenberg's plan to end the Hungarian Revolution of 1848, and Franz Joseph took the throne at eighteen.

Largely considered a reactionary, he spent his early reign resisting constitutionalism. After Schwarzenberg's death in 1852 the emperor effectively became his own prime minister, and he was forced to issue the February Patent of 1861 to borrow money abroad. Austria lost influence in Italy after the Second Italian War of Independence in 1859 and the war of 1866. The Austro-Prussian War of 1866 ended in the Peace of Prague, which settled the German Question in favour of Prussia, though he ceded no territory to it. His main foreign-policy goal had been unification of Germany under the Habsburgs. In 1854 he married his cousin Elisabeth of Bavaria, whom he had chosen in place of the bride his mother favoured.

In the Compromise of 1867 he granted Hungary greater autonomy and created the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary, which he then ruled peacefully for 45 years. In 1873 he joined the League of Three Emperors with Wilhelm I of Germany and Alexander II of Russia. His troops occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina after the Congress of Berlin in 1878, and in 1908 he annexed it, causing the Bosnian Crisis. In 1903 he used the last veto by a Catholic ruler on a papal election, against Cardinal Rampolla.

He suffered personal tragedies: the execution of his brother Maximilian of Mexico in 1867, the suicide of his son Rudolf in 1889, and the assassinations of his wife Elisabeth in 1898 and of his nephew and heir, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. Austria-Hungary's declaration of war on Serbia then began the First World War. Told of the killing, he said that a superior power had restored the order he had been unable to maintain.

Franz Joseph died at Schönbrunn on the evening of 21 November 1916, at the age of 86, of pneumonia caught after a walk with King Ludwig III of Bavaria. After almost 68 years on the throne he was succeeded by his grandnephew Charles I, and he is buried in the Imperial Crypt in Vienna. Franz Josef Land in the Arctic was named for him in 1873.
franz-joseph-ii-prince-of-liechtenstein: Franz Joseph was born on 16 August 1906 at Schloss Frauenthal in Austria-Hungary, the first child of Prince Alois of Liechtenstein and Archduchess Elisabeth Amalie of Austria. Emperor Franz Joseph I was his godfather. He spent his youth on family estates, notably the castle of Groß Ullersdorf in Moravia, attended the Schottengymnasium in Vienna and took a diploma in forestry engineering in 1930. On 26 February 1923 his father renounced the succession in his favour, worried about his own age, and in 1930 he was appointed deputy of his childless grand-uncle, Prince Franz I.

On 31 March 1938, after the Anschluss of Austria, Franz I made him regent. It was speculated that Franz I did not wish to remain in control if Nazi Germany invaded, because his wife, Elisabeth von Gutmann, was of Jewish relation. Franz I died on 25 July 1938, and Franz Joseph became prince and settled permanently in the principality. Liechtenstein stayed neutral in World War II. He supported Prime Minister Josef Hoop's policy of non-provocative diplomacy towards Germany and tied the country as closely as possible to Switzerland. He met Hitler in Berlin in March 1939, a visit he later said was made to flatter Hitler's ego, while a small German National Movement staged a failed coup at home.

Near the end of the war he granted asylum to Russian emigrés of the First Russian National Army, and the principality refused Soviet demands for their repatriation in August 1945; about a hundred later moved to Argentina. In 1945 the family lost its estates in Czechoslovakia and Poland without compensation, and it later sold artworks, among them Leonardo da Vinci's Ginevra de' Benci in 1967. The family bank and the principality's role as a tax haven brought rapid economic growth from a poor agricultural state.

Women received the vote after a referendum among men only in 1984. In the same year Franz Joseph handed most day-to-day decisions to his son Hans-Adam on 26 August, while remaining sovereign. He used his veto once, in 1985, against a hunting law he called silly. His wife, Countess Georgina von Wilczek, whom he married in 1943, died on 18 October 1989, and he died on 13 November 1989 after a long period of poor health. He had ruled for 51 years, and was succeeded by Hans-Adam II.
franz-liszt: Liszt was born on 22 October 1811 in the village of Doborján (now Raiding, Austria), in the Kingdom of Hungary. His father, Adam Liszt, was a land steward in the service of Prince Nikolaus II Esterházy and an amateur musician who knew Joseph Haydn. Franz improvised at the piano before the age of five and gave his first public concert at Sopron in 1820, aged nine. In 1823 the family moved to Paris. The Conservatoire refused him entry because it did not accept foreigners, so he studied under Anton Reicha and Ferdinando Paer. He gave concerts from 8 March 1824 and toured France and England, where he played for King George IV.

In 1833 Liszt began a relationship with Countess Marie d'Agoult. They lived together for four years and travelled in Switzerland and Italy; the journeys later inspired Années de pèlerinage. They had three children, among them Cosima, who married Hans von Bülow and later Richard Wagner. Liszt's tours in the 1830s and 1840s produced what was called Lisztomania, a popularity that earlier virtuosos had not known. He is credited as the first pianist to give solo recitals in the modern sense, the term first applying to his concert at the Hanover Square Rooms in London on 9 June 1840.

In July 1848 he settled in Weimar, where he arranged festivals of the music of Hector Berlioz and Wagner and gave the premiere of Lohengrin. His planned marriage to Princess Carolyne was stopped by a Vatican official in Rome in October 1861. In January 1869 he agreed to give masterclasses in Weimar, and from 1872 he travelled regularly among Rome, Weimar and Budapest, a life he called his vie trifurquée. He taught, by some estimates, over 400 pupils.

Most of Liszt's music is for the piano, and it is often marked by difficulty. Weimar saw the first fifteen Hungarian Rhapsodies, shaped by the Romani bands he had heard in Hungary, and the Grandes Études de Paganini, published in 1851, which include La campanella. He also wrote 137 secular vocal pieces, now relatively obscure. In an essay of 1855 on Berlioz's Harold in Italy he coined the term program music and argued that it was artistically superior to absolute music. His late works, from about 1869, push the limits of tonality. Romantic music fell out of favour in the early twentieth century, and only a few of his pieces, such as the Liebesträume and the Hungarian Rhapsodies, stayed in print.
franz-marc: Franz Marc was born in Munich on 8 February 1880. His father, Wilhelm Marc, was a landscape painter, and his mother was a devout Calvinist. At 17 he wanted to study theology, as his older brother Paul had, but two years later he enrolled in an arts programme. After a year of military service he began studies at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich in 1900. He spent time in Paris in 1903 and 1907, copying paintings in museums, and found a strong affinity with the work of Vincent van Gogh. He married twice, first Marie Schnür and then Maria Franck, and both were artists.

In 1906 Marc travelled with his brother, a Byzantine expert, to Thessaloniki and Mount Athos. In 1910 he became a friend of the artist August Macke. A critic, Morgan Meis, writes that Marc became an artist in the winter of 1910 to 1911, when his animals began to emerge on the canvas with color as the main thing. In 1911 he founded the journal Der Blaue Reiter with Macke, Wassily Kandinsky and others who had split from the Neue Künstlervereinigung. The first Blue Rider exhibition was held at the Thannhauser Galleries in Munich between December 1911 and January 1912, and travelled to Berlin, Cologne, Hagen and Frankfurt.

In 1912 Marc met Robert Delaunay, whose use of color and the Cubist method influenced him. He painted The Tiger and Red Deer in 1912, and The Tower of Blue Horses, The Foxes and Fate of the Animals in 1913. His work is characterised by bright primary color and a near-cubist treatment of animals. Marc gave colors a meaning, using blue for masculinity and spirituality, yellow for feminine joy and red for violence. He made some sixty prints in woodcut and lithography. He wrote to his wife that Fate of the Animals was like a premonition of the war.

Marc was drafted into the Imperial German Army as a cavalryman in 1914. By 1916 he was a lieutenant, had been awarded the Iron Cross, and had turned to camouflage, painting canvas covers to hide artillery from aerial observation. The government had listed notable artists to be withdrawn from combat for their own safety, but he was killed instantly by a shell splinter at the Battle of Verdun before orders reached him. In 1936 and 1937 the Nazis condemned him as a degenerate artist and ordered about 130 of his works removed from German museums. The Blue Horses was auctioned in Lucerne in 1939. Most of his work survived the war, and the Franz Marc Museum at Kochel am See opened in 1986.
franz-schubert: Franz Schubert was born in Himmelpfortgrund, now part of Alsergrund in Vienna, on 31 January 1797, the twelfth child of the parish schoolmaster Franz Theodor Florian Schubert and Maria Elisabeth Katharina Vietz. His father gave him lessons from the age of five, and his brother Ignaz taught him the piano, though Schubert surpassed him within a few months. In 1808, aged eleven, he entered the Stadtkonvikt school, where he came to know the orchestral music of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven. He left in November 1813 for teacher training and in 1814 taught the youngest pupils at his father's school, while continuing private lessons in composition with Antonio Salieri until 1817.

Schubert was immensely prolific. In 1815 he composed over 20,000 bars of music, including about 140 Lieder. In 1816 Franz von Schober invited him to lodge at his mother's house, and Schubert gave up teaching to devote himself to composition. In 1817 he met the baritone Johann Michael Vogl, who sang many of his songs. In March 1821 Vogl sang Erlkönig at a concert that was extremely well received. Publishers remained distant, and Anton Diabelli agreed to print the first seven opus numbers only on commission.

In 1822 he began the Symphony in B minor, known as the Unfinished Symphony, with two movements and sketches of a third; why he left it unfinished is still discussed. In 1823 he wrote his first large-scale song cycle, Die schöne Müllerin, and the later cycle Winterreise, of 1827, is widely considered one of the pinnacles of Lieder. In his career he wrote roughly 630 songs, seven complete symphonies, seven masses and a large body of piano and chamber music. In March 1828 he gave a concert of his works to critical acclaim, the only one of his career.

Schubert's health deteriorated in the late 1820s, and symptoms of syphilis had first appeared in 1823. At the beginning of November 1828 he fell ill with headaches, fever, swollen joints and vomiting, and he died on 19 November 1828. The cause was officially attributed to typhoid fever, but some historians believe it was syphilis. During his lifetime his appreciation was limited to a small circle of admirers in Vienna, and about 100 opus numbers were published, mainly songs, chamber music and small piano pieces. Many larger works stayed hidden in cabinets and file boxes until George Grove and Arthur Sullivan travelled to Vienna in October 1867 and found manuscripts of six of the symphonies. Mendelssohn, Schumann, Liszt and Brahms discovered and championed his works.
franz-von-papen: Franz von Papen was born on 29 October 1879 in Werl, Westphalia, into a wealthy noble Catholic family. His father was a Prussian cavalry officer. Papen entered a cadet school at the age of 11 and trained for the German General Staff, which he joined as a captain in March 1913. He became a military attaché in the United States in December 1913 and also observed the Mexican Revolution, where he was involved in selling arms to the government of General Victoriano Huerta.

He later commanded a battalion on the Western Front, fighting on the Somme and at Vimy Ridge, and ended the war on the General Staff in the Middle East as a lieutenant colonel. After 1920 he entered politics as a monarchist on the national conservative wing of the Centre Party.

President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Papen chancellor on 1 June 1932, on the advice of General Kurt von Schleicher. His cabinet was nicknamed the cabinet of barons, and he had little support in the Reichstag. He governed by presidential decree, launched the Preußenschlag against the government of Prussia led by the Social Democratic Party, and dissolved the Reichstag twice. Hindenburg removed him in favour of Schleicher.

Papen met Adolf Hitler secretly in Cologne on 4 January 1933 and on 22 January agreed to support him as chancellor with himself as vice-chancellor. Hindenburg appointed Hitler on 30 January. Papen believed Hitler could be contained, but Hitler and his allies quickly marginalised him. On 17 June 1934 he gave a speech at the University of Marburg calling for an end to SA terror. During the Night of the Long Knives his office was ransacked and associates including Herbert von Bose, Erich Klausener and Edgar Julius Jung were shot. Papen resigned, then served as ambassador in Vienna from 1934 to 1938 and in Ankara from 1939 to 1944. He joined the Nazi Party in 1938.

Papen was captured on 14 April 1945 and was one of the defendants at the main Nuremberg trial. The tribunal found no solid evidence that he had been involved in the annexation of Austria. It acquitted him, saying that his actions were political immoralities that were not punishable under the charge of conspiracy to commit crimes against peace. A West German denazification court later sentenced him to eight years of hard labour, but he was released on appeal in 1949. His memoirs of 1952 downplayed his involvement and portrayed him as a tragic patriot. He died on 2 May 1969. He is largely remembered for his role in Hitler's rise to power.
frascati: Frascati is a city in the Metropolitan City of Rome Capital, in Lazio, on the Alban Hills 20 kilometres south-east of Rome and close to the ancient city of Tusculum. The most important archaeological find nearby is a patrician Roman villa of the late Republic, probably belonging to Lucullus. In the first century CE its owner was Gaius Sallustius Crispus Passienus, who married Agrippina the Younger, mother of Nero.

According to the Liber Pontificalis Frascati was a little village in the ninth century. Its name probably comes from a local tradition of collecting firewood, called frasche in Italian. After the destruction of Tusculum in 1191 the population increased and the bishopric moved to Frascati. Raids impoverished it, and baronial families such as the Colonna held it until Pope Pius II fortified it with walls in 1460. In 1538 Pope Paul III conferred the title of civitas on it, with the name Tusculum Novum, and building of the cathedral began in 1598.

On 1 May 1527 a Landsknecht company that had sacked Rome approached the town but turned aside at a shrine of the Virgin Mary, and a church commemorates the event. On 15 September 1616 the first public and free school in Europe was established on the initiative of Saint Joseph Calasanz. Frascati was annexed to the French Empire in 1809, and in 1837 it was the only town to open its doors to 5,000 people fleeing plague in Rome. In 1943 it held the German general headquarters for the Mediterranean zone and was heavily bombed, and about half its buildings were destroyed. It was liberated on 4 June 1944.

From the sixteenth century popes, cardinals and Roman nobles built villas on the slopes as status symbols, designed for social life rather than farming, among them Villa Aldobrandini, Villa Falconieri and Villa Mondragone. The cathedral, rebuilt after the bombing, holds the tombstone of Charles Edward Stuart. The town produces a white wine of its name and hosts scientific laboratories, among them the Laboratori Nazionali di Frascati, where the first Italian particle accelerator was developed in the late 1950s.
fraser-river: The Fraser rises at Fraser Pass in the Canadian Rocky Mountains, near the border with Alberta, and flows for 1,375 kilometres into the Strait of Georgia just south of Vancouver. It drains 220,000 square kilometres and discharges about 20 million tons of sediment into the ocean each year. It turns sharply south at Giscome Portage and meets the Nechako River at Prince George. South of Williams Lake it cuts the Fraser Canyon. At Hell's Gate the walls force the whole river through a gap only 35 metres wide. Yale is the head of navigation, and below it the river crosses the Fraser Valley and splits around Lulu Island and Sea Island before reaching the sea.

The river is named after Simon Fraser, who led a North West Company expedition in 1808 from the site of present-day Prince George almost to its mouth. On 14 June 1792 the Spanish explorers Dionisio Alcalá Galiano and Cayetano Valdés anchored in the North Arm, the first Europeans officially to enter it. Alexander Mackenzie explored the upper reaches in 1793, and Fraser traced the river in 1808 and confirmed it was not connected to the Columbia.

The Hudson's Bay Company built the original Fort Langley in 1827, the first settlement of mixed European and Indigenous ancestry in southern British Columbia. In 1828 George Simpson went down the canyon and wrote that the passage would be certain death in nine attempts out of ten, so Fort Vancouver stayed the company's main Pacific depot. After the Oregon Treaty of 1846 the Fraser was the essential route between the Interior and the Lower Coast, and in 1858 the Fraser Canyon Gold Rush brought prospectors. The worst floods came in 1894 and 1948. In 1998 it was designated a Canadian Heritage River.

The Fraser is the largest producer of salmon in Canada, and holds white sturgeon, steelhead trout and all five Pacific salmon species. Its banks are rich farmland, its water serves pulp mills, and a few dams on its tributaries make electric power, but the main flow has never been dammed. The estuary is a site of hemispheric importance in the Western Hemisphere Shorebird Reserve Network.
frauenfeld: Frauenfeld is the capital of the canton of Thurgau in Switzerland and lies along both banks of the Murg river. The earliest traces of human settlement are La Tène graves east of Langdorf, and a Roman road from Oberwinterthur to Pfyn ran through what is now the Allmend. Two Roman villas have been found, at Thalbach and Oberkirch, and by the 9th century a church stood at Oberkirch. By the end of the 1220s a fortified tower with a mill and chapel had been built, and a village grew around it on land owned by Reichenau Abbey. The tower grew into Frauenfeld Castle.

Frauenfeld is first mentioned in 1246 as Vrowinvelt, and in 1286 as a city. By then it had been integrated into the Habsburg territories, and it belonged to the Habsburg district of Kyburg. How the city came into being is not clear. In 1374 the Habsburgs gave the right of judgment for all Thurgau to the Duke of Frauenfeld, and the castle became the centre of the Habsburg district of Frauenfeld. The Landsberger family held it until 1534. In 1460 the Swiss Confederation captured Thurgau, including Frauenfeld.

Under the Confederation Frauenfeld became the centre from which the Confederates managed Thurgau. After 1499 it was the home of a Confederation court, and after 1504 the Thurgau governor lived there, after 1532 in the castle. The Reformation affected the city, and Catholic and Protestant councils shared its government. Protestants had no church of their own until 1645. The assembly of the Confederacy, the Tagsatzung, met at Frauenfeld in the 18th century, and the fall of the old Confederacy in 1798 ended those gatherings. Fires in 1771 and 1788 destroyed nearly all the houses, so the present old city dates from the end of the 18th century.

The constitution of 1798, under the Helvetic Republic, made Frauenfeld the capital of the new canton of Thurgau, although Weinfelden, geographically central, was the main alternative. Since 1832 the cantonal parliament has met twice a year alternately in Frauenfeld and Weinfelden. On 25 May 1799 French and Austrian forces fought a battle in the city, and the Austrians were victorious. The city walls were demolished between 1808 and 1834. The old city is included in the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites, and the castle, which holds the Historical Museum, and the town hall are among ten buildings of national significance. The Thurgauer Zeitung, founded in 1798 as a weekly journal, is still published.
frauenkirche-munich: A late Romanesque church stood beside the town's first ring of walls from the 12th century and served as the second city parish after the older Alter Peter. The late Gothic cathedral that replaced it was commissioned by Duke Sigismund and the people of Munich in the 15th century and raised in about twenty years by Jörg von Halsbach. Because no stone quarry lay nearby, and for financial reasons, brick was chosen. Construction began in 1468, and when the money ran out in 1479 Pope Sixtus IV granted an indulgence. The church was consecrated in 1494. Its size was striking: it could hold 20,000 standing people in a city of about 13,000 inhabitants.

The church is of red brick, designed very plainly, with its buttresses moved into the interior. It is 109 metres long, 40 metres wide and 37 metres high, a hall church whose nave and two aisles are of equal height and are divided by a double row of 22 pillars. Heinrich von Straubing designed the arches. The twin towers stand just over 98 metres high; the north tower is 98.57 metres and the south 98.45, though a legend says they differ by one metre. Plans for tall open-work spires were never carried out for lack of money, and in 1525 the towers received domes in a cheaper design, possibly modelled on the Dome of the Rock.

Inside are the tomb monument of Emperor Louis IV, Gothic stained glass and choir stalls carved by Erasmus Grasser between 1495 and 1502. The stalls burned in the Second World War, but their figures had been moved and survive. The crypt holds the tombs of the Archbishops of Munich and Freising and of members of the Wittelsbach dynasty. A black mark at the entrance, the Devil's Footstep, is linked by legend to the devil, who stood there and mocked the church for seeming to have no windows.

In 1919 Eugen Leviné, leader of a short-lived Bavarian Socialist Republic, had the church declared a revolutionary temple. In the later stages of the Second World War air raids collapsed the roof, badly damaged a tower and destroyed or lost most of its historical contents. A restoration in several stages began soon after the war and was completed in 1994. Its domed towers have made it a symbol of Munich.
fredegund: Fredegund was born into a low-ranking family around 543 and gained power through her association with King Chilperic I. She was originally a servant of Chilperic's first wife Audovera, and she won the king's affection and persuaded him to put Audovera in a convent and divorce her. Chilperic then put Fredegund aside and married Galswintha, daughter of the Visigothic king Athanagild, after his half-brother and rival Sigibert I of Austrasia had married Galswintha's younger sister Brunhilda. The marriage deteriorated, and Galswintha died, probably strangled on the orders of Chilperic or Fredegund, who succeeded her as queen. Brunhilda began a feud with Fredegund that lasted more than 40 years.

Gregory of Tours, the main source, records that an epidemic of dysentery in 580 struck Chilperic and their sons Chlodobert and Dagobert. Fredegund burned tax records she feared were unjust and urged Chilperic to do the same, but the two sons died, and she then made large donations to churches and the poor. Gregory also reports that she quarrelled with her daughter Rigunth, and that Rigunth's journey to her Visigothic fiancé in Spain ended in robbery and the loss of most of her treasure.

Fredegund is said to have ordered the assassination of Sigibert in 575 and to have made attempts on the lives of Sigibert's son Childebert II, King Guntram of Burgundy and Brunhilda. Gregory suggests she drove the persecution of Bishop Praetextatus, who was stabbed during Easter Mass in 586. After Chilperic was murdered in 584 she took refuge in the cathedral in Paris and became regent for her infant son Chlothar II, protected by Guntram until his death in 592. She commanded the Neustrian armies, and in 593 she led troops to a victory over Brunhilda's at the Battle of Droizy. She kept the support of the clergy and gave land to the Bishop of Le Mans.

Fredegund died of natural causes on 8 December 597 in Paris. Her tomb, a mosaic of marble and copper, stands in Saint Denis Basilica. Her reputation has been poor, mostly because of Gregory of Tours, who calls her murderous and cruel. Historians note that he was a Gallo-Roman bishop appointed through Sigibert and Brunhilda, who receive almost no criticism from him, so his account may be exaggerated. Bishop Leudovald, said to have been a target of her plots, was still favoured by the Neustrian monarchy after her death. Composers later dramatised her story, among them Camille Saint-Saëns and Paul Dukas, who completed Ernest Guiraud's opera Frédégonde in 1895.
frederic-chopin: Frédéric François Chopin was born in Żelazowa Wola, 46 kilometres west of Warsaw, in the Duchy of Warsaw. The baptismal record gives his birthday as 22 February 1810, but the composer and his family used 1 March, now generally accepted. His father, Nicolas Chopin, was a Frenchman from Lorraine who had emigrated to Poland in 1787 and insisted on Polish at home; his mother was Justyna Krzyżanowska. In October 1810 the family moved to Warsaw, where his father taught French at the Warsaw Lyceum. His first professional tutor, from 1816 to 1821, was the pianist Wojciech Żywny. A child prodigy, Chopin gave public concerts by the age of seven.

Chopin wrote his early works in Warsaw, among them six works for piano and orchestra, including two piano concertos. He left Poland at 20, less than a month before the November 1830 Uprising, and at 21 settled in Paris. He gave only about thirty public performances, preferring the salon, and lived by selling compositions and giving piano lessons, for which he was in high demand. He befriended Franz Liszt and was admired by Robert Schumann. After a failed engagement to Maria Wodzińska in 1836 to 1837 he kept up an often troubled relationship with the writer George Sand. Their brief and unhappy visit to Mallorca in 1838 to 1839 proved one of his most productive periods of composition.

More than 230 of Chopin's works survive, all involving the piano. His influences included Bach and Mozart, Polish folk music and the Paris salons. He took the nocturne, invented by John Field, to a deeper level of sophistication, was the first to write ballades and scherzi as individual concert pieces, and established the free-standing prelude with his Op. 28, published in 1839. His mazurkas were written for the concert hall rather than the dance hall, and his waltzes for the salon.

In his last years Jane Stirling supported him financially. He died in Paris on 17 October 1849 at the age of 39. Debussy dedicated his 1915 piano Études to Chopin's memory, and the Fryderyk Chopin Institute, created by the Polish parliament, hosts the International Chopin Piano Competition.
frederick-augustus-i-of-saxony: Frederick Augustus was the second, but eldest surviving, son of Frederick Christian, Elector of Saxony, and Maria Antonia Walpurgis of Bavaria. His father died of smallpox in 1763 while he was a minor, so his mother served as regent until 1768. Two earlier electors of Saxony had been kings of Poland, but his youth ruled him out in the Polish royal election of 1764. When the Polish Sejm ratified the constitution of 1791 it named him successor to King Stanisław August Poniatowski. After Stanisław's death in 1798 he declined the Polish crown, fearing entanglement in disputes with Austria, Prussia and Russia, which had begun partitioning Poland in 1772.

Saxony was drawn into the war against revolutionary France and left the coalition in August 1796. Frederick Augustus took no part in founding the Confederation of the Rhine. In autumn 1806 he joined Prussia, but Napoleon crushed the Prussian and Saxon troops at Jena and Auerstedt. In the peace signed at Poznań on 11 December 1806 Saxony had to join the Confederation of the Rhine and cede parts of Thuringia to the Kingdom of Westphalia, and in exchange became a kingdom. He was proclaimed King of Saxony on 20 December 1806.

After the Treaty of Tilsit in July 1807 he was also named Duke of Warsaw. The duchy had an initial area of about 104,000 square kilometres and about 2,600,000 inhabitants, most of them Poles. In 1809 Polish and Saxon troops defeated an Austrian attempt to take it, and the duchy gained Kraków and other regions. Napoleon dictated its constitution, which joined it hereditarily to the Saxon royal house.

In 1813 Saxony became the central arena of war. Frederick Augustus secretly pursued an alliance with Austria, concluded on 20 April, but after Napoleon's victory at Lützen on 2 May he submitted to Napoleon's ultimatum. At the Battle of Leipzig Saxon and Polish troops fought for Napoleon, though larger Saxon formations went over to the Coalition during the battle.

After Leipzig the allies took Frederick Augustus prisoner. He was kept near Berlin and denied a place at the Congress of Vienna. Prussia and Russia had agreed in the Treaty of Kalisz of February 1813 to compensate Prussia with Saxon territory, and the allies divided Saxony on 7 January 1815. By the treaty of 21 May 1815, 57 percent of its territory and 42 percent of its population passed to Prussia. He abdicated as Duke of Warsaw on 22 May. Greeted warmly on his return in July 1815, he oversaw few political reforms in his last twelve years. He died in 1827, received the epithet The Just, and is buried in the Roman Catholic cathedral of Dresden.
frederick-augustus-iii-of-saxony: Frederick Augustus was born in Dresden on 25 May 1865, the eldest son of King George of Saxony and Maria Anna of Portugal. Like his father and grandfather he was educated at Leipzig University. He entered the Royal Saxon Army in 1877 as a second lieutenant at the age of twelve and, given his rank, advanced rapidly: Generalmajor in 1894, Generalleutnant in 1898 and General der Infanterie in 1902, commanding the XII (1st Royal Saxon) Corps until he became king in October 1904. In July 1902 Emperor Wilhelm II appointed him à la suite of the German Marine Infantry during a visit to Kiel.

Frederick Augustus did not care for the formalities and luxuries of royalty. He often dressed in civilian clothes, spoke the vernacular Upper Saxon dialect and was sometimes seen playing skat with his subjects in the pubs of Dresden. Several jokes at his own expense were recorded; when a lady on a station platform asked him to move her trunk, he is said to have answered that he was not a porter and only looked like one.

He was promoted Generalfeldmarschall on 9 September 1912. His marriage to Archduchess Louise of Austria, made in Vienna on 21 November 1891, ended in divorce by royal decree in 1903 after she left Dresden while pregnant; they had seven children.

When the revolution broke out in November 1918 he made no attempt to defend the monarchy and would not use loyal troops against a workers' uprising in the Altmarkt. He left Dresden Castle for Moritzburg Castle. Hermann Fleissner proclaimed the Free State of Saxony on 10 November, and on 13 November the king signed his abdication on one sheet of paper with a single sentence: I renounce the throne. He released the Saxons from their oath of loyalty and withdrew to Sibyllenort Palace, which he owned, near Breslau. He died there on 18 February 1932 and was buried in Dresden.
frederick-banting: Frederick Banting was born on 14 November 1891 on his family's farm near Alliston, Ontario, the youngest of five children. He was a shy boy who struggled at school, and he failed French and English composition in his matriculation examinations before passing in July 1910. He enrolled at the University of Toronto, failed his first year, then entered the medical programme in 1912 and specialised in surgery. He joined the Royal Canadian Army Medical Corps in 1915 and served in England and France. At the Battle of Cambrai in 1918 he was struck by shrapnel, and he was awarded the Military Cross for exceptional bravery in attending the wounded under fire. After the war he set up a practice in London, Ontario, which proved unsuccessful.

Preparing a talk on the pancreas for 1 November 1920, Banting read reports suggesting that diabetes resulted from a lack of a hormone made in the islets of Langerhans. An article by Moses Barron on closing the pancreatic duct suggested to him a way to extract the hormone before digestive enzymes destroyed it. John Macleod, professor of physiology at the University of Toronto, provided facilities and a student, Charles Best, and the biochemist James Collip later helped. In November 1921 Banting obtained insulin from the pancreas of fetal calves. The first injection was given to 14-year-old Leonard Thompson at Toronto General Hospital on 11 January 1922.

Banting and Macleod shared the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Banting split his half with Best, and Macleod split the other with Collip. At 32 he was the youngest laureate in the field. Parliament granted him a life annuity of $7,500, and he was knighted in 1934. He researched silicosis, cancer and drowning, and from 1938 he worked with the Royal Canadian Air Force on the problems of high-altitude pilots, helping Wilbur Franks with the G-suit. He was also a keen amateur painter and friend of the Group of Seven artists A. Y. Jackson and Lawren Harris.

In February 1941 Banting was a passenger on a Lockheed aircraft bound for England to test the Franks flying suit. After leaving Gander, Newfoundland, both engines failed and the plane crashed at Musgrave Harbour. Banting survived the impact and gave first aid, but died of his injuries the next day, 21 February. He is buried in Mount Pleasant Cemetery in Toronto. His former home in London, Ontario, was declared a National Historic Site of Canada in 1997 and contains a museum of the history of insulin. The Banting Research Foundation was created in 1925, and the American Diabetes Association has awarded Banting Medals since 1941. In 1991 his birthday was made World Diabetes Day.
frederick-barbarossa: Frederick was born in mid-December 1122, probably at Hagenau, the son of Duke Frederick II of Swabia of the Hohenstaufen family and Judith of Bavaria of the rival House of Welf. Descent from the two leading families of the empire made him an acceptable candidate to the princes who elected the king. He could neither read nor write and did not speak Latin until later in life. In 1147 he joined the Second Crusade, and after his father's death that April he succeeded him as Duke of Swabia.

When his uncle Conrad III died in February 1152, Frederick and the prince-bishop of Bamberg both said that the dying king had handed him the royal insignia. The princes chose Frederick at Frankfurt on 4 March 1152, and he was crowned at Aachen on 9 March. He sought to restore the empire to the position it held under Charlemagne and Otto the Great. He made six expeditions into Italy. The first, in 1154–55, brought the destruction of Tortona and the suppression of the republican commune of Rome led by Arnold of Brescia, who was hanged.

The Diet of Roncaglia in 1158 began a long struggle with Pope Alexander III. The Lombard League opposed him, and the cities beat him at the Battle of Legnano on 29 May 1176, where he was wounded and for a time believed dead. In the Peace of Venice in 1177 he was formally reconciled with Alexander. His use of Roman law gave him trained lawyers to administer his lands, and from 1165 he pursued policies to encourage trade; the number of mints in Germany rose ninefold in the reigns of Frederick and his son Henry.

In 1188 at the Diet of Mainz Frederick took the crusader's vow. On the advice of local Armenians he followed a shortcut along the Saleph River, and he drowned there on 10 June 1190. Accounts differ: one says he swam across against advice, another that he was thrown from his horse and drowned weighed down by armour. Most of his army abandoned the crusade before reaching Acre.

Legend says he sleeps with his knights in a cave in the Kyffhäuser mountains and will wake to restore Germany. The nickname Barbarossa, Red Beard, was first used by the Florentines in 1298. In the 19th and early 20th centuries the Risorgimento, the German Empire and the Nazi movement each used him as a symbol.
frederick-christian-elector-of-saxony: Frederick Christian was born on 5 September 1722, the third but eldest surviving son of Frederick Augustus II, Elector of Saxony and, as Augustus III, King of Poland, and Maria Josepha of Austria. He was a weak child, suffered paralysis in one foot and depended on a wheelchair early in life. His mother repeatedly tried to induce him to take monastic vows and give up his rights of succession to his younger brothers, but he refused. The early deaths of his two older brothers, one stillborn in 1721 and Joseph Augustus in 1728, made him heir. On 13 June 1747 he married his cousin Maria Antonia of Bavaria by proxy at Munich, and again in person at Dresden on 20 June.

Frederick Christian succeeded his father on 5 October 1763. He had already written in his diary that princes exist for their subjects, not subjects for their princes, and that his subjects' wealth, public credit and a well-standing army made up a prince's true happiness, which showed his openness to the ideas of the Enlightenment. One of his first acts was to dismiss the unpopular prime minister Count Heinrich von Brühl, whose failed economic policy and catastrophic foreign policy had drawn the electorate into the Seven Years' War.

He began to rebuild the wrecked finances of the plundered and devastated country through reforms known as the Rétablissements, which pared down court expenses and simplified administration on principles of economy. Most members of his government, such as Thomas von Fritsch, Friedrich Ludwig Wurmb and Christian Gotthelf Gutschmied, were of middle-class origin.

Frederick Christian died of smallpox on 17 December 1763 and was buried in the Hofkirche in Dresden. His eldest son, Frederick Augustus III, was a minor, so the electorate was governed jointly by the boy's uncle Francis Xavier and the Dowager Electress Maria Antonia until his majority.
frederick-douglass: Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey was born into slavery in Talbot County, on the Eastern Shore of Maryland. His mother, Harriet Bailey, was enslaved, and his father, who may have been her master, was apparently white; Douglass later wrote that he searched in vain for his father's name. He did not know his age. Records of his former owner, Aaron Anthony, led the historian Dickson J. Preston to place his birth in February 1818, and Douglass chose to celebrate 14 February.

At six he was moved to the Wye House plantation. After Anthony's death he was sent to Baltimore, to Hugh and Sophia Auld, and in 1835 he was hired out as a ship caulker, where white workers who feared competition from enslaved labour abused him. In 1837 he met Anna Murray, a free Black woman, who encouraged him and gave him money. He escaped to the North in September 1838 and settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts, taking the surname Douglass on the suggestion of Nathan Johnson, who had read Walter Scott's The Lady of the Lake.

Douglass became a leader of the abolitionist movement in Massachusetts and New York. His Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845) was an immediate bestseller, reprinted nine times in three years. Fearing that publicity would draw the attention of his former owner, friends sent him to tour Ireland and Britain from August 1845. On his return in 1847, with £500 from English supporters, he began the North Star in Rochester, New York, which he later merged into Frederick Douglass' Paper.

In 1848 he was the only Black person at the Seneca Falls Convention, where he spoke for women's suffrage. During the Civil War he argued that African Americans should fight, published Men of Color to Arms! in March 1863, and two of his sons joined the 54th Massachusetts Infantry Regiment. After the war he campaigned for the rights of freed people, became president of the Freedman's Savings Bank in 1874 shortly before its failure, and in 1872 was nominated, without his knowledge, as vice president on the Equal Rights Party ticket.

Douglass wrote two further autobiographies, My Bondage and My Freedom (1855) and Life and Times of Frederick Douglass (1881, revised 1892). On 20 February 1895 he attended a meeting of the National Council of Women in Washington, D.C., received a standing ovation and died of a heart attack shortly after returning home. His funeral was held at the Metropolitan African Methodist Episcopal Church.
frederick-henry-prince-of-orange: Frederick Henry was born in Delft on 29 January 1584, the youngest child of William the Silent and Louise de Coligny, daughter of the Huguenot leader Gaspard de Coligny. His father was assassinated six months later, on 10 July 1584. He was trained in arms by his half-brother Maurice of Orange, one of the finest generals of his age. In 1625, after Maurice threatened to legitimize his own illegitimate children if he did not marry, Frederick Henry married his first cousin once removed, Countess Amalia of Solms-Braunfels. A son by Margaretha Catharina Bruyns, Frederick Nassau de Zuylestein, had been born to him in 1624.

Maurice died without legitimate issue on 23 April 1625, and Frederick Henry succeeded to his estates and to the stadtholderates of Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht, Overijssel and Guelders, and to the posts of captain and admiral-general of the Union; he added Groningen in 1640.

During his twenty-two years at the head of the government the power of the stadtholderate reached its peak, and Dutch writers speak of a Period of Frederick Henry. His chief sieges were Grol in 1627, 's-Hertogenbosch in 1629, Maastricht in 1632, Breda in 1637, Sas van Gent in 1644 and Hulst in 1645. The capture of 's-Hertogenbosch, the main Spanish base, earned him the epithet stedendwinger, city forcer.

For most of his rule the alliance with France against Spain was the pivot of his foreign policy, but in his last years he gave it up to conclude a separate peace with Spain. His chief opponent in the later 1640s was Andries Bicker, burgomaster of Amsterdam, who wanted peace and a smaller army. He built the country houses Huis Honselaarsdijk, Huis ter Nieuwburg and Huis ten Bosch and renovated the Noordeinde Palace in The Hague.

Frederick Henry died in The Hague on 14 March 1647 and was buried at Delft beside his father and brother. The Treaty of Münster was signed on 30 January 1648, its negotiations delayed by his illness and death. His widow commissioned a mausoleum in the Oranjezaal, a painted ballroom with scenes from his life and allegories of good government. Of their nine children only William II, Prince of Orange, survived him as a son, and he was the paternal grandfather of William III, later King of England, Scotland and Ireland.
frederick-i-elector-of-brandenburg: Frederick was born at Nuremberg on 21 September 1371, the second son of Burgrave Frederick V of the House of Hohenzollern and Elisabeth of Meissen. He entered early into the service of his brother-in-law, the Habsburg duke Albert III of Austria. After Albert's death in 1395 he fought for King Sigismund of Hungary against invading Ottoman forces, and with his elder brother John he took part in the disastrous defeat at the Battle of Nicopolis in 1396.

Back in Franconia he divided his father's inheritance with John, who received Bayreuth while he kept Ansbach. He was Burgrave of Nuremberg as Frederick VI from 1397 to 1427 and Margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach from 1398. In 1401 he married Elisabeth of Bavaria-Landshut.

From September 1399 he fought on the side of Rupert III of the Palatinate, his sister's husband, against King Wenceslaus, who was deposed, and Rupert was elected King of the Romans on 21 August 1400. After Rupert's death in 1410 Sigismund sought the throne. Jobst of Moravia then ruled Brandenburg, and Sigismund disputed his vote and named Frederick to represent Brandenburg at the election of 20 September 1410.

Jobst won a majority in October, but he died under suspicious circumstances in January 1411, which cleared the way for Sigismund. In gratitude Sigismund made Frederick Oberster Hauptmann and Verwalter der Marken in 1411, and Frederick fought the rebellious Brandenburg nobility, in particular the Von Quitzow family, and restored security.

At the Council of Constance on 30 April 1415 Sigismund granted Frederick the titles of Margrave and Prince-elector of Brandenburg. On 21 October 1415 the Brandenburg estates in a Landtag asked him to rule in Berlin, and the king formally enfeoffed him with the margraviate on 18 April 1417. Constant feuding with the nobility led him to withdraw to Cadolzburg in 1425 and hand the regency of the mark to his son John in 1426, though he remained elector.

After 1427 he organised the imperial war against the Hussites and in August 1431 joined the papal legate Cardinal Julian Cesarini in the disastrous Battle of Domažlice. He then helped to mediate the Compacta of Prague at the Council of Basel in 1433. He died on 20 September 1440, and his second son Frederick II succeeded him as elector. He was the first Hohenzollern to rule the Margraviate of Brandenburg.
frederick-i-elector-of-saxony: Frederick was born on 11 April 1370, the eldest son of Frederick III, Landgrave of Thuringia, and Catherine of Henneberg. After the death of his uncle William I, Margrave of Meissen, in 1407, he became governor of the Margraviate of Meissen together with his brother William II and his cousin Frederick IV, the son of Balthasar, until their possessions were divided in 1410 and 1415. On 7 February 1402 he had married Catherine of Brunswick-Lüneburg, daughter of Henry the Mild, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg; they had seven children, among them Frederick II, who succeeded him as elector.

Frederick took part in several wars before his elevation. In the German town war of 1388 he assisted Frederick V of Hohenzollern, burgrave of Nuremberg, and in 1391 he helped the Teutonic Order against Wladislaus II of Poland. He supported Rupert III, Elector Palatine of the Rhine, in his struggle with King Wenceslaus for the German throne, probably because Wenceslaus had refused to give him his sister Anna in marriage. In 1409 he and his brother William founded the University of Leipzig for German students who had left the University of Prague after the events relating to the Western Schism.

The danger from the Hussites led him to ally with Emperor Sigismund, and he took a leading part in the war against them, with considerable success in its early years. In this campaign he spent large sums and received places in Bohemia and elsewhere in pledge from Sigismund, who rewarded him on 6 January 1423 with the vacant electoral Duchy of Saxony-Wittenberg. His formal investiture followed at Ofen on 1 August 1425. On 16 August 1426 the Saxon army was almost annihilated at Aussig, while he was trying to rouse the German princes to join the war. After the death of his brother William he ruled all the possessions of the House of Wettin except Thuringia.

Frederick died at Altenburg in 1428 and was buried as the first Wettin in the centre of what is now the Princes Chapel in Meissen Cathedral. Called the Belligerent or the Warlike, he secured the Saxon electorship for the House of Wettin and thereby established the dynasty's future importance in German politics.
frederick-i-grand-duke-of-baden: Frederick was born in Karlsruhe on 9 September 1826, the third son of Leopold, Grand Duke of Baden, and Princess Sophie of Sweden. He became heir presumptive on the death of his father in 1852 and the accession of his brother as Grand Duke Louis II. Because of his brother's mental ill-health he served as regent ad interim of Baden from 1852 to 1855 and took the title of grand duke in 1856. His brother died in 1858. In 1856 he married Princess Louise, daughter of Prince Wilhelm of Prussia and Princess Augusta of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach; the couple had three children.

Frederick was considered a relatively liberal supporter of constitutional monarchy. During his reign civil marriage became possible in Baden, and in 1904 direct elections to the Lower House of the Parliament of Baden were introduced. He was present at the proclamation of the German Empire at Versailles in 1871, as the only son-in-law of King Wilhelm I of Prussia and one of the reigning sovereigns of Germany. At the ceremony he shouted loudly, 'His Majesty, Emperor Wilhelm!'

He also played a part in the history of Zionism. In 1896 he met Theodor Herzl, the founder of political Zionism, through their mutual acquaintance the Reverend William Hechler, and helped Herzl obtain an audience with his nephew Wilhelm II, German Emperor. After some persuasion by the grand duke, the emperor accepted the appeal. The audience took place in Palestine on 2 November 1898, during the emperor's visit to inaugurate the Church of the Redeemer in Jerusalem.

Frederick died at his summer residence on the island of Mainau in southern Germany on 28 September 1907. His son Frederick II of Baden succeeded him and married Princess Hilda of Nassau, without issue. His daughter Victoria married King Gustav V of Sweden and had children, and his younger son, Prince Louis, died unmarried in 1888. Mainau is now owned by the Lennart Bernadotte Foundation, created by Frederick's great-grandson Count Lennart Bernadotte.
frederick-i-of-denmark: Frederick was born on 7 October 1471, the youngest son of King Christian I and Dorothea of Brandenburg, and belonged to the House of Oldenburg. Not originally destined for the throne, he was elected co-duke of Schleswig and Holstein in 1482, with his elder brother, King John of Denmark. When he came of age in 1490 the two duchies were divided between the brothers, and he lived chiefly at Gottorf Castle.

In 1500 he persuaded his brother to conquer Dithmarschen. The expedition failed at the Battle of Hemmingstedt, where a third of all the knights of Schleswig and Holstein died. When King John died in 1513, Jutish nobles offered Frederick the throne, but he declined, rightly believing that most of the Danish nobility would stay loyal to John's son, Christian II.

In late 1522 Jutland nobles and bishops, dissatisfied with Christian II's burgher-friendly policies, approached Frederick. The uprising was proclaimed at the Viborg Landsting on 25 January 1523; Frederick allied with Lübeck, made Johan Rantzau his commander and was acclaimed king on 26 March. Christian II fled to the Low Countries on 2 April. At Roskilde in August the coronation charter was adopted, restoring noble and clerical privileges, and it is regarded as the most restrictive ever imposed on a Danish monarch. Copenhagen surrendered on 6 January 1524 after an eight-month siege. Frederick recognised Gustav Vasa as king of Sweden in the Treaty of Malmö of 1524, which ended the Kalmar Union.

Risings in 1524 and 1525 demanded Christian II's return. In 1525 Søren Norby invaded Blekinge with 8,000 men, and Rantzau defeated the rebels. Frederick governed largely from Gottorf and left daily administration to councillors, notably Mogens Gøye. He was formally Catholic and the protector of the Church in his charter, but he let Lutheran preaching spread, appointed the reformer Hans Tausen his chaplain in 1526 when Tausen was threatened with trial for heresy, and from 1527 authorised the closure of Franciscan houses in 28 towns. He married his daughter Dorothea to Albert, duke of Prussia, in 1526 and allied with Hesse in 1528 without joining the Schmalkaldic League.

Frederick died at Gottorp on 10 April 1533 and was buried in Schleswig Cathedral. His reign is seen as a period of stability amid religious upheaval, but the balance he kept dissolved at his death and led to the Count's Feud of 1534 to 1536, which ended with the accession of his son Christian III and the establishment of Lutheranism as the state religion. Contemporary accounts differ: his chancellor Wolfgang Utenhof praised him, while the councillor Johan Friis complained of his avarice. The historian Benito Scocozza called him a prisoner of the nobility. His reign also began the custom of naming Danish kings alternately Christian and Frederick.
frederick-i-of-prussia: Frederick was born in Königsberg on 11 July 1657, the third son of Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg, and Louise Henriette of Orange-Nassau. His cousin on his mother's side was King William III of England. On the death of his father on 29 April 1688 he became Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg and Duke of Prussia, two lands ruled in personal union as Brandenburg-Prussia. Soon after succeeding he founded a new city next to Dorotheenstadt and named it Friedrichstadt after himself. Unlike his father, who had sought an alliance with Louis XIV, he opposed France, took Brandenburg into the League of Augsburg and in 1689 captured Bonn, yet he styled his court on that of Louis XIV.

Frederick wanted the more prestigious title of king, but under Germanic law no kingdom could exist within the Holy Roman Empire except Bohemia. Frederick argued that Prussia had never been part of the Empire and that he ruled it with full sovereignty. Emperor Leopold I agreed in the Crown Treaty of 16 November 1700, ostensibly in exchange for an alliance against Louis XIV in the War of the Spanish Succession and 8,000 Prussian troops. Frederick crowned himself on 18 January 1701 in Königsberg. The Sejm of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth called this illegal. Because Hohenzollern sovereignty over the Duchy of Prussia depended on the male line continuing, Frederick took the style King in Prussia rather than King of Prussia.

England recognised him first, and he provided it with troops, though he often withheld them until he got the ceremonial concessions he wanted. His royal title applied to Prussia only, and in Brandenburg he remained an elector under the emperor. He founded the Prussian Academy of Arts in 1696 and the Academy of Sciences in 1700. His grandson Frederick the Great, who first styled himself King of Prussia in 1772, called him the mercenary king, because he profited from hiring out Prussian troops.

Frederick married three times: Elizabeth Henrietta of Hesse-Kassel in 1679, Sophia Charlotte of Hanover, with whom he had the future Frederick William I, and in 1708 Sophia Louise of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. He died in Berlin on 25 February 1713 and is entombed in Berlin Cathedral. Frederick the Great wrote of him that he was great in small matters, and small in great matters.
frederick-i-of-wurttemberg: Frederick was born on 6 November 1754 in Treptow an der Rega, now Trzebiatów in Poland, the eldest son of Frederick II Eugene, Duke of Württemberg, and Sophia Dorothea of Brandenburg-Schwedt. His uncle, Duke Charles Eugene, would not give any relative a role in government, so Frederick took up a military career at the court of Frederick the Great and entered the Prussian army in 1774. In 1780 he married Augusta of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. He resigned in 1781, and Catherine II made him Governor of Eastern Finland, but she ordered him out of Russia after his wife appealed to her for protection in 1786. Augusta died in 1788. In 1797 he married Charlotte, the eldest daughter of George III.

Frederick became Duke of Württemberg as Frederick III on 23 December 1797. The French army occupied the duchy in 1800, and the duke fled to Vienna. When the Reichsdeputationshauptschluss reorganised the Holy Roman Empire, he was raised to prince-elector on 25 February 1803, and he gained ecclesiastical territories and former free cities. In exchange for a large auxiliary force for France, Napoleon allowed him to make Württemberg a kingdom on 26 December 1805. He was crowned at Stuttgart on 1 January 1806 as Frederick I. Württemberg left the Empire and joined Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine, and neighbouring princes' lands were mediatized and annexed.

In the German campaign of 1813 Frederick changed sides to the Allies, helped by his ties to the British Prince Regent and to Emperor Alexander I of Russia. He attended the Congress of Vienna, where he was confirmed as king and kept the lands he had won, even though his harsh treatment of the mediatized princes made him a target of their organisation. Austria preferred an alliance with middle-sized states like Württemberg. In 1810 he banished the composer Carl Maria von Weber from the kingdom.

Frederick joined the German Confederation in 1815 and died at Stuttgart on 30 October 1816. His son William I of Württemberg, by his first marriage, succeeded him. His daughter Catharina married Napoleon's youngest brother, Jérôme Bonaparte, in 1807. He was very tall and obese; Napoleon remarked that God had made him to show how far human skin could be stretched without bursting.
frederick-ii-grand-duke-of-baden: Frederick, known as Fritz, was born on 9 July 1857 in Karlsruhe, the son of Grand Duke Frederick I of Baden and Princess Louise of Prussia. He was a first cousin of the German emperor Wilhelm II and an uncle of Gustaf VI Adolf of Sweden. At the University of Heidelberg he belonged to the Suevia Corps, a student fraternity. On 20 September 1885 he married Princess Hilda of Nassau, the only daughter of the exiled Duke Adolphe of Nassau, who later became Grand Duke of Luxembourg. The marriage had no surviving children.

In October 1880 Frederick joined the Prussian Army in the 1st Regiment of Foot Guards at Potsdam. After his marriage he moved to the 5th Baden Infantry Regiment in Freiburg im Breisgau, which he commanded from 22 March 1889. He then commanded the 4th Guards Infantry Brigade in Berlin from 1891 to 1893 and the 29th Division in Freiburg from 1893. On 27 January 1897 Wilhelm II appointed him commanding general of the VIII Army Corps in Koblenz, where Paul von Hindenburg served under him as chief of staff. In 1902 he left active service to support his ageing father.

Frederick became head of the House of Zähringen on 28 September 1907, when his father died, and on 7 October 1907 succeeded him in the largely ceremonial post of general inspector of the V Army Inspectorate in Karlsruhe. He was the last sovereign Grand Duke of Baden. He abdicated on 22 November 1918, during the German Revolution of 1918 to 1919, which ended the grand duchy. The Weimar-era state of Baden grew out of the area of his former realm. He died on 9 August 1928, and the headship of the house passed to his first cousin Prince Maximilian of Baden, the last chancellor of Imperial Germany.
frederick-ii-of-denmark: Frederick was born on 1 July 1534 at Haderslevhus Castle, the son of Duke Christian of Schleswig and Holstein, later King Christian III, and Dorothea of Saxe-Lauenburg. His father's victory in the Count's Feud had restored royal power, and Christian III's coronation charter made the king's eldest son heir apparent. Frederick's education was thorough but centred on theology, and a wider princely programme planned by the Danish Chancellor was never carried out. He learned to write clearly but struggled with reading and spelling.

In 1554 he was allowed his own court at Malmö Castle in Scania, under a court master, and began political training there. His closest political tutor was his brother-in-law, Elector Augustus of Saxony.

Christian III died on 1 January 1559, and within weeks Frederick joined his uncles in Holstein in a campaign under Johan Rantzau that conquered Ditmarschen, which King John had failed to subdue in 1500. He had not consulted the Council of the Realm, and the councillor Johan Friis had warned of a threat from Sweden. In 1560 he installed his brother Magnus of Holstein as bishop of Ösel-Wiek, and in 1562 he made peace with Tsar Ivan IV in the Treaty of Mozhaysk. The competition with Sweden broke into the Northern Seven Years' War in 1563.

In peacetime Frederick moved his court from residence to residence, hunting and feasting with councillors, and he did most of his business with the Council one to one. The crown's revenues rose after the war, paying for a larger fleet, the first national road network, the kongevej, and Kronborg at Elsinore. In 1583 England agreed to pay annually for permission to sail in what he called the king's sound. He issued a Marriage Ordinance in 1582 that allowed divorce on grounds including infidelity and leprosy.

In 1572 Frederick married his cousin Sophie of Mecklenburg-Güstrow, and they had seven children. He was a patron of the University of Copenhagen, where he raised the budget, supported poor students and funded study abroad. He backed Paracelsian medicine and, through his interest in alchemy and astrology, the rise of Tycho Brahe, who received the island of Ven and other fiefs to fund his work at Uraniborg.

He died on 4 April 1588 at Antvorskov, aged 53, and was buried at Roskilde Cathedral. Danish historians long portrayed him as unlettered and brutish, a view begun by Troels Frederik Lund in 1906 and continued by Erik Arup. Historians such as Poul Grinder-Hansen and Paul Douglas Lockhart now regard his reign, especially the later years, as a success.
frederick-iii-elector-of-saxony: Frederick was born at Torgau on 17 January 1463, the son of Ernest, Elector of Saxony, and Elisabeth of Bavaria, and succeeded his father in 1486. Lucas Cranach the Elder became his court painter in 1504. With his childhood friend Johann von Staupitz he founded the University of Wittenberg in 1502. He was among the German princes who pressed Emperor Maximilian I to reform, and in 1500 he became president of the newly formed council of regency. He collected relics in his Castle Church, whose inventory of 1518 listed 17,443 items, and money was paid to venerate them in the belief that this shortened time in purgatory.

Pope Leo X backed Frederick as a candidate for emperor in 1519 and awarded him the Golden Rose of virtue on 3 September 1518 to persuade him. Frederick instead helped secure the election of Charles V, agreeing to support him if he repaid a debt to the Saxons dating from 1497.

Martin Luther began teaching theology at Wittenberg in 1508 and so was a subject of the elector. After Luther's protest against indulgences in 1517 and his excommunication in January 1521, Frederick ensured that he would be heard at the Diet of Worms in 1521. When Emperor Charles V declared Luther an outlaw, Frederick secured an exemption from the Edict of Worms for Saxony. He is described as acting less from belief in Luther's views than from a belief in a fair trial for his subjects and the rule of law, and from a wish to protect the reputation of Saxony's university.

On Luther's way home from Worms, masked horsemen intercepted him in the forest and took him to Wartburg Castle at Eisenach, where he lived disguised as Junker Jörg. This was planned by Frederick. Luther called the castle his Patmos and translated the New Testament from Greek into German there.

Frederick had little personal contact with Luther, and his treasurer Degenhart Pfaffinger spoke on his behalf. He is considered to have remained a Roman Catholic all his life, though he gradually inclined towards the doctrines of the Reformation, and he is said to have converted on his deathbed. He died on 5 May 1525. Since Saxony was an electorate, neither the popes nor the Habsburg emperors wished to affect an imperial election by acting against him.
frederick-iii-holy-roman-emperor: Frederick was born on 21 September 1415 at Innsbruck, the eldest son of Duke Ernest of Inner Austria and Cymburgis of Masovia. His father died in 1424, making the nine-year-old duke of Inner Austria, which comprised Styria, Carinthia and Carniola, with his uncle Frederick IV of Austria as regent. Relatives kept him from ruling until 1435, and his younger brother Albert VI began a long rivalry by asserting a claim to co-rule. In 1436 he made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. From 1439 he was regent for Sigismund in Tyrol and for his nephew Ladislaus the Posthumous in the duchy of Austria. On 2 February 1440 the prince-electors met at Frankfurt and unanimously elected him King of the Romans.

In 1452 he travelled to Italy to receive his bride, Eleanor of Portugal, and to be crowned emperor. He was crowned with the German crown as King of Italy on 16 March, married that afternoon, and crowned emperor on 19 March. He was the last Holy Roman Emperor crowned in Rome. His reign of 41 years was the longest in the empire's history. His style was hesitant, and Enea Silvio Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, said he wanted to conquer the world while remaining seated. Historians now see his delaying as a way of coping with far-flung possessions.

He prevailed over his Habsburg rivals largely by outliving them. He gained Lower Austria from Ladislaus in 1457 and Upper Austria from Albert VI, who besieged him in Vienna in 1462. He failed against Matthias Corvinus of Hungary, who defeated him in 1485 and held Vienna until his death. Frederick fled to Graz and later Linz. Ottoman raids struck Carniola, Styria and Carinthia, prompting the Carinthian Peasant Revolt of 1478. In 1486 Maximilian was elected king in his father's lifetime, and he joined the empire's reform first under pressure in Frederick's last years. His personal motto was the string A.E.I.O.U., which he never explained.

Frederick's son Maximilian married Mary of Burgundy, heir to the Burgundian lands, which gave rise to the Habsburg saying that others should wage wars while Austria should marry. In 1493 his left leg was amputated at Linz on 8 June, a well-documented medieval operation, and he died on 19 August 1493, aged 77. His tomb in St Stephen's Cathedral, made by Nikolaus Gerhaert, is among the most important sculptures of the late Middle Ages.

The Austrian historian Adam Wandruszka calls him the true founder of the Habsburg imperial position, and German historians tend to be more critical than Austrian ones. He collected 110 books that formed the core of the later Bibliotheca Regia, forerunner of the Austrian National Library.
frederick-iii-of-denmark: Frederick was born on 18 March 1609 at Haderslev in Slesvig, the second-eldest son of Christian IV and Anne Catherine of Brandenburg. Until the death of his older brother Christian in June 1647 he had no prospect of the throne. He was educated at Sorø Academy and studied in the Netherlands and France, with interests in theology, natural sciences and Scandinavian history, and he is described as reserved, a prince who seldom laughed and wrote little.

His collection of books became the foundation of the Royal Library in Copenhagen. As a young man he administered the Prince-Archbishopric of Bremen and the Prince-Bishopric of Verden on his father's behalf, and on 1 October 1643 he married Sophie Amalie of Brunswick-Lüneburg.

Christian IV died on 28 February 1648, and Frederick was elected only after signing a charter, the Haandfæstning, that curtailed royal power in favour of the Rigsraadet, the royal council. He nevertheless held more effective power than the charter allowed, and in 1651 he removed two of the council's most influential members, his brothers-in-law Corfitz Ulfeldt and Hannibal Sehested.

He declared war on Sweden in 1657, but in January and February 1658 Charles X Gustav marched across the frozen Belts, and Frederick had to accept the treaties of Taastrup and Roskilde. When the Swedish army landed at Korsør on 17 July 1658, Frederick is said to have refused to flee Copenhagen, saying "I will die in my nest", and led the defence with the mayor Hans Nansen. A Dutch fleet defeated Charles X in the Battle of the Sound on 29 October. The Treaty of Copenhagen of May 1660 confirmed the loss of Scania, Halland and Blekinge, while Bornholm and parts of Schleswig returned to Denmark.
