Frederick used his popularity to turn the elective monarchy into an absolute one by the Revolution of 1660. At the Estates in September 1660 he played the different Estates against one another and won support for a hereditary monarchy and the annulment of the Haandfæstning. In 1665 the Kongeloven, or Lex Regia, set down absolute rule in writing and led to the abolition of the Council of the Realm.

Frederick changed the administration from a chancellery to colleges and replaced fiefs with amt counties. He died at Copenhagen Castle in 1670 and is buried in Roskilde Cathedral. Absolute monarchy lasted until 1814 in Norway and 1848 in Denmark.
frederick-iv-duke-of-austria: Frederick was the youngest son of Duke Leopold III and Viridis, a daughter of Bernabò Visconti, Lord of Milan. His father died at the Battle of Sempach in 1386, and Frederick and his elder brothers William, Leopold IV and Ernest were placed under the tutelage of their uncle Duke Albert III of Austria. After Albert's death in 1395 the brothers claimed their rights, and when Frederick came of age in 1402 he was assigned the scattered Habsburg lands in Swabia known as Further Austria and lived in Freiburg im Breisgau. Leopold IV ceded Tyrol to him in 1406, and after Leopold's death in 1411 Frederick became sole ruler in Further Austria.

His early years were marked by conflict. Tyrolean nobles opposed him in 1406 and 1407 and gave him the nickname "of the Empty Pockets", and he faced a rebellion in the Bishopric of Trent and the Appenzell Wars, which ended in peace in 1410 though Appenzell became a protectorate of the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1411. In 1415, during the Western Schism, he helped Antipope John XXIII flee the Council of Constance. King Sigismund placed him under the Imperial ban, and Frederick lost the western Aargau, the Freiamt and the County of Baden to the Swiss, though with local support he kept Tyrol.

In 1420 he moved his Tyrolean court from Meran to Innsbruck. His rule there stabilised after several noble rebellions, partly because silver mining began successfully and brought prosperity. After the death of his brother Ernest on 10 June 1424 he also became regent of Inner Austria for his nephews Frederick V, the later Emperor Frederick III, and Albert VI. In his last years Prince-Bishop Alexander of Trent instigated another rebellion against his Tyrolean rule.

Frederick died at Innsbruck on 24 June 1439, a rich man despite his nickname, and was buried in the Cistercian abbey of Stams. He had married Elizabeth of the Palatinate in 1407; she and their infant daughter died shortly after the birth on 27 December 1408. In 1411 he married Anna, daughter of Duke Frederick I of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. Of their children only Sigismund, born in 1427, survived to adulthood. He succeeded his father in Tyrol and Further Austria and was called der Münzreiche, "Rich in Coin".
frederick-lugard: Frederick John Dealtry Lugard was born at Madras on 22 January 1858, the son of an army chaplain, and was brought up in Worcester. He was educated at Rossall School and Sandhurst and was commissioned into the 9th Foot in 1878. He served in the Second Anglo-Afghan War, the Sudan campaign of 1884 to 1885 and the Third Anglo-Burmese War, and won the Distinguished Service Order in 1887.

After a failed attachment to a divorcee, for whom he left his post in Burma, he made a fresh start in Africa, where he led two unsuccessful expeditions in 1888 and 1889 against the Swahili trader Mlozi in the Karonga War near Lake Malawi.

In 1889 Lugard joined the Imperial British East Africa Company and from 1890 to 1892 was military administrator of Uganda. He preferred blood brotherhood ceremonies to written treaties, and made one with Waiyaki Wa Hinga at Dagoretti in 1890. In 1894 he secured treaties in Borgu for the Royal Niger Company and reached Nikki weeks before a French rival, though Nikki was later integrated into French Dahomey.

He organised the West African Frontier Force in 1897. On 1 January 1900 he proclaimed the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria as its first high commissioner. The Sultan of Sokoto and many Fula princes had refused to meet their treaty obligations, and a campaign against Kano and the Sokoto Caliphate in 1903 brought the whole protectorate under British control. He stopped slave raiding, abolished the slave trade, and reorganised taxation. He was knighted in 1901 and resigned in 1906.

He then served as Governor of Hong Kong from 1907 to 1912 and was the first chancellor of the University of Hong Kong, founded in 1911. Returning to Nigeria in 1912, he amalgamated the northern and southern protectorates in 1914 and was governor-general until 1919. From 1922 to 1936 he was the British member of the League of Nations' Permanent Mandates Commission.

Lugard is remembered above all for indirect rule, in which colonial officials governed through existing rulers. In The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa (1922) he argued that Africa could be administered both for its inhabitants' welfare and for the world's benefit, on three principles: decentralisation, continuity and cooperation. He held racist and paternalistic views, describing Africans as like children, and scholars have criticised indirect rule for building hierarchies and increasing ethnic conflict. He is also criticised for keeping the North apart from the South. He died on 11 April 1945, aged 87, and the barony he had held since 1928 became extinct.
frederick-roberts-1st-earl-roberts: Frederick Sleigh Roberts was born at Cawnpore, India, on 30 September 1832, the son of General Sir Abraham Roberts, of an Anglo-Irish family from County Waterford, who then commanded the 1st Bengal European Regiment. His mother was Isabella Bunbury, born in Edinburgh. He was educated at Eton, Sandhurst and the Addiscombe Military Seminary, and entered the East India Company Army as a second lieutenant in the Bengal Artillery on 12 December 1851. In the Indian Rebellion of 1857 he fought at the siege and capture of Delhi and the relief of Lucknow, and won the Victoria Cross for actions at Khudaganj on 2 January 1858.

Roberts transferred to the British Army in 1861 and served in the Umbeyla campaign of 1863, the Abyssinian expedition of 1867 and 1868 and the Lushai campaign of 1871 and 1872. In October 1878 he took command of the Kurram Valley Field Force in the Second Anglo-Afghan War. His success at the Battle of Peiwar Kotal in December 1878 brought him the thanks of Parliament and promotion to major general. After his Indian command he became commander-in-chief of British forces in Ireland from 1 October 1895, was promoted field marshal in May 1895, and published a memoir, Forty-one Years in India, in 1897.

On 23 December 1899 he sailed for South Africa with Lord Kitchener as chief of staff to take overall command in the Second Boer War, replacing General Redvers Buller after a string of early defeats. He reached Cape Town on 10 January 1900. After the relief of Kimberley he forced the Boer general Piet Cronjé to surrender with about 4,000 men at Paardeberg on 27 February 1900 and captured the Free State capital Bloemfontein on 13 March. His attempt to reorganise the army's supply system on the Indian model contributed to a typhoid epidemic that cost the British more men than combat did. He became the last Commander-in-Chief of the Forces on 3 January 1901; the post was abolished in February 1904.

In retirement Roberts was president of the National Service League from 1905 to 1914 and campaigned for compulsory military training to prepare for a great European war; his speeches appeared in 1907 as A Nation in Arms. He died of pneumonia at St Omer, France, on 14 November 1914 while visiting Indian troops, lay in state in Westminster Hall and was buried in St Paul's Cathedral after a state funeral. His son Frederick was killed at the Battle of Colenso in December 1899 and was awarded a posthumous Victoria Cross. A statue of Roberts by Harry Bates was unveiled in Calcutta in 1898, with copies in Glasgow and on Horse Guards Parade in London.
frederick-the-fair: Frederick was born in Vienna, the second son of King Albert I of Germany and Elisabeth of Gorizia-Tyrol, and a grandson of the first Habsburg king of Germany, Rudolph I. In 1298 his father invested him and his elder brother Rudolph III with the duchies of Austria and Styria. After Rudolph's early death in 1307 and the assassination of Albert in 1308, Frederick ruled both duchies for himself and his younger brothers. The royal title passed to Count Henry VII of Luxembourg, and Frederick had to abjure all claims to the German crown, receiving in return the confirmation of his fiefs.

Frederick had been a friend of his cousin Louis IV of Bavaria, who also grew up at the Austrian court. They came to arms in 1313, when Bavarian nobles entrusted Frederick with the guardianship of the sons of the late Duke Stephen I of Lower Bavaria. Louis beat him at the Battle of Gammelsdorf on 9 November 1313. After Henry VII died, the electors met at Frankfurt-Sachsenhausen on 19 October 1314 and gave Frederick four of seven votes, two of which were contested. The next day a second election chose Louis with five votes. Louis was crowned at Aachen and Frederick at Bonn on 25 November 1314.

Frederick suffered a crushing defeat at Morgarten in 1315 against the Swiss Confederacy. After years of war, with the support of his brother Leopold I, his army was beaten near Mühldorf on 28 September 1322, and he and 1,300 nobles were captured. Louis held him at Trausnitz Castle for three years. In the Treaty of Trausnitz of 13 March 1325 Frederick recognised Louis as the legitimate ruler and promised to return to captivity if he could not persuade his brothers to submit. Leopold refused, and Frederick went back to Munich as a prisoner, even though the Pope had released him from his oath.

Louis, impressed, renewed their friendship, and the two agreed to rule jointly, which the Pope and electors opposed. A treaty at Ulm on 7 January 1326 had Frederick govern Germany as king while Louis was to be crowned emperor. After Leopold died in 1326 Frederick withdrew to rule only Austria and Styria. He died on 13 January 1330 at Gutenstein Castle and was buried at Mauerbach Charterhouse, and later in St. Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna. His return to captivity inspired Schiller's poem Deutsche Treue.
frederick-the-great: Frederick was born on 24 January 1712 in the Berlin Palace, the son of Crown Prince Frederick William of Prussia. In his youth he was more interested in music and philosophy than war, which led to clashes with his authoritarian father. In 1730 he plotted to flee to Britain with Hans Hermann von Katte and other junior officers. The plan was betrayed and both were imprisoned at Küstrin and accused of treason. The king had Katte beheaded on 6 November and forced his son to watch. On 12 June 1733 Frederick married Elisabeth Christine, a match arranged under Austrian influence; they had no children, and after his accession he separated from her.

Frederick succeeded on 31 May 1740 to a highly militarised state: Prussia's army was the fourth largest in Europe though its population was only the twelfth largest, and the military absorbed 86 per cent of the budget. By 1770 he had doubled the army. After the death of Emperor Charles VI on 29 October 1740 he disputed Maria Theresa's right to the Habsburg lands and asserted a claim to Silesia, resting on old and ambiguous Hohenzollern claims. He withdrew from the War of the Austrian Succession once Austria guaranteed his possession of Silesia, and used the peace after the Treaty of Dresden to fortify the province and expand his army.

He wished to join Pomerania, Brandenburg and East Prussia by annexing Polish territory, and had called Poland an artichoke to be eaten leaf by leaf. The First Partition of Poland gave him Royal Prussia in 1772, after which he styled himself King of Prussia. In 1778 he entered the War of the Bavarian Succession, in which he checked Austrian attempts to exchange the Austrian Netherlands for Bavaria. He commanded the army in sixteen major battles.

In the Anti-Machiavel and his Political Testament Frederick wrote that the sovereign was the first servant of the state. With Grand Chancellor Samuel von Cocceji he reformed the courts, abolished most uses of judicial torture and removed special courts for special social classes, a reform completed after his death in the Prussian Law Code of 1794. He drained the Oderbruch marshland and founded about 1,200 villages. A religious sceptic, he tolerated Jews and Catholics, though not without prejudice. He played the flute, composed sonatas and met Johann Sebastian Bach in 1747. He died on 17 August 1786, succeeded by his nephew Frederick William II.
frederick-v-of-the-palatinate: Frederick was born on 26 August 1596 at the hunting lodge in Deinschwang, the son of the Elector Frederick IV and Louise Juliana of Orange-Nassau, a daughter of William the Silent. In 1604 he was sent to Sedan, to the court of his uncle Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Duke of Bouillon, where the Calvinist theologian Daniel Tilenus taught him that Protestant princes had a duty to intervene when their fellow believers were harassed.

His father died on 19 September 1610. A dispute followed over guardianship, since the nearest male relative, Wolfgang William of Neuburg, was a Catholic and the dying elector had named John II of Zweibrücken instead. Emperor Matthias intervened in 1613 and Frederick began personal rule before his eighteenth birthday. On 14 February 1613 he married Elizabeth Stuart, daughter of James VI of Scotland and I of England.

Frederick presented himself as a leader of the Protestant princes and head of the Protestant Union, and built the Hortus Palatinus garden at Heidelberg. In 1619 the Bohemian Estates, in revolt against the Catholic Ferdinand II, elected him king. He was the only elector to vote against Ferdinand's election as emperor. Historians have concluded that he acted chiefly from a sense of duty to fellow Protestants, though trade in Upper Palatinate iron and Bohemian tin and glass also counted. He was crowned in St. Vitus Cathedral on 4 November 1619.

He found a weak crown and a divided country. He and Elizabeth spoke no Czech, so court posts went mostly to foreigners. James opposed the venture and the Protestant Union did not support him. He was defeated at the Battle of White Mountain on 8 November 1620 and fled to Breslau the next day. Pamphleteers on both sides mocked his flight.

Ferdinand II declared Frederick's lands and titles forfeit in 1621. Imperial forces took the Palatinate, and an imperial edict formally deprived him of it in 1623. He lived in exile, mostly at The Hague, where he kept a government-in-exile and built a summer palace at Rhenen. In 1632 he met Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, who would restore him only if he held the Palatinate as a Swedish fief and granted Lutherans equal rights. Frederick refused and died at Mainz on 29 November 1632.

His eldest surviving son, Charles I Louis, regained the electorate in 1648 under the Peace of Westphalia. Another son was Prince Rupert of the Rhine, and his daughter Sophia was named heir presumptive to the British throne; her son became George I in 1714.
frederick-vi-of-denmark: Frederick was born at Christiansborg Palace in Copenhagen on 28 January 1768, the eldest of two children of Christian VII and Caroline Mathilde. His father suffered increasing mental illness, and from 1770 to 1772 the king's physician Johann Friedrich Struensee was de facto regent and the queen's lover. Struensee had the boy raised on the principles of Rousseau's Émile. In a palace coup on 17 January 1772 he was deposed and later executed, and the queen was exiled, so that the four-year-old Frederick never saw his mother again. Real power then lay with the queen dowager Juliana Maria and Ove Høegh-Guldberg.

The sixteen-year-old crown prince was confirmed on 4 April 1784, and on 14 April he seized full power as regent, dismissing ministers loyal to the queen dowager. He ruled under his father's name until 1808. With the minister Andreas Peter Bernstorff he introduced reforms in the spirit of enlightened absolutism: the abolition of serfdom in Denmark in 1788, of hanging in 1789, and in 1803 of Dano-Norwegian involvement in the transatlantic slave trade.

He became king on 13 March 1808. After the British bombardment of Copenhagen in 1807 he allied Denmark-Norway with France, and the Gunboat War with Britain lasted until the Treaty of Kiel in 1814, which cost him the Norwegian crown. He refused a request from the Allies to change sides after the French defeat in Russia in 1812. Many historians have called him stubborn and misguidedly loyal to Napoleon, but others argue he stayed in the alliance to protect Norway, which depended on grain imports and was a target of Swedish ambitions. After 1814 he gave up his liberal ideas, and censorship and a poor economy marked the years. In 1834 he created the consultative Assemblies of the Estate.

Frederick patronised astronomy and in 1832 offered gold medals to anyone who discovered a comet with a telescope. He had no surviving legitimate sons, and died at Amalienborg Palace on 3 December 1839, succeeded by his half-cousin Christian. He was buried in Roskilde Cathedral. Of eight children by his wife Marie Sophie only two daughters, Caroline and Wilhelmine, lived to adulthood. The Royal Frederick University in Oslo was named in his honour.
frederick-vii-of-denmark: Frederick was born on 6 October 1808 at Levetzau's Palace, part of the Amalienborg Palace complex in Copenhagen, the second but eldest surviving child of Prince Christian Frederick, the future Christian VIII, and Duchess Charlotte Frederica of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. After his parents divorced he had a rather neglected childhood, and his youth was marked by private scandals.

His first two marriages ended in scandal and divorce: in 1828 to his second cousin Princess Vilhelmine Marie, a daughter of Frederick VI, divorced in 1837, and in 1841 to Duchess Caroline Charlotte Mariane of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, divorced in 1846. On 7 August 1850 he married morganatically Louise Christina Rasmussen, a milliner and former ballet dancer, whom he created Lensgrevinde Danner. The marriage aroused indignation among the nobility and the bourgeoisie, but she seems to have steadied him.

Frederick succeeded in January 1848 and was at once met by demands for a constitution. The Schleswig-Holsteiners wanted an independent state, while the Danes wished to keep South Jutland Danish. The king soon yielded to the Danes, and in March he accepted the end of absolutism, which led to the June Constitution of 1849. During the First War of Schleswig in 1848 to 1851 he appeared as the national leader, though he took no active part in the fighting.

He behaved on the whole as a constitutional monarch but kept interfering in politics: in 1854 he helped bring down the conservative Ørsted cabinet, and in 1859-60 he accepted a liberal government appointed on his wife's initiative. The National Liberal Party was in office from 1854, and free trade was introduced in 1857. Disputes over Schleswig-Holstein pushed the National Liberals to a more resistant course against the Germans, and shortly before his sudden death the king was ready to sign the November Constitution for Denmark and Schleswig.

Frederick had no legitimate children. In 1852 his second cousin Prince Christian of Glücksburg was chosen heir presumptive, and when Frederick died in 1863 at Glücksburg of erysipelas, Christian became Christian IX. Frederick was buried in Roskilde Cathedral. His death ended the male line of the Oldenburg kings, and the rival claims to the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein led to the Second War of Schleswig. He became one of the best-loved Danish kings, and as a keen antiquarian he helped arouse wide interest in Danish antiquities.
frederick-william-i-of-prussia: Frederick William was born in Berlin on 14 August 1688, the son of King Frederick I of Prussia and Princess Sophia Charlotte of Hanover. A Huguenot governess, Marthe de Roucoulle, raised him in his first years. When the plague of the Great Northern War devastated Prussia, he and a party at court brought down the leading minister Johann Kasimir Kolbe von Wartenberg after an investigation exposed large-scale embezzlement. The episode made him resent crime, corruption and waste, and it was the first time he took an active part in politics. He married his first cousin Sophia Dorothea of Hanover on 28 November 1706, and they had fourteen children.

His father had paid heavily for the royal title and enlarged palaces at great expense, which ruined the state's finances. On taking the throne in 1713 Frederick William dismissed his father's Cabinet of Three Counts and reorganized the finances. He raised excise taxes, subjected the nobility to a land tax and dictated Regulations for State Officials, which set out every public servant's duties; a minister who missed a committee meeting lost six months' pay. He encouraged commerce and farming, reclaimed marshes and stored grain in good years to sell in bad ones.

He expanded the Prussian Army from 38,000 men in 1713 to 80,000 in 1740, so that about one man in twenty-five served. With Leopold I, Prince of Anhalt-Dessau, he reformed training, tactics and conscription, introducing the canton system, and the iron ramrod raised the infantry's rate of fire. Peasants bore military obligations, while the middle class paid an annual tax in place of service. In 1717 he sold the Brandenburg Gold Coast to the Dutch West India Company, preferring to spend on the army. In 1732 he invited Salzburg Protestants to settle in East Prussia, which plague had depopulated in 1709. He joined the Great Northern War briefly, in alliance with Peter the Great, and gained part of Swedish Pomerania with new Baltic ports.

Frederick William had a short temper and sometimes struck servants and even his own children with a cane, and a hereditary disease gave him gout and stomach pains. His relations with his eldest surviving son, the future Frederick II, were hostile. After the prince tried to flee to England with his tutor Hans Hermann von Katte, the king had Katte beheaded in front of him. He died in 1740, aged 51, and was interred at the Garrison Church in Potsdam. His reforms left his son the most formidable army in Europe.
frederick-william-ii-of-prussia: Frederick William was born in Berlin on 25 September 1744, the eldest son of Prince Augustus William of Prussia and Duchess Luise of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. In 1747 his uncle, King Frederick II, took him from his family and had him educated in the spirit of the Enlightenment under the tutor Nicolas de Béguelin, though not for affairs of state. The shy boy could not meet his uncle's demand for audacity, and was punished for rebelliousness.

His father was dismissed from the army in 1757, and after his death Frederick William was confirmed in December 1758 as Prince of Prussia, the heir presumptive. Relations with his uncle cooled. Frederick II arranged his marriages, to Elisabeth Christine of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel in 1765, ended after four years, and to Frederica Louisa of Hesse-Darmstadt in 1769, and kept him ignorant of day-to-day politics.

Frederick William acceded on 17 August 1786. He lightened the burdens of the people, reformed the oppressive French system of tax-collecting, cut customs dues, built roads and canals and ended the state monopolies on coffee, tobacco and sugar. The codification known as the Allgemeines Preußisches Landrecht, begun under Frederick II, was completed in 1794. He turned the kingdom's culture from French towards German: the French Theatre in Berlin became the National Theater on the Gendarmenmarkt, where he declared "We are Germans, and we intend to remain so."

Prussia was isolated in foreign policy when Frederick II died. In reaction to the French Revolution the king ended the German dualism between Prussia and Austria, and at home he tightened censorship and religious control. A devout Protestant, he joined the Rosicrucians in 1781. He was a keen cellist with a court orchestra of 70 musicians, and he patronised the building of the Brandenburg Gate and the Marmorpalais in Potsdam.

In October 1797 Frederick William withdrew to the Marmorpalais, and on 9 November he handed government to his son, Frederick William III. He died there on 16 November 1797, aged 53, and was buried on 11 December in a vault of the old Berlin Cathedral. A eulogy called him the happy enlarger of his country, and his contemporaries called him the Kind One.
frederick-william-iv-of-prussia: Frederick William was born on 15 October 1795, the son of King Frederick William III of Prussia and Queen Louise, and was his mother's favourite son. His tutors included the historian and statesman Friedrich Ancillon. When Louise died in 1810 he saw her death as a punishment from God, and he later tried to live in a way that would absolve him of his guilt. The execution of Louis XVI in 1793 had helped create the conditions for his later orientation toward tradition and historical continuity. After Prussia lost the Battle of Jena-Auerstedt on 14 October 1806 he and his brother William were taken to Königsberg and then fled with their parents to Memel.

He became king in 1840 and was also sovereign prince of Neuchâtel until 1848. Called the romanticist on the throne, he was deeply religious and believed he ruled by divine right. His ideal was a state governed by the Christian estates rather than a constitutional monarchy. He reconciled with the Catholic population by authorising the Cologne Cathedral Building Association in 1840, and in 1842 he founded the civil class of the Order Pour le Mérite on the advice of Alexander von Humboldt. He also promoted architecture, including the Neues Museum in Berlin.

The overthrow of the French July Monarchy in February 1848 set off revolution across Europe. About 300 demonstrators were killed in the Berlin barricade fighting of March, and the king blamed foreigners in his manifesto To my dear Berliners. In December 1848 he dissolved the Prussian National Assembly and imposed a constitution. The Frankfurt Parliament elected him Emperor of the Germans on 28 March 1849. He refused, writing that he did not want it because Austria would then be separated from Germany. He sent troops to put down the Dresden uprising in May 1849, and his Erfurt Union lost the support of Hanover and Saxony by the winter of 1849.

His strokes began on 14 July 1857 and affected his speech. On 7 October 1858 he signed a regency charter for his brother William, and the new regent dismissed the reactionary minister president Otto Theodor von Manteuffel, starting what is called the New Era. Frederick William suffered further strokes in 1859 and 1860 and died on 2 January 1861. He was buried in the Friedenskirche in Potsdam, and his heart was buried separately beside his parents in the Charlottenburg mausoleum. The Berlin-Potsdam palace landscape and Museum Island, which he extended, and the Cologne Cathedral, which he helped to complete, are now UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
fredericton: Fredericton lies in the west-central part of New Brunswick on the Saint John River, which flows through the city from west to east and is its dominant natural feature. The Nashwaak River, a major tributary, joins it here. The downtown stands on flat, low-lying ground on both banks, and the region's water and arable soil make it good farmland. The climate is warm-summer humid continental, with short, warm summers and long, cold winters.

There is evidence of a camp here 12,000 years ago, and the Wolastoqiyik farmed upriver. In the late 1600s French colonists built Fort Nashwaak on the north bank as the capital of Acadia, and it withstood a British attack in 1696. In 1713 Acadians escaping the British takeover of Nova Scotia settled the site and called it Pointe Ste-Anne. It was destroyed in 1758, when its population of about 83 was exiled in the expulsion of the Acadians.

Modern Fredericton begins with the arrival of United Empire Loyalists from New England in 1783. New Brunswick was separated from Nova Scotia the next year, and Pointe-Ste-Anne was renamed Fredericstown after Frederick, second son of George III. It became the capital because its position was thought easier to defend than that of the larger Saint John. Its streets, Charlotte, Brunswick, George, King and Queen, were laid out in a grid and named in keeping with Loyalist sympathies. The Legislative Building went up in 1790, and King's College, now the University of New Brunswick, became the first English-language university in Canada.

It was a British garrison town from 1784 to 1869, and its military compound is preserved as a National Historic Site of Canada. In the 1960s the province's Equal Opportunity program centralised government services there, which increased jobs and population.

Fredericton is an educational and cultural centre of the province. The University of New Brunswick and St. Thomas University are based there, with the Beaverbrook Art Gallery and the Playhouse, the main venue of Theatre New Brunswick. The 2021 census counted 63,116 people in the city, and English is the mother tongue of about 80 per cent.
free-imperial-city: In the 13th and 14th centuries the emperor promoted some cities to the status of Imperial Cities, essentially for fiscal reasons. These had been founded by the German kings and emperors and gradually gained independence as their magistrates took over administration and justice; examples are Colmar, Haguenau, Memmingen and Ravensburg. Free Cities such as Basel, Augsburg, Cologne and Strasbourg began under a prince-bishop and slowly won independence from him. Over time the difference blurred, and from the 15th century the collective term free imperial city was used. Like other Imperial Estates they could wage war, make peace and control their trade, and some joined City Leagues such as the Hanseatic League.

Free imperial cities held imperial immediacy, subject only to the emperor, unlike territorial cities under a prince or ecclesiastical lord. They were admitted to the Imperial Diet as individual Estates in 1489, at first with only an advisory vote; the Peace of Westphalia confirmed their full vote as a third college. The Reichsmatrikel of 1521 listed 85 such cities, and the number was about 50 from 1648 to 1803. Their territories were mostly small, though Bern, Zürich, Luzern, Ulm, Nuremberg and Hamburg held substantial hinterlands.

Their constitutions were at first republican, but between 1548 and 1552, after the defeat of the Schmalkaldic League, the democratic constitutions of 28 cities were replaced by rule of a small council of patricians. Below them stood the burghers, who held citizenship that could be inherited or bought, and below those the Beisassen, a disenfranchised population that might be half of a city's people. Conflicts that sometimes amounted to class warfare broke out in cities such as Lübeck, Frankfurt and Hamburg in the 17th century.

Some cities were lost earlier: Donauwörth was annexed by Bavaria in 1607, and Louis XIV took Strasbourg and the ten cities of the Décapole. After 1795 the revolutionary armies annexed cities west of the Rhine. In the reorganisation of 1803 all but six free cities lost their independence: Hamburg, Bremen, Lübeck, Frankfurt, Augsburg and Nuremberg. The Empire was dissolved in 1806, and by 1811 all had lost their independence. The Congress of Vienna made Hamburg, Lübeck, Bremen and Frankfurt free cities again in 1815. Frankfurt was annexed by Prussia in 1866; the other three became states of the German Empire in 1871, and Bremen and Hamburg remain states of the Federal Republic.
freetown: The area around the Sierra Leone estuary has been inhabited for millennia, and the earliest known group was the Bullom people. In the sixteenth century the Mane people invaded and established chiefdoms, integrating with the Bullom. In 1787 some 400 formerly enslaved black people sent from London under the Committee for the Relief of the Black Poor founded the Province of Freedom and the settlement of Granville Town on land bought from the Koya Temne subchief King Tom and the regent Naimbana. Some historians question how well the Koya leaders understood the agreement, since they had a different conception of property.

After this colony collapsed, the directors of the Sierra Leone Company were eager to recruit new settlers, and Lieutenant John Clarkson, an abolitionist, was sent to Nova Scotia to register emigrants. Freetown was founded on 11 March 1792 by 1,196 African Americans under Clarkson at the foot of the Cotton Tree, as a settlement for free and freed African American, Afro-Caribbean and Liberated African slaves, whose descendants are the Creole people.

The Temne attacked the colony in 1801 and were repulsed. The British made Freetown a Crown Colony in 1808, and from 1808 to 1874 it was the capital of British West Africa. It was also the base of the Royal Navy's Eastern Squadron, which enforced the ban on the slave trade and brought most of the slaves it freed from trading ships to Freetown. Fourah Bay College, the oldest university in West Africa, was founded there in 1827.

Freetown is the capital and largest city of Sierra Leone, a major port on the Atlantic with a harbour in the estuary of the Sierra Leone River. The Krio language of the Creole people is by far the most widely spoken language in the city. Landmarks of its founding include the Cotton Tree, King's Yard Gate, whose inscription declares any slave who passes through it free, and the ruins of the slave fortress on Bunce Island, a boat ride away. St George's Cathedral opened in 1828.
freiberg: Freiberg lies on the northern slope of the Ore Mountains, on the Freiberger Mulde, a tributary of the Mulde. Its centre is about 412 m above sea level, about 31 km west-southwest of Dresden. The nucleus of the town was the forest village of Christiansdorf in the valley of the Münzbach stream. The unwalled town grew on the two slopes of the valley and on the ridge to the west, so that the streets running to the east of the main axis are very steep. The east is the Lower Town, with its lower market, and the west the Upper Town, with the upper market.

The town was founded around 1168, after a silver discovery led to the first Berggeschrey, or mining rush, and for centuries it was a centre of the mining industry in the Ore Mountains. It belonged to the Margraviate of Meissen from 1186, to the Electorate of Saxony from 1423 and to the Kingdom of Saxony from 1806. A fire destroyed the town in 1484, and its Renaissance quarter was built afterwards. The Bergakademie, the mining academy, was established in 1765 by Prince Franz Xaver, regent of Saxony, on plans by Friedrich Wilhelm von Oppel and Friedrich Anton von Heynitz.

Silver mining was discontinued in 1913 because the price of silver had fallen. After it resumed before the Second World War, mining of lead, zinc and tin continued until 1969, and the town was dominated by mining and smelting for around 800 years. In 1944 a subcamp of the Flossenbürg concentration camp was built outside the town, housing over 500 women, including survivors of Auschwitz, until its evacuation in April 1945.

Freiberg has around 41,000 inhabitants. Its historic centre is under monument protection, and together with mining monuments such as the Reiche Zeche ore mine it has been part of the World Heritage Site of the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region since 2019. Freiberg Cathedral holds two organs by Gottfried Silbermann, a tulip pulpit and the Golden Gate, and its choir became a burial place of the Albertine Wettins. The university, the oldest of mining and metallurgy in the world, has since 1969 turned the town towards semiconductor and solar technology. The Christmas market keeps the mining traditions of the Ore Mountains.
freiburg-im-breisgau: Freiburg lies at the south-western foothills of the Black Forest, on the Dreisam River, in the Breisgau, one of the warmest regions of Germany and part of the Upper Rhine Plain. Its city limits reach from the summit of the Schauinsland, at 1,284 metres, to a point 3 kilometres east of the French border, and Switzerland lies 42 kilometres to the south. The city stands in the wine-growing region of Baden, not far from the volcanic hills of the Kaiserstuhl, and serves as a gateway to the Black Forest. The dialect spoken there is Low Alemannic, related to Alsatian and to Basel German.

Konrad and Duke Berthold III of the House of Zähringen founded Freiburg in 1120 as a free market town, and its name means free town or, probably, fortified town of free citizens. It was incorporated in the early 12th century and soon became a commercial, intellectual and ecclesiastical centre for the Upper Rhine. Its university, the Albert-Ludwigs-Universität, was founded in 1457, and the minster was built between c. 1200 and 1513. The city's flag, a St George's Cross, dates from about 1368 and is identical to England's, since Saint George is the patron of both.

Freiburg remained Catholic through the Reformation, though villages around it ruled by the Margrave of Baden turned Protestant. It was part of the Diocese of Konstanz until 1821, when it became the seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Freiburg. A dispute between Baden and the Holy See delayed the archbishop's formal start until 1827.

Freiburg is the fourth-largest city in Baden-Württemberg, with a built-up area of about 355,000 people. Its old town is crossed by runnels called Bächle, fed from the Dreisam. The minster is the main landmark, and the university has counted Max Weber, Edmund Husserl, Martin Heidegger and Friedrich Hayek among its scholars. In 1995 the city council resolved to allow only low-energy buildings on municipal land, and the districts of Vauban and Rieselfeld were built in the late 1990s on principles of sustainability.
freikorps: After 1918 the term Freikorps referred to loosely affiliated paramilitary groups formed in Germany after its defeat in World War I. Their ranks were mostly demobilised soldiers, young men and conservative nationalists who blamed socialists and communists for Germany's problems. Historians agree that some 500,000 men were formal members, with another 1.5 million taking part informally. Many veterans who could not return to civilian life found a sense of belonging in a military structure that continued the comradeship of the trenches. Others joined from anger at defeat, or to exact revenge on those they held responsible.

The government of Friedrich Ebert used the Freikorps against socialist and communist uprisings. Defence Minister Gustav Noske relied on them to suppress the Spartacist uprising, which ended with the summary executions of Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg on 15 January 1919. In late April 1919 Noske sent brigades totalling some 30,000 men to Bavaria against the Bavarian Soviet Republic, where they acted with particular brutality: at Perlach on 5 May a dozen men, members of the Social Democratic Party, were shot, and the next day twenty members of a Catholic club were beaten, shot and bayoneted to death.

In Eastern Europe the units fought in East Prussia, Latvia, Silesia and Poland, justifying their campaign as defence against Bolsheviks and Slavs. The historian Nigel Jones records a massacre of 500 Latvian civilians and the slaughter of some 3,000 people at the capture of Riga. The Iron Division was defeated by the Estonian and Latvian armies at the Battle of Cēsis. After the failed Kapp Putsch of March 1920 the army commander Hans von Seeckt removed Freikorps members from the army, and by 1921 only a small core remained.

Many former members went on to the Black Reichswehr, which Seeckt organised in 1923 and later disbanded after a failed putsch at Küstrin, and to the Nazi Sturmabteilung. Future Nazi figures such as Martin Bormann, Reinhard Heydrich and Rudolf Höss served in Freikorps units, although recent research finds that former members were no more likely to join Nazi organisations than the average German man. During the Night of the Long Knives in 1934, Hitler had Freikorps leaders, among them Hermann Ehrhardt, targeted for killing or arrest.
freising: Freising lies on the Isar river in Upper Bavaria, north of Munich, and is the capital of the district of Freising. It is built around two hills. One is the Cathedral Hill, with the former bishop's residence and Freising Cathedral, and the other is Weihenstephan Hill, where the former Weihenstephan Abbey stands, which houses what is described as the oldest working brewery in the world. Freising is described as the oldest town between Regensburg and Bolzano. Archaeological finds show settlement in the late Stone Age and Bronze Age, but no proof has been found of continuous settlement before the 8th century CE. The earliest recorded tornado in Europe struck Freising in 788.

Around 700 the Frankish Agilolfing dukes built a simple palace on the highest hill as part of the Duchy of Bavaria. Saint Corbinian was sent to Bavaria by the Church to spread Christianity and built a Benedictine monastery and school on the hill, where a sanctuary already stood. According to his life by Bishop Arbeo, a bear killed his packhorse on the way to Rome and was made to carry his luggage over the Alps. The bear still appears in the city's coat of arms. Saint Boniface established Freising as a diocese after Corbinian's death, and between 764 and 783 Bishop Arbeo founded a library and scriptorium. In 996 Emperor Otto III granted Freising city rights.

Monks from Freising built a toll bridge on the Salt Road in the 10th century, at the village that became Munich, and in 1158 Duke Henry the Lion destroyed it and built another downriver. The present Romanesque cathedral was begun in 1159 and finished in 1205. During the Thirty Years' War King Gustavus Adolphus demanded 30,000 guilders in 1632 to spare the city, yet his army sacked it. The bishopric, more than a thousand years old, was abolished when church lands were secularised in the early 19th century, and the diocese's seat moved to Munich in 1821.

Freising remains the seat of diocesan administration, and the Diocesan Museum is there. Manuscripts made in its monastery between 900 and 1200 include the Freising manuscripts in Slovenian, regarded as the first continuous text in a Slavic language written in Roman script, and the chronicle of the two cities by Otto of Freising. The Cathedral Library, founded by Bishop Arbeo, is one of the largest church libraries in Germany. The Weihenstephan campus holds institutes of the Technical University of Munich and a university of applied sciences. The town has about 50,000 inhabitants.
frejus: Fréjus lies in the Var department on the coast of south-eastern France, next to Saint-Raphaël, with which it forms one urban agglomeration, and below the Massif de l'Esterel. It stood at an important crossroads formed by the Via Julia Augusta, between Italy and the Rhône, and the Via Domitia. Tacitus called its port claustra maris, the gateway to the sea. Its origins probably lie with the Celto-Ligurian people who settled round the natural harbour of Aegytna, and the Phocaeans of Marseille later set up an outpost on the site.

Julius Caesar refounded the city as Forum Julii to counter Massalia, the later Marseille, which had sided with Pompeius in the civil war. The date is unclear, but 49 BCE is most likely. Octavius brought the galleys taken from Mark Antony at Actium in 31 BCE to Forum Julii, and between 29 and 27 BCE it became a colony for veterans of the 8th legion. Augustus made it the capital of the new province of Narbonensis in 22 BCE, and its port became the only naval base of the Roman fleet of Gaul until the reign of Claudius.

Under Tiberius the major monuments were built: the amphitheatre, the aqueduct, the lighthouse, the baths and the theatre. The walls, 3.7 km long, protected 35 hectares and about six thousand inhabitants. Gnaeus Julius Agricola, later the conqueror of Britain, was born there in 40 CE. A bishop was elected in 374, and Saint Léonce, bishop from 433, built the first cathedral with its baptistery. Muslim raiders attacked repeatedly between the 7th and 9th centuries, and silt clogged the port and left a swampy plain between the town and the sea.

Fréjus has the richest concentration of Roman architecture in France after Arles. Its amphitheatre and theatre survive, and the aqueduct from Mons, 42 km long, is largely well preserved. The baptistery of the cathedral dates from the 5th century, and remains of the ancient harbour, with the lighthouse and the quay of Augustus, can be seen. The Malpasset Dam above the town ruptured on 2 December 1959, killing over 400 people. Napoleon landed at Fréjus on 9 October 1799, returning from Egypt. The town is a resort that hosts three to four times its regular population in summer.
frelimo: After the Second World War Portugal, under the Estado Novo regime, maintained that Mozambique and its other possessions were overseas territories of the mother country, and calls for independence grew. FRELIMO was founded in Dar es Salaam, Tanganyika, on 25 June 1962, when three regionally based nationalist organisations, the Mozambican African National Union, the National Democratic Union of Mozambique and the National African Union of Independent Mozambique, merged.

Eduardo Mondlane was elected president and Uria Simango vice-president. The movement could not be based in the colony, where the police controlled nationalist activity, and Tanzania under Julius Nyerere was sympathetic. Convinced by events such as the Mueda massacre that peaceful agitation would not bring independence, FRELIMO launched its first offensive in September 1964.

During the war of independence FRELIMO received support from the Soviet Union, China and the Scandinavian countries. By the late 1960s it had set up liberated zones in the north, where it replaced colonial structures, encouraged collectives and increased access to education and healthcare, and by 1969 it controlled about one third of the territory, mostly in rural areas. The 2nd Party Congress of July 1968 approved socialist goals.

After Mondlane was assassinated in February 1969, a triumvirate of Simango, Samora Machel and Marcelino dos Santos took over, and in November Machel and dos Santos ousted Simango. Portugal's Operation Gordian Knot inflicted heavy losses in 1970. After the Carnation Revolution of April 1974 in Lisbon, Portugal and FRELIMO negotiated a transitional government, and independence came in June 1975, with Machel as the first president.

FRELIMO became a Marxist–Leninist vanguard party at its 3rd Congress in February 1977 and nationalised land, banks, health and education. A civil war against RENAMO, supported by Rhodesia and later South Africa, lasted from 1976 to 1992. Machel died in an air crash in 1986 and Joaquim Chissano succeeded him on 6 November 1986. In 1989 the party dropped Marxism–Leninism for democratic socialism, and a constitution of 1990 introduced a multi-party system. The Rome General Peace Accords were signed in 1992, and FRELIMO won the first multi-party election in 1994 with 53.3 per cent of the vote.

FRELIMO has won a majority of seats in the Assembly of the Republic at every election since 1994. Its voluntary quota of 1992 required 30 per cent of its candidates to be women, and women's share of parliamentary seats rose from 26 per cent in 1994 to 40 per cent in 2015. The presidents it has put forward were Samora Machel, Joaquim Chissano, Armando Guebuza, Filipe Nyusi and, from 15 January 2025, Daniel Chapo.
fremantle: Fremantle lies on a series of limestone hills that the Noongar call Booyeembara, with the sandplain to the east called Gardoo. The suburb is bounded by the Swan River to the north and north-west and the Indian Ocean to the west. It has a Mediterranean climate, and its regular afternoon sea breeze is known as the Fremantle Doctor.

The Whadjuk Noongar people, who called the area Walyalup, meaning place of the woylie, have lived there for millennia. The area from Arthur Head to Point Marquis, called Manjaree, was a major meeting and trading place where bush paths converged. The first Europeans to visit were Dutch explorers under Willem de Vlamingh in 1697. In 1827 Captain James Stirling explored the coast, and his favourable report was welcomed by the British Government, which had for some time been suspicious of French colonial intentions towards the west of Australia.

The settlement struggled in its first decades. In 1850, with the advent of penal transportation, Fremantle became Australia's primary destination for convicts, and Fremantle Prison operated long after transportation ended in 1868. In 1897 the engineer C. Y. O'Connor deepened the harbour and removed the limestone bar across the entrance to the Swan River. This made Fremantle a port for commercial shipping at the height of the Western Australian gold rush, and a gateway for miners bound for Coolgardie, Kalgoorlie and Southern Cross. The city was declared a city in 1929.

During the Second World War Fremantle was the home of the largest base for Allied submarines in the Southern Hemisphere. Up to 125 American, 31 British and 11 Free Dutch submarines operated from it, and the port's batteries formed a coastal defence system called Fremantle Fortress. Australia's defence of the America's Cup was held there in 1987.

Fremantle is known for its well-preserved heritage architecture, including convict-built structures and hundreds of gold rush buildings in locally quarried limestone. Its Inner Harbour handles almost the entire container trade of Western Australia, and the city is the western terminus of the railway from Perth, whose first line opened in 1881. Ferries run from the port to Rottnest Island and upriver to Perth.
french-antilles: Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc, a French trader and adventurer, sailed to the Caribbean in 1625 hoping to settle on St Christopher, or St Kitts. Returning to France in 1626, he won the support of Cardinal Richelieu, who became a shareholder in the Compagnie de Saint-Christophe, later reorganised as the Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique. In 1635 d'Esnambuc took one hundred settlers to Martinique to clear land for sugar plantations and founded Saint-Pierre, the first permanent French colony. He died in 1636, and his nephew Jacques Dyel du Parquet became governor of Martinique in 1637. Du Parquet built Fort Saint Louis in 1638, founded a settlement on Saint Lucia in 1643 and led an expedition to Grenada in 1649.

In 1651 the company dissolved itself and sold its rights. The du Parquet family bought Martinique, Grenada and Saint Lucia, the sieur d'Houël bought Guadeloupe, Marie-Galante, La Désirade and the Saintes, and the Knights of Malta bought Saint Barthélemy and Saint Martin. In 1665 the Knights sold their islands to the new Compagnie des Indes occidentales.

The French settled permanently on Martinique and Guadeloupe after being driven from Saint Kitts by the British. Fort Royal on Martinique, now Fort-de-France, was a major port for French warships. Woodcutters from Martinique and Guadeloupe set up timber camps on Dominica from 1690 and gradually became permanent settlers. France imported slaves from West Africa, Martinique and Guadeloupe to work its plantations there, and the Antillean Creole language developed in this period. France ceded Dominica to Great Britain in 1763. In 1783 the Spanish king allowed French planters, with their slaves and free people of colour from the French islands, to settle in Trinidad, whose population rose from just under 1,400 in 1777 to over 15,000 by the end of 1789.

Guadeloupe and Martinique are French overseas departments. Saint Martin and Saint Barthélemy, once attached to Guadeloupe, have held separate status as overseas collectivities since 2007. Antillean Creole survives beyond them: it is spoken on Dominica and Saint Lucia, which became independent from Britain, and in Grenada French loanwords, buildings, cuisine and place names recall the French years.
french-colonial-empire: French colonisation of the Americas began in the sixteenth century with the voyages of Giovanni da Verrazzano and Jacques Cartier. Spain's defence of its American monopoly and the French Wars of Religion prevented steady settlement, and early attempts in Brazil and Florida failed. After 1598 Henry IV encouraged trade with Asia and Africa. French presence in Senegal began in 1626, with Saint-Louis founded in 1659 and Gorée in 1677, and Fort Dauphin in Madagascar in 1642. Plantation economies based on forced African labour were especially lethal for the enslaved.

A series of wars with Britain, from the War of the Austrian Succession to the Napoleonic Wars, destroyed most of the first empire and nearly expelled France from the Americas. Spain returned Louisiana to France in 1800, and France sold it to the United States in 1803. At the end of the Napoleonic Wars Britain restored Guadeloupe, Martinique, French Guiana, Réunion and the small Indian possessions, but kept Saint Lucia, Tobago, the Seychelles and Mauritius.

The second empire began with the invasion of Algeria in 1830, fully conquered by 1903. The historian Ben Kiernan estimates that 825,000 Algerians died in the conquest by 1875. France forced a protectorate on Tahiti in 1842, ruled Morocco as a protectorate from 1912 to 1956, and held mandates over Syria and Lebanon. On the eve of the First World War the empire was the second largest in the world, after the British. In the Second World War Free France and Vichy France struggled for the colonies, and by 1943 all but Indochina under Japanese control had joined the Free French.

After 1945 the French Union replaced the empire in name while Paris kept control. Demonstrations in Algeria in May 1945 were repressed with an estimated 6,000 to 45,000 killed, and the Malagasy Uprising of 1947 with estimates from 11,000 to 89,000 dead. France lost Indochina and Algeria in costly wars, and most other colonies became independent after 1960.

The ideological basis of French colonialism was the civilising mission, which aimed to spread French language, institutions and values; some French politicians contested it. Colonial subjects lived under unequal legal systems and rarely received full citizenship. France sent few settlers to most colonies, Algeria being the main exception. Remaining possessions were integrated into France as overseas departments and territories, and links with former colonies persist through La Francophonie and the CFA franc.
french-directory: The Directory grew out of the Constitution of the Year III, which the National Convention debated from 4 July to 17 August 1795 and adopted on 22 August. It was a long document of 377 articles, against 124 in the constitution of 1793. Of five million eligible voters, 1,057,390 approved it in a referendum and 49,978 opposed it. The Convention required that five hundred of its own members remain in the new legislature.

In October 1795 royalists and constitutional monarchists, hostile to that rule, tried to seize power in Paris and were put down. The elections that followed returned 379 members of the old Convention, and the Convention required that every Director be a former member who had voted for the execution of Louis XVI.

The Directory began with an empty treasury and almost worthless assignats. It stopped printing them in 1796, replaced them with the mandats territoriaux, which also collapsed, and then returned to silver and gold coin, which brought falling prices and wages. Bread shortages in Paris in 1796 fed the Conspiracy of the Equals of François-Noël Babeuf, which the government crushed.

The main task was the war against Britain and Austria. The Directory annexed Belgium and the left bank of the Rhine, and set up twenty-nine short-lived sister republics in Italy, Switzerland and the Netherlands, which sent France money and art treasures. By the Treaty of Campoformio of 17 October 1797 France received the Ionian Islands, Belgium and the left bank of the Rhine as far south as Andernach.

The royalists triumphed in the elections of 1797 and were then put down by a coup, and in 1798 the Directors disqualified Jacobin candidates. In 1799 Britain, Austria and Russia formed a Second Coalition. Bonaparte returned from Egypt and, with Abbé Sieyès and others, overthrew the Directory on 9 November 1799.

Five Directors held executive power. The presidency was an entirely ceremonial post, held first by Jean-François Rewbell, chosen by lot on 2 November 1795, and passed on every three months. Louis Gohier was the last president.

Under the Directory the middle and upper classes replaced the nobility at the top of Paris society, and enormous fortunes were made by army suppliers and property speculators. Young Parisians known as Incroyables and Merveilleuses dressed in extravagant costumes and attended the Bals des victimes. The Goncourt brothers reported 640 balls in Paris in 1797 alone. Crime and highway robbery increased, and the death penalty was applied to robberies on the main roads.
french-equatorial-africa: French Equatorial Africa accounted for a little less than an eighth of Africa, across the present-day Central African Republic, Chad, the Republic of the Congo, Gabon and most of Cameroon. The greater part of it extended over a granite plateau framed by the Tibesti, Ouadaï and Fertit massifs, with two basins, that of Chad and that of the Congo. The highest point was Mount Emi Koussi, at 3,415 metres, in Tibesti. The climate ran from arid Saharan in the north to humid tropical in the south, with savannahs in the centre where millet, peanuts and cassava were grown, and tropical forests in the south that supplied ebony and okoumé.

The federation was established in 1910 with four colonial possessions: French Gabon, French Congo, Ubangi-Shari and French Chad. The Governor-General was based in Brazzaville with deputies in each territory. In 1911 France ceded parts of the territory to German Kamerun after the Agadir Crisis, and it was returned after Germany's defeat in World War I.

France granted private companies contracts to exploit ivory and rubber, and Ubangi-Shari had a concession system like that of the Congo Free State, with similar atrocities. The writer André Gide travelled there and was told of mutilations, executions and the burning of children, and his Travels in the Congo, published in 1927, was fiercely critical of the concession companies. The number of victims remains unknown. The French authorities long tolerated indigenous slavery, but acted against the slave trade of the Sultan of Dar Kuti in 1908 and 1911, and annexed his territory in 1912.

Until 1934 the AEF was a federation of colonies, and in that year it became a unitary entity with a single budget. In August 1940 the whole federation except Gabon rallied to the Free French Forces, and Gabon followed after the Battle of Gabon on 12 November 1940. Félix Eboué was installed as Governor-General, and the federation became the strategic centre of Free French activities in Africa. In the September 1958 referendum the territories voted to become autonomous within the French Community and the federation was dissolved. They formed an interim Union of Central African Republics in 1959 and became fully independent in August 1960.
french-first-republic: Under the Legislative Assembly, France was already at war with Prussia and Austria. In July 1792 the Duke of Brunswick, commanding the Austro-Prussian army, issued the Brunswick Manifesto, threatening the destruction of Paris if the royal family were harmed. On 10 August 1792 citizens stormed the Tuileries Palace, killing six hundred of the king's Swiss guards. In the first week of September mobs broke into the city's prisons and killed over half of the prisoners in the September Massacres.

The Convention met for the first time on 21 September 1792 and unanimously abolished the monarchy. The Republic was never formally proclaimed, but acts were dated from the year I of the Republic, and on 25 September it was declared one and indivisible. From 1792 to 1802 France was at war with the rest of Europe, and it also fought internal conflicts such as the wars in Vendée.

Louis XVI was tried for treason from December 1792, convicted on 16 January 1793 and executed on 21 January. Food riots and hunger continued, and on 6 April 1793 the Convention created the Committee of Public Safety, which adopted a policy of terror under which perceived enemies were guillotined at an increasing rate. The Constitution of 1793 was ratified in early August, but the rights it guaranteed were suspended under the committee.

After Robespierre was executed on 28 July 1794, the Jacobin club was closed. The Constitution of the Year III restored freedom of worship, and on 3 November 1795 the Directory was established, with a Council of Elders of 250 members, a Council of Five Hundred and an executive of five directors. Hyperinflation of the paper assignats and military disasters in 1798 and 1799 brought it down after four years.

The Consulate began with the coup of 18 Brumaire, on 9 November 1799, planned by members of the Directory itself, with Napoleon Bonaparte as a co-conspirator and then First Consul. It had four bodies: a Council of State that prepared draft laws, a Tribunate that debated them, a Legislative Body of three hundred that voted on them without debate or amendment, and a Conservative Senate of sixty irremovable members appointed by Bonaparte. On 18 May 1804 the Senate proclaimed Napoleon Emperor of the French, which ended the Republic.
french-flanders: French Flanders lies in the northernmost part of France, in the Nord department of the Hauts-de-France region, and roughly corresponds to the arrondissements of Lille, Douai and Dunkirk on the border with Belgium. With French Hainaut and Cambrésis it makes up the department. The landscape is flat and low-lying, with fertile plains where wheat, sugar beet and chicory are grown. Maritime Flanders, or the Westhoek, runs along the North Sea coast and includes Dunkirk, while inland Flanders is rural, with towns such as Cassel, Hazebrouck and Bailleul and the hills around Cassel. The Lys and the Yser cross the region.

The region was once part of the feudal County of Flanders and later of the Southern Netherlands. It came under English and then Spanish control, became part of the Spanish Netherlands, and was retained by Spain at the end of the Eighty Years' War. It was separated from the county in 1659 by the Peace of the Pyrenees, which ended the French-Spanish conflict, and further parts were added by treaties in 1668 and 1678 under Louis XIV. It then became part of the province of Flanders and Hainaut, and most of it later fell within the department of Nord.

Some western parts had separated in 1237 and formed the County of Artois, which France gained in 1659; they now lie in Pas-de-Calais. Rich in coal and facing the North Sea, French Flanders was fought over many times between the Middle Ages and World War II, when the name was applied to all of Nord-Pas de Calais under German occupation.

French is the main language, but about 20,000 people speak French Flemish, a West Flemish dialect of Dutch, and the traditional language of Walloon Flanders is Picard. Many local schools teach Flemish, partly to revive it, though it has no official recognition as a regional language. The region is known for red-brick architecture, stepped gables and belfries, for the Carnival of Dunkirk and the giant puppet parades of the north, and for dishes such as carbonade flamande, potjevleesch and Maroilles cheese. Its flag and arms follow those of the County of Flanders, a black lion on gold.
french-foreign-legion: Louis Philippe, King of the French, created the Foreign Legion on 10 March 1831 to bring foreign nationals into the French Army from the foreign regiments of the old kingdom. Its recruits included soldiers from the recently disbanded Swiss and German regiments of the Bourbon monarchy. The royal ordinance allowed the foreigners to serve only outside France. The French expeditionary force that had occupied Algiers in 1830 needed reinforcements, so the Legion was sent by sea from Toulon to Algeria. It was first divided into six national battalions: Swiss, Poles, Germans, Italians, Spanish and Dutch-Belgian.

The Legion was initially stationed only in Algeria, where it took part in the conquest, described as a genocide, and in the drying of marshes near Algiers. It served in the First Carlist War in Spain from 1835, the Crimean War in 1854 and the Italian campaign of 1859. It was part of the French intervention in Mexico from 1863 to 1867 and the Tonkin campaign and Sino-French War of the 1880s. French law kept it out of metropolitan France except in an invasion, so it was not in the army that capitulated at Sedan in 1870.

It helped extend the French colonial empire in Africa. After 1871 volunteers from Alsace and Lorraine joined it, and it fought in many critical battles on the Western Front in the First World War. Its numbers swelled in the First Indochina War, and it suffered heavy losses at Dien Bien Phu, which fell on 7 May 1954.

In the Algerian War its parachute regiments fought the National Liberation Front. By the mid-1960s the Legion had lost its home in French Algeria, and Charles de Gaulle, who considered disbanding it, cut it from 40,000 to 8,000 men and moved it to metropolitan France. Over its history it has lost nearly 40,000 men.

The Legion is the only unit of the French Army open to people of any nationality, and most of its commissioned officers are French, with about 10 per cent promoted from the ranks. Legionnaires may apply for French citizenship after three years' service, or at once if wounded in the line of duty, a provision known as Français par le sang versé. Its flags bear the motto Honneur et Fidélité rather than Honneur et Patrie. It marches at 88 steps a minute, against 116 for other French units, and always comes last in a parade. Its marching song is Le Boudin.
french-invasion-of-russia: Napoleon began the campaign to force the Russian Empire to comply with the continental blockade of the United Kingdom. France had been at war with the major European powers since 1792, and Napoleon had won the War of the Third Coalition, the War of the Fourth Coalition and the War of the Fifth Coalition. Russia had learned from earlier defeats at Austerlitz and Friedland. Between 1810 and 1812 it built and rebuilt fortresses, created military intelligence offices and formally established the corps system. In April 1812 Alexander I issued an ultimatum demanding that French troops leave Prussia and the Grand Duchy of Warsaw. Napoleon chose war, and called it the Second Polish War to win support from Polish nationalists.

The multinational Grande Armée crossed the Neman River on 24 June 1812. Estimates of its size vary, with figures of 400,000 to 500,000 men commonly given, and only about half the soldiers were French. The Russian armies under Barclay de Tolly and Pyotr Bagration, together about 180,000 to 220,000 men, retreated eastward and used scorched earth tactics. Heat, disease, desertion and supply failures cost the French heavily before they took Smolensk in August. Mikhail Kutuzov then became commander-in-chief.

At the Battle of Borodino on 7 September, more than 250,000 troops fought and at least 70,000 were killed or wounded. The French took the main positions but failed to destroy the Russian army. Kutuzov decided at the council at Fili to abandon Moscow, and Napoleon entered it on 14 September to find it deserted and set ablaze by its military governor Fyodor Rostopchin. He waited five weeks for a peace offer that never came and left on 19 October. After losing the Battle of Maloyaroslavets he had to retrace his earlier route. Snow, frost, hunger, typhus and attacks by peasants and Cossacks followed. Napoleon left the army at Smorgonie on 5 December and returned to Paris.

Estimates of the losses differ. Richard K. Riehn gives 685,000 men entering Russia and fewer than 70,000 known survivors, while Adam Zamoyski estimates that as many as 400,000 of the 550,000 to 600,000 who crossed the Neman died, counting prisoners who died in captivity. About 100,000 prisoners were taken, and more than 50,000 died. The campaign is also said to have claimed around a million soldiers and civilians. The saying that General Winter defeated Napoleon is disputed, since Minard's map shows the French losses were highest in summer and autumn, owing to inadequate logistics and disease. The campaign remains present in Russian culture through Leo Tolstoy's War and Peace and Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture.
french-revolution: Between 1715 and 1789 the French population grew from 21 to 28 million, and the middle class tripled in size. The benefits of rising prosperity were largely restricted to the rentier and mercantile classes, while living standards fell for wage labourers and peasant farmers who rented their land. An economic recession from 1785 and bad harvests in 1787 and 1788 led to high unemployment and food prices.

The state's finances were in crisis. The nobility and the Church benefited from exemptions, so the tax burden fell mainly on the lower classes, and the parlements could block new tax laws. By 1788 half of state revenue went on servicing the debt. Reforms proposed by the finance minister Calonne in 1786 were rejected, and the notables and parlements argued that new taxes could be approved only by an Estates-General, last held in 1614.

The Estates General met in May 1789, and in June the representatives of the Third Estate re-constituted themselves as a National Assembly. On 14 July a crowd, joined by soldiers, attacked the Bastille, a royal fortress with large stores of arms. Its governor surrendered after fighting that cost the lives of 83 attackers. The Bastille held only seven prisoners but was a potent symbol of the Ancien Régime. The Assembly then abolished feudalism, placed the Catholic Church under state control and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.

Military defeats after the outbreak of war in April 1792 led to the insurrection of 10 August 1792. The monarchy was replaced by the First Republic in September, and Louis XVI was executed in January 1793. Political power then passed to the Committee of Public Safety, dominated by Jacobins led by Maximilien Robespierre. About 16,000 people were sentenced by the Revolutionary Tribunal and executed in the Reign of Terror, which ended in July 1794.

The Directory replaced the Committee in November 1795 but faced internal unrest, a weak economy and an expensive war. It ended with the coup of 18 Brumaire on 9 November 1799 and the Consulate, with Napoleon Bonaparte as First Consul. The Revolution also began the French Revolutionary Wars, which lasted until Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo in 1815, involved every major European power and redrew the map of Europe.

Historians disagree about the role of ideology: Jonathan Israel holds that the radical Enlightenment was the primary driving force, while Cobban argues that the revolutionaries mostly sought practical solutions to immediate problems.
french-revolutionary-wars: As early as 1791 the other monarchies of Europe looked with outrage on the French Revolution and considered whether to intervene in support of King Louis XVI or to profit from the chaos. On 27 August 1791 Emperor Leopold II and King Frederick William II of Prussia issued the Declaration of Pillnitz, threatening vague but severe consequences if anything befell the king and his family. Leopold meant it as a non-committal gesture, but it was seen in France as a serious threat. France declared war on Austria and Prussia in the spring of 1792, and their coordinated invasion was turned back at the Battle of Valmy in September.

The wars fall into the War of the First Coalition, from 1792 to 1797, and the War of the Second Coalition, from 1798 to 1802. In 1793 France declared war on Great Britain and the Dutch Republic, and drafted hundreds of thousands of men by mass conscription. After reverses, the French regained the initiative at Fleurus in June 1794 and occupied Belgium, the Rhineland and the south of the Netherlands. In 1795 the Batavian Republic was founded, and Prussia signed the Peace of Basel on 6 April, ceding the west bank of the Rhine to France. In Italy in 1796 and 1797 Napoleon Bonaparte drove the Habsburg forces out of the peninsula, and Austria agreed to the Treaty of Campo Formio on 17 October 1797.

In 1798 Napoleon invaded Egypt and won at the Battle of the Pyramids, but Nelson sank his fleet at the Battle of the Nile. The allies gradually pushed the French out of Italy until the French victory at Zurich in September 1799 made Russia drop out of the war. Napoleon failed at the siege of Acre in 1799 and returned to France. Austria signed the Treaty of Lunéville on 9 February 1801. Britain and France signed the Treaty of Amiens in 1802, which is generally taken as the transition to the Napoleonic Wars.

France had conquered territories in Italy, the Low Countries and the Rhineland. The wars spread revolutionary principles over much of Europe, and French armies, mobilized by mass conscription, replaced eighteenth-century armies with their rigid protocols and aristocratic officer classes. Scholars identify the era as the beginning of modern war. The peace with Britain lasted less than a year, though it was the longest period of peace between the two countries between 1793 and 1815.
french-union: The first official use of the term Union française came in the Declaration on Indochina of 24 March 1945. The Union was established by the constitution of the Fourth Republic of 27 October 1946, which held that there were no French colonies and that metropolitan France, the overseas departments and the overseas territories together formed a single France. Its stated goal was the assimilation of the overseas territories into a greater France inhabited by French citizens. It ended the indigène status of colonial subjects.

It had five components: metropolitan France, including the four departments of Algeria; the old colonies that became overseas departments in 1946, Guadeloupe, Guiana, Martinique and Réunion; the new colonies, renamed overseas territories; the associated states, namely Cambodia, Laos, the State of Vietnam, Morocco and Tunisia; and United Nations trust territories such as French Cameroons and French Togoland.

The Union had a President, who was the President of the Republic, a High Council and an Assembly. The Assembly had members from the Council of the Republic, the National Assembly and the regional assemblies of the overseas territories, but ultimately had no power. The High Council met only three times, first in 1951. In practice colonial areas were represented, but all power remained in the French Parliament, and local assemblies had limited authority. Some African leaders, among them Félix Houphouet-Boigny and Leopold Senghor, supported the Union and its investment. African students educated in France came to see a contradiction between the claim of equality and reality, and resistance grew.

The associated states of Indochina moved toward independence between 1949 and 1954, and all three withdrew from the Union in 1954: Vietnam on 20 July, Cambodia in 1955 and Laos in 1957. On 31 January 1956, in response to the Algerian War, the system changed from assimilation to autonomy, allowing territories to develop local government and eventually independence.

In 1958 Charles de Gaulle's Fifth Republic replaced the Union with the French Community, in a constitutional referendum held on 28 September. More than 95% of voters in Guinea, with a turnout of 85.5%, rejected the constitution and so chose independence. French officials there destroyed furniture, lightbulbs and windows, and over 3,000 civil servants and army health officials left. In most other territories upward of 90% approved. The Community did not last long, as most African states left it by 1962, and mentions of it were removed from the French constitution in the 1990s.
french-wars-of-religion: Tensions between Catholics and Protestants had been building since the 1530s. After the Affair of the Placards in October 1534, when Protestant radicals put up posters rejecting the Catholic doctrine of the real presence, Protestantism was clearly defined as heresy. The accidental death of Henry II in July 1559 left a political vacuum and a struggle for power between his widow Catherine de' Medici and powerful nobles: a Catholic faction led by the Guise and Montmorency families and Protestants headed by the House of Condé and Jeanne d'Albret, queen of Navarre. Spain and Savoy supported the Catholics, and England and the Dutch Republic the Protestants.

Catherine, ruling as regent for her son Charles IX, at first backed the moderates known as Politiques. Her Edict of Saint-Germain of January 1562 was opposed by the Guise, and fighting broke out in March after the massacre of Vassy. Condé seized Orléans on 2 April 1562, and the Huguenots took towns along the Loire. In 1572 Catherine backed the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre in Paris, in which Catholic mobs killed between 5,000 and 30,000 Protestants throughout France. The wars were commonly counted in eight numbered phases, ended by edicts and peaces such as Amboise and Longjumeau.

The Catholic League, formed by Henri, Duke of Guise, opposed concessions. When the Duke of Anjou died in 1584 the Calvinist Henry of Navarre became heir to Henry III, and the League allied with Philip II of Spain. On 23 December 1588 Henry III had the Duke of Guise killed at Blois, and in July 1589 a Dominican friar, Jacques Clément, stabbed the king to death. Navarre, now Henry IV, abjured Protestantism on 25 July 1593 and was crowned at Chartres on 27 February 1594.

Between two and four million people died from violence, famine or disease directly caused by the conflict, and the power of the monarchy was severely damaged. The Peace of Vervins with Spain was signed in May 1598. The Edict of Nantes granted the Huguenots substantial rights, but it was less a sign of genuine toleration than a grudging truce with guarantees for both sides.

Henry IV was assassinated in 1610, and the political freedoms of the Huguenots, which detractors called a state within the state, caused trouble in the 17th century. Their revolts ended with the Siege of La Rochelle and the Peace of La Rochelle in 1629. Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685.
frere-jacques: The earliest known version of the melody is in a French manuscript, titled Recueil de Timbres de Vaudevilles and held by the Bibliothèque Nationale, which the library dates between 1775 and 1785. There the tune is labelled Frère Blaise. A publication of 1825 printed the words with a description of the melody in solfège but without musical notation. The words and music appear together in Charles Lebouc's popular collection of children's rounds, Récréations de l'enfance, issued by Rouart, Lerolle in Paris. The musicologist Sylvie Bouissou has found some evidence that Jean-Philippe Rameau wrote the music, since a manuscript at the French National Library lists him as author of this piece among 86 canons.
