The French song asks a friar, Frère Jacques, whether he is sleeping and tells him to sound the bell for matins, the midnight or very early morning prayers. The usual English version, Brother John, keeps the rhythm but reverses the sense, so that the bells wake the sleeper. English friar comes from the Old French frere, which comes in turn from the Latin frater.

Several origins have been proposed. A link with the 17th-century surgeon Frère Jacques Beaulieu was explored without evidence, and Martine David and A. Marie Delrieu suggest the song mocked the Dominican friars, known in France as the Jacobin order, for sloth. Resemblances exist with a piece by Girolamo Frescobaldi first published around 1615, with a French song of 1650 and with a Hungarian folk tune.

The tune is one of the simplest repeating canons, like Three Blind Mice, and it has spread easily. In 1926 officers of the Whampoa Military Academy used it for the patriotic song Revolution of the Citizens, and in China it is also widely thought of as a folk song called Two Tigers. Gustav Mahler set it in a minor key in the third movement of his Symphony No. 1, calling it by its German name, Bruder Martin. Leonard Bernstein used it to explain counterpoint in his Young People's Concerts. The Beatles' Paperback Writer has the title sung beneath its last verse, and the French group Les Frères Jacques took its name from the song's friar.
fretilin: Fretilin was founded on 20 May 1974 as the Timorese Social Democratic Association (ASDT). It renamed itself Fretilin on 11 September 1974 and took a more radical stance, proclaiming itself the sole legitimate representative of the East Timorese people. After a coup by the Timorese Democratic Union (UDT) on 11 August 1975, Fretilin hastily formed an armed wing, Falintil, which emerged victorious after a three-week civil war.

Fretilin declared East Timor's independence from Portugal on 28 November 1975 and inaugurated an 18-member cabinet drawn from its Central Committee, with Francisco Xavier do Amaral as president and Nicolau dos Reis Lobato as vice president and prime minister. Falintil fought the Indonesian armed forces during their invasion on 7 December 1975 and the occupation that followed. The two leaders fell out under the pressure of the occupation, and in September 1977 Lobato had do Amaral arrested for high treason. Lobato, as president, was killed by Indonesian forces on 31 December 1978, and his successor, António Duarte Carvarino, was tracked down and executed on 2 February 1979. From September 1977 to February 1979 only three of the 52 members of the Central Committee survived.

Fretilin survived the military collapse and was slowly rebuilt under the relatively moderate and nationalist leadership of Xanana Gusmão. Between March 1981 and April 1984 it was known as the Partido Marxista–Leninista Fretilin and Marxism-Leninism was its declared ideology; in 1984 the old name returned and revolutionary politics was dropped to further national unity and win the support of the UDT and the Catholic Church.

In the first elections, in 2001, Fretilin polled 57.4% of the vote and took 55 of the 88 seats in the Assembly, a working majority short of the two-thirds it had hoped for to draft the constitution. It formed the government until independence in 2002. In June 2007 it again came first, but with 29% of the vote and 21 seats, and its secretary-general, Mari Alkatiri, spoke of a minority government. On 6 August José Ramos-Horta announced that a coalition led by the CNRT of Xanana Gusmão would govern instead. Fretilin denounced the decision as unconstitutional, and its supporters in Dili held violent protests.

The CNRT was in power from 2007 to 2017. After the July 2017 election Alkatiri formed a coalition government, but his minority government soon fell, and a second general election in May 2018 was won by the CNRT as part of the Alliance for Change and Progress. Francisco Guterres of Fretilin was president from 2017 to 2022, and lost his bid for a second term to José Ramos-Horta.
friday-mosque-of-herat: The mosque stands on ground where religious buildings had been located for many centuries. The first known building was a Zoroastrian temple converted into a mosque in the 7th century; it was later enlarged by the Ghaznavids, and in the second half of the 11th century a smaller mosque with a wooden roof was founded under the Khwarazmian dynasty. An earthquake in 1102 almost destroyed it, and a later fire ruined the rebuilt mosque. The Ghurids seized Herat in 1175, and at the end of the 12th century Sultan Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad chose the plot of the burned mosque and additional land in the elevated north-eastern quarter, which had a direct water supply for its fountain.
When he died in 1203 he was buried in a mausoleum in the mosque. His son Sultan Ghayath-ul-din Mahmood continued the work, which was completed in 1210 with a madrasa added.

The Ghurids built the original mosque entirely of brick on a four-iwan plan around a courtyard with a water basin, now disappeared. The qibla faces west, about 20 degrees off the true direction of Mecca. The present complex is 180 metres long and 120 metres wide, with 460 domes, 444 pillars and 12 minarets, grouped around a courtyard 82 by 60 metres. At the south-east corner stands the Ghurid portal, which has not served as an entrance since unknown times; its brick mosaic and terracotta Kufic inscriptions, glazed blue on the front, survive. Stucco ornament of the Ghurid period has been uncovered in the southern and western iwans.

After the Mongols conquered Herat in 1221 the mosque fell into ruin, and rebuilding began only after 1245 under Shams al-Din Kart. An earthquake in 1364 nearly destroyed it again. The last Kart ruler commissioned a bronze basin in 1375 that is still in the mosque.

Under the Timurid Shah Rukh (1405 to 1444) the courtyard facades received glazed tile mosaic and a marble mihrab, and Mir Ali-Shir Nava'i, adviser to Sultan Husayn Bayqara, remodelled it with a marble minbar and more tilework. The Timurid period corresponds to the time of its highest magnificence.

A major renovation took place in 1942 and 1943, with a tile studio established by UNESCO, and a fuller reconstruction followed from 1951 to 1973 that left little of the original Ghurid plasterwork or Timurid decoration visible. In the Soviet-Afghan War a rocket brought down a minaret in 1986, killing many people, and repairs were not finished until 1995. During the Taliban's rule in Herat from 1996 to 2001 the mosque was closed to non-Muslims. The roofs were renovated in 2002, and parts of old Ghurid decoration were found in 2004.
fridtjof-nansen: Fridtjof Wedel-Jarlsberg Nansen was born on 10 October 1861. The family originated in Denmark, where the trader Hans Nansen, an early explorer of the White Sea region, became borgmester of Copenhagen in 1654. In 1880 Nansen passed his university entrance examination and chose to study zoology at the Royal Frederick University in Christiania, saying later that he thought it offered a life in the open air. He later worked as a curator at the University Museum of Bergen, where his research on the nervous system of lower marine creatures earned him a doctorate and helped establish the neuron doctrine.

Earlier attempts on the Greenland interior, by Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld in 1883 and Robert Peary in 1886, had set out from Disko Bay and turned back after about 160 kilometres. Nansen proposed to travel from east to west, so that his party would have no line of retreat. The sealer Jason picked up his party at Ísafjörður on 3 June 1888, and after weeks of drifting along the coast they crossed the interior on skis. Between thirty and forty thousand people crowded the streets of Christiania to welcome the party in 1889.

He then planned to reach the North Pole by drifting with the current. The naval engineer Colin Archer built the ship Fram, with a rounded hull designed to be pushed upwards by pack ice, and it left Christiania on 24 June 1893. On 14 March 1895 Nansen and Hjalmar Johansen left the ship to dash for the pole, reaching 86°14′ N before turning back. They met the British explorer Frederick Jackson at Cape Flora on 17 June. After 1896 Nansen turned chiefly to oceanography, and in 1905 he spoke out for ending the union with Sweden.

In 1921 Nansen became High Commissioner for Refugees at the League of Nations, with the task of resettling about two million Russian refugees. He introduced the Nansen passport for stateless people, recognised by more than 50 countries, and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922. He died of a heart attack on 13 May 1930, and his ashes were laid under a tree at Polhøgda. The Nansen International Office for Refugees, set up afterwards, received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1938.
friedberg-hesse: Friedberg is the capital of the Wetteraukreis district, about 30 kilometres north of Frankfurt am Main in the Wetterau region. It stands on the river Usa just before it flows into the Wetter, on a basalt plateau, and extends west into the Taunus up to the 518-metre Steinkopf. It has been populated at least since Roman times: relics of a Mesolithic settlement have been found in the suburb of Bruchenbrücken, and Castle Hill was the site of a Roman military camp on the limes, presumably the castellum in monte tauno of Roman records of the 1st century, though this is still discussed. The remains of Roman baths survive. The Roman settlement was abandoned in the retreat from the Rhine frontier by 260 CE.

The Hohenstaufen dynasty of the Holy Roman Empire refounded the old city at a point convenient for important trade routes. It at first rivalled Frankfurt with an important annual trading fair and rapid growth, but its fortunes soon dwindled. Friedberg consisted of two entities, the city and the castle, which were politically independent and in permanent, often malicious competition, and which once ended with angry citizens ransacking and destroying the castle. The city became a Free Imperial City of the Holy Roman Empire by a charter of 1211.

From the 14th to the 15th century the castle was a noble republic in which twelve noble families shared a single castle. Between 1337 and 1498 its constitution developed, with knightly families holding the right to elect a burgrave, two Baumeister and twelve Regimentsburgmannen, who represented the community, kept up the buildings and governed its affairs. The arrangement was unusual in being sustained by many families under a formal constitution. Under Napoleon Friedberg was incorporated in the Grand Duchy of Hesse, or Hesse-Darmstadt.

Friedberg's old town once housed a prosperous Jewish community. Many Jews fled to Palestine and the United States before the Holocaust, and all who remained were deported to Treblinka in 1942. The medieval Jewish ceremonial bath, the Judenbad, a memorial to the old synagogue burned down, and a plaque at a school remain. From about 1956 to 2007 the town was the home of a United States Army installation, Ray Barracks.

Friedberg has seven districts: Bruchenbrücken, Friedberg, Dorheim, Ockstadt, Bauernheim, Fauerbach and Ossenheim. Its most prominent feature is the castle's Adolfsturm, whose crown was restored in the 1980s. The main station lies on the Main-Weser Railway and is the northern terminus of Frankfurt's S-Bahn line S6.
friedrich-durrenmatt: Friedrich Reinhold Dürrenmatt was born on 5 January 1921 in Konolfingen, in the canton of Bern, the son of a Protestant pastor. His grandfather Ulrich Dürrenmatt was a conservative politician. The family moved to Bern in 1935. In 1941 he began studying philosophy and literature at the University of Zürich but moved to Bern after one semester and also studied natural science. As a student he was briefly a member of the Fröntler, a far-right movement, an activity he later attributed to a wish to rebel against his father. In 1943 he decided to become an author and left academic life.

Like Bertolt Brecht, Dürrenmatt explored epic theatre, and he has been called its most original theorist after Brecht. His first play, It Is Written, premiered in April 1947 amid fights and protests in the audience. It sets a sensation-craving cynic against a religious fanatic in a city under siege. From 1948 to 1949 he wrote sketches for the anti-Nazi Cabaret Cornichon in Zürich. His first major success was Romulus the Great, set in 476 CE during the last days of the Roman Empire.

The Visit (1956) is his most widely performed and translated play, a grotesque mixture of comedy and tragedy about a wealthy woman who offers her hometown a fortune if its people avenge the wrongs done to her. The Physicists (1962) is a satire on the responsibility of science for dangerous changes to the world. He also wrote radio plays and detective novels, among them The Judge and His Hangman (1950) and Suspicion (1951). In 1970 he announced his intention to abandon literature and adapt established works for the theatre instead.

Dürrenmatt married the actress Lotti Geißler in 1946, and they had three children. After her death in 1983 he married Charlotte Kerr in 1984. In 1990 he gave a speech for Václav Havel, Switzerland, a Prison, after learning that he and 800,000 other left-leaning Swiss had been spied on for five decades by the Swiss secret service. He died of heart failure on 14 December 1990 in Neuchâtel. Over 1,000 of his paintings and drawings have been exhibited since 2000 in the Centre Dürrenmatt Neuchâtel, designed by Mario Botta around his former home.
friedrich-ebert: Friedrich Ebert was born in Heidelberg on 4 February 1871, the seventh of nine children of a tailor. His family could not afford university, so he trained as a saddle-maker from 1885 to 1888 and then travelled as a journeyman. He joined the Social Democratic Party in Mannheim in 1889. He read Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels but cared more for practical and organisational questions that would improve workers' lives.

After settling in Bremen in 1891 he worked on a socialist newspaper, ran a pub that became a centre of socialist and union activity, and was elected to the Bremen assembly in 1900. In 1905 he became Secretary-General of the party and moved to Berlin, and in 1913, after August Bebel's death, he was elected party leader.

In August 1914 Ebert led the party's Reichstag members to vote almost unanimously for war loans, regarding the war as a defensive measure against the autocratic regime of the Tsar. He backed the Burgfrieden, the truce among parties for the duration of the war, a stance that contributed to a split in 1917 when opponents of the war formed the Independent Social Democratic Party. Two of his four sons were killed in the war. In October 1918 he persuaded his party to join the government of Prince Maximilian of Baden, arguing that it was a duty. He did not favour a republic, and told the prince that he hated social revolution like sin.

After the revolution reached Berlin on 9 November 1918, Ebert and the party leadership sided with the civil service, army, police and judiciary against those who wanted a more radical revolution. He and General Wilhelm Groener planned the return of army units to Berlin in December. On 11 February 1919 the National Assembly, meeting at Weimar, elected him provisional president, and he was sworn in under the new constitution on 21 August 1919. He denounced the Treaty of Versailles as unbearable but accepted it after Hindenburg concluded the army could not resume the war.

Ebert suffered from gallstones. A Magdeburg court in December 1924 fined a journalist who had called him a traitor, yet said that, in strict legal terms, he had committed treason by his role in the January 1918 strike. He gave evidence and delayed medical help. In February 1925 he underwent an emergency appendectomy and died of septic shock on 28 February, aged 54. Paul von Hindenburg succeeded him on 12 May. Historians remain divided. Some defend his actions as the price of preventing a socialist state on the model promoted by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, while leftist critics call him a traitor who paved the way for the far right.
friedrich-engels: Friedrich Engels was born on 28 November 1820 in Barmen, in Prussia, now part of Wuppertal. He was the eldest of nine children of Friedrich Engels Sr., a prosperous cotton mill owner, in a devout Pietist Protestant family. He grew up in the Wupper valley, an early industrial centre known as the German Manchester, and saw polluted rivers, dangerous working conditions and the contrast between the merchant elite's houses and the poverty of the workers.

In September 1841 he began a year of military service in Berlin, where he attended the University of Berlin as a non-matriculated student and joined the Young Hegelian circle known as Die Freien. In 1842 his father sent him to Manchester to work in a cotton mill in which the family had an investment, and his experience of the industrial working class led to The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845).

In August 1844 Engels met Karl Marx for the second time in Paris, and over ten days they found their complete agreement in all theoretical fields. Their first joint work was The Holy Family (1845). After moving to Brussels they wrote The German Ideology, which argued that social structures, politics and ideas are determined by the economic base; it was never published in their lifetimes. The Communist League commissioned them to write the Manifesto of 1848, and Engels fought in the Revolutions of 1848 before exile in England.

In November 1850 he returned to Manchester and the firm of Ermen & Engels to support Marx financially. He led a double life as a respectable cotton merchant and a clandestine communist, became a partner in 1864, and over twenty years sent the Marx family between 3,000 and 4,000 pounds, which effectively funded Das Kapital. He retired in 1870 and moved to London, where he joined the General Council of the International Working Men's Association.

Anti-Dühring (1878) explained their shared scientific socialism in response to Eugen Dühring's influence in Germany, and a section of it appeared separately as Socialism: Utopian and Scientific (1880). After Marx's death in 1883 Engels devoted his life to editing his writings, completing the second and third volumes of Das Kapital. His application of dialectics to science, in works such as Dialectics of Nature, was later controversially developed into the state ideology of the Soviet Union. He died of cancer in London on 5 August 1895, and his ashes were scattered off Beachy Head.
friedrich-hayek: Friedrich August von Hayek was born in Vienna on 8 May 1899 to August von Hayek, a medical doctor and part-time botany lecturer at the University of Vienna, and Felicitas Hayek, née von Juraschek. In his teens Hayek fought in the First World War, and he said later that this experience, together with a wish to help avoid the mistakes that led to the war, drew him into economics. At the University of Vienna he first studied philosophy, psychology and economics, and he earned doctorates in law in 1921 and in political science in 1923.

With the help of Ludwig von Mises, Hayek directed the Austrian Institute for Business Cycle Research in the late 1920s. He joined the London School of Economics in 1931 at the invitation of Lionel Robbins. In Prices and Production (1931) he argued that the business cycle resulted from a central bank's credit expansion, which, by holding interest rates artificially low, caused capital to be misallocated. Building on Mises, he argued that central planners could never have enough information to allocate resources reliably.

The Road to Serfdom (1944) grew from his concern at the view in British academia that fascism was a capitalist reaction to socialism; Hayek argued that fascism, Nazism and state socialism shared roots in central economic planning. In 1950 he left London for the University of Chicago's Committee on Social Thought, and from 1962 until 1968 he taught at the University of Freiburg, where he worked on Law, Legislation and Liberty. On 9 October 1974 it was announced that he would share the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics with Gunnar Myrdal.

Hayek also wrote on psychology. The Sensory Order (1952) set out a learning and memory model close to what became known as Hebbian learning. In social and political philosophy he based his views on the limits of human knowledge and on spontaneous order, favouring a market order in which the state mostly enforces abstract legal rules. In 1975 Margaret Thatcher, newly elected leader of the Conservative Party, held up his book The Constitution of Liberty at a meeting and said that this was what the party believed. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1991 and died on 23 March 1992.
friedrich-schiller: Johann Christoph Friedrich Schiller was born on 10 November 1759 in Marbach, in the Duchy of Württemberg, the only son of the military doctor Johann Kaspar Schiller and Elisabetha Dorothea Schiller. He grew up in a devoutly Lutheran family and spent much of his youth studying the Bible. His parents wanted him to become a priest, and the village priest taught him Latin and Greek. In 1773 he entered the Karlsschule Stuttgart, an elite military academy founded by Karl Eugen, Duke of Württemberg, and graduated as a doctor of medicine in 1780.

At the school he read Rousseau and Goethe and wrote The Robbers, a play about two aristocratic brothers, one of whom leads rebellious students into the Bohemian forest as Robin Hood-like bandits. Its critique of social corruption astounded its first audience and made him an overnight sensation.

In 1780 Schiller became a regimental doctor in Stuttgart, a post he disliked. He left his regiment without permission to see the first performance of The Robbers in Mannheim, was arrested, sentenced to 14 days of imprisonment and forbidden by the duke to publish further works. In 1782 he fled Stuttgart and went by way of Frankfurt, Mannheim, Leipzig and Dresden to Weimar. On 26 May 1789 he gave his inaugural lecture as professor of History and Philosophy at the University of Jena and wrote historical works there. On 22 February 1790 he married Charlotte von Lengefeld.

From 1788 until his death he kept a productive but complicated friendship with Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, who convinced him to return to playwriting. Together they founded the Weimar Theater and wrote the Xenien, satirical short poems aimed at their opponents. The Duke of Saxe-Weimar ennobled him in 1802.

Schiller's philosophical work was concerned above all with human freedom, a theme that runs through his histories and plays: the Wallenstein trilogy concerns the Thirty Years' War, and Don Carlos the revolt of the Netherlands against Spain. His On the Aesthetic Education of Man, first published in 1794, was prompted by his disillusion with the French Revolution and its descent into violence, and argues that a people's moral character can be raised by first touching their souls with beauty. He died of tuberculosis in Weimar in 1805, aged 45. A skull long believed to be his was shown by DNA tests in 2008 not to be.
friedrich-schlegel: Friedrich Schlegel was born on 10 March 1772 at Hanover, where his father, Johann Adolf Schlegel, was pastor at the Lutheran Market Church. The family was fervently Protestant, but as a young man he rejected religion in favour of atheism and individualism. He studied law for two years at Göttingen and Leipzig and met Friedrich Schiller, then in 1793 devoted himself entirely to literary work. In 1796 he moved to Jena, where his brother August Wilhelm lived, and collaborated with Novalis, Ludwig Tieck, Fichte and Caroline Schelling. In 1797 he quarrelled with Schiller, who disliked his polemical work.

Schlegel published Die Griechen und Römer in 1797 and a history of Greek and Roman poetry in 1798, then turned to Dante, Goethe and Shakespeare. With his brother he founded the journal Athenaeum, in which fragments, aphorisms and essays set out the principles of the Romantic school. They are generally recognised as deep and significant expressions of the subjective idealism of the early Romanticists. In 1799 he published the first part of the novel Lucinde, seen as an account of his affair with Dorothea Veit, which caused a scandal in German literary circles. It contributed to the failure of his academic career in Jena.

In Paris from 1802 he studied Sanskrit and Persian. In 1808 he published Über die Sprache und Weisheit der Indier, arguing that a people originating from India founded the first European civilizations. He compared Sanskrit with Latin, Greek, Persian and German and noted many similarities in vocabulary and grammar. The common features he asserted are now generally accepted with significant revisions, while the Out-of-India model has been discredited. He was the first to notice what became known as Grimm's law, and he was a pioneer of comparative linguistics.

Schlegel married Dorothea Veit in Paris in April 1804, and in 1808 the couple joined the Catholic Church in Cologne Cathedral. From then on he increasingly opposed political and religious liberalism. In 1809 he moved to Vienna and was appointed imperial court secretary at the military headquarters, editing the army newspaper and issuing proclamations against Napoleon. After the Congress of Vienna he was councillor of legation at the Austrian embassy in Frankfurt, and in 1820 he started a conservative Catholic magazine, Concordia. He died on 12 January 1829 at Dresden while preparing a series of lectures.
friedrichstadt: Friedrichstadt was founded in 1621 by Dutch settlers. Duke Friedrich III of Holstein-Gottorp persuaded them to bring capital and knowledge to the region in return for freedom to practise their Mennonite and Remonstrant faiths, and for the chance to reclaim fen and marsh land around the town. One of the settlers was Johannes Narssius. Dutch became an official language, and the town took its name from the duke.

By 1630 many of the Arminians had already returned to the Netherlands. Between 1633 and 1637 the duke sent an embassy to Tsar Michael I of Russia and to Shah Safi of Persia, hoping to make Friedrichstadt a European trade terminus. The delegation was led by the jurist Philip Crusius and the merchant Otto Brugman; their secretary, the scholar Adam Olearius, later wrote a book about the journey. The aim of a regular trade route that avoided the passage round Africa was not achieved, and the town did not prosper as expected.

The town lies in the district of Nordfriesland, on the river Eider, about 12 km south of Husum. Besides Remonstrants and Mennonites, Unitarians, Quakers, Catholics and Jews also settled there. Natives include Johannes Thedens, governor-general of the Dutch East Indies in 1741–1743, and the folklorist Wilhelm Mannhardt. The painter Jürgen Ovens, a pupil of Rembrandt, lived in the town and is buried in St. Christophorus Church.
frisia: Frisia is a cross-border cultural region in northwestern Europe along the Wadden Sea, taking in the north of the Netherlands and parts of northwestern Germany. It is commonly divided into West Frisia, roughly the Dutch province of Friesland, East Frisia in Lower Saxony, and North Frisia, between the Eider River and the Danish border, which belonged to the Danish Duchy of Schleswig until 1864. The name comes from the Latin Frisii, possibly from a Proto-Germanic word meaning curly or crisp, presumably referring to the hair of the tribesmen.

The people later known as Frisii began settling in the 6th century BCE, and in Roman times lived, according to Pliny the Elder, on terps, man-made hills. The Frisians of the early Middle Ages were, according to archaeology, descendants of Anglo-Saxon immigrants from the German Bight. The Frisian Realm of 650 to 734 had its centre in Utrecht and its law written down as the Lex Frisionum. It ended at the Battle of the Boarn in 734, when the Franks conquered the western part up to the Lauwers; they took the area east of it in 785. From the 7th to the 10th centuries Frisian merchants took a large part in the luxury trade, with districts in cities such as Hedeby, York and Cologne.

In the 12th century Frisian noblemen and the city of Groningen founded the Upstalsboom League under the slogan of Frisian freedom, to counter feudalising tendencies; it collapsed after 1337. In 1464 a nobleman of the Cirksena family became count of East Frisia, with the help of the Hanseatic League, and Friesland was conquered in 1498 by Duke Albert of Saxony-Meissen. West Friesland had fallen to the count of Holland in 1289. Friesland joined the nascent Dutch Republic in 1577 and Groningen was conquered by the Dutch in 1594.

About half a million Frisians in the province of Friesland speak West Frisian, several thousand people in Nordfriesland and Heligoland speak North Frisian dialects, and a small number in four villages speak Saterland Frisian. Friesland has been called Fryslân since 1996. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries Frisian freedom became the slogan of a regionalist movement demanding equal rights for the Frisian language and culture within the Netherlands.
fritigern: Fritigern was a Thervingian Gothic chieftain whose name is reconstructed as Frithugairns, desiring peace. The earliest references concern the years between an attack on the Thervingi by the emperor Valens and the Hunnic raids of about 376. Socrates Scholasticus, Sozomen and Zosimus report a civil war between Fritigern and Athanaric, another prominent Thervingian ruler; Ammianus Marcellinus and Philostorgius do not mention it. According to Socrates, Fritigern asked for Roman aid and, with Valens, defeated Athanaric. Before or during this conflict he became an Arian Christian. Athanaric seems to have prevailed, since he later led the Thervingi against the Huns.

In 376 the Thervingi, pressed by the Huns who had already conquered their kinsmen the Greuthungi, were allowed by Valens to cross the Danube. In the winter of 376-377 famine struck them. The Roman governors Lupicinus and Maximus sold them food at extreme prices, so that many Goths sold their children into slavery, and invited several leaders to a feast where some were killed and others taken hostage.

Fritigern escaped, became leader of the Thervingi and declared war. His forces beat Lupicinus at the Battle of Marcianople, and by 377 they held most of Thracia. He held a wagon fort through the winter and won Hunnic and Alanic cavalry to his side.

On the night of 8 August he sent envoys proposing peace and an alliance in exchange for territory in Thrace, with a private letter to Valens. Valens refused and marched. At the Battle of Adrianople the Goths won a decisive victory, the Roman army was routed and Valens was killed. Fritigern besieged Adrianople without success. Theodosius I succeeded Valens in January 379, and peace was declared on 3 October 382.
fritzlar: Fritzlar lies mainly on the north bank of the Eder river in the Schwalm-Eder district of northern Hesse, about 160 kilometres north of Frankfurt. The surrounding country is fertile farmland with wooded basalt peaks, many of them topped by medieval castles or castle ruins. The town stood at the crossroads of several important trade routes, and an imperial residence stood there from the time of Charlemagne. This made it a frequent place for royal visits and for assemblies and synods of German princes and church leaders in the early Middle Ages.

Saint Boniface established a church and monastery dedicated to Saint Peter at Fritzlar. Under its first abbot, Saint Wigbert, the Benedictine monastery became a centre of religious and worldly learning, and Wigbert built a stone basilica in 732. Across the Eder, on the Büraburg, Boniface also set up Germany's first bishopric outside the old Roman frontiers, which was absorbed into the diocese of Mainz after its only bishop, Witta, died in 747. In 774 the Saxons destroyed Fritzlar but spared the basilica, which gave rise to a legend that two angels had driven off the invaders. In 782 Charlemagne granted the monastery imperial protection and substantial territory.

In 919 an assembly at Fritzlar proclaimed Henry I, duke of Saxony, king of the Germans. King Conrad I of Germany had died in December 918 without a son and urged his brother Eberhard to nominate Henry. Henry was proclaimed by the leaders of the Franks and Saxons, and Burchard I, Duke of Swabia, soon swore allegiance, although Duke Arnulf of Bavaria did not submit until Henry marched into Bavaria in 921.

In 1079 Emperor Henry IV gave Fritzlar to the archbishop of Mainz, and that year Saxon partisans of the rival king Rudolf of Swabia attacked Henry there, sacking the town and church. A Thuringian landgrave sacked it again in 1232, when much of the population was killed. After the Reformation it remained a Catholic enclave of Mainz within Protestant Hesse. The Thirty Years' War and an outbreak of plague cut its population from about 2,000 to 600. In 1803 it passed to Hesse-Kassel, which Prussia annexed in 1866.

Fritzlar is a small town of about 15,000 people with a medieval centre ringed by a wall and watch towers. The Grey Tower, at thirty-eight metres, is the highest surviving urban defence tower in Germany, and the city hall, first documented in 1109, is described as the oldest in Germany still used for its original purpose. The Romanesque-Gothic Church of St. Peter dominates the town.
friuli: Friuli covers about 8,240 square kilometres between the Livenza river in the west, the Carnic Alps in the north, the Julian Alps and the Timavo river in the east and the Adriatic Sea in the south. The Tagliamento crosses its hills and flows into a large flood plain, and the lagoons of Marano and Grado lie to the south. The historical capital and most important city is Udine, which was also the capital of the medieval Patria del Friuli.

In prehistory the area belonged to the Castellieri culture and the Raeti, and in the 4th century BCE the Carni settled there. From the 2nd century BCE the Romans colonised it. Aquileia became the fourth largest city of Italy under the empire, a river port that dominated trade between the Adriatic and northern Europe. In 452 Attila razed it to the ground. The Patriarchate of Aquileia ranked among the highest ecclesiastical authorities in Italy from the mid-6th century.

In 568 the Lombards took the region, and King Alboin established the Duchy of Friuli, the first Lombard duchy, which he gave to his relative Gisulf I, with its capital at Forum Iulii. The historian Paul the Deacon was born in Friuli. After the Frankish conquest the region became the March of Friuli in 846. On 3 April 1077 Emperor Henry IV granted the county of Friuli to Sigaerd, Patriarch of Aquileia, and the patriarchal state became one of the best organised polities of medieval Italy. It had a parliament from the 12th century, which met for the last time in 1805, when Napoleon Bonaparte abolished it.

Venice conquered the patriarchate in 1420 but left Friuli its own parliament. On 27 February 1511 starving citizens of Udine began a revolt known as Joibe Grasse, which spread through the whole territory and was put down by 1 March, when Venice sent about a hundred cavalry. From 1516 the Habsburg Empire controlled eastern Friuli. In 1866 central and western Friuli were annexed by Italy with the Veneto, while the east stayed under Austria until the First World War.

Friuli forms the major part of the autonomous region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia, with the provinces of Udine, Pordenone and Gorizia. Its people, the Friulians, speak the Friulian language, which around 350,000 people claim as their native language. Slovene, German and Venetian dialects are also spoken in parts of the region.
frombork: Frombork lies on the Vistula Lagoon in Braniewo County, in the historical region of Warmia. The town was founded as a defensive stronghold on an Old Prussian site, after the Teutonic Knights, granted control of the region by the imperial Golden Bull of Rimini, conquered it. According to a local legend, its name, Frauenburg in German, honours Gertruda, the widow of the stronghold's lord, who offered the settlement to the bishop. The name is a common one, since it usually marks a fortified chapel, church or monastery dedicated to the Virgin Mary.

The village is first mentioned in a document of 1278 signed by Bishop Heinrich Fleming, and on 8 July 1310 Bishop Eberhard of Neisse granted the town Lübeck city rights. The Brick Gothic cathedral was built between 1329 and 1388. The town was plundered and burned in 1414 during the Hunger War, joined the anti-Teutonic Prussian Confederation in 1440, and was recognised as part of the Polish Kingdom by the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466. It was devastated again in 1520, in the Polish–Teutonic War.

Nicolaus Copernicus lived and worked there as a canon in 1512–16 and from 1522 until his death. In 1519 he wrote to the King of Poland asking for help against the Teutonic Knights; the letter was intercepted, and the Knights took and burned the town after Copernicus and other canons had left. He wrote De revolutionibus orbium cœlestium in Frombork, and after its publication in 1543 he died there and was buried in the cathedral. Between 1626 and 1635 Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden occupied the town and sent many cultural treasures, including Copernicus's manuscripts, to Sweden. Prussia took the town in 1772 and it became part of the German Empire in 1871.

Heavily damaged in the Second World War, the town passed to Poland in 1945, regained its city rights in 1959, and was rebuilt in 1966–1973 by Polish Boy Scouts and others, in time for the 500th anniversary of Copernicus's birth. The fortified Cathedral Hill holds the cathedral, the Copernicus Tower and the Old Bishop's Palace, which houses the Nicolaus Copernicus Museum, listed as a Historic Monument of Poland. The cathedral is the seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Warmia. Archaeologists found a grave believed to be Copernicus's in 2005; DNA tests confirmed it in 2008, and he was reburied in the cathedral in 2010.
fructuoso-rivera: Rivera was a rancher who joined the army of José Gervasio Artigas in 1810 and eventually rose to the rank of general. When the Banda Oriental was occupied by the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves and Artigas was forced into exile in 1820, Rivera stayed in the newly created Cisplatina province and briefly served in the Imperial Brazilian Army, reaching the rank of brigadier.

He first met Juan Antonio Lavalleja in 1825, in an event known as the Abrazo del Monzón. In the same year the Thirty-Three Orientals led by Lavalleja and their Argentine supporters began their fight against the Empire of Brazil, and Rivera joined them, though it is unclear whether he did so voluntarily. He became an important commander in the Cisplatine War and took part in the Battle of Rincón and the Battle of Sarandí.

After Uruguayan independence was proclaimed in 1828 through the Treaty of Montevideo, arguments between Rivera and Lavalleja turned into fighting, and José Rondeau became the first provisional governor. Rivera held the presidency from 6 November 1830 until 24 October 1834 and survived an unsuccessful assassination attempt and coup by Lavalleja's supporters in 1832. On 11 April 1831 he organised the Salsipuedes Massacre: Charrúa leaders and warriors were lured to a meeting and killed by the military, and surviving women and children were marched to Montevideo and held in household servitude.

Rivera backed Manuel Oribe as his successor but came into conflict with him. In October 1838 he defeated Oribe, who fled to Buenos Aires. Rivera's supporters wore red armbands and Oribe's white, the origin of the division between Colorados and Blancos. Rivera held the presidency again from 1 March 1839 to 1 March 1843. Oribe, backed by Juan Manuel de Rosas, invaded Uruguay, and in December 1842 he defeated Rivera at the Battle of Arroyo Grande and began the Great Siege of Montevideo.

Rivera's power was limited to the capital until he was forced into exile in Brazil in 1847; he stayed there until 1853. A triumvirate of Venancio Flores, Lavalleja and Rivera was created on 25 September 1853. Lavalleja died on 22 October, and Rivera died on 13 January 1854 on his way to Montevideo. He is regarded as the founder of the Colorado Party, which ruled Uruguay without interruption from 1865 until 1958, and a Riverista tendency within it remains a counterpoint to the Batllista and other factions.
fruela-ii-of-asturias: Fruela was a son of Alfonso III of Asturias and his wife Jimena. In 910 he and two of his brothers deposed their father and divided the kingdom among themselves. Fruela, the youngest brother, took the original portion, Asturias; Ordoño took Galicia; and García, the eldest, took León. Although Fruela called himself king of a much-diminished Asturias, evidence suggests that his role was subordinate to the king of León. As king of Asturias he had the task of consolidating the region later called Castile and keeping its counts in check.

Fruela married twice, first in 910 to Nunilo Jimena, daughter of the Navarrese king, and by 917 to Urraca, daughter of the Banu Qasi governor of Tudela. He had at least three sons, Alfonso, Ramiro and Ordoño, none of whom inherited the throne. Bishop Pelayo gives all three to Nunila, while Ibn Khaldun gives Ordoño and Ramiro to Urraca.

Fruela kept good relations with his brother Ordoño, who held the hegemony. They cooperated in the Reconquista, and Fruela signed Ordoño's diplomas as Froila frater confirmat, 'Fruela the brother confirms'. When Ordoño died in 924 the magnates ignored his heirs and elected Fruela king. He had never been popular with the nobles and his subjects, and some doubt that his election was regular and see it as a likely usurpation.

He had Gebuldo and Aresindo, sons of Olmundo, who claimed descent from King Witiza, assassinated, which alienated the nobility further. One chronicler relates that for this he was condemned to a reign of only fourteen months. According to Ramón Menéndez Pidal, he also exiled Frunimio, bishop of León and a relation of Olmundo. He reigned for fourteen months and died of leprosy in August 925.

After Fruela's death several claimants competed for his lands. They included Ramiro, who appears to have married the widowed queen Urraca and used the royal title but was eventually unsuccessful, the sons of Ordoño II and Fruela's own young sons. There is some debate about the immediate succession.
frumentius: According to the fourth-century historian Tyrannius Rufinus, who cites Frumentius' brother Edesius as his authority, the two were born in Tyre, in present-day Lebanon. As children, about 316, they accompanied their uncle Meropius on a voyage to 'India'. On the return voyage their ship stopped at a harbour on the Red Sea, where local people massacred the whole crew but spared the two boys, who were taken as slaves to the King of Axum. Edesius became the king's cupbearer and Frumentius his secretary and treasurer. Shortly before his death the king freed them, but the widowed queen persuaded them to stay and help her educate the young heir, Ezana, and administer the kingdom during his minority.

Frumentius, especially, used his influence to spread Christianity. He first encouraged Christian merchants in the country to practise their faith openly and helped them find places for prayer, and later he converted some of the local people. When Ezana came of age Edesius went back to Tyre, where he was ordained a priest, while Frumentius travelled as far as Alexandria and asked Athanasius, Patriarch of Alexandria, to send a bishop and priests as missionaries to Ethiopia. By Athanasius' own account he judged Frumentius the most suitable person, and consecrated him bishop, traditionally in 328, or according to others between 340 and 346.

Frumentius returned and set up his see at Axum, where he converted and baptised Ezana, who built many churches and spread Christianity through the country. Frumentius founded the first monastery of Ethiopia, Dabba Selama in Dogu'a Tembien. Around 356 the Roman emperor Constantius II wrote to Ezana and his brother Saizana asking them to replace Frumentius with Theophilos the Indian, who supported Arianism, as the emperor did. Athanasius, a leading opponent of Arianism, had appointed Frumentius, and the king refused the request.

Frumentius died about 383. He was called Kesate Birhan, meaning Revealer of Light, and Abba Salama, meaning Father of Peace, and was the first Abuna, the title of the head of the Oriental Orthodox Churches in Ethiopia. His appointment began the tradition that the Patriarch of Alexandria appointed the bishops of Ethiopia. Ethiopian traditions credit him with the first Geʽez translation of the New Testament and with a part in developing the Geʽez script from an abjad into an abugida. The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Churches celebrate his consecration on 18 Taḫśaś, the Coptic Orthodox Church keeps his feast on 18 December, the Eastern Orthodox Church on 30 November and the Catholic Church on 20 July.
fuad-i-of-egypt: Fuad was born in Giza Palace in Cairo, the youngest son of Isma'il Pasha, and spent his childhood with his exiled father in Naples. He was educated at the military academy in Turin. Before becoming sultan he played a major role in the establishment of Egyptian University, now called Cairo University, and was its first rector from 1908 until his resignation in 1913.

In 1911, after the Italian invasion of Tripoli and Cyrenaica, he sought to establish himself as Arab Muslim ruler of Libya under the Italian crown, but the Italian government preferred direct colonial administration. In 1913 Azzam Pasha suggested him for the throne of Albania, but the European Allied powers chose a German prince in March 1914. He was president of the Egyptian Geographic Society from 1915 until 1918.

Fuad succeeded his elder brother Hussein Kamel as Sultan of Egypt in 1917. After the Egyptian Revolution of 1919 the United Kingdom ended its protectorate and recognised Egypt as a sovereign state on 28 February 1922, and on 15 March 1922 Fuad issued a decree changing his title from Sultan to King of Egypt. The 1923 Constitution granted him vast powers. He made frequent use of his right to dissolve parliament, cabinets were dismissed at royal will, and parliaments never lasted their full four-year term. In 1930 he abrogated the constitution and replaced it with one that limited the role of parliament to advice only, but large-scale public dissatisfaction compelled him to restore the earlier constitution in 1935.

Fuad had eighty-seven volumes of correspondence of his ancestors copied, translated and arranged from European archives, and later gathered old documents from Egyptian archives into what became the Royal Archives in the 1930s. His effort to portray his great-grandfather Muhammad Ali, his grandfather Ibrahim and his father as nationalists and benevolent monarchs became an enduring influence on Egyptian historiography.

Fuad married first Princess Shivakiar in 1895, a marriage that ended in divorce in 1898, and second Nazli Sabri on 24 May 1919. His second marriage produced five children, among them the future King Farouk and Princess Fawzia, who became queen consort of Iran. Fuad died on 28 April 1936 at the Koubbeh Palace in Cairo, reportedly of heart failure, and was buried at the Khedival mausoleum in the al-Rifa'i Mosque. He was succeeded by Farouk I, who was 16 years old and studying in England.
fuhrer: Führer has been used as a military title in Germany since at least the 18th century. A company's temporary or less qualified commander, for example, was a Kompanieführer, while a fully qualified commanding officer was a Kompaniechef. The first political use of the word was for Georg Ritter von Schönerer (1842–1921), the pan-German Austrian nationalist, whose followers called him the Führer. According to the historian Richard J. Evans, this probably introduced the term to the German far right, though the Nazis may also have been influenced by Benito Mussolini's informal title of Duce, which likewise means leader.

Adolf Hitler took the title to denote his function as head of the Nazi Party. He received it in 1921, when he resigned in anger at party founder Anton Drexler's plan to merge with another party and returned only on condition that he be made chairman with dictatorial powers. After he became Chancellor on 30 January 1933, a law of 1934 merged the offices of president and chancellor on the death of President Paul von Hindenburg. Hitler then became Führer und Reichskanzler, although Reichskanzler was quietly dropped from everyday use. Soldiers swore allegiance to him as Führer of the German Reich and Nation, and on 23 June 1941 he declared himself Germanic Führer, to assert leadership over peoples the Nazis counted as Nordic-Germanic.

The slogan Ein Volk, ein Reich, ein Führer, meaning One People, One Empire, One Leader, was among the most repeated of the Nazis and appeared on countless posters. It stressed the leader's absolute control over almost every part of German society, with the churches formally the main exception. The term spread from the party to the state, the armed forces, the nation and finally all Germanic peoples. Hitler kept up a pretence of legality, issuing thousands of decrees based on the Reichstag Fire Decree, and his vague orders set subordinates against one another. Lower ranks also used the word: Gauleiter led Nazi regions, and the SS and SA used Führer in their rank titles.

In German the word remains common in compounds such as Reiseführer, travel guide, and Führerschein, driving licence. Because of its link with Hitler, the isolated word usually has negative connotations when it means a political leader.
fuhrerprinzip: The political-science term Führerprinzip was coined by Hermann von Keyserling, a Baltic German philosopher. As an ideology it sees an organisation as a hierarchy of leaders, each with absolute responsibility in his own area, owed absolute obedience and personal loyalty by those below and answerable to those above. Rudolf Hess described it as unconditional authority downwards and responsibility upwards. Adolf Hitler proclaimed it the law of the Nazi Party as early as July 1921, when he left the party in a quarrel with its founder Anton Drexler and returned only when the committee accepted his demand to replace Drexler as chairman.

The Nazi Party split into a northern faction led by Otto and Gregor Strasser, which disagreed about whether the principle was essential, and a southern faction led by Hitler. At the Bamberg Conference on 14 February 1926 Hitler defeated the opposition and made it the managing principle of the party. In 1934 he imposed it on the government and civil society, and organisations in schools, sports associations and factories were led by appointed leaders rather than elected committees. The armed forces swore a Führer Oath to Hitler personally from 1934. The legal theorist Carl Schmitt defended it as the foundation of the total state.

Propaganda supported the idea in films such as Der Herrscher and Kolberg, and appealed to the memory of Frederick the Great and Otto von Bismarck. Hermann Göring told the British ambassador that none of the leadership counted for more than the stones they stood on, and that the Führer alone decided.

After the Second World War, defendants at the Nuremberg trials of 1945 and 1946 and at the Eichmann trial in 1961 argued that the Führerprinzip voided their responsibility, since they were officers following superior orders. In Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963) Hannah Arendt described Eichmann as an ordinary administrator who denied personal responsibility, the figure she called the banality of evil. Eichmann said he had been doing his job and had tried to act in accordance with Immanuel Kant's categorical imperative.
fujian: Fujian is bordered by Zhejiang to the north, Jiangxi to the west, Guangdong to the south and the Taiwan Strait to the east. The province is mostly mountainous, traditionally described as eight parts mountain, one part water and one part farmland, and its highest point is Mount Huanggang, at 2,157 metres. The name Fujian, 'happy establishment', combines the names of Fuzhou and Jianzhou, which is now Nanping. Because of the mountains and successive waves of migration, it is one of China's most culturally and linguistically diverse provinces.

Excavations at Keqiutou on Pingtan Island show that Fujian had entered the Neolithic by the middle of the sixth millennium BCE. The kingdom of Minyue was located there; its name joins Min, perhaps an ethnic name and also that of the main river, with Yue, after the State of Yue in Zhejiang, whose royal family fled to Fujian after Chu annexed that kingdom in 306 BCE. King Wuzhu built a fortified city at Fuzhou, and his kingdom reached into eastern Guangdong, eastern Jiangxi and southern Zhejiang.

A first wave of settlers from the north arrived in the early fourth century, mainly from eight families of central China, among them Chen, Lin, Huang and Zheng, which remain the commonest surnames in the province. In the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period a second wave came with the brothers Wang Chao, Wang Shengui and Wang Shenzhi, who set up a Kingdom of Min with its capital at Fuzhou. The name Fujian was first used for an administrative region in 985.

From 1357 to 1366 Muslims of Quanzhou took part in the Ispah Rebellion before the Yuan crushed it, and the city then lost its foreign trade. Under the Ming, Fujian became a province, and Changle served as the base for Zheng He's expeditions. A sea trade ban hampered it, and the Qing imposed another ban of about twenty years against Koxinga's Ming loyalists on Taiwan.

Fujian has a population of about 41.5 million, with Fuzhou as its capital. Quanzhou is its largest prefecture-level city by population, and Xiamen was one of China's first special economic zones. Southern Min, or Hokkien, is spoken by much of the ethnic Chinese population of Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines, because of emigration. The province has four UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them the Fujian Tulou, earth buildings of the Hakka, listed in 2008.
fujiwara-clan: The clan descended from the Nakatomi clan and, as legend held, through them from the ancestral god Ame-no-Koyane. Its founder, Nakatomi no Kamatari (614–669), was rewarded by Emperor Tenji with the honorific Fujiwara, after the wisteria field on Mount Tono where Kamatari and the then Prince Naka, whom he had befriended in a game of kemari, conspired against the Soga clan. Kamatari led a coup against the Soga in 645 and began the sweeping reforms known as the Taika Reform.

The surname passed to the descendants of his second son Fujiwara no Fuhito (659–720), who married his daughter Kōmyōshi to Emperor Shōmu, the first empress consort of Japan who was not herself of the imperial family. Fuhito's four sons founded four branches, of which the Hokke, or Northern branch, came to lead the whole clan.

During the Heian period the Hokke built a hereditary claim to the posts of regent for a minor emperor (sesshō) and for an adult one (kampaku). The clan's strategy was to marry its daughters to emperors, so that its male heads were often the emperor's father-in-law, uncle or maternal grandfather. Fujiwara no Yoshifusa was the first non-imperial person to become regent for a minor emperor, in 858, when his grandson was enthroned as Emperor Seiwa, and his adopted son Mototsune became the first kampaku.

The family reached its peak under Fujiwara no Michinaga (966–1027), grandfather of three emperors and father of six empresses or consorts; he never took the title of kampaku, as he held more power than the office gave. Under the Fujiwara the court produced kana scripts, the Pillow Book of Sei Shōnagon and the Tale of Genji by Murasaki Shikibu, herself a Fujiwara.

Their control weakened with Emperor Go-Sanjō (reigned 1068–73), the first emperor since Uda whose mother was not a Fujiwara, and with the cloistered rule begun in 1087. The Hōgen Disturbance of 1156 and the Heiji Disturbance of 1160 brought the Taira to power and ended Fujiwara dominance, and the Kamakura shogunate was founded in 1192.

A northern branch, the Northern Fujiwara, ruled the Tōhoku region in the 12th century. In the 13th century the Hokke split into five regent houses: Konoe, Takatsukasa, Kujō, Nijō and Ichijō, which kept a monopoly on the offices of sesshō and kampaku until they were abolished in the Meiji era. Younger branches turned to the arts and produced scholars such as Fujiwara no Shunzei and Fujiwara no Teika. Emperors and crown princes often took their principal consorts from the Fujiwara until the marriage of the Crown Prince Hirohito in January 1924, and Fumimaro Konoe and Morihiro Hosokawa, both descended from the clan, became prime ministers.
fukui-prefecture: Fukui Prefecture lies in the Chūbu region of Honshū and borders Ishikawa Prefecture to the north, Gifu Prefecture to the east, Shiga Prefecture to the south and Kyoto Prefecture to the southwest. It covers about 4,190 square kilometres and faces the Sea of Japan, within the historic Hokuriku region. The western part, formerly Wakasa, is a narrow plain between the mountains and the sea. The larger eastern part, formerly Echizen, has wider plains and holds the capital and most of the population. The area lies within Japan's snow country, and parts of it are protected as Hakusan National Park and the Echizen-Kaga Kaigan and Wakasa Wan Quasi-National Parks.

The Kitadani Dinosaur Quarry on the Sugiyama River, in the city of Katsuyama, has yielded dinosaurs such as Fukuiraptor, Fukuisaurus, Koshisaurus, Fukuivenator, Fukuititan and Tambatitanis, and fossils from the prefecture are shown at the Fukui Prefectural Dinosaur Museum.

Fukui originally consisted of the old provinces of Wakasa and Echizen before the prefecture was formed in 1871. During the Edo period the daimyō of the region bore the surname Matsudaira and descended from Tokugawa Ieyasu. The Matsudaira clan was headquartered at Fukui Castle, which stood on the site of the modern prefectural offices. Fukui was heavily bombed in World War II, and the castle, surrounded by a moat, was demolished; the prefectural government buildings were built on its site.

Fukui is the capital and largest city, and other major cities include Sakai, Echizen and Sabae. Sabae produces 90 per cent of Japan's domestically made glasses, and Fukui has long been a centre of papermaking, with makers of traditional Echizen paper. The prefecture is also known for sake, rice and soba noodles, and its people speak a distinctive accent, Fukui-ben.

Among its historic sites are Eihei-ji, a Buddhist training temple founded by Dōgen in 1244 on about 33 hectares; the Ichijōdani Asakura Family Historic Ruins; the National Treasures of Myōtsū-ji, its three-storied pagoda and main hall; and Maruoka Castle, built in 1576 and the oldest standing castle in Japan. Nuclear power stations stand along Wakasa Bay.
fukuoka: Fukuoka is built along Hakata Bay, bordered by mountains on three sides and open to the Genkai Sea on the north. It is the point of Japan's main islands nearest to the Asian mainland, and Busan in South Korea lies about 180 kilometres away. People have lived in the area since the Jomon period, and settlers of the Yayoi period were among the earliest to arrive. Distance from Kyoto, Osaka and later Edo gave the city a distinctive local culture and dialect.

The Book of the Later Han records that an envoy from the region visited the court of Emperor Guangwu in 57 CE and received a gold seal, which was found in the 17th century. By the end of the Asuka period the port, sometimes called the Port of Dazaifu, had grown into the regional government headquarters for Kyushu and a trade centre with Tang China. Trade continued to grow after the Kōrokan declined at the end of the Heian period, and monks who had studied in China founded temples there. Eisai founded Shōfuku-ji, described as the oldest Zen temple in Japan, and is credited with bringing tea to Japan; Enni, who built Joten-ji, is credited with bringing udon from China.

From 1268 Kublai Khan sent envoys to make the Kamakura shogunate acknowledge his suzerainty, and the shogunate refused. During the Muromachi period Hakata was the first free city in Japanese history, governed by a council of 12 wealthy merchants called Tongyoji, and it remained Japan's main port for trade with mainland Asia, particularly with the Song and Yuan dynasties of China and with Korea. The name Fukuoka, combining the characters for good fortune and hill, was given by the daimyō Kuroda Nagamasa to his new castle town after the Fukuoka district of Bizen Province, the ancestral home of his clan.

In the early 20th century the city gained the Fukuoka Medical College in 1903 and a streetcar service in 1910. In World War II it was a regional military centre, and it was firebombed on 19 June 1945, an attack that destroyed 21.5 per cent of its urban area.

Fukuoka is the capital of Fukuoka Prefecture and the most populous city on Kyushu, with a population of over a million and a half in seven wards. It was designated a city by government ordinance on 1 April 1972. Its oldest festival, Hakata Gion Yamakasa, is held for two weeks each July and is said to date from 1241. The city museum displays the gold seal of 57 CE.
fukuoka-prefecture: Fukuoka Prefecture lies at the northernmost point of Kyūshū, on the Kanmon Straits, which connect the Tsushima Strait and the Seto Inland Sea across from Yamaguchi Prefecture on the island of Honshu. It extends south towards the Ariake Sea and borders Saga, Kumamoto and Ōita prefectures. The prefecture faces the sea on three sides, and it includes a number of small islands off the north coast. Fukuoka is the capital and the largest city on Kyūshū, and other major cities include Kitakyushu, Kurume and Ōmuta. The prefecture includes the former provinces of Chikugo, Chikuzen and Buzen.

The prefecture's religious history is old. Kōra taisha, Sumiyoshi-jinja and Hakozaki-gū are its chief Shinto shrines. The oldest of its Buddhist temples, Kanzeon-ji at Dazaifu, was founded in the 7th century by the emperor to honour his mother, and together with its Kaidan-in it was one of three places in Japan where Buddhist monks could be ordained.

Monks who had studied in China sailed back and founded temples in the heart of Hakata, now Fukuoka City. Eisai founded Shōfuku-ji, known as the oldest Zen temple in Japan, and Kūkai established Tocho-ji. Enni built Jōten-ji, and he is also credited with first bringing udon noodles to Japan. During the Tokugawa shogunate the daimyo Arima Toyōji was relocated to the region and moved his family temple to Kurume, where it became the Zen temple Bairin-ji.

The prefecture contains much of Kyūshū's industry, with automobiles, semiconductors and steel among its major products; the tire maker Bridgestone was founded there. Kyushu University is in Fukuoka. The Kyushu National Museum at Dazaifu covers the history of Kyūshū from prehistory to the Meiji era, with emphasis on its cultural exchange with China and Korea. The Hakata Gion Yamakasa festival is held each July, and the Genko Historical Museum displays arms and armour of the 13th-century Mongol invasions.
fulbert-youlou: Youlou, whose last name means grape in Lari, was born in Madibou, a younger child in a family of three boys. He was baptised at nine, received the Christian name Fulbert, and entered the Petit Séminaire of Brazzaville in 1929. He completed his studies in Cameroon and Libreville, and at Yaoundé met Barthélemy Boganda and André-Marie Mbida, later nationalist leaders. He served as a priest in the parish of Saint-François de Brazzaville, directing youth organisations and Catholic groups.

In the territorial elections of 1947 he stood for the African college in the district of Pool and was heavily defeated. In 1955 a Kongo council chose him as its candidate for the legislative elections, and his bishop tried to dissuade him. He was banned from wearing the cassock and celebrating Mass. Some supporters regarded him as the reincarnation of Jesus-Matswa, and he became a symbol of resistance to colonial rule.

On 17 May 1956 Youlou founded the Union démocratique de défense des intérêts africains, an anti-communist party of Liberal Christian persuasion whose symbol was the crocodile. In September 1957 it won a majority in the Assembly with 23 seats, and rivalry with Jacques Opangault's African Socialist Movement turned violent. In the referendum of 28 September 1958 he supported the Yes vote on the French Community. On 28 November 1958 the socialist deputies left the Assembly, and Youlou proclaimed the Republic, was named head of the provisional government and became prime minister on 8 December.

In August 1960 he led the country into independence. He favoured economic liberalism, pursued a pro-Western policy he called moderate and in December 1960 held a conference in Brazzaville that created the anti-communist groupe de Brazzaville. In August 1962 he announced a one-party state, and in August 1963 the unions refused his proposed system. Union leaders were imprisoned, and the revolution of the Trois Glorieuses followed. Charles de Gaulle despised him, France refused to assist him, and he resigned in the face of overwhelming opposition.

Youlou was imprisoned after his resignation and on 25 March 1965 fled to Léopoldville with the help of his successor, Alphonse Massamba-Débat. A popular tribunal in Congo-Brazzaville tried him in absence from 8 June 1965 on charges including misappropriation of public funds, and sentenced him to death. He answered with a book, J'accuse la Chine, in 1966. Later regimes held him responsible for the country's problems, and his name was struck from public discourse. He died of hepatitis in Madrid in 1972, and was buried in Madibou without official ceremony. The National Conference of 1991, which restored multi-party democracy, rehabilitated his memory.
fulda: Fulda lies on the river Fulda in the German state of Hesse and is the administrative seat of the Fulda district. Since 1974 it has been included in the district as a city with special status. Its station is an interchange between local and long-distance services on the Hanover to Würzburg high-speed line, and the Roman Catholic Diocese of Fulda has its seat in the cathedral.

In 744 Saint Sturm, a disciple of Saint Boniface, founded the Benedictine monastery of Fulda as one of Boniface's outposts in the reorganisation of the church in Germany. Carolingian rulers and leading families supported it with large donations, and in 751 it was placed directly under the Papal See. Boniface was killed by the Frisians in 754 and his relics were brought to Fulda. Between 790 and 819 the abbey church was rebuilt on the model of Old St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. Rabanus Maurus was abbot from 822 to 842, and the abbey owned the Codex Fuldensis and works by Cicero and Bede. Its school became a centre of learning.

On Christmas day 1235 five boys died in a house fire, and local people accused the Jewish community of killing them for ritual purposes. Jews were tortured and 34 were killed after two confessed. Emperor Frederick II investigated and found them innocent. In the Counter-Reformation Prince-abbot Balthasar von Dernbach called in the Jesuits in 1571 and ordered his subjects, most of them Lutheran, to return to the Catholic faith or leave. He also ordered the Fulda witch trials, in which hundreds were arrested.

Fulda became a bishopric in 1752 and the prince-bishops ruled until Napoleon I dissolved the bishopric in 1802. The cathedral was remodelled in 1704–12 and the Stadtschloss in 1707–12 by Johann Dientzenhofer, which give the city its title of Baroque City. After 1814–15 most of the territory went to the Electorate of Hesse, which Prussia annexed in 1866.

From 1938 to 1943 a Nazi forced labour camp for Romani people stood at Fulda. In the Cold War the Fulda Gap, an old east-west invasion route, was presumed to be where a conventional war between NATO and Soviet forces would begin, and American cavalry regiments were stationed in the city until 1993. The crypt of the abbey church still holds the relics of Boniface.
fulgencio-batista: Fulgencio Batista y Zaldívar was born on 16 January 1901 in Veguita, in the municipality of Banes, Cuba, to parents who had fought in the Cuban War of Independence. He was of Spanish, African and Chinese descent, and possibly of some Taíno descent. His mother named him Rubén and gave him her surname, and he was legally Rubén Zaldívar until 1939. When he then tried to register as a presidential candidate, no birth certificate existed for Fulgencio Batista, and he had to pay the local judge 15,000 pesos.

Batista joined the Sergeants' Revolt of 1933, which overthrew Gerardo Machado. Contemporaries claimed he was drawn in mainly because he was the only sergeant with a car. He then became army chief of staff with the rank of colonel and controlled the armed forces behind a short-lived five-member presidency. In January 1934 he, conspiring with the United States envoy Sumner Welles, forced President Ramón Grau San Martín to resign, and he ruled through puppet presidents until he was elected president in 1940. He carried out social reforms and pro-union policies, and Cuba entered the Second World War on the side of the Allies on 9 December 1941.

After four years in the United States he returned, and on 10 March 1952, three months before an election in which he stood a distant third, he seized power with army backing and cancelled the vote. He suspended the 1940 constitution and revoked most political liberties, including the right to strike. Havana became a centre of gambling and prostitution run for the American Mafia, and United States companies owned large shares of Cuba's sugar lands, mines and utilities. After Fidel Castro's attack on the Moncada Barracks on 26 July 1953, Batista relied increasingly on police violence. Estimates of those killed range from hundreds to 20,000, a figure that is disputed.

From December 1956 to December 1958 Castro's 26th of July Movement waged guerrilla war against the government. Rebels under Che Guevara defeated Batista's forces at Santa Clara on New Year's Eve 1958, and on 1 January 1959 Batista fled to the Dominican Republic under Rafael Trujillo's protection. He later found asylum in Portugal, living on Madeira and in Estoril, and died of a heart attack in Marbella, Spain, on 6 August 1973.
fulk-king-of-jerusalem: Fulk was born in late 1089 or 1090, the son of Count Fulk IV of Anjou and Bertrada of Montfort. He became sole count of Anjou when his father died on 14 April 1109, and count of Maine in 1110 through his marriage to Eremburga, daughter of Elias of Maine. He subdued rebellious castellans and clashed with King Henry I of England over Maine, for which he did homage to Henry in 1113. In 1120 he became a major sponsor of the Knights Templar and made an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

In 1128 his son Geoffrey married Empress Matilda, and in 1129 Fulk left Anjou to Geoffrey and went to Jerusalem to marry Melisende, daughter of King Baldwin II. As her dowry the couple received Acre and Tyre.

Baldwin II died on 21 August 1131, and Fulk and Melisende were crowned on 14 September in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the first monarchs crowned there. In Antioch, Princess Alice seized power, and in 1132 Fulk marched north, fought Count Pons of Tripoli and won the regency for the young Princess Constance.

At home he appointed Angevins to key offices and tried to exclude Melisende from power. In 1134 Hugh II of Jaffa, her cousin, was accused of plotting to murder the king. Hugh allied with the Muslims of Ascalon and lost the support of the other lords. Fulk besieged Jaffa until Patriarch William of Malines negotiated peace, with three years of exile for Hugh. Melisende then forced Fulk to share rule, and William of Tyre wrote that he did nothing without her consent.

Fulk and Melisende made little attempt to expand by conquest. They blockaded Fatimid-ruled Ascalon and guarded the borders against Imad al-Din Zengi. In 1137 Zengi defeated Fulk's army near Montferrand, and Fulk gave up the fortress in return for his freedom. That year Emperor John II Komnenos demanded the submission of Antioch, and Fulk affirmed the Byzantine claim. In 1142 he avoided a confrontation with John by saying that the kingdom could not support so large an army.

On 7 November 1143 Fulk rode out with Melisende for a picnic near Acre. They flushed a hare, he spurred his horse after it, and the horse stumbled and threw him. The saddle struck his head, and he died on 10 November. He was buried beside the gate on the right side of the Holy Sepulchre. Melisende promptly made herself sole ruler, despite the coronation of their son Baldwin III on 25 December. The Arab chronicler Ibn al-Qalanisi judged Fulk an unsound and unsuccessful successor to Baldwin II, while William of Tyre described him as faithful, gentle and an experienced warrior.
funj-sultanate-of-sennar: The Christian kingdoms of Makuria and Alodia in Nubia began to decline from the 12th century. By the 13th century central Sudan seemed to have broken into petty states, and between the 14th and 15th centuries many Bedouin moved in, bringing Islam and Arabic. Tradition names one of them, Abdallah Jammah of the Abdallabi, who created a tribal federation and destroyed what was left of Alodia. In the early 16th century the federation was attacked from the south by the Funj, nomadic pastoralists who followed their own religion. The Funj founded their capital Sennar on the Blue Nile and ruled a population that included Nubians, Beja, Bedouin and Hamaj.

In 1525 the Ottoman admiral Selman Reis called the kingdom weak and easily conquerable, and noted a yearly tribute of 9,000 camels paid to Ethiopia. The Funj exported horses to Ethiopia, and in 1618 and 1619 war with the Ethiopian emperor Susenyos devastated many eastern provinces. The state reached its peak in the late 17th century, when it stretched from the Third Cataract to the edge of the Ethiopian Highlands, east to the Red Sea and west to Kordofan. Under Badi III, Sennar was a prosperous and cosmopolitan trading city.

In the 18th century the monarchy lost power to merchants, scholars and discontented nobles. About 1718 Unsa III was overthrown by the Funj aristocracy, and the Hamaj seized power in a coup in 1762. From the late 18th century the sultanate broke up in civil wars. In 1821 the last sultan, greatly weakened, surrendered to the Turco-Egyptian conquest.

The sultan, called mek, was chosen by the royal court from the sons of earlier rulers and Funj noblewomen, and a council of 20 elders had a say in decisions. Provinces were governed by a manjil, subdivided among makks, and each manjil had to travel to Sennar yearly to pay tribute. The army was feudal, and most warriors were slaves taken in annual raids on the Nuba mountains. The Funj adopted Islam, but its observance among the populace remained thin until the 18th century. Trade in gold, caravans and slaves to Egypt supplied the sultans' wealth.
fur-trade: The fur trade is a worldwide industry dealing in the acquisition and sale of animal fur. Since the establishment of a world fur market in the early modern period, the furs of boreal, polar and cold temperate mammals have been the most valued. Historically the trade stimulated the exploration and colonisation of Siberia, northern North America, and the South Shetland and South Sandwich Islands. Fur was relied on to make warm clothing, a critical consideration before coal was distributed for heating.

Before the European colonisation of the Americas, Russia was a major supplier of fur pelts to Western Europe and parts of Asia. Its trade developed in the early Middle Ages through exchanges at posts around the Baltic and Black seas, with Leipzig the main market, and Kievan Rus' was the first supplier. Russians settled in Siberia, rich in Arctic fox, lynx, sable, sea otter and ermine, and in a search for sea otter pelts, first used in China, and later the northern fur seal, the Russian Empire expanded into Alaska. From the 17th to the second half of the 19th century Russia was the world's largest supplier of fur.

European contact with North America made it a major supplier in the 17th century. The trade began as early as the 1500s between Europeans and First Nations. In 1578 there were 350 European fishing vessels at Newfoundland, and sailors traded metal implements, particularly knives, for the natives' well-worn beaver pelts, which the new felt-hat industry found especially useful. By the 1580s beaver wool was the major material of the French felt-hatters. In 1599 Captain Chauvin obtained a monopoly from Henry IV and tried to found a colony at Tadoussac.

The maritime fur trade was ship-based and sought sea otter furs from the peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast and Alaska, mostly to be traded in China for tea, silks and porcelain. Russians pioneered it, and the British and Americans entered in the 1780s. It boomed around the turn of the 19th century and declined from the 1810s.

Beaver felt hats were an expensive status symbol in Europe, and the demand was such that the beaver in Europe and European Russia had largely disappeared through exploitation. Today the trade has diminished and rests on pelts from fur farms and regulated trapping, and it is controversial: animal rights organisations oppose it, citing the way animals are killed. Fur has been replaced in some clothing by synthetic imitations.
furstenwalde: Fürstenwalde, called Pśibor pśi Sprjewje in Lower Sorbian, is the most populous town in the Oder-Spree District of Brandenburg. It lies in the glacial valley of the Spree river north of the Rauen Hills, about 60 kilometres east of Berlin and 30 kilometres west of Frankfurt (Oder). It stands on the western part of the historic Lubusz Land, and its station is a stop on the railway line from Berlin to Frankfurt (Oder).

The settlement was first mentioned in a deed of 1272 and was founded in the course of the German Ostsiedlung migration at a ford across the Spree, probably near the site of a former Slavic settlement. The Margraves of Brandenburg of the Ascanian line had acquired the Lebus Land from Poland in 1248 or 1249. The town's importance rose as a staple port and terminal for the transport of goods on the river.

In 1373 Emperor Charles IV enforced the renunciation of the Wittelsbach margrave Otto VII of Brandenburg by the Treaty of Fürstenwalde, and from 1373 to 1415 the town was part of the Bohemian Crown. The collegiate church in Lebus had been destroyed, and Bishop Wenceslaus moved the seat of the Bishopric of Lebus to Fürstenwalde, where St Mary's Church was raised to a cathedral. The last Catholic bishop, Georg von Blumenthal, was besieged in his palace by Lutheran robbers led by Nickel von Minckwitz and had to escape through a window in disguise. The bishopric was secularized during the Reformation in 1555 and was completely disbanded when Joachim Frederick became Margrave of Brandenburg in 1598.

From the 18th century Fürstenwalde was part of the Kingdom of Prussia, and from 1815 to 1947 it lay in the Province of Brandenburg.
